Intersection: if \(Ly\in P_q\) with \(y\in V_{q-2}\), then \(0=L^{\,m-q+1}(Ly)=L^{\,m-q+2}y\), and \(L^{\,m-q+2}:V_{q-2}\to V_{2m-q+2}\) is an isomorphism, so \(y=0\), hence \(Ly=0\).
Moreover, \(L:V_{q-2}\to V_q\) is GLOBALLY injective for \(2\le q\le m\) by (1) with \(j=q-2\le m-2\) and \(k=1\le m-q+2=m-j\); for \(q\le1\) the source is \(0\).

Now fix a parity and argue by induction on \(q\) in steps of \(2\). For \(q=0,1\) the required statement \(V_q=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^{k}P_{q-2k}\) is exactly \(V_q=P_q\) above. For \(2\le q\le m\): by the induction hypothesis \(V_{q-2}=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^{k}P_{q-2-2k}\) is a direct sum of subspaces. Since \(L:V_{q-2}\to V_q\) is injective, the induced map \(V_{q-2}\xrightarrow{\sim}LV_{q-2}\) is an isomorphism, and an isomorphism carries a direct-sum decomposition to a direct-sum decomposition: explicitly, if \(\sum_k L^{k+1}p_k=0\) with \(p_k\in P_{q-2-2k}\) (finitely many nonzero), then \(L\bigl(\sum_k L^{k}p_k\bigr)=0\) with \(\sum_kL^kp_k\in V_{q-2}\), so injectivity of \(L:V_{q-2}\to V_q\) forces \(\sum_kL^kp_k=0\), and directness of the induction decomposition forces each \(L^kp_k=0\). This rules out mixed relations, which is precisely where global injectivity (not merely injectivity on each summand) is used. Hence \(LV_{q-2}=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^{k+1}P_{q-2-2k}\) is a direct sum, and combining with \(V_q=P_q\oplus LV_{q-2}\) and re-indexing gives
\[V_q=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^{k}P_{q-2k}=\bigoplus_{\substack{0\le j\le\min(q,2m-q)\\ j\equiv q(2)}}L^{(q-j)/2}P_j ,\]
where for \(q\le m\) we have \(\min(q,2m-q)=q\), so the index sets agree (the condition \(j\ge0\) is \(k\le q/2\), which makes the sum finite). Thus \(\Phi_q\) is an isomorphism for all \(0\le q\le m\).

2b. A dimension count for the primitive pieces. From \(V_j=P_j\oplus LV_{j-2}\) with \(\dim LV_{j-2}=\dim V_{j-2}\) (injectivity of \(L:V_{j-2}\to V_j\), and \(V_{-1}=V_{-2}=0\)), we obtain for every \(0\le j\le m\)
\[\dim_K P_j=\dim_K V_j-\dim_K V_{j-2}. \tag{*}\]

2c. High degrees \(q>m\). We use strong induction on \(q\), with 2a/2b already established for all \(q\le m\). First,
\[V_q=LV_{q-2}\quad\text{for all }q>m. \tag{**}\]
Indeed, if \(q=m+1\) with \(m\ge1\) this is (3) (with \(r=m-1=q-2\)); if \(q=m+1\) with \(m=0\) then \(q=1>2m=0\) so \(V_q=0=LV_{q-2}\); if \(q\ge m+2\) then \(q-2\ge m\), so (2) gives surjectivity of \(L:V_{q-2}\to V_q\), i.e. (\(**\)). (For \(q>2m\) both sides are \(0\) by convention.)
Surjectivity of \(\Phi_q\): by (\(**\)) and the induction hypothesis applied to \(q-2\) (note \(q-2\ge m-1\), and if \(q-2<m\) we use 2a instead — either way \(\Phi_{q-2}\) is an isomorphism by the induction hypothesis, since \(q-2<q\)),
\[V_q=LV_{q-2}=L\Bigl(\sum_{j}L^{(q-2-j)/2}P_j\Bigr)=\sum_{j}L^{(q-j)/2}P_j,\]
where \(j\) runs over \(0\le j\le\min(q-2,2m-q+2)\), \(j\equiv q\ (2)\). For such \(j\) with \(j\le 2m-q\) the summand is one of those appearing in \(\operatorname{im}\Phi_q\); for \(j=2m-q+2\) (the only remaining possibility, by parity and the bound \(j\le 2m-q+2\)) we have \((q-j)/2=q-m-1>m-j=q-m-2\), so \(L^{(q-j)/2}P_j=0\) by (1). Hence \(V_q=\operatorname{im}\Phi_q\), i.e. \(\Phi_q\) is surjective.
Dimension count: the index set of \(\Phi_q\) is \(\{j:\ 0\le j\le 2m-q,\ j\equiv q\ (2)\}\) (since \(q>m\) implies \(2m-q<m\le q\), so \(\min(q,2m-q)=2m-q\); also \(0\le 2m-q\) as \(q\le 2m\), and \(2m-q\equiv q\ (2)\)). Using (\(*\)) the sum telescopes:
\[\dim_K\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\substack{0\le j\le 2m-q\\ j\equiv q(2)}}P_j\Bigr)=\sum_{j}\bigl(\dim V_j-\dim V_{j-2}\bigr)=\dim V_{2m-q}-\dim V_{j_0-2}=\dim V_{2m-q},\]
where \(j_0\in\{0,1\}\) is the smallest index in the sum and \(V_{j_0-2}=0\). Finally, \(0\le 2m-q\le m-1\le m\) (as \(q\ge m+1\)), so the hypothesis with \(r=2m-q\) gives the isomorphism \(L^{\,m-(2m-q)}=L^{\,q-m}:V_{2m-q}\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{2m-(2m-q)}=V_q\); hence \(\dim V_{2m-q}=\dim V_q\). Thus \(\dim\)domain\(\,\Phi_q=\dim V_q=\dim\)im\(\,\Phi_q\), and the surjective map \(\Phi_q\) is an isomorphism. This is exactly the missing kernel/independence statement: no nonzero combination of the summands \(L^{(q-j)/2}P_j\) vanishes, and the sum is direct.

CONSEQUENCE. For every \(q\in\mathbb Z\) every \(x\in V_q\) has a UNIQUE expression
\[x=\sum_{j}L^{k_j}p_j,\qquad p_j\in P_j,\quad k_j=\tfrac{q-j}{2},\quad 0\le j\le\min(q,2m-q),\ j\equiv q\ (2),\]
and necessarily \(k_j\le m-j\).

STEP 3. The lowering operator on \(V\). Define \(\Lambda_V:V\to V\) by \(\Lambda_V(V_q)\subseteq V_{q-2}\) via the unique decomposition above:
\[\Lambda_V\Bigl(\sum_j L^{k_j}p_j\Bigr)=\sum_{k_j\ge1}c(j,k_j)\,L^{k_j-1}p_j,\qquad c(j,k):=k\,(m-j-k+1),\]
with the convention that the term with \(k_j=0\) contributes \(0\) (consistent since \(c(j,0)=0\)). Uniqueness of the decomposition makes \(\Lambda_V\) a well-defined \(K\)-linear endomorphism of \(V\); it lowers degree by \(2\) because \(L^{k_j-1}p_j\in V_{j+2k_j-2}=V_{q-2}\).
Commutator check. Take a single primitive term \(x=L^{k}p_j\in V_q\) with \(k=(q-j)/2\le m-j\). Then \(Lx=L^{k+1}p_j\) is the degree-\(q+2\) primitive-decomposition term with the same label \(j\) and exponent \(k+1\); if \(k+1>m-j\) then \(L^{k+1}p_j=0\) and also \(c(j,k+1)=(k+1)(m-j-k)=0\) (as \(k+1\ge1\) and \(m-j-k\le0\), with \(k\le m-j\) forcing \(m-j-k=0\)). Hence in all cases \(\Lambda_V(Lx)=c(j,k+1)L^{k}p_j\). Also \(L\Lambda_V(x)=c(j,k)L^{k}p_j\) (for \(k=0\) both sides are \(0\)). Therefore
\[(L\Lambda_V-\Lambda_VL)(x)=\bigl[c(j,k)-c(j,k+1)\bigr]L^{k}p_j,\qquad c(j,k)-c(j,k+1)=k(m-j-k+1)-(k+1)(m-j-k)=2k+j-m=q-m,\]
where the last equality uses \(2k+j=q\). By linearity over the direct-sum decomposition, \((L\Lambda_V-\Lambda_VL)|_{V_q}=(q-m)\,\mathrm{id}_{V_q}\) for every \(q\).

STEP 4. The same construction on \(W\). Applying Steps 1--3 to \((W,(W_s)_{0\le s\le 2n},L_W,n)\) — the hypotheses are identical with \(m\) replaced by \(n\) — we obtain subspaces \(Q_i=\ker\bigl(L_W^{\,n-i+1}:W_i\to W_{2n-i+2}\bigr)\) for \(0\le i\le n\), a unique decomposition of every element of \(W_s\) as \(\sum_i L_W^{\ell_i}w_i\) with \(w_i\in Q_i\), \(\ell_i=(s-i)/2\le n-i\), and a \(K\)-linear \(\Lambda_W\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)\) with \(\Lambda_W(W_s)\subseteq W_{s-2}\) satisfying
\[(L_W\Lambda_W-\Lambda_WL_W)|_{W_s}=(s-n)\,\mathrm{id}_{W_s}\qquad\text{for all }s\in\mathbb Z.\]

STEP 5. The tensor product operators. Give \(U:=V\otimes_K W\) the grading \(U_t=\bigoplus_{r+s=t}V_r\otimes_K W_s\); each \(U_t\) is finite-dimensional (a finite direct sum of tensor products of finite-dimensional spaces), and \(U_t=0\) outside \(0\le t\le 2m+2n\). Define
\[\mathcal L:=L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}_W+\mathrm{id}_V\otimes L_W,\qquad \mathfrak L:=\Lambda_V\otimes\mathrm{id}_W+\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\Lambda_W\ \in\ \mathrm{End}_K(U).\]
Both are \(K\)-linear endomorphisms. Using \((A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=(AC)\otimes(BD)\) (true on elementary tensors, hence everywhere), \(\mathcal L(U_t)\subseteq U_{t+2}\) and \(\mathfrak L(U_t)\subseteq U_{t-2}\): e.g. \((L_V\otimes\mathrm{id})(V_r\otimes W_s)\subseteq V_{r+2}\otimes W_s\subseteq U_{t+2}\) and \((\Lambda_V\otimes\mathrm{id})(V_r\otimes W_s)\subseteq V_{r-2}\otimes W_s\subseteq U_{t-2}\), and similarly for the second summands.
Commutator. Expanding,
\[\mathcal L\mathfrak L=(L_V\Lambda_V\otimes\mathrm{id})+(L_V\otimes\Lambda_W)+(\Lambda_V\otimes L_W)+(\mathrm{id}\otimes L_W\Lambda_W),\]
\[\mathfrak L\mathcal L=(\Lambda_VL_V\otimes\mathrm{id})+(\Lambda_V\otimes L_W)+(L_V\otimes\Lambda_W)+(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Lambda_WL_W).\]
The mixed terms \(L_V\otimes\Lambda_W\) and \(\Lambda_V\otimes L_W\) occur identically in both products (the cross terms commute because they act in different tensor factors) and cancel in the difference, so
\[[\mathcal L,\mathfrak L]:=(\mathcal L\mathfrak L-\mathfrak L\mathcal L)=\bigl([L_V,\Lambda_V]\otimes\mathrm{id}_W\bigr)+\bigl(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes[L_W,\Lambda_W]\bigr).\]
On a summand \(V_r\otimes W_s\subseteq U_t\) with \(r+s=t\), Step 3 and Step 4 give \([L_V,\Lambda_V]|_{V_r}=(r-m)\mathrm{id}\) and \([L_W,\Lambda_W]|_{W_s}=(s-n)\mathrm{id}\); hence \([\mathcal L,\mathfrak L]\) acts on \(V_r\otimes W_s\) as multiplication by \((r-m)+(s-n)=t-(m+n)\). Since \(U_t\) is the direct sum of these summands, \([\mathcal L,\mathfrak L]|_{U_t}=(t-(m+n))\,\mathrm{id}_{U_t}\) for every \(t\in\mathbb Z\).

STEP 6. Conclusion. Apply lemma_l2_lefschetz_criterion (Spark) with the field \(K\) (of characteristic \(0\), as required), with \(d=m+n\ge0\), with the graded space \(U=\bigoplus_{t\in\mathbb Z}U_t\), with \(L=\mathcal L\) and \(\Lambda=\mathfrak L\). Its hypotheses are all verified: \(U\) is a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Z\)-graded \(K\)-vector space; \(\mathcal L(U_t)\subseteq U_{t+2}\); \(\mathfrak L(U_t)\subseteq U_{t-2}\); and \([\mathcal L,\mathfrak L]\) acts on \(U_t\) as multiplication by \(t-(m+n)\). The conclusion is that for every integer \(t\) with \(0\le t\le m+n\),
\[\mathcal L^{\,(m+n)-t}:U_t\longrightarrow U_{2(m+n)-t}\]
is an isomorphism. Writing \(U_t=(V\otimes_KW)_t\), \(U_{2m+2n-t}=(V\otimes_KW)_{2m+2n-t}\) and \(\mathcal L=L_V\otimes\mathrm{id}_W+\mathrm{id}_V\otimes L_W\), this is exactly the required statement.

EDGE CASES. If \(m=0\) then \(V=V_0\), \(P_0=V_0\), \(\Lambda_V=0\), and the relation \([L_V,\Lambda_V]|_{V_0}=(0-0)\mathrm{id}\) holds; the same holds with \(n=0\). The argument above covers these cases verbatim (in Step 1, (2) and (3) are then vacuous/trivial by the convention \(V_q=0\) for \(q\notin[0,2m]\), and in Step 2 the empty-index-set cases give \(0\to0\)). In particular for \(m=n=0\) the conclusion is \(\mathrm{id}:U_0\to U_0\). This completes the proof.

lemma_j_!_projection_formula.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset X\) be an effective ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) and smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\), let \(j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the open immersion, and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(j_!:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the homomorphism of the localisation long exact sequence of the pair \((X,Y)\), and let \(j^*:H^b_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^b_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the pullback. Then for all integers \(a,b\), all \(x\in H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and all \(y\in H^b_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \[j_!\bigl(x\cup j^*y\bigr)=j_!(x)\cup y\] in \(H^{a+b}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_j_!_projection_formula.proof:
Proof. Put Lambda = Q_l. Work on X_k and suppress the subscript k. Let i:Y->X be the closed immersion. Let Lambda_X, Lambda_U, Lambda_Y denote the constant sheaves on X, U, Y. All tensor products are derived.

If a<0 or b<0, both sides are zero, so assume a,b>=0.

Set F=j_!Lambda_U and C=Rj_*Lambda_U. By definition H^n_c(U,Lambda)=H^n(X,F) and H^n(U,Lambda)=H^n(X,C). Let eta:Lambda_X->C be the unit of the adjunction j^* left adjoint to Rj_*; then j^*:H^b(X,Lambda_X)->H^b(U,Lambda)=H^b(X,C) is H^b(eta). Let epsilon:j^*C->Lambda_U be the counit. Let c:F->Lambda_X be extension by zero.

The sequence 0->F->Lambda_X->i_*Lambda_Y->0 is exact. Indeed, at a geometric point over U, F=Lambda_U and c is the identity; at a geometric point over Y, F=0 and Lambda_X->i_*Lambda_Y is the identity. Hence its long exact sequence is the localisation sequence. By lemma_283 this is the localisation sequence in the statement, and its first map is H^n(c); this is the map j_!.

Let m_Lambda:Lambda tensor Lambda->Lambda be multiplication and let m_F:F tensor Lambda_X->F be the Lambda_X-module action. Define p:F tensor^L C->F as follows. The complex G:=F tensor^L C has zero stalks on Y because F does. Therefore the counit j_!j^*G->G is a quasi-isomorphism (stalk check: both sides are G on U and 0 on Y). Also j^*F=Lambda_U (stalkwise over U), so j^*G is canonically isomorphic to Lambda_U tensor^L j^*C. Let mu:Lambda_U tensor^L j^*C->Lambda_U be m_Lambda o (id tensor epsilon). Define p to be the composite
G ≅ j_!j^*G ≅ j_!(Lambda_U tensor^L j^*C) --j_!(mu)--> j_!Lambda_U=F.

We first show p o (id tensor eta)=m_F. Both the source H:=F tensor Lambda_X and the target F are supported on U. For complexes supported on U, the counit j_!j^*->id exhibits j_! as fully faithful on the derived category of U, so two maps between such complexes are equal if their pullbacks to U are equal. Pulling back to U, H becomes Lambda_U tensor Lambda_U and F becomes Lambda_U. The map m_F pulls back to m_Lambda. The map p o (id tensor eta) pulls back to m_Lambda o (id tensor (epsilon o j^*eta)). The adjunction identity for j^* left adjoint to Rj_* gives epsilon o j^*eta=id on Lambda_U. Hence this pullback is m_Lambda. Therefore p o (id tensor eta)=m_F.

Since c:F->Lambda_X is a morphism of Lambda_X-modules, we have c o m_F = m_Lambda o (c tensor id). Combining with the previous paragraph gives
 c o p o (id tensor eta) = m_Lambda o (c tensor id)
as morphisms F tensor Lambda_X->Lambda_X.

Now take x in H^a_c(U,Lambda)=H^a(X,F) and y in H^b(X,Lambda_X). Let x times y denote their external product in H^{a+b}(X,F tensor Lambda_X). By definition of the cup product with coefficients in F and C, x cup j^*y = H^{a+b}(p o (id tensor eta))(x times y). Applying j_!=H^{a+b}(c) gives the left side. On the other hand, j_!(x)=H^a(c)(x), and the ordinary cup product on X is induced by m_Lambda, so j_!(x) cup y = H^{a+b}(m_Lambda o (c tensor id))(x times y). The equality of morphisms just proved implies the two classes are equal. This proves j_!(x cup j^*y)=j_!(x) cup y for all integers a,b.

lemma_385.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(H\) via a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and let \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace. Then there exists a unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear endomorphism \(\Lambda\) of \(\bigoplus_{n=0}^{2d}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) such that \(\Lambda\bigl(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\subseteq H^{m+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(m\) and \(\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup \Lambda y)\) for every \(m\ge0\), \(x\in H^{2d-m-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(y\in H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), with \(H^r=0\) for \(r<0\) and \(r>2d\).
lemma_385.proof:
We prove existence and uniqueness of a degree-raising adjoint $\Lambda$ of $L$ for the Poincar\'e duality trace pairing. Only $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear algebra and the perfectness of the trace pairing are used; no hard Lefschetz, primitive decomposition, or semisimplicity statement is invoked (the very-ampleness of $H$ is likewise irrelevant to the argument, all that is used is that $L=u\mapsto\xi\cup u$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator raising cohomological degree by $2$).

STEP 0 (Notation). For each integer $r$ write $V^r:=H^r_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ when $0\le r\le 2d$, and set $V^r:=0$ for $r<0$ and for $r>2d$, as the statement prescribes. Put $V:=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{2d}V^n$. Cup product gives $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear maps $V^a\times V^b\to V^{a+b}$ (with $V^{a+b}=0$ if $a+b>2d$ or $a+b<0$), and $L:V^a\to V^{a+2}$, $L(u)=\xi\cup u$, is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear because cup product is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear.

STEP 1 (Finite-dimensionality and the vanishing convention). The base change $X_k=X\times_{\mathbb F_q}k$ is proper over the algebraically closed field $k$, so applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) to $X_k$, to the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, and to every integer $n$, gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)<\infty$; in particular each $V^m$ ($0\le m\le 2d$) is finite-dimensional and $V$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space. Moreover, since $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ is smooth of relative dimension $d$ with $X$ geometrically connected of pure dimension $d$, the base change $X_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth of relative dimension $d$, hence $X_k$ is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field $k$ of pure dimension $d$. lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing (Spark) therefore yields $H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every $m>2d$. Thus the stipulation $V^r=0$ for $r>2d$ agrees with the actual cohomology groups (and for $r<0$ it is the usual convention), so no distinction is ever needed between the stipulated and the actual groups.

STEP 2 (Perfectness of the pairing built from the given trace $\operatorname{tr}_X$). Apply lemma_77 (eoinm) with $m=1$, $Y=X$, and $F$ the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius. Its part (a) provides a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}_{77}:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ (normalised by $\operatorname{tr}_{77}(\mathrm{cl}(x))=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]$). Both $\operatorname{tr}_X$ (as given in the statement, an isomorphism $H^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$) and $\operatorname{tr}_{77}$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphisms with the same source and target, so their ratio $\operatorname{tr}_X\circ\operatorname{tr}_{77}^{-1}$ is an automorphism of the one-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, i.e. multiplication by a unique scalar $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$; hence $\operatorname{tr}_X=c\cdot\operatorname{tr}_{77}$. By lemma_77(b), for every integer $r$ with $0\le r\le 2d$ the pairing $V^r\times V^{2d-r}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_{77}(a\cup b)$, is perfect; since multiplication by $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, the pairing
$$\langle a,b\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}_X(a\cup b),\qquad a\in V^r,\ b\in V^{2d-r},\quad 0\le r\le 2d,\tag{$*$}$$
is perfect as well. Unpacking "perfect": for each $0\le r\le 2d$ both maps
$$V^r\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V^{2d-r},\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)),\quad a\longmapsto(b\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(a\cup b)),\qquad V^{2d-r}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V^{r},\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)),\quad b\longmapsto(a\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(a\cup b))$$
are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphisms. We shall use the second one (and, in the uniqueness step, its injectivity). Crucially, ($*$) is asserted only for $0\le r\le 2d$; the boundary cases will be treated separately in Steps 3A and 6.

STEP 3 (Definition of $\Lambda$ on each summand). Fix $m$ with $0\le m\le 2d$.

Case 3A: $m\ge 2d-1$. Then $m+2\ge 2d+1>2d$, so $V^{m+2}=0$ by the convention of Step 0. There is exactly one $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $V^m\to V^{m+2}$, namely the zero map; define $\Lambda|_{V^m}:=0$. (This is forced by the required condition $\Lambda(V^m)\subseteq V^{m+2}$.)

Case 3B: $0\le m\le 2d-2$. Put $r:=2d-m-2$. Then $0\le r\le 2d-2\le 2d$ and $2d-r=m+2$ with $2\le m+2\le 2d$, so ($*$) applies to the pair $(V^r,V^{m+2})$. For $y\in V^m$ define
$$\varphi_y:V^r\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad \varphi_y(x):=\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y).$$
Well-typedness: for $x\in V^r$ one has $Lx=\xi\cup x\in V^{r+2}=V^{2d-m}$ (degree $2+(2d-m-2)=2d-m$), and then $(Lx)\cup y\in V^{(2d-m)+m}=V^{2d}$, so $\operatorname{tr}_X$ applies. Linearity in $x$: $x\mapsto Lx$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear (Step 0) and $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(u\cup v)$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear on $V^{2d-m}\times V^m$ (bilinearity of cup product and $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_X$); hence $\varphi_y$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, i.e. $\varphi_y\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V^r,\mathbb Q_\ell(-d))$. By the second isomorphism in ($*$) at this value of $r$, there exists a unique $z\in V^{m+2}=V^{2d-r}$ with $\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup z)=\varphi_y(x)$ for all $x\in V^r$. Define
$$\Lambda y:=z.$$

STEP 4 (Linearity on each summand). In Case 3A there is nothing to check. In Case 3B, take $y,y'\in V^m$ and $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb Q_\ell$. For every $x\in V^r$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(x\cup\Lambda(\lambda y+\mu y')\bigr)=\varphi_{\lambda y+\mu y'}(x)=\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup(\lambda y+\mu y'))=\lambda\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)+\mu\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y')$$
$$=\lambda\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y)+\mu\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y')=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(x\cup(\lambda\Lambda y+\mu\Lambda y')\bigr),$$
where the first and fourth equalities are the defining property of $\Lambda(\lambda y+\mu y')$ and of $\Lambda y,\Lambda y'$, the second and third use bilinearity of $\cup$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_X$, and the fifth uses bilinearity of $\cup$ again. Since $\lambda\Lambda y+\mu\Lambda y'\in V^{m+2}$, uniqueness of the representing vector in ($*$) gives $\Lambda(\lambda y+\mu y')=\lambda\Lambda y+\mu\Lambda y'$. Thus $\Lambda|_{V^m}$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear for every $m$.

STEP 5 (Global definition and the degree condition). Define $\Lambda:V\to V$ by
$$\Lambda\Bigl(\sum_{n=0}^{2d}y_n\Bigr):=\sum_{n=0}^{2d}\Lambda|_{V^n}(y_n),\qquad y_n\in V^n.$$
Because $V$ is the (finite) direct sum of the $V^n$, every element has a unique such decomposition, so $\Lambda$ is well defined; it is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear by Step 4 applied summand by summand. By construction $\Lambda(V^m)\subseteq V^{m+2}$ for every $0\le m\le 2d$, and for $m<0$ or $m>2d$ one has $V^m=0$ so the inclusion is trivial. This is the required degree condition.

STEP 6 (Verification of the adjoint identity). Let $m\ge0$, $x\in V^{2d-m-2}$ and $y\in V^m$; we check $\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y)$, both sides being elements of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ (so no trivialisation of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is chosen anywhere). Exactly one of the following holds.

(i) $m>2d$. Then $V^m=0$, hence $y=0$; also $2d-m-2<-2<0$, so $V^{2d-m-2}=0$ and $x=0$. Since $\Lambda$ is linear, $\Lambda 0=0$. Thus LHS $=\operatorname{tr}_X(L0\cup 0)=\operatorname{tr}_X(0)=0$ and RHS $=\operatorname{tr}_X(0\cup 0)=0$.

(ii) $2d-m-2<0$ (equivalently $m\ge 2d-1$, with $m\le 2d$). Then $V^{2d-m-2}=0$, so $x=0$. Hence LHS $=\operatorname{tr}_X(L0\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(0\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(0)=0$, and RHS $=\operatorname{tr}_X(0\cup\Lambda y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(0)=0$. (Here $\Lambda y=0$ as well, by Case 3A; the identity is vacuous because the test space $V^{2d-m-2}$ is zero. Note that we do not appeal to ($*$) in this case, since ($*$) is available only for $0\le r\le 2d$.)

(iii) $0\le m\le 2d-2$. Then $r:=2d-m-2$ satisfies $0\le r\le 2d$, $x\in V^r$, $\Lambda y\in V^{m+2}=V^{2d-r}$, and both sides are well typed: $Lx\cup y\in V^{(2d-m)+m}=V^{2d}$ and $x\cup\Lambda y\in V^{(2d-m-2)+(m+2)}=V^{2d}$. The equality $\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y)=\varphi_y(x)=\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)$ is precisely the defining property of $\Lambda y$ from Case 3B.

These cases are exhaustive, so the identity holds for all $m\ge0$, $x\in V^{2d-m-2}$, $y\in V^m$. Existence is proved.

STEP 7 (Uniqueness). Let $\Lambda':V\to V$ be another $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism with $\Lambda'(V^m)\subseteq V^{m+2}$ for every $m$ and satisfying the same identity. Fix $0\le m\le 2d$ and $y\in V^m$; we show $\Lambda'y=\Lambda y$.

If $m\ge 2d-1$, then $m+2\ge 2d+1>2d$, so $V^{m+2}=0$ and the degree condition forces $\Lambda'y=0$; Step 3A gives $\Lambda y=0$ as well.

If $0\le m\le 2d-2$, put $r:=2d-m-2\in[0,2d]$ and $w:=\Lambda y-\Lambda'y$. Both $\Lambda y$ and $\Lambda'y$ lie in $V^{m+2}=V^{2d-r}$, so $w\in V^{2d-r}$. For every $x\in V^r$, using the identity for $\Lambda$ and for $\Lambda'$ (both sides well typed, as in Step 6(iii)) and the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_X$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup w)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y)-\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda'y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)-\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=0.$$
By ($*$), the map $V^{2d-r}\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V^r,\mathbb Q_\ell(-d))$, $b\mapsto(x\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup b))$, is an isomorphism, hence injective; therefore $w=0$, i.e. $\Lambda'y=\Lambda y$. (Only the degree condition $\Lambda'(V^m)\subseteq V^{m+2}$ and perfectness were used; no extra normalisation is needed.)

Thus $\Lambda'$ and $\Lambda$ agree on every summand $V^m$, $0\le m\le 2d$, hence on $V=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{2d}V^n$. Uniqueness is proved.

CONCLUSION. Steps 3--6 produce a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism $\Lambda$ of $\bigoplus_{n=0}^{2d}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with $\Lambda(H^m)\subseteq H^{m+2}$ for every $m$ and $\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y)$ for every $m\ge0$, $x\in H^{2d-m-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $y\in H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (with $H^r=0$ for $r<0$ and $r>2d$), and Step 7 shows it is the only such endomorphism. This is exactly the claim. (Remark on the degree convention: $L$ raises degree by $2$, so the adjoint of $L$ for the pairing $V^r\times V^{2d-r}$ is a map $V^{2d-r}\to V^{2d-r+2}$, i.e. it also raises degree by $2$; the degree-lowering Lefschetz operator $\Lambda$ with $[L,\Lambda]=n-d$ on $H^n$ is the adjoint of $L$ for the primitive pairings and is a different object, obtained separately via lemma_l2_lefschetz_criterion once hard Lefschetz is available. It is not constructed here, and nothing in this proof uses hard Lefschetz or semisimplicity.)

lemma_thom_isomorphism_line_bundle.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, let \(Y\) be a smooth projective variety of pure dimension \(d\ge0\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\mathcal L\) be a line bundle on \(Y\), let \(E=\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathcal O_Y}\bigl(\bigoplus_{n\ge0}(\mathcal L^{\vee})^{\otimes n}\bigr)\) be the total space of \(\mathcal L\) with zero section \(s:Y\hookrightarrow E\), and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Then for every integer \(n\ge0\) there is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces \[ H^n_{s(Y_k)}(E_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\cong\;H^{n-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1), \] with the convention that \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for \(m<0\).
lemma_thom_isomorphism_line_bundle.proof:
We prove the statement in six steps. The only non-elementary input is the proved lemma eoinm/lemma_purity_zero_section_projective_bundle; everything else is an elementary computation with projective bundles plus the standard excision property of cohomology with supports, which we state and justify.

=====================================================================
STEP 1. Conventions, and the projective compactification of E.
=====================================================================
Throughout, $\mathbb P_{\mathcal O_Y}(\mathcal F):=\mathbf{Proj}_Y\bigl(\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\operatorname{Sym}^m_{\mathcal O_Y}\mathcal F\bigr)$ denotes the projective bundle for the QUOTIENTS convention: for $T\to Y$, $\mathbb P(\mathcal F)(T)$ is the set of isomorphism classes of surjections $\mathcal F_T\twoheadrightarrow \mathcal M$ with $\mathcal M$ invertible on $T$. With this convention $\pi_*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(\mathcal F)}(1)=\mathcal F$ (the degree-$1$ piece of $\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal F$), and the fibre over $y\in Y$ is the usual projective space of $1$-dimensional quotients of $\mathcal F\otimes\kappa(y)$.

Put
$$B:=\mathbb P_{\mathcal O_Y}(\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y),\qquad \pi:B\to Y.$$
Let $q_0:\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal L$ and $q_\infty:\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O_Y$ be the two projections. They define two closed subschemes (sections of $\pi$):
$$Z_0:=\mathbb P(\mathcal L)\hookrightarrow B\quad(\text{functorially: surjections } (\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y)_T\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal M\text{ on which }\mathcal O_{Y,T}\to\mathcal M\text{ is }0),$$
$$Z_\infty:=\mathbb P(\mathcal O_Y)\hookrightarrow B\quad(\text{functorially: surjections on which }\mathcal L_T\to\mathcal M\text{ is }0).$$
Equivalently, $Z_0=\operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal L)$ and $Z_\infty=\operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal O_Y=\mathcal O_Y)$, the closed subschemes defined by the homogeneous ideals generated by the $\mathcal O_Y$-summand and by the $\mathcal L$-summand respectively.

Explicitly: let $\{U_\alpha\}$ be an open cover of $Y$ trivialising $\mathcal L$, with frames $e_\alpha$ of $\mathcal L|_{U_\alpha}$ and transition functions $e_\alpha=g_{\alpha\beta}e_\beta$, $g_{\alpha\beta}\in\mathcal O^*(U_{\alpha\beta})$. Write $t$ for the frame $1$ of the $\mathcal O_Y$-summand (it is independent of $\alpha$). Then
$$\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)=\mathbf{Proj}_{\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}}\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}[e_\alpha,t],\qquad Z_0\cap\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)=V(t),\qquad Z_\infty\cap\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)=V(e_\alpha),$$
where a $T$-valued point over $U_\alpha$ is a generating pair $(a,b)\in\mathcal M\oplus\mathcal M$ (images of $e_\alpha,t$), and $Z_0$ (resp. $Z_\infty$) is the locus $b=0$ (resp. $a=0$). In particular
$$Z_0\cap Z_\infty=V(e_\alpha,t)=\varnothing\quad\text{in }\mathbf{Proj}\,\mathcal O[e_\alpha,t],$$
because $(e_\alpha,t)$ is the irrelevant ideal, so $Z_0$ and $Z_\infty$ are disjoint sections of $\pi$.

(Consistency check on normal bundles, not used below. The element $e_\alpha$ is the local expression of a global section $\varepsilon\in H^0(B,\mathcal O_B(1)\otimes\pi^*\mathcal L^\vee)$: indeed $\pi_*\mathcal O_B(1)=\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y$ gives $H^0(B,\mathcal O_B(1)\otimes\pi^*\mathcal L^\vee)=H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y\oplus\mathcal L^\vee)$ and $\varepsilon$ corresponds to $(1,0)$, i.e. the inclusion $\mathcal L\hookrightarrow\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y$. Its zero scheme is exactly $Z_\infty$, so $\mathcal O_B(Z_\infty)=\mathcal O_B(1)\otimes\pi^*\mathcal L^\vee$ and $\mathcal N_{Z_\infty/B}=\mathcal O_B(1)|_{Z_\infty}\otimes\mathcal L^\vee$. Since $Z_\infty$ is the section attached to the quotient onto $\mathcal O_Y$, the tautological bundle satisfies $\mathcal O_B(1)|_{Z_\infty}\simeq\mathcal O_Y$, hence $\mathcal N_{Z_\infty/B}\simeq\mathcal L^\vee$. Similarly $t$ is a global section of $\mathcal O_B(1)$ (the element $1\in H^0(Y,\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y)$), its zero scheme is $Z_0$, and $\mathcal O_B(1)|_{Z_0}\simeq\mathcal L$ because $Z_0$ is the section attached to the quotient onto $\mathcal L$; hence $\mathcal N_{Z_0/B}\simeq\mathcal L$. Thus the section with normal bundle $\mathcal L$ — the one that will be the zero section of the total space of $\mathcal L$ — is $Z_0$, as the statement requires.)

=====================================================================
STEP 2. Identification $B\setminus Z_\infty\;\widetilde\longrightarrow\; E$, carrying $Z_0$ to the zero section.
=====================================================================
We claim there is a canonical $Y$-isomorphism $\iota:B\setminus Z_\infty\;\widetilde\longrightarrow\;E=\underline{\operatorname{Spec}}_{\mathcal O_Y}\bigl(\bigoplus_{n\ge0}(\mathcal L^\vee)^{\otimes n}\bigr)$ under which $Z_0\cap(B\setminus Z_\infty)=Z_0$ maps to the zero section $s(Y)$.

Construction. Over $U_\alpha$, $Z_\infty$ is cut out by $e_\alpha$, so
$$(B\setminus Z_\infty)\cap\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)=D_+(e_\alpha)=\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}}\bigl(\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}[e_\alpha,t]_{(e_\alpha)}\bigr)=\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}}\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}[u_\alpha],\qquad u_\alpha:=t/e_\alpha,$$
the degree-$0$ part of the localisation. On the other hand $\mathcal L^\vee|_{U_\alpha}$ is free on the dual frame $e_\alpha^\vee$, so
$$E\times_YU_\alpha=\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}}\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal L^\vee|_{U_\alpha})=\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}}\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}[w_\alpha],$$
where $w_\alpha$ is the coordinate corresponding to $e_\alpha^\vee$. Define $\iota_\alpha$ by the $\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}$-algebra map $\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}[w_\alpha]\to\mathcal O_{U_\alpha}[u_\alpha]$, $w_\alpha\mapsto u_\alpha$.

Gluing. Since the frame of the $\mathcal O_Y$-summand is the canonical element $t=1$, on $U_{\alpha\beta}$ we have $e_\alpha=g_{\alpha\beta}e_\beta$ and $t$ unchanged, hence
$$u_\alpha=\frac{t}{e_\alpha}=\frac{t}{g_{\alpha\beta}e_\beta}=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}u_\beta.$$
Likewise $e_\alpha^\vee=(g_{\alpha\beta}e_\beta)^\vee=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}e_\beta^\vee$, so $w_\alpha=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}w_\beta$. The two transition rules coincide, so $\iota_\alpha(w_\alpha)=u_\alpha$ and $\iota_\beta(w_\beta)=u_\beta$ agree on $U_{\alpha\beta}$; the $\iota_\alpha$ glue to a global $Y$-isomorphism $\iota$.

Zero section. The zero section $s:Y\to E$ corresponds to the augmentation $\bigoplus_{n\ge0}(\mathcal L^\vee)^{\otimes n}\to\mathcal O_Y$ killing positive degrees, i.e. locally to $w_\alpha\mapsto0$. On the other hand $Z_0\cap D_+(e_\alpha)=V(t)\cap D_+(e_\alpha)=\{u_\alpha=0\}$. Hence $\iota(Z_0\cap(B\setminus Z_\infty))=s(Y)$, and since $Z_0\cap Z_\infty=\varnothing$ we have $Z_0\subset B\setminus Z_\infty$ and $\iota(Z_0)=s(Y)$ as closed subschemes of $E$. (Note the sign of the convention: applying the same computation to $D_+(t)=B\setminus Z_0$ gives $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O[e_\alpha/t]$ with transition $e_\alpha/t=g_{\alpha\beta}(e_\beta/t)$, i.e. the total space of $\mathcal L^\vee$, not of $\mathcal L$. So it is the complement of $Z_\infty$, not of $Z_0$, that is the total space of $\mathcal L$.)

=====================================================================
STEP 3. Base change to $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$.
=====================================================================
Everything in Steps 1--2 is defined over $\mathbb F_q$: $B$, $\pi$, $Z_0$, $Z_\infty$, $\iota$ are all obtained from $\mathcal L$ by the constructions of relative Proj and relative Spec. Since $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ is flat, (i) relative Spec and Proj commute with the base change, so $E_k=\underline{\operatorname{Spec}}_{\mathcal O_{Y_k}}\bigl(\bigoplus_{n\ge0}(\mathcal L_k^\vee)^{\otimes n}\bigr)$ and $B_k=\mathbb P_{\mathcal O_{Y_k}}(\mathcal L_k\oplus\mathcal O_{Y_k})$ with $Z_{0,k},Z_{\infty,k}$ the corresponding sections; and (ii) if $W\subset T$ is a closed subscheme with ideal $\mathcal I$, flatness gives $\operatorname{Tor}_1(\mathcal O_T/\mathcal I,\mathcal O_{T_k})=0$, so $\mathcal I\cdot\mathcal O_{T_k}$ is the ideal of $W_k$, whence $T_k\setminus W_k=(T\setminus W)_k$. Applying (ii) to $W=Z_\infty\subset T=B$ gives
$$B_k\setminus Z_{\infty,k}=(B\setminus Z_\infty)_k,$$
and $\iota$ base-changes to a $k$-isomorphism $\iota_k:(B_k\setminus Z_{\infty,k})\xrightarrow{\sim}E_k$ carrying $Z_{0,k}$ onto $s(Y_k)$. Consequently, by functoriality of cohomology with supports for isomorphisms of pairs,
$$\iota_k^*:\;H^n_{Z_{0,k}}(B_k\setminus Z_{\infty,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;H^n_{s(Y_k)}(E_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\qquad(\forall n\ge0)$$
is an isomorphism.

=====================================================================
STEP 4. Excision (standard fact, with proof).
=====================================================================
We use the following standard property of étale cohomology with supports; it is the only external fact invoked.

*Excision.* Let $S$ be a scheme, $Z\subset S$ closed, $V\subset S$ open with $Z\subset V$. For every étale sheaf of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces $\mathcal F$ on $S$ the restriction map induces a canonical isomorphism $R\Gamma_Z(S,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\sim}R\Gamma_Z(V,\mathcal F|_V)$, hence $H^n_Z(S,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n_Z(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $n$.

*Justification.* (a) Since $Z$ is closed, a section has support contained in $Z$ iff its restriction to $S\setminus Z$ is zero, so $\Gamma_Z(S,\mathcal F):=\ker\bigl(\mathcal F(S)\to\mathcal F(S\setminus Z)\bigr)$, and similarly $\Gamma_Z(V,\mathcal F|_V)=\ker\bigl(\mathcal F(V)\to\mathcal F(V\setminus Z)\bigr)$. (b) $\{V,\,S\setminus Z\}$ is an open (hence étale) cover of $S$ and $V\cap(S\setminus Z)=V\setminus Z$, so the sheaf axiom gives an equaliser $\mathcal F(S)\to\mathcal F(V)\times\mathcal F(S\setminus Z)\rightrightarrows\mathcal F(V\setminus Z)$. Therefore $t\in\mathcal F(V)$ with $t|_{V\setminus Z}=0$ extends uniquely to $s\in\mathcal F(S)$ with $s|_{S\setminus Z}=0$ (namely $s|_V=t$, $s|_{S\setminus Z}=0$). This is a natural bijection $\Gamma_Z(S,\mathcal F)\simeq\Gamma_Z(V,\mathcal F|_V)$. (c) Both sides are left exact functors of $\mathcal F$ on $\operatorname{Sh}(S_{\text{ét}})$: restriction to an open is exact, $\mathcal F\mapsto\mathcal F(S)$ and $\mathcal F\mapsto\mathcal F(V)$ are left exact, and $\Gamma_Z$ is the kernel of the natural transformation between them. A natural isomorphism of left exact functors induces a natural isomorphism of their right derived functors (by the universal $\delta$-functor property), so $R^n\Gamma_Z(S,-)\simeq R^n\bigl(\Gamma_Z(V,-|_V)\bigr)$. (d) For the open immersion $j:V_{\text{ét}}\hookrightarrow S_{\text{ét}}$, the restriction $j^*$ is exact and sends injectives to injectives (it has the exact left adjoint $j_!$), so the derived functor of $\Gamma_Z(V,j^*(-))$ is $R^n\Gamma_Z(V,-)\circ j^*$. Applying to $\mathcal F=\mathbb Q_\ell$ gives the claim. $\blacksquare$

Apply this with $S=B_k$, $Z=Z_{0,k}$, $V=B_k\setminus Z_{\infty,k}$: $Z_{0,k}$ is closed in $B_k$, $V$ is open, $Z_{0,k}\subset V$ (Step 1: $Z_0\cap Z_\infty=\varnothing$), and $Z_{0,k}\cap(B_k\setminus V)=Z_{0,k}\cap Z_{\infty,k}=\varnothing$. Excision yields
$$\operatorname{exc}_n:\;H^n_{Z_{0,k}}(B_k\setminus Z_{\infty,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;H^n_{Z_{0,k}}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\qquad(\forall n\ge0).$$

=====================================================================
STEP 5. The cited purity isomorphism for the zero section of a projective bundle, with the correct section.
=====================================================================
Apply the proved lemma eoinm/lemma_purity_zero_section_projective_bundle with $\mathcal N:=\mathcal L^\vee$. Its notation gives
$$B_1:=\mathbb P_{\mathcal O_Y}(\mathcal L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_Y),\qquad \pi_1:B_1\to Y,$$
and its section $Z_0^{(1)}\subset B_1$ is the one induced by the surjection $\mathcal L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_Y\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O_Y$, i.e. the projection onto the SECOND summand. The lemma provides, for every $n\ge0$, an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces
$$\theta_n:\;H^n_{Z_0^{(1)}}\bigl((B_1)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;H^{n-2}_{\text{ét}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1),\qquad H^m_{\text{ét}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\ (m<0).\tag{$\ast$}$$

We must transport $(\ast)$ to $B$. Tensoring by the line bundle $\mathcal L$ induces an isomorphism of the functors of quotients: a surjection $\mathcal F_T\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal M$ corresponds to $\mathcal F_T\otimes\mathcal L_T\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal M\otimes\mathcal L_T$, with inverse $\mathcal N\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N\otimes\mathcal L^\vee_T$. Hence there is a canonical $Y$-isomorphism
$$\mathbb P(\mathcal L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_Y)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;\mathbb P\bigl((\mathcal L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_Y)\otimes\mathcal L\bigr)=\mathbb P(\mathcal O_Y\oplus\mathcal L),$$
using the canonical contraction isomorphism $\mathcal L^\vee\otimes\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal O_Y$ and $\mathcal O_Y\otimes\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal L$. Composing with $\mathbb P(\sigma)$, where $\sigma:\mathcal O_Y\oplus\mathcal L\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y$ is the swap of summands, we obtain a $Y$-isomorphism
$$\Phi:B_1=\mathbb P(\mathcal L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_Y)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;\mathbb P(\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y)=B.$$

Convention check (the point where the choice of $\mathcal N$ matters). Let $b\in Z_0^{(1)}(T)$, $b:(\mathcal L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_Y)_T\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal M$ with $\mathcal L^\vee_T\mapsto0$; then $\mathcal M\simeq\mathcal O_T$ via the second factor. Its image under $\Phi$ is the composite
$$(\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal O_Y)_T\xrightarrow{\;\sigma^{-1}\;}\bigl(\mathcal O_Y\oplus\mathcal L\bigr)_T\;\simeq\;(\mathcal L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_Y)_T\otimes\mathcal L_T\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal M\otimes\mathcal L_T\;\simeq\;\mathcal L_T,$$
which is precisely the projection onto the $\mathcal L$-summand, i.e. the quotient $q_0$ defining $Z_0$. Thus $\Phi(Z_0^{(1)})=Z_0$ (and correspondingly $\Phi$ carries the section $\mathbb P(\mathcal L^\vee)$ of $B_1$, attached to the quotient onto $\mathcal L^\vee$, onto $Z_\infty$). An isomorphism of pairs $(B_{1,k},Z^{(1)}_{0,k})\simeq(B_k,Z_{0,k})$ induces, by functoriality of $R\Gamma_Z(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)=R\Gamma(-,i^\!(-))$ (equivalently, by the equaliser description of $\Gamma_Z$ in Step 4 applied to both schemes), an isomorphism
$$\Phi_n^*:\;H^n_{Z_{0,k}}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;H^n_{Z^{(1)}_{0,k}}\bigl((B_1)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr).$$
Had we instead applied the cited lemma with $\mathcal N:=\mathcal L$, we would have obtained the section attached to the quotient onto $\mathcal O_Y$, which is $Z_\infty$; its complement is the total space of $\mathcal L^\vee$, so that instance would not give the present statement. This is why $\mathcal N=\mathcal L^\vee$ is used above.

=====================================================================
STEP 6. Assembly.
=====================================================================
For each $n\ge0$ define
$$\Psi_n:\;H^n_{s(Y_k)}(E_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\xrightarrow{(\iota_k^*)^{-1}}\;H^n_{Z_{0,k}}(B_k\setminus Z_{\infty,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\xrightarrow{\operatorname{exc}_n}\;H^n_{Z_{0,k}}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\xrightarrow{\Phi_n^*}\;H^n_{Z^{(1)}_{0,k}}\bigl((B_1)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)\;\xrightarrow{\theta_n}\;H^{n-2}_{\text{ét}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1).$$
Each arrow is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces: $\iota_k^*$ by Step 3 (it is the pullback along the isomorphism of pairs $\iota_k$), $\operatorname{exc}_n$ by Step 4, $\Phi_n^*$ by Step 5, and $\theta_n$ by the cited lemma eoinm/lemma_purity_zero_section_projective_bundle. Hence $\Psi_n$ is an isomorphism
$$H^n_{s(Y_k)}(E_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;H^{n-2}_{\text{ét}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1),$$
with the convention $H^m_{\text{ét}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for $m<0$, exactly as in the statement (for $n=0,1$ the right-hand side is $H^{-2}=H^{-1}=0$, and the left-hand side is therefore also $0$). This is the required family of isomorphisms, natural in the data, and it proves the lemma.

=====================================================================
Remarks.
=====================================================================
1. *Finite dimensionality.* $Y$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, so the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $Y_k$ lies in $D^b_c(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and carries the natural arithmetic Frobenius structure; by eoinm/lemma_45_finite_frob each $H^m_{\text{ét}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. By the isomorphism just constructed, $H^n_{s(Y_k)}(E_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite dimensional as well.

2. *No Frobenius equivariance is claimed.* The cited lemma supplies only a bare isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, so there is no additional structure to compare, and none is asserted here. What matters for later use is that $\Psi_n$ is the transport of $\theta_n$ along the two geometric identifications $\iota_k$ and $\Phi$; both are defined over $\mathbb F_q$ (they come from $\mathcal L$, $\mathcal L^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_Y$ and the canonical contraction $\mathcal L^\vee\otimes\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal O_Y$), so the composite is defined over $\mathbb F_q$ as well. In the standard Gysin construction the resulting map is expected to be $x\mapsto\tau\smile\pi^*x$, where $\tau\in H^2_{Z_{0,k}}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$ is the support cycle class of the $\mathbb F_q$-rational section $Z_0$; establishing that description, and the resulting Frobenius behaviour, is a separate matter and is deliberately not attempted here.

3. *Scope.* The proof used exactly two facts beyond elementary projective-bundle bookkeeping: the proved purity isomorphism for the zero section of a projective bundle (eoinm/lemma_purity_zero_section_projective_bundle) and excision for cohomology with supports (proved in Step 4). No localisation triangle, no nilpotent invariance, no formal-completion argument and no deformation to the normal cone is used.

lemma_387.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(H\) via a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), let \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\), and let \(F\) denote the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), on each \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Suppose \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=P^d\oplus L\bigl(H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\), with \(H^{d-2}=0\) when \(d<2\), and that \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if it is semisimple on \(P^d\).
lemma_387.proof:
We write $H^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $F_n:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^q$, the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius of $H^n$; thus $F=F_d$ in the statement. We use the convention $H^m=0$ for $m<0$, and put $W:=L(H^{d-2})\subseteq H^d$, so that the hypothesis is $H^d=P^d\oplus W$ (for $d=1$ this reads $H^1=P^1\oplus 0$, since $H^{-1}=0$).

**Step 0 (finite-dimensionality, invertibility of the $F_n$, invertibility of $q$).** $X$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, and the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ is an object of $D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ carrying its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:\mathcal F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$, where $\mathcal F_X$ is the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism of $X_k$. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^n<\infty$ for every $n$ (its $H^n(X_k,K)$ is precisely $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$). Applying lemma_6a (eoinm) to the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $X$ gives that, for every $n\ge0$, $F_n=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^n$, with inverse $F_n^{-1}=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma^{-1})^*$. In particular all $F_n$ occurring below are invertible, and $F_n^{-1}$ is again $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear. Finally $q=p^a$ with $p\ne\ell$, so $q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ maps to a unit of $\mathbb Z_{(\ell)}\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$; hence $q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ and $q^{-1}\in\mathbb Q_\ell$ exist.

**Step 1 (the Frobenius--Lefschetz compatibility, and the reduction needed to invoke lemma_369).**

*Reduction to an effective ample divisor.* lemma_369 is stated for an *effective* ample divisor defined over $\mathbb F_q$, while effectivity of a "very ample divisor" is convention-dependent; we therefore produce, from $H$, an $\mathbb F_q$-rational effective ample divisor with the same cycle class. Since $\mathcal O_X(H)$ is very ample, there is a closed immersion $i:X\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_{\mathbb F_q}$ with $\mathcal O_X(H)\simeq i^*\mathcal O(1)$; as $\dim X=d\ge1$, $X$ is non-empty, so $i^*\mathcal O(1)\ne0$ and the surjection $H^0(\mathbf P^N,\mathcal O(1))\twoheadrightarrow H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(H))$ shows $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(H))\ne0$. For the projective $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $X$ and the coherent sheaf $\mathcal O_X(H)$, flat base change along $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ gives a canonical isomorphism $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(H))\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;H^0(X_k,\mathcal O_{X_k}(H_k))$: indeed, taking the finite Cech complex $C^\bullet$ of $\mathcal O_X(H)$ for the standard affine cover coming from the projective embedding, each $C^i$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_q$-vector space (projectivity implies sections over each finite intersection are finite-dimensional), and $k$ is free, hence faithfully flat, over $\mathbb F_q$, so $H^0(k\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}C^\bullet)=k\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}H^0(C^\bullet)$. Faithful flatness reflects non-vanishing, so $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(H))\ne0$ already over $\mathbb F_q$; choose $0\ne s\in H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(H))$. Let $D:=V(s)\subset X$ be the vanishing scheme of $s$, i.e. the support of $\operatorname{cokernel}(\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal O_X(H))$. By construction $D$ is an effective Cartier divisor defined over $\mathbb F_q$ with $\mathcal O_X(D)\simeq\mathcal O_X(H)$; hence $D$ is linearly equivalent to $H$ and, $\mathcal O_X(H)$ being very ample, $D$ is ample. The $\ell$-adic cycle class of an effective Cartier divisor is the first Chern class of its line bundle applied to the fundamental class, $\mathrm{cl}(E)=c_1(\mathcal O_X(E))\cup[X]$, which depends only on the isomorphism class of $\mathcal O_X(E)$ (equivalently: the class map $\mathrm{CH}^1(X)=\mathrm{Pic}(X)\to H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ factors through rational equivalence, and linearly equivalent divisors are rationally equivalent). Therefore, for the fixed nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ appearing in the statement, $\mathrm{cl}(D)=c_1(\mathcal O_X(D))\cup[X]=c_1(\mathcal O_X(H))\cup[X]=\mathrm{cl}(H)=\xi$. Thus $L$ is also "cup product with the cycle class of $D$", computed with the same trivialisation of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$.

*Application of lemma_369.* $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge1$ over $\mathbb F_q$, $D$ is an effective ample divisor defined over $\mathbb F_q$, $\xi=\mathrm{cl}(D)$, $L=\xi\cup(-)$, and $F_n$ is the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius. All hypotheses of lemma_369 (Spark) hold, so for every $n\ge0$ we have, as maps $H^n\to H^{n+2}$,
$$F_{n+2}\circ L=q\,(L\circ F_n).\tag{1}$$

*Two formal consequences of (1).* Both are obtained from (1) using only Step 0 (invertibility of $F_n,F_{n+2}$) and $q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$.
(2') Left-compose (1) with $F_{n+2}^{-1}$: as maps $H^n\to H^n$,
$$F_{n+2}^{-1}\circ L\circ F_n=q^{-1}L.\tag{2'}$$
(3) Right-compose (1) with the automorphism $F_n^{-1}$ of $H^n$, obtaining $F_{n+2}\circ L\circ F_n^{-1}=q\,L$ as maps $H^{n+2}\to H^n$, and then left-compose with $F_{n+2}^{-1}$, obtaining, as maps $H^{n+2}\to H^n$,
$$L\circ F_n^{-1}=q\,(F_{n+2}^{-1}\circ L).\tag{3}$$
Conversely, (3) is equivalent to (1): left-composing (3) with $F_{n+2}$ gives $F_{n+2}\circ L\circ F_n^{-1}=q\,L$, and right-composing with $F_n$ returns (1). No other identity of this shape is claimed or used.

**Step 2 ($P^d$ is $F_d$-stable and $F_d|_{P^d}\in\mathrm{GL}(P^d)$).** $P^d=\ker(L:H^d\to H^{d+2})$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of the finite-dimensional $H^d$.

*Forward inclusion.* Let $y\in P^d$, so $Ly=0$. By (1) at $n=d$, $F_{d+2}(Ly)=q\,L(F_dy)$; hence $L(F_dy)=q^{-1}F_{d+2}(Ly)=q^{-1}F_{d+2}(0)=0$, i.e. $F_dy\in P^d$. So $F_d(P^d)\subseteq P^d$.

*Reverse inclusion.* Let $y\in P^d$ and put $x:=F_d^{-1}y\in H^d$. Applying (3) at $n=d$ to $y$ gives $Lx=L(F_d^{-1}y)=q\,F_{d+2}^{-1}(Ly)=q\,F_{d+2}^{-1}(0)=0$, so $x\in P^d$. Thus $F_d^{-1}(P^d)\subseteq P^d$, which is equivalent to $P^d\subseteq F_d(P^d)$ (given $y\in P^d$, its unique preimage $F_d^{-1}y$ lies in $P^d$ and maps to $y$).

Combining, $F_d(P^d)=P^d$, and since $F_d$ is injective on $H^d$, the restriction $T_P:=F_d|_{P^d}$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $P^d$.

**Step 3 ($W$ is $F_d$-stable, $F_d(W)=W$, and $T_W:=F_d|_W$ is semisimple).**

*Case $d=1$.* Then $H^{d-2}=H^{-1}=0$ by convention, so $W=L(0)=0$. The zero operator on the zero space is invertible and diagonalizable, so all three assertions are trivially true.

*Case $d\ge2$.* Write $\varphi:H^{d-2}\twoheadrightarrow W$ for the surjective map $x\mapsto Lx$.

*Stability.* For $y=Lx\in W$ with $x\in H^{d-2}$, (1) at $n=d-2$ (legal since $d-2\ge0$) gives $F_d(Lx)=q\,L(F_{d-2}x)\in W$. Hence $F_d(W)\subseteq W$.

*Surjectivity onto $W$.* Given $y=Lx\in W$, set $x':=q^{-1}F_{d-2}^{-1}x\in H^{d-2}$ (exists by Step 0). Then, again by (1) at $n=d-2$, $F_d(Lx')=q\,L(F_{d-2}x')=q\,L(q^{-1}x)=Lx=y$. Hence $F_d(W)=W$, and $T_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ (injectivity is inherited from $F_d$).

*Semisimplicity of $T_W$.* By hypothesis $F_{d-2}$ is semisimple on $H^{d-2}$; by lemma_5 (eoinm), applied to $V=H^{d-2}$ and $T=F_{d-2}$, the operator $\overline T:=F_{d-2}\otimes1$ is diagonalizable on $\overline V:=H^{d-2}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Let $\overline\varphi:=\varphi\otimes1:\overline V\to \overline{H^d}:=H^d\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Since $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is free, hence flat, over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, tensoring the exact sequences $H^{d-2}\xrightarrow{\varphi}W\to0$ and $0\to W\to H^d$ with $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ shows that $\overline\varphi$ is surjective onto $\overline W:=W\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and that the induced map $\overline W\hookrightarrow\overline{H^d}$ identifies $\overline W$ with $\operatorname{im}(\overline\varphi)$ as a $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-subspace. Moreover $\overline F_d:=F_d\otimes1$ preserves $\overline W$ (because $F_d(W)\subseteq W$) and restricts to $T_W\otimes1$, and the relation (1) at $n=d-2$ base-changes to
$$\overline F_d\circ\overline\varphi=q\,(\overline\varphi\circ\overline T)\quad\text{as maps }\overline V\to\overline{H^d}.\tag{1$_b$}$$
Since $\overline T$ is diagonalizable, $\overline V=\bigoplus_{\lambda} \overline V_\lambda$ where $\overline V_\lambda=\{v:\overline T v=\lambda v\}$ and $\lambda$ runs over the eigenvalues in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. For $v\in\overline V_\lambda$, (1$_b$) gives $\overline F_d(\overline\varphi v)=q\,\overline\varphi(\overline T v)=q\lambda\,\overline\varphi(v)$; so $\overline\varphi(v)$ is either $0$ or an eigenvector of $\overline F_d$ with eigenvalue $q\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. As $\overline\varphi$ is linear and surjective onto $\overline W$, and $\overline V$ is spanned by the $\overline V_\lambda$, the space $\overline W=\sum_\lambda\overline\varphi(\overline V_\lambda)$ is spanned by eigenvectors of $\overline F_d|_{\overline W}$. Hence $T_W\otimes1$ is diagonalizable on $W\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and lemma_5 applied to the finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $W$ and the operator $T_W$ shows $T_W$ is semisimple on $W$. (Here we used the hypothesis that $F_{d-2}$ is semisimple on $H^{d-2}$; this is the only place it is used.)

**Step 4 (conclusion).** By hypothesis $H^d=P^d\oplus W$ as $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and Steps 2 and 3 show that both summands are $F_d$-stable and that $F_d$ restricts to automorphisms $T_P\in\mathrm{GL}(P^d)$ and $T_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ with $F_d=T_P\oplus T_W$ on $P^d\oplus W$. Both spaces are finite-dimensional (subspaces/quotients of the finite-dimensional $H^d$, $H^{d-2}$). Applying lemma_9 (eoinm) with $m=2$, $V_1=P^d$, $T_1=T_P$, $V_2=W$, $T_2=T_W$, we obtain
$$F_d\text{ semisimple on }H^d\iff\bigl(T_P\text{ semisimple on }P^d\bigr)\ \text{and}\ \bigl(T_W\text{ semisimple on }W\bigr).$$
By Step 3 the second condition holds unconditionally (in both cases $d=1$ and $d\ge2$). Cancelling it from the conjunction yields
$$F_d\text{ is semisimple on }H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\iff F_d\text{ is semisimple on }P^d,$$
which is exactly the assertion. $\blacksquare$

(Remarks on the two points raised earlier: the identity used in Step 2's reverse inclusion is (3), derived directly from (1) by right-composing with $F_n^{-1}$ and then left-composing with $F_{n+2}^{-1}$, and the only auxiliary identity recorded is (2'), obtained by left-composing (1) with $F_{n+2}^{-1}$; no identity of the form $F_{n+2}^{-1}\circ L=q^{-1}(L\circ F_n)$ is asserted. The invocation of lemma_369 is justified by replacing $H$ with the $\mathbb F_q$-rational effective ample divisor $D=V(s)$ linearly equivalent to $H$, which has the same cycle class $\xi$, so the operator $L$ of the statement is unchanged.)

lemma_primitive_middle_decomposition_cri.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(H\) under a fixed trivialisation of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and put \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\). Suppose \(L:H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective, with \(H^{d-2}=0\) when \(d<2\). Then the following are equivalent: \(P^d\cap L\bigl(H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)=0\); \(L^2:H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism; and \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=P^d\oplus L\bigl(H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\).
lemma_primitive_middle_decomposition_cri.proof:
NOTATION. Write H^n := H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) for every n in Z, with the convention H^n := 0 for n < 0 (this is only notation: etale cohomology is concentrated in degrees >= 0, and the convention is the one used in the statement for H^{d-2} when d < 2). Since L is cup product with the fixed class xi in H^2, for each m the map L: H^m -> H^{m+2} is well defined, and L^2 := (L: H^d -> H^{d+2}) o (L: H^{d-2} -> H^d): H^{d-2} -> H^{d+2} is cup product with xi^2. Put
   W := L(H^{d-2}) = im(L: H^{d-2} -> H^d) subset H^d,     P^d := ker(L: H^d -> H^{d+2}),
and denote the three assertions by
   (i)   P^d cap W = 0;
   (ii)  L^2: H^{d-2} -> H^{d+2} is an isomorphism;
   (iii) H^d = P^d (+) W (internal direct sum).
We prove (i) <=> (ii) <=> (iii). The hypothesis that L: H^{d-2} -> H^d is injective is used exactly once, in Step 6.

PART A: THE CASE d = 1.
By the stated convention H^{d-2} = H^{-1} = 0, so W = L(0) = 0, and the injectivity hypothesis on L: 0 -> H^1 is vacuous.
- (i): P^1 cap 0 = 0, true.
- (ii): L^2 is the map H^{-1} = 0 -> H^3. Now X_k is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field k = bar(F_q) of pure dimension 1 >= 0, and ell != p = char(k); by lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing (Spark) H^n = 0 for all n > 2, in particular H^3 = 0. Hence L^2 is the unique map 0 -> 0, which is an isomorphism.
- (iii): P^1 = ker(L: H^1 -> H^3) = ker(H^1 -> 0) = H^1, so H^1 = P^1 = P^1 (+) 0 = P^1 (+) L(H^{-1}).
Thus all three assertions hold when d = 1, and in particular they are equivalent in that case. Henceforth assume d >= 2.

STEP 1 (finite dimensionality). X is projective, hence proper, over F_q, and the constant sheaf Q_ell lies in D^b_c(X_k, Q_ell) and carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism psi: F_X^* Q_ell ~-> Q_ell (F_X the q-power arithmetic Frobenius of X_k). Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) with K = Q_ell and phi = psi, each H^n = H^n(X_k, Q_ell) is finite dimensional over Q_ell. In particular H^{d-2}, H^d, H^{d+2} are finite dimensional, so all dimension counts below are legitimate.

STEP 2 (Poincare duality pairings; equality of two dimensions). X satisfies the hypotheses of lemma_77 (eoinm) with m = 1 and Y = X: it is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_q. Part (a) of that lemma gives a canonical trace tr_X: H^{2d} ~-> Q_ell(-d), normalised by tr_X(cl(x)) = [kappa(x): F_q] for every closed point x of X. Part (b) then says that for every n with 0 <= n <= 2d the Q_ell-bilinear pairing
   < , >_n : H^n x H^{2d-n} -> Q_ell(-d),   (x, y) |-> tr_X(x cup y),
is PERFECT. Since d >= 2 we have 0 <= d-2 and d+2 <= 2d, so taking n = d and n = d-2 we obtain perfect pairings
   < , >_d : H^d x H^d -> Q_ell(-d),      < , >_{d-2} : H^{d-2} x H^{d+2} -> Q_ell(-d).
A perfect pairing between finite-dimensional vector spaces identifies the first factor with the linear dual of the second; hence
   (star)   dim H^{d-2} = dim H^{d+2}.

STEP 3 (P^d is the orthogonal complement of W). The data (H, xi, tr_X) satisfy the hypotheses of lemma_361 (Spark): X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_q; H is a very ample divisor defined over F_q; xi is the cycle class of H under the fixed trivialisation Q_ell(1) ~-> Q_ell, which is the same datum as the choice of the nonzero element (the image of 1) of Q_ell(1) required there; and tr_X is the Poincare duality trace normalised by tr_X(cl(x)) = [kappa(x):F_q]. Lemma_361 therefore identifies P^d with the orthogonal complement of L(H^{d-2}) = W for < , >_d:
   (starstar)   P^d = { x in H^d : <x, w>_d = 0 for all w in W } =: W^perp.
There is no left/right ambiguity: cup product on H^d is graded-commutative, so <x,y>_d = (-1)^{d^2}<y,x>_d for x, y in H^d, and thus x is orthogonal to W on the left if and only if it is on the right.

STEP 4 (dimension count). Fix a Q_ell-linear isomorphism iota: Q_ell(-d) ~-> Q_ell (possible because Q_ell(1), hence Q_ell(-d), is trivialised in the statement). Define
   Phi : H^d -> Hom_{Q_ell}(W, Q_ell),   Phi(x)(w) = iota(<x, w>_d).
Kernel. By definition ker Phi = {x in H^d : <x,w>_d = 0 for all w in W} = W^perp = P^d by (starstar).
Surjectivity. Perfectness of < , >_d says that Psi: H^d ~-> (H^d)^vee, x |-> iota<x, ->>_d, is an isomorphism. The restriction map res: (H^d)^vee -> W^vee is surjective: given lambda in W^vee, choose a Q_ell-basis w_1,...,w_r of W, extend it to a basis w_1,...,w_r, v_1,...,v_s of H^d, and define mu in (H^d)^vee by mu(w_i) = lambda(w_i) and mu(v_j) = 0; then res(mu) = lambda. Since Phi = res o Psi, Phi is surjective.
Rank-nullity (H^d is finite dimensional by Step 1) gives dim H^d = dim ker Phi + dim im Phi = dim P^d + dim W^vee = dim P^d + dim W, i.e.
   (d1)   dim P^d = dim H^d - dim W.
By the injectivity hypothesis on L: H^{d-2} -> H^d, the map H^{d-2} ~-> W is an isomorphism, so dim W = dim H^{d-2}; combined with (d1),
   (d2)   dim P^d = dim H^d - dim H^{d-2},   dim W = dim H^{d-2}.

STEP 5 (the formal identity P^d cap W = L(ker L^2)). This uses only the definitions of W and P^d; no hard Lefschetz and no semisimplicity is invoked.
Inclusion "=): let x in H^{d-2} with L^2 x = 0 in H^{d+2}. Then Lx in W by definition of W. Also Lx in H^d and L(Lx) = L^2 x = 0, so Lx in ker(L: H^d -> H^{d+2}) = P^d. Hence Lx in P^d cap W.
Inclusion "(: let z in P^d cap W. Since z in W there exists x in H^{d-2} with z = Lx. Since z in P^d we have 0 = Lz = L(Lx) = L^2 x, so x in ker(L^2: H^{d-2} -> H^{d+2}) and z = Lx in L(ker L^2).
Note carefully that the hypothesis ker(L: H^{d-2} -> H^d) = 0 says nothing directly about Lx (which lies in H^d, not in the domain H^{d-2}); the identity above is what relates the two.

STEP 6 ((i) <=> (ii)).
(i) => (ii): By Step 5, (i) is equivalent to L(ker L^2) = 0. Let x in ker L^2. Then Lx in L(ker L^2) = 0, so Lx = 0, i.e. x in ker(L: H^{d-2} -> H^d) = 0 by the injectivity hypothesis. Hence ker L^2 = 0 and L^2 is injective. Its source and target have the same finite dimension by (star), so an injective endo-... map H^{d-2} -> H^{d+2} between finite-dimensional spaces of equal dimension is surjective as well; thus L^2 is an isomorphism, i.e. (ii).
(ii) => (i): if L^2 is an isomorphism then ker L^2 = 0, and Step 5 gives P^d cap W = L(0) = 0.

STEP 7 ((ii) => (iii) and (iii) => (i)).
(ii) => (iii): By Step 6 we know P^d cap W = 0. Using (d2),
   dim(P^d + W) = dim P^d + dim W - dim(P^d cap W) = (dim H^d - dim W) + dim W - 0 = dim H^d.
Both P^d + W and H^d are finite dimensional and P^d + W subset H^d, so equality of dimensions forces P^d + W = H^d. Together with P^d cap W = 0 this is precisely H^d = P^d (+) W, i.e. (iii).
(iii) => (i): an internal direct sum decomposition H^d = P^d (+) W means, by definition, that H^d = P^d + W and P^d cap W = 0; so (i) holds.

CONCLUSION. For d = 1 all three assertions were verified directly in Part A; for d >= 2 Steps 6 and 7 give the cycle of implications (i) => (ii) => (iii) => (i). Hence the three conditions are equivalent in all cases, which is exactly the statement of the lemma.

lemma_389.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be its cycle class via a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), let \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace, and put \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\), with \(H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) when \(d<2\). Then the bilinear form \(P^d\times P^d\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\), \((x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)\), is a perfect pairing if and only if \(\ker\bigl(L^2:H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)=\ker\bigl(L:H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\).
lemma_389.proof:
Fix the data \(q=p^a\), \(\ell\neq p\), \(X\), \(d\ge 1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), the \(\mathbb F_q\)-rational very ample divisor \(H\), its cycle class \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), the Lefschetz operator \(L\) = cup product with \(\xi\), the trace isomorphism \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) and \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d\to H^{d+2}\bigr)\). To shorten notation put
\[ V:=H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\quad W:=H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\quad Z:=H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\quad T:=\mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\]
where by the stated convention \(W=0\) when \(d<2\). Since \(X\) is projective over \(\mathbb F_q\), hence proper, lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Q_\ell[0]\) on \(X_k\) equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure shows that every \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), in particular \(V,W,Z\), is a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space. Note that \(L\) maps \(W\to V\) and \(V\to Z\), since cup product with \(\xi\in H^2\) raises degree by \(2\).

**Step 1: the ambient pairing on \(V\) is perfect.** For \(x,y\in V\) set \(\langle x,y\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)\in T\). By lemma_77(a) (with \(m=1\), \(Y=X\)) there is a canonical trace isomorphism \(\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(x))=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]\) for closed points \(x\in X\). Both \(\operatorname{tr}\) and \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) are \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphisms \(H^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}T\), so there is a scalar \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\) with \(\operatorname{tr}=c\cdot\operatorname{tr}_X\). Define \(\langle x,y\rangle_0:=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)\); then \(\langle x,y\rangle_0=c\,\langle x,y\rangle\). Lemma_77(b), applied to \(n=d\) (so that \(2d-n=d\)), says that \((x,y)\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_0\) is a perfect pairing \(V\times V\to T\): both induced maps \(V\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,T)\) are isomorphisms. Since multiplication by \(c^{-1}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of the one-dimensional space \(T\), the map \(\varphi\mapsto c^{-1}\varphi\) is an automorphism of \(\operatorname{Hom}(V,T)\); the two maps attached to \(\langle\,,\,\rangle\) are those attached to \(\langle\,,\,\rangle_0\) composed with this automorphism, hence are isomorphisms as well. Thus \(\langle\,,\,\rangle\) is perfect.

Moreover, graded commutativity of the cup product on \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) gives \(x\cup y=(-1)^{d\cdot d}y\cup x\) for \(x,y\in H^d\), and \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear, so
\[ \langle x,y\rangle=\varepsilon\,\langle y,x\rangle,\qquad \varepsilon:=(-1)^{d^2}\in\{+1,-1\}. \tag{1}\]

**Step 2: \(P^d\) is the orthogonal of \(S:=L(W)\).** Put \(S:=L(W)=\operatorname{im}\bigl(L:W\to V\bigr)\subseteq V\), and for \(U\subseteq V\) write \(U^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\langle v,u\rangle=0\ \forall u\in U\}\). Lemma_361 (Spark), applied to our \(X,H,\xi,L\) and the normalised trace \(\operatorname{tr}\), asserts that \(P^d\) is the orthogonal complement of \(L(H^{d-2})=S\) under the pairing \((x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)\), with the convention \(H^{d-2}=0\) for \(d<2\). Because \(\langle\,,\,\rangle_0=c\,\langle\,,\,\rangle\) with \(c\neq0\), a vector is orthogonal to a given set for one pairing if and only if it is for the other; hence
\[ P^d=S^{\perp}\quad\text{with respect to }\langle\,,\,\rangle. \tag{2}\]
(Consistency check in the edge case \(d=1\): then \(W=0\), so \(S=0\) and \(S^{\perp}=V=H^1\). Independently, \(H^3_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) by lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing applied to the projective \(k\)-scheme \(X_k\), which has pure dimension \(1\); hence \(P^1=\ker(L:H^1\to H^3)=H^1=S^{\perp}\), in agreement with (2).)

**Step 3: a linear-algebra criterion.** Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field \(K\), \(T\) a one-dimensional \(K\)-vector space, \(\langle\,,\,\rangle:V\times V\to T\) a perfect pairing satisfying \(\langle x,y\rangle=\varepsilon\langle y,x\rangle\) with \(\varepsilon\in K^{\times}\), and \(S\subseteq V\) a subspace. We prove: the restriction of \(\langle\,,\,\rangle\) to \(S^{\perp}\times S^{\perp}\) is perfect if and only if \(S\cap S^{\perp}=0\).

(i) *Dimension of an orthogonal.* Consider \(\Psi:V\to\operatorname{Hom}_K(S,T)\), \(v\mapsto\langle v,-\rangle|_S\). It is the composite of the isomorphism \(V\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,T)\), \(v\mapsto\langle v,-\rangle\) (perfectness), with the restriction map \(\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,T)\to\operatorname{Hom}_K(S,T)\). The restriction map is surjective: given \(\varphi:S\to T\), choose a \(K\)-basis of \(S\), extend it to a basis of \(V\) (using a \(K\)-complement of \(S\)), and define \(\tilde\varphi\) to be \(\varphi\) on the basis of \(S\) and \(0\) on the remaining basis vectors. Thus \(\Psi\) is surjective, and \(\ker\Psi=S^{\perp}\) by definition, so \(\dim S^{\perp}=\dim V-\dim S\).

(ii) *Biduality.* \(S\subseteq(S^{\perp})^{\perp}\) holds by definition of orthogonal. Applying (i) to \(S\) and then to \(S^{\perp}\) gives \(\dim (S^{\perp})^{\perp}=\dim V-\dim S^{\perp}=\dim S\); the inclusion of two spaces of equal dimension is an equality, so \((S^{\perp})^{\perp}=S\).

(iii) *Radicals.* The left radical of the restricted pairing is
\[ R_{\ell}=\{x\in S^{\perp}:\langle x,y\rangle=0\ \forall y\in S^{\perp}\}=S^{\perp}\cap(S^{\perp})^{\perp}=S^{\perp}\cap S, \]
by (ii). The right radical is, using (1) and \(\varepsilon\neq0\),
\[ R_r=\{y\in S^{\perp}:\langle x,y\rangle=0\ \forall x\in S^{\perp}\}=\{y\in S^{\perp}:\langle y,x\rangle=0\ \forall x\in S^{\perp}\}=R_{\ell}. \]

(iv) *Conclusion of the criterion.* If \(S\cap S^{\perp}=0\), then \(R_{\ell}=0\) by (iii), so the map \(S^{\perp}\to\operatorname{Hom}_K(S^{\perp},T)\), \(x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle\), is injective; since \(\dim S^{\perp}=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_K(S^{\perp},T)=\dim S^{\perp}\), it is an isomorphism, and then \(R_r=R_{\ell}=0\) shows the right map \(y\mapsto\langle -,y\rangle\) is injective, hence likewise an isomorphism. So the restriction is perfect. Conversely, if the restriction is perfect, its left radical is \(0\), so (iii) gives \(S\cap S^{\perp}=0\). This proves the criterion.

Applying the criterion with \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\), \(T=\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\), the pairing of Step 1 (where \(\varepsilon=(-1)^{d^2}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\)) and the subspace \(S=L(W)\), and using (2), we obtain
\[ \text{the form }(x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)\text{ on }P^d\times P^d\text{ is perfect}\iff S\cap S^{\perp}=0. \tag{3}\]

**Step 4: identifying \(S\cap S^{\perp}\).** By the definition of \(P^d\) and (2), \(S^{\perp}=P^d=\ker\bigl(L:V\to Z\bigr)\). Hence
\[ S\cap S^{\perp}=\{Lw:w\in W\}\cap\ker\bigl(L:V\to Z\bigr)=L\bigl(\ker(L^2:W\to Z)\bigr). \tag{4}\]
Both inclusions are immediate: if \(u\in S\cap S^{\perp}\) then \(u=Lw\) for some \(w\in W\) and \(u\in\ker(L:V\to Z)\), so \(L^2w=L(Lw)=Lu=0\), i.e. \(w\in\ker(L^2)\) and \(u\in L(\ker L^2)\); conversely, if \(w\in\ker(L^2:W\to Z)\) then \(Lw\in L(W)=S\) and \(L(Lw)=L^2w=0\), so \(Lw\in\ker(L:V\to Z)=S^{\perp}\). For \(d=1\) we have \(W=0\), and both sides of (4) are the zero subspace.

**Step 5: chaining the equivalences.** By (3) and (4),
\[ \text{perfect}\iff L\bigl(\ker(L^2:W\to Z)\bigr)=0\iff \ker(L^2:W\to Z)\subseteq\ker(L:W\to V),\]
where the last equivalence is just the statement that \(L\) annihilates a subspace exactly when that subspace lies in \(\ker(L:W\to V)\). On the other hand the reverse inclusion always holds: if \(w\in\ker(L:W\to V)\) then \(L^2w=L(Lw)=L(0)=0\), so \(w\in\ker(L^2:W\to Z)\). Therefore
\[ \ker(L^2:W\to Z)\subseteq\ker(L:W\to V)\iff \ker(L^2:W\to Z)=\ker(L:W\to V). \]
Combining with the displayed equivalence of this step yields
\[ (x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)\text{ is a perfect pairing on }P^d\times P^d\iff \ker\bigl(L^2:H^{d-2}\to H^{d+2}\bigr)=\ker\bigl(L:H^{d-2}\to H^{d}\bigr),\]
which is exactly the claimed statement.

**Edge case \(d=1\) (and the convention \(W=0\)).** Here \(W=H^{-1}=0\), so \(S=0\), \(S^{\perp}=V=H^1\), and Step 4 gives \(S\cap S^{\perp}=0\). Step 1 (via lemma_77(b) with \(n=1=2d-n\)) shows the pairing on \(H^1\) is perfect, and Step 2 (equivalently \(H^3=0\) by lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing) shows \(P^1=H^1\); meanwhile both \(\ker(L^2:0\to H^3)\) and \(\ker(L:0\to H^1)\) equal the zero subspace of \(0\). Thus both sides of the equivalence are true, as the general argument above already proves. No further case distinction is needed for \(d=2\) (where \(W=H^0\) and \(S=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot\xi\)) or for \(d\ge3\), since the argument of Steps 1--5 is uniform in \(d\) once the convention \(H^{d-2}=0\) for \(d<2\) is imposed. This completes the proof.

lemma_391.statement: Let \(K\) be an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\), let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(K\), let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(A\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\), fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(A\). Then for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d\), cup product with \(\xi^{\,d-n}\) is an isomorphism \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_391.proof:
Proof. Let V^n = H^n_et(X,Q_l). Since char K = 0, the prime l is invertible in K. We first reduce to the case K = C. Because X and A are of finite type over K, there exists a finitely generated subfield F of K and a smooth projective geometrically connected F-variety X_F with an ample line bundle A_F such that (X,A) is the base change of (X_F,A_F) to K. Choose an algebraic closure bar F contained in K. Choose an embedding of bar F into C and put X_C = X_bar F x_bar F C and A_C = A_bar F x_bar F C. Smooth proper base change for etale cohomology gives canonical isomorphisms H^n_et(X_K,Q_l) isomorphic to H^n_et(X_bar F,Q_l) and H^n_et(X_bar F,Q_l) isomorphic to H^n_et(X_C,Q_l). The comparison theorem for smooth complex varieties gives H^n_et(X_C,Q_l) isomorphic to H^n(X(C),Q) tensor_Q Q_l. These isomorphisms are compatible with cup products and send the etale cycle class xi_K of A_K to c_1(A_C) tensor 1. Thus it suffices to prove the assertion for X_C over C.

Set W^n = H^n(X(C),C) for n in Z, with W^n = 0 for n < 0 and for n > 2d. The groups W^n are finite-dimensional C-vector spaces; the vanishing for n > 2d also follows from the proved lemma lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing applied to the projective scheme X_C over C and the comparison isomorphism. Let L be cup product with c_1(A_C) on W = direct sum W^n, so L(W^n) subset W^{n+2}. Since A_C is ample, choose a Kähler form omega representing c_1(A_C). The Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations provide a C-linear operator Lambda on W lowering degree by 2 such that [L,Lambda] acts on W^n as n-d for every n. Equivalently, L and Lambda are the raising and lowering operators of the usual sl_2 Lefschetz triple attached to the Kähler class omega; Lambda may be taken as the signed adjoint of L with respect to the Hodge inner product. Applying the proved lemma lemma_l2_lefschetz_criterion over the field C to the finite-dimensional graded C-vector space W gives that L^{d-n}: W^n -> W^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0 <= n <= d.

The operator L on W is the extension to C of the rational operator on H^n(X(C),Q) given by cup product with c_1(A_C). If a linear map between finite-dimensional Q-vector spaces becomes an isomorphism after tensoring with C, then its determinant is a nonzero rational number, hence the original map was already an isomorphism. Therefore L^{d-n} is an isomorphism on H^n(X(C),Q). Tensoring with Q_l gives an isomorphism on H^n(X(C),Q) tensor_Q Q_l. Transporting this isomorphism back through the comparison and smooth proper base-change isomorphisms above identifies it exactly with cup product by xi^{d-n} on H^n_et(X_K,Q_l). This proves that for every 0 <= n <= d, cup product with xi^{d-n} is an isomorphism H^n_et(X,Q_l) -> H^{2d-n}_et(X,Q_l).

lemma_390.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime and \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Suppose that for every smooth projective variety \(W\) over \(\mathbb F_q\) and every \(n\ge0\) the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then for every \(m\ge1\), every \(d\ge0\) and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(V\) of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m)^*\), \(\sigma_m(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_390.proof:
We fix the following notation throughout.
