Put \(K:=\mathbb F_q\), \(L:=\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(\sigma:k\to k\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and write \(\sigma_m:=\sigma^m\), so \(\sigma_m(c)=c^{q^m}\). Note \(\sigma_m|_L=\mathrm{id}_L\) and \(\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^m}=k\). Fix \(m\ge 1\), \(d\ge 0\), and a smooth projective geometrically connected \(L\)-scheme \(V\) of pure dimension \(d\); we must prove semisimplicity of \((\mathrm{id}_V\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m)^*\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\). (The case \(m=1\) is contained in the argument below, where it becomes tautological.)

STEP 1. The auxiliary variety \(X\) over \(\mathbb F_q\).
Let \(X\) be the scheme \(V\) equipped with the composite structure morphism \(V\to\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}K\); only the structure morphism is changed, the underlying scheme is that of \(V\). We verify that \(X\) is a smooth projective variety over \(K\), in the sense in which the hypothesis of the lemma uses that phrase.
\(\bullet\) Finite type and separated: \(V\to\operatorname{Spec}L\) is projective, hence of finite type and separated; \(\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}K\) is finite, hence of finite type and separated; both properties are stable under composition.
\(\bullet\) Smooth: \(L/K\) is a finite separable extension (finite fields are perfect), so \(\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}K\) is finite \'etale, hence smooth; \(V\to\operatorname{Spec}L\) is smooth by hypothesis; smooth morphisms are stable under composition.
\(\bullet\) Projective: the composition of projective morphisms is projective (if \(Y\hookrightarrow\mathbb P(E)\) over \(X\) and \(X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P(F)\) over \(S\) with \(E,F\) locally free of finite rank, then \(Y\hookrightarrow\mathbb P(E)\times_S\mathbb P(F)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Segre}}\mathbb P(F\otimes_{\mathcal O_S}E)\) over \(S\) is a closed immersion). Here \(V\to\operatorname{Spec}L\) is projective by hypothesis, and \(\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}K\) is projective: writing \(L=K[T]/(f)\) with \(f\in K[T]\) of degree \(m\), \(\operatorname{Spec}L\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_K\) is a closed immersion, and \(\operatorname{Spec}L\) is proper over \(K\) (finite morphisms are proper), so its image is closed in \(\mathbb P^1_K\).
\(\bullet\) Reduced/irreducible (in case the convention for \emph{variety} demands it): \(V\) is geometrically connected over \(L\), so \(V_{\overline L}\to V\) is surjective (base change of \(\operatorname{Spec}\overline L\to\operatorname{Spec}L\)) with connected source, whence \(V\) is connected; thus \(X\) is connected. \(X\) is smooth over the field \(K\), hence regular. Regular local rings are domains, so no point of the noetherian scheme \(X\) can lie on two irreducible components (that would give a local ring with two minimal primes); the finitely many irreducible components are therefore pairwise disjoint closed subsets covering \(X\), hence each is also open. Connectedness forces exactly one irreducible component, so \(X\) is irreducible, and regular implies reduced.
Geometric connectedness is \emph{not} part of the convention for \emph{variety} used in the hypothesis: both the conjecture and the conclusion of this lemma explicitly add the words \emph{geometrically connected} when that property is needed. (Indeed Step 3 shows that \(X_k\) is a disjoint union of \(m\) non-empty clopen subschemes when \(m>1\), so \(X\) is typically not geometrically connected over \(K\).)
Thus \(X\) is a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\); in particular it is proper over \(K\), and the hypothesis of the lemma applies to \(W=X\).

STEP 2. Frobenius on \(X\) is semisimple and the cohomology is finite dimensional.
The constant sheaf \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) on \(X_k\) is an object of \(D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) (\(X_k\) is of finite type over the algebraically closed field \(k\)), and pullback of a constant sheaf is the constant sheaf, so \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius trivialisation \(\psi:F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\), where \(F_X:=\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma\). Since \(X\) is proper over \(K\), eoinm/lemma_45_finite_frob applied to \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell[0]\) with \(\varphi=\psi\) shows that \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) for every \(n\), and that the induced \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism is the pullback \(F_X^*\). eoinm/lemma_6a (with the field \(\mathbb F_q\)) likewise gives that \(F_X^*:=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), with inverse the geometric Frobenius. The hypothesis applied to \(W=X\) says precisely:
\[(*)\qquad F_X^*\ \text{is semisimple on } H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{for every } n\ge0.\]

STEP 3. Decomposition of \(X_k\) into the \(m\) conjugate components.
Since \(X\) is \(V\) with the \(K\)-structure factoring through \(L\), there is a canonical isomorphism of \(k\)-schemes
\[X_k=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k\;\cong\;V\times_{\operatorname{Spec}L}\operatorname{Spec}(L\otimes_K k).\]
Consider the \(k\)-algebra homomorphism
\[\theta:L\otimes_K k\longrightarrow \prod_{i\in\mathbf Z/m\mathbf Z}k,\qquad \lambda\otimes c\longmapsto (\sigma^i(\lambda)c)_{i\in\mathbf Z/m}.\]
Choose \(\alpha\in L\) with \(L=K[\alpha]\) (finite extensions of finite fields are simple), let \(f\in K[T]\) be its minimal polynomial (separable of degree \(m\)) and put \(\alpha_i:=\sigma^i(\alpha)\), \(i\in\mathbf Z/m\); these are the \(m\) distinct roots of \(f\) in \(k\) (the restrictions \(\sigma^i|_L\), \(i=0,\dots,m-1\), are the \(m\) distinct elements of \(\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)\)). The map \(\lambda\otimes c\mapsto c\,\overline{g_\lambda}(T)\) for \(\lambda=g_\lambda(\alpha)\) identifies \(L\otimes_K k\) with \(k[T]/(f)\), and since \(f=\prod_i (T-\alpha_i)\) with the \(\alpha_i\) distinct, the Chinese remainder theorem identifies \(k[T]/(f)\) with \(\prod_i k[T]/(T-\alpha_i)\cong\prod_i k\) by evaluation at \((\alpha_i)_i\). Under these identifications \(\theta\) is exactly evaluation, hence \(\theta\) is a \(k\)-algebra isomorphism.
For \(j\in\mathbf Z/m\) let \(e_j\in L\otimes_K k\) be THE element characterised by \(\theta(e_j)=(\delta_{ij})_{i\in\mathbf Z/m}\). The \(e_j\) are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with \(\sum_j e_j=1\). Put \(V_j:=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal O_{X_k}e_j)\subseteq X_k\); this is open and closed, \(V_j=\{x\in X_k:e_j(x)=1\}\), and \(X_k=\bigsqcup_{j\in\mathbf Z/m}V_j\) as a disjoint union of clopen subschemes. Since \(\theta\) identifies \((L\otimes_K k)e_j\) with \(k\) via \(\lambda\otimes c\mapsto\sigma^j(\lambda)c\), we have \(V_j\cong V\times_{L,\,\sigma^j}\operatorname{Spec}k\); in particular
\[V_0=V\times_{L,\,\mathrm{id}}\operatorname{Spec}k=V_k.\]

STEP 4. The \(q\)-Frobenius cyclically permutes the components, and its \(m\)-th power restricts to the \(q^m\)-Frobenius on \(V_0\).
The comorphism of \(F_X=\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma\) on \(\mathcal O_{X_k}=\mathcal O_V\otimes_K k\) is \(\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma\) (checked on affine opens of \(V\) and glued); it is \(\sigma\)-semilinear and sends \(\lambda\otimes c\) to \(\lambda\otimes\sigma(c)\).

Claim: \((\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma)(e_j)=e_{j+1}\) (indices mod \(m\)).
Proof of the claim. In the model \(A:=k[T]/(f)\) of Step 3, \(\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma\) corresponds to the \(\sigma\)-semilinear map \(\tau:\sum_i c_iT^i\mapsto\sum_i\sigma(c_i)T^i\). It is well defined because \(\sigma(f)=f\) (as \(f\in K[T]\)), and it satisfies \(\tau(c\,\overline{g_\lambda})=\sigma(c)\,\overline{g_\lambda}\), i.e.\ \(\tau(\lambda\otimes c)=\lambda\otimes\sigma(c)\), so it does represent \(\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma\). Let \(p_j\in k[T]\) be the Lagrange polynomial of degree \(<m\) with \(p_j(\alpha_i)=\delta_{ij}\); then \(e_j\) is the class of \(p_j\). For every \(\beta\in k\) algebraic over \(K\) and every \(p=\sum_i c_iT^i\in k[T]\),
\[\sigma(p)(\sigma(\beta))=\textstyle\sum_i\sigma(c_i)\sigma(\beta)^i=\sigma\bigl(\sum_i c_i\beta^i\bigr)=\sigma(p(\beta)).\]
Hence for every \(i\in\mathbf Z/m\), using \(\alpha_{i+1}=\sigma(\sigma^i\alpha)=\sigma(\alpha_i)\) and \(\sigma(\delta_{ij})=\delta_{ij}\),
\[\sigma(p_j)(\alpha_{i+1})=\sigma\bigl(p_j(\sigma^i\alpha)\bigr)=\sigma\bigl(p_j(\alpha_i)\bigr)=\sigma(\delta_{ij})=\delta_{ij}.\]
Thus \(\sigma(p_j)\) takes the value \(1\) at \(\alpha_{j+1}\) and \(0\) at every \(\alpha_i\) with \(i\ne j\); two polynomials of degree \(<m\) agreeing at the \(m\) distinct roots of \(f\) are congruent modulo \(f\), so \(\tau(\overline{p_j})=\overline{p_{j+1}}\), i.e.\ \((\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma)(e_j)=e_{j+1}\). This proves the claim.

Consequences.
(i) Since \(V_j=\{e_j=1\}\), \(F_X^{-1}(V_j)=\{(\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma)(e_j)=1\}=\{e_{j+1}=1\}=V_{j+1}\); as \(F_X\) is an automorphism, \(F_X(V_i)=V_{i-1}\). Hence with \(f:=F_X^{\,m}\) we have \(f(V_i)=V_i\) and \(f^{-1}(V_i)=V_i\) for every \(i\).
(ii) \((\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma)^m=\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma^m=\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma_m\). In the model \(k[T]/(f)\) this is \(\sum_i c_iT^i\mapsto\sum_i\sigma_m(c_i)T^i\); since \(\sigma_m\) fixes each \(\alpha_i\in L\), \(\sigma_m(p_j)(\alpha_i)=\sigma_m(p_j(\alpha_i))=\sigma_m(\delta_{ij})=\delta_{ij}\), so \((\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma_m)(e_j)=e_j\) for every \(j\); thus \(f\) preserves every \(V_j\).
(iii) Identify \(\psi:(\mathcal O_{X_k})e_0\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal O_V\otimes_{L,\mathrm{id}}k=\mathcal O_{V_k}\) by \(\psi((b\otimes c)e_0)=b\otimes c\). This is well defined because the balancing relation \((b\lambda)\otimes c=b\otimes(\lambda c)\) in \(\mathcal O_V\otimes_K k\) is respected: \(\psi(((b\lambda)\otimes c)e_0)=b\lambda\otimes c\) and \(\psi((b\otimes\lambda c)e_0)=b\otimes\lambda c=b\lambda\otimes c\), since \(L\) acts on the \(k\)-factor of the target through the identity; the inverse is \(b\otimes c\mapsto (b\otimes c)e_0\). Then, using (ii),
\[\psi\bigl((\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma_m)((b\otimes c)e_0)\bigr)=\psi\bigl((b\otimes\sigma_m(c))(\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma_m)(e_0)\bigr)=\psi\bigl((b\otimes\sigma_m(c))e_0\bigr)=b\otimes\sigma_m(c),\]
which is exactly the comorphism of \(F_V^{(m)}:=\mathrm{id}_V\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m\). Thus \(f|_{V_0}=F_V^{(m)}\) under the identification \(V_0=V_k\). The map \(F_V^{(m)}:V_k\to V_k\) is a well defined morphism of schemes over \(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}\) (equivalently of \(L\)-schemes), because \(\sigma_m|_L=\mathrm{id}\); it is \emph{not} a morphism of \(k\)-schemes, since \(\sigma_m\) is not the identity on \(k\). This is harmless: pullback of \('etale\) sheaves is defined for every morphism of schemes, and it carries the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) to the constant sheaf.

STEP 5. Block diagonality of \(f^*\) and stability of the \(V_k\)-summand.
Let \(\iota_j:V_j\hookrightarrow X_k\) be the clopen immersion. Because \(V_j\) is open and closed, \((\iota_j)_*=(\iota_j)_!\) is exact and fully faithful, \(\iota_j^*(\iota_j)_*=\mathrm{id}\), \(\iota_i^*(\iota_j)_!=0\) for \(i\ne j\), and \(\sum_j(\iota_j)_!\iota_j^*\cong\mathrm{id}\) on sheaves on \(X_k\); hence \(\mathbb Q_\ell\cong\bigoplus_j(\iota_j)_*\mathbb Q_\ell|_{V_j}\). The functor \((\iota_j)_*\) is exact and has the exact left adjoint \(\iota_j^*\), hence preserves injectives, and \(\Gamma(X_k,(\iota_j)_*(-))=\Gamma(V_j,-)\); therefore \((\iota_j)_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_j,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective with image \(W_j:=\{x:\iota_i^*x=0\ \text{for all }i\ne j\}\), and
\[H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbf Z/m} W_j,\qquad W_j\xrightarrow{\ \iota_j^*\ }\ \sim H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_j,\mathbb Q_\ell),\]
with inverse \((\iota_j)_*\); equivalently \(x\mapsto(\iota_j^*x)_j\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \(H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigoplus_j H^n(V_j,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
Since \(f(V_j)=V_j\), the corestriction \(f_j:=f|_{V_j}:V_j\to V_j\) is defined and \(f\circ\iota_j=\iota_j\circ f_j\) (the square with the \(\iota_j\) is cartesian, as \(f^{-1}(V_j)=V_j\); equivalently, on stalks \(f^{-1}(\iota_j)_*G\cong(\iota_j)_*(f_j)^{-1}G\), both being the stalk at \(f_j(x)\) for \(x\in V_j\) and \(0\) for \(x\notin V_j\), using \(f(x)\in V_j\Leftrightarrow x\in V_j\)). By functoriality of pullback, \(\iota_j^*\circ f^*=(f_j)^*\circ\iota_j^*\). Hence, if \(x\in W_j\) and \(i\ne j\), then \(\iota_i^*(f^*x)=(f_i)^*(\iota_i^*x)=0\), so \(f^*x\in W_j\): each summand \(W_j\) is \(f^*\)-stable. Moreover, for \(y\in H^n(V_j,\mathbb Q_\ell)\),
\[\iota_j^*\bigl(f^*(\iota_j)_*y\bigr)=(f_j)^*\bigl(\iota_j^*(\iota_j)_*y\bigr)=(f_j)^*y,\]
and since \(f^*(\iota_j)_*y\in W_j\) and \(\iota_j^*:W_j\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(V_j,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is the inverse of \((\iota_j)_*\), this says \(f^*(\iota_j)_*y=(\iota_j)_*(f_j)^*y\); i.e.\ \(f^*|_{W_j}\) is carried by \((\iota_j)_*\) onto \((f_j)^*\).
Taking \(j=0\) and using contravariance \((F_X^{\,m})^*=(F_X^*)^m\), we obtain: with \(T:=(F_X^*)^m\), the summand \(W_0\cong H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_0,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is \(T\)-stable, and \(T|_{W_0}\) is conjugate via the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \((\iota_0)_*\) to \((f_0)^*=(F_V^{(m)})^*\):
\[(\iota_0)_*\circ (F_V^{(m)})^*=T|_{W_0}\circ(\iota_0)_*.\]

STEP 6. Linear algebra and conclusion.
Let \(V_n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) (finite dimensional by Step 2) and \(F:=F_X^*\). By \((*)\), \(F\) is semisimple. By eoinm/lemma_5, \(F\otimes 1\) is diagonalisable on \(V_n\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\); in an eigenbasis of \(F\) the operator \(T=F^m=(F\otimes1)^m\) is again diagonal (with eigenvalues \(\lambda^m\)), hence \(T\otimes1\) is diagonalisable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\); applying eoinm/lemma_5 again, \(T\) is semisimple on \(V_n\). The subspace \(W_0\subseteq V_n\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspace with \(T(W_0)\subseteq W_0\), so eoinm/lemma_358 yields that \(T|_{W_0}\in\mathrm{GL}(W_0)\) is semisimple on \(W_0\) (it is invertible because \(T\) is invertible and \(W_0\) is a stable subspace of a finite-dimensional space).
The operator \((F_V^{(m)})^*\) on \(H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is invertible by eoinm/lemma_6a (applied with the field \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), whose algebraic closure is \(k\), and \(\sigma_m(c)=c^{q^m}\)); that same lemma identifies \((F_V^{(m)})^*=(\mathrm{id}_V\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m)^*\) with the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Since \((\iota_0)_*:H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}W_0\) intertwines \((F_V^{(m)})^*\) with \(T|_{W_0}\), eoinm/lemma_8 gives that \((F_V^{(m)})^*\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). By eoinm/lemma_5 this is equivalent to diagonalisability over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
As \(n\ge0\), \(m\ge1\), \(d\ge0\) and \(V\) were arbitrary, the statement of the lemma is proved.

lemma_386.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic zero, let d >= 1 be an integer, let V = direct sum_{n in Z} V_n be a finite-dimensional Z-graded K-vector space with V_n = 0 for n < 0 and n > 2d, and let L in End_K(V) satisfy L(V_n) subset V_{n+2} for every n. Suppose that L^{d-n}: V_n -> V_{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= d. Then there exists Lambda in End_K(V) such that Lambda(V_n) subset V_{n-2} for every n and L Lambda - Lambda L acts on V_n as multiplication by n - d for every 0 <= n <= 2d.
lemma_386.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_386.

CONVENTIONS. By hypothesis V_n = 0 for n < 0 and for n > 2d; we use this convention freely, so that all statements about graded pieces outside [0,2d] are vacuous and all maps into or out of them are zero. L^a denotes the a-th power of L (L^0 = id), so L^a(V_j) subset V_{j+2a} for all a >= 0. The hypothesis (HL) is: for every 0 <= n <= d, L^{d-n}: V_n -> V_{2d-n} is an isomorphism (for n = d this is the identity of V_d). K has characteristic 0, so all integers occurring below act as honest scalars.

STEP 1. Injectivity below the middle and surjectivity above it.
(a) If 0 <= j < d, then L: V_j -> V_{j+2} is injective. Indeed d - j >= 1 and L^{d-j} = L^{d-j-1} o L as maps V_j -> V_{2d-j}, while L^{d-j}: V_j -> V_{2d-j} is an isomorphism by (HL); a map whose composite with L is injective forces L injective.
(b) If d <= j <= 2d - 1, then L: V_j -> V_{j+2} is surjective. Let y in V_{j+2}. Since j >= d we have 2d - j - 2 <= d - 2 <= d, so (HL) applied to the index 2d - j - 2 says that L^{d-(2d-j-2)} = L^{j+2-d}: V_{2d-j-2} -> V_{2d-(2d-j-2)} = V_{j+2} is an isomorphism. Choose z in V_{2d-j-2} with L^{j+2-d} z = y. Since j >= d, j + 1 - d >= 1, and x := L^{j+1-d} z lies in V_{2d-j-2 + 2(j+1-d)} = V_j and satisfies L x = L^{j+2-d} z = y. For j >= 2d the target V_{j+2} is 0 and surjectivity is vacuous.

STEP 2. Primitive spaces and their dimensions.
For 0 <= m <= d define P^m := ker( L^{d-m+1}: V_m -> V_{2d-m+2} ). (For m = d this is ker(L: V_d -> V_{d+2}); for m = 0,1 the target is V_{2d+2} = 0 resp. V_{2d+1} = 0, so P^0 = V_0 and P^1 = V_1.)
Factor L^{d-m+1} = L o L^{d-m}, where L^{d-m}: V_m -> V_{2d-m} is the isomorphism from (HL). Hence P^m = (L^{d-m})^{-1}( ker( L: V_{2d-m} -> V_{2d-m+2} ) ), and since L^{d-m} is a bijection,
  dim P^m = dim ker( L: V_{2d-m} -> V_{2d-m+2} ).
Because 2d - m >= d, Step 1(b) shows this last L is surjective, so its kernel has dimension dim V_{2d-m} - dim V_{2d-m+2}. Now dim V_{2d-m} = dim V_m (the isomorphism L^{d-m}), and dim V_{2d-m+2} = dim V_{m-2}: for m >= 2 this is because L^{d-(m-2)} = L^{d-m+2}: V_{m-2} -> V_{2d-m+2} is an isomorphism by (HL) (m-2 <= d); for m <= 1 both V_{m-2} and V_{2d-m+2} (degrees 2d+1, 2d+2) are 0. Therefore
  (2.1)   dim P^m = dim V_m - dim V_{m-2}   for every 0 <= m <= d.

STEP 3. Powers of L on primitive parts. Fix 0 <= m <= d and r >= 0.
(a) If 0 <= r <= d - m, then L^r: P^m -> V_{m+2r} is injective: L^{d-m} = L^{d-m-r} o L^r as maps V_m -> V_{2d-m}, and L^{d-m}: V_m -> V_{2d-m} is injective (it is an isomorphism).
(b) If r >= d - m + 1, then L^r P^m = 0: writing r = (r - (d-m+1)) + (d-m+1), L^r = L^{r-(d-m+1)} o L^{d-m+1}, and L^{d-m+1} vanishes on P^m by definition.

STEP 4. Lefschetz decomposition. For each n set R(n) := { r in Z : max(0, n-d) <= r <= floor(n/2) }. We claim that for every n the addition map gives a direct-sum decomposition
  (4.1)   V_n = direct sum over r in R(n) of L^r P^{n-2r}.
First note that for r in R(n) the index m := n - 2r lies in [0,d]: r <= floor(n/2) gives m >= 0; if n <= d then m <= n <= d; if n > d then r >= n - d gives m = n - 2r <= 2d - n < d.

Case n <= d. Then R(n) = {0,1,...,R} with R = floor(n/2).
Directness. Suppose sum_{r=0}^{R} L^r p_r = 0 with p_r in P^{n-2r}, and let r_0 be maximal with p_{r_0} nonzero. Apply L^a with a := d - n + r_0 (>= 0 since n <= d). Each term L^{a+r} p_r lies in V_{n-2r+2(a+r)} = V_{n+2a}. For r < r_0 we have a + r = d - n + r_0 + r >= d - n + (r+1) + r = d - (n-2r) + 1, since r_0 >= r+1; hence L^{a+r} p_r = 0 by Step 3(b) applied to m = n - 2r. For r = r_0, with m_0 := n - 2r_0, we get L^{a+r_0} p_{r_0} = L^{d-n+2r_0} p_{r_0} = L^{d-m_0} p_{r_0}, which is nonzero by Step 3(a) (injectivity of L^{d-m_0} on P^{m_0}; note d - m_0 = d - n + 2r_0 and r_0 <= d - m_0 as required). Thus the sum is nonzero, contradiction. Hence all p_r = 0.
Spanning. For each r in R(n) we have r >= 0 >= n - d, i.e. r <= d - (n - 2r), so L^r: P^{n-2r} -> V_n is injective by Step 3(a); thus dim L^r P^{n-2r} = dim P^{n-2r}. The sum is direct by the previous paragraph, so by (2.1)
  dim ( sum_{r=0}^{R} L^r P^{n-2r} ) = sum_{r=0}^{R} ( dim V_{n-2r} - dim V_{n-2r-2} ) = dim V_n - dim V_{n-2R-2} = dim V_n,
telescoping, and n - 2R - 2 is -1 or -2, so V_{n-2R-2} = 0. A subspace of the finite-dimensional space V_n having the same dimension is all of V_n.

Case n > d. Then 2d - n < d, so (HL) at the index 2d - n says L^{n-d}: V_{2d-n} -> V_{2d-n+2(n-d)} = V_n is an isomorphism. Apply L^{n-d} to the already-established decomposition (4.1) in degree 2d - n:
  V_n = direct sum over s in R(2d-n) of L^{n-d+s} P^{2d-n-2s}.
Put r := n - d + s. Then 2d - n - 2s = 2d - n - 2(r - n + d) = n - 2r, so the summands are L^r P^{n-2r}. Since R(2d-n) = {0,...,floor((2d-n)/2)}, r runs over {n-d, ..., n-d + floor((2d-n)/2)}. Writing t := n - d >= 1, the top end is t + floor((d-t)/2) = floor((d+t)/2) = floor(n/2). Hence r runs over {n-d,...,floor(n/2)} = R(n), which is exactly (4.1).

Uniqueness. By (4.1), every v in V_n is written uniquely as v = sum_{r in R(n)} L^r p_r with p_r in P^{n-2r}.

STEP 5. Definition of Lambda. For 0 <= m <= d and s >= 0 set c(m,s) := s(d - m - s + 1), an element of the prime field of K (with c(m,0) = 0). Define Lambda on V_n as follows: for v = sum_{r in R(n)} L^r p_r (unique, p_r in P^{n-2r}) put
  Lambda v := sum over r in R(n) with r >= 1 of c(n-2r, r) L^{r-1} p_r.
Since p_r in V_{n-2r}, L^{r-1} p_r in V_{n-2r+2r-2} = V_{n-2}; hence Lambda(V_n) subset V_{n-2}. Uniqueness of the decomposition makes Lambda a well-defined K-linear endomorphism of V (and V_n = 0 outside [0,2d] needs no definition).

Auxiliary identity (*). For all 0 <= m <= d, all s >= 0 and all p in P^m,
  ( * )   Lambda( L^s p ) = c(m,s) L^{s-1} p,
where the right side is 0 when s = 0 (we read L^{-1}p as 0, matching c(m,0) = 0).
Proof of (*). Case s = 0: p in P^m subset V_m and 0 in R(m) (as 0 <= m <= d), so p is the s = 0 summand of its own decomposition and Lambda p = 0 = c(m,0) L^{-1}p.
Case s >= 1 with s in R(m+2s): then L^s p is, by uniqueness of the decomposition of V_{m+2s}, exactly the s-summand element (its primitive part p lies in P^m = P^{(m+2s)-2s}); hence Lambda(L^s p) = c(m,s) L^{s-1}p by definition. (Note s in R(m+2s) implies s <= d - m: indeed s >= max(0, m+2s-d) gives s <= d - m whenever m+2s > d, and s <= (d-m)/2 <= d-m when m+2s <= d.)
Case s >= 1 with s not in R(m+2s): since floor((m+2s)/2) = s + floor(m/2) >= s, the only way to fail is s < max(0, m+2s-d), i.e. m + 2s > d and s < m + 2s - d, i.e. s >= d - m + 1. Then L^s p = 0 by Step 3(b), so Lambda(L^s p) = 0. If s = d - m + 1 then c(m,s) = s(d-m-s+1) = s*0 = 0; if s >= d - m + 2 then s - 1 >= d - m + 1, so L^{s-1} p = 0 by Step 3(b) again. In both subcases c(m,s) L^{s-1}p = 0, proving (*) in this case as well.

STEP 6. The commutator. Fix n, an index r in R(n), m := n - 2r and p in P^m; put x := L^r p in V_n. Using (*) with s = r and with s = r + 1:
  (L Lambda - Lambda L)(x) = L( Lambda(L^r p) ) - Lambda( L^{r+1} p ) = c(m,r) L^r p - c(m,r+1) L^r p = ( c(m,r) - c(m,r+1) ) x.
Now compute the scalar explicitly:
  c(m,r) = r(d - m - r + 1) = r(d-m) - r^2 + r,
  c(m,r+1) = (r+1)(d - m - r) = (r+1)(d-m) - r(r+1) = (r+1)(d-m) - r^2 - r,
  c(m,r) - c(m,r+1) = - (d-m) + 2r = m + 2r - d = n - d,
since m + 2r = n. Hence (L Lambda - Lambda L) x = (n - d) x for every generator x = L^r p of V_n (the elements L^r p with r in R(n), p in P^{n-2r} span V_n by (4.1)), and by K-linearity for every v in V_n.

STEP 7. Conclusion. The operator Lambda constructed in Step 5 lies in End_K(V), satisfies Lambda(V_n) subset V_{n-2} for every n, and satisfies (L Lambda - Lambda L)|_{V_n} = (n - d) id_{V_n} for every 0 <= n <= 2d (and for all n, since V_n = 0 otherwise). This is exactly the required conclusion. QED.

REMARKS. (i) The normalisation is the one demanded by the statement: the coefficient is n - d, matching the sign convention of the converse criterion lemma_l2_lefschetz_criterion (which, conversely, deduces (HL) from such a pair (L, Lambda)); no geometric input and no trace pairing are used, and no unnormalised adjointness is invoked (which would give the wrong coefficient, e.g. Lambda(Lp) = p instead of 2p in degree m = 0, d = 2). (ii) The proof used only the hypothesis (HL) and characteristic zero (to interpret the integer scalars c(m,r)); the case d >= 1 given in the statement is more than enough, and the argument covers every degree 0 <= n <= 2d, including the top degrees n > d where the decomposition is transported from degree 2d - n by the hard-Lefschetz isomorphism L^{n-d}.

lemma_dual_short_exact_perfectness.statement: Let K be a field. Let 0 -> A --f--> B --g--> C -> 0 and 0 -> C' --g'--> B' --f'--> A' -> 0 be exact sequences of finite-dimensional K-vector spaces. Suppose the pairings < , >_B : B x B' -> K and < , >_C : C x C' -> K are perfect, and g and g' are adjoint: < g(b), c' >_C = < b, g'(c') >_B for all b in B and c' in C'. Define a pairing < , >_A : A x A' -> K by < a, a' >_A = < f(a), b' >_B for any b' in B' with f'(b') = a'. Then this pairing is well-defined and perfect.
lemma_dual_short_exact_perfectness.proof:
Proof. Recall that a bilinear pairing V x W -> K of finite-dimensional K-vector spaces is perfect iff the induced maps V -> W^* and W -> V^* are isomorphisms. We prove bilinearity and both nondegeneracies, then conclude by a dimension count.

Well-definedness. Let a in A and a' in A'. Choose b' in B' with f'(b') = a'. If b'' is another element of B' with f'(b'') = a', then b' - b'' lies in ker(f') = im(g'), so b' - b'' = g'(c') for some c' in C'. Then
<f(a), b' - b''>_B = <f(a), g'(c')>_B = <g(f(a)), c'>_C = 0,
because g o f = 0 by exactness of the first sequence. Hence the value <f(a),b'>_B depends only on a and a', not on the chosen lift b'.

Bilinearity. If b'_1 and b'_2 lift a'_1 and a'_2, then lambda b'_1 + mu b'_2 lifts lambda a'_1 + mu a'_2. Therefore
<a, lambda a'_1 + mu a'_2>_A = <f(a), lambda b'_1 + mu b'_2>_B = lambda <a,a'_1>_A + mu <a,a'_2>_A.
Similarly, if b' lifts a', then for a_1,a_2 in A and lambda,mu in K,
<lambda a_1 + mu a_2, a'>_A = <f(lambda a_1 + mu a_2), b'>_B = lambda <a_1,a'>_A + mu <a_2,a'>_A.
Thus the pairing is bilinear.

Left nondegeneracy. Suppose a in A satisfies <a,a'>_A = 0 for every a' in A'. Let b' be any element of B'. Since f' is surjective, a' = f'(b') lies in A'. By definition,
<f(a), b'>_B = <a, f'(b')>_A = 0.
Thus f(a) pairs trivially with every b' in B'. Since the B-pairing is perfect, f(a)=0. Since f is injective, a=0.

Right nondegeneracy. Suppose a' in A' satisfies <a,a'>_A = 0 for every a in A. Choose b' in B' with f'(b') = a'. Then for every a in A,
<f(a), b'>_B = <a,a'>_A = 0.
By exactness, im(f) = ker(g), so b' annihilates ker(g) under the B-pairing.

Define a linear functional phi on im(g) subset C by phi(g(b)) = <b,b'>_B. This is well-defined: if g(b_1)=g(b_2), then b_1-b_2 in ker(g)=im(f), so b_1-b_2=f(a) for some a in A, and hence
<b_1-b_2,b'>_B = <f(a),b'>_B = 0.
It is linear because the B-pairing is linear in its first argument. Since im(g) is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space C, extend phi to a linear functional Phi on C, for example by extending a basis of im(g) to a basis of C and defining Phi arbitrarily on the added basis vectors.

Because the C-pairing is perfect, there exists c' in C' such that Phi(c) = <c,c'>_C for all c in C.

Now for every b in B,
<b,b'>_B = phi(g(b)) = Phi(g(b)) = <g(b),c'>_C = <b,g'(c')>_B,
where the last equality is the assumed adjointness of g and g'. Hence <b,b' - g'(c')>_B = 0 for all b in B. Perfectness of the B-pairing gives b' = g'(c'). Therefore
a' = f'(b') = f'(g'(c')) = 0,
by exactness of the second sequence. Thus the pairing is right nondegenerate.

Dimension count and perfectness. The left nondegeneracy says the induced map A -> (A')^* is injective. The right nondegeneracy says the induced map A' -> A^* is injective. From exactness, dim(B)=dim(A)+dim(C) and dim(B')=dim(C')+dim(A'). Perfect pairings imply dim(B)=dim(B') and dim(C)=dim(C'). Hence dim(A)=dim(A'). Therefore the injective maps A -> (A')^* and A' -> A^* are isomorphisms between finite-dimensional spaces of the same dimension. The defined pairing is perfect.

lemma_open_immersion_derived_projection_.statement:
Let \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) be an open immersion of schemes, let \(\Lambda\) be a field, let \(F\) be a complex of sheaves of \(\Lambda\)-modules on \(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\) and let \(G\) be a complex of sheaves of \(\Lambda\)-modules on \(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\). Then the canonical morphism
\[
\theta_{F,G}\colon j_!\!\left(F\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\Lambda} j^{*}G\right)\longrightarrow j_!F\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\Lambda} G,
\]
the \((j_!\dashv j^{*})\)-adjoint of \(F\to j^{*}j_!F\to j^{*}j_!F\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\Lambda}j^{*}G\cong j^{*}(j_!F\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\Lambda}G)\), is an isomorphism in \(D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\Lambda)\).
lemma_open_immersion_derived_projection_.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_open_immersion_derived_projection_formula",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Proof. Let j:U

↪ X be an open immersion of schemes, let Λ be a field, let F ∈ D(U_et,Λ) and G ∈ D(X_et,Λ). We prove θ_{F,G}: j_!(F ⊗^L_Λ j^*G) → j_!F ⊗^L_Λ G is an isomorphism.

1. Geometric stalks. For a scheme Y and a geometric point ȳ:Spec(Ω)→Y, the stalk functor S_ȳ:Sh(Y_et,Λ)→Mod_Λ is a filtered colimit over étale neighbourhoods of ȳ, hence exact and conservative: a morphism of sheaves, and hence a morphism of complexes, is an isomorphism iff all geometric stalks are isomorphisms. For sheaves A,B on Y, (A⊗_ΛB)_ȳ≅A_ȳ⊗_ΛB_ȳ. For complexes K,L, using the usual total complex with direct sums, S_ȳ(K⊗_ΛL)≅S_ȳ(K)⊗_ΛS_ȳ(L) termwise.

2. K-flatness over a field. Let C be an acyclic complex of Λ-modules. Each short exact sequence 0→B^n(C)→C^n→B^{n+1}(C)→0 splits because Λ is a field, so C is contractible. If C is contractible and K is any complex of Λ-modules, then K⊗_ΛC is contractible (the contracting homotopy is id_K⊗s with the usual sign). Hence tensoring with any complex preserves acyclicity of complexes of Λ-modules. Now let A be an acyclic complex of sheaves of Λ-modules on Y and let K be any complex of sheaves. By the stalk formula above, (K⊗_ΛA)_ȳ≅K_ȳ⊗_ΛA_ȳ is acyclic for every geometric point ȳ, so K⊗_ΛA is acyclic. Thus every complex of sheaves of Λ-modules is K-flat. In the standard K-flat construction of the derived tensor product, the identity map on any complex is a K-flat quasi-isomorphism, so F⊗^L_ΛG is canonically represented by the termwise tensor product F⊗_ΛG.

3. The extension-by-zero functor. For H∈Sh(U_et,Λ) and V→X étale, put V_U=V×_XU and define (j_!H)(V) to be the set of sections s∈H(V_U) whose support Supp(s)={v∈|V_U|:s_ṽ≠0}, viewed as a subset of |V|, is closed in |V|. If f:W→V is étale, Supp(f^*s)=f^{-1}Supp(s), so restriction is well defined. The presheaf is a sheaf: uniqueness follows from H being a sheaf; existence follows by gluing on U_et, and closedness of the glued support descends along the surjective étale map ∐V_i→V because surjective étale maps are open and hence quotient maps on underlying topological spaces. For any étale sheaf H on a scheme W and any section t∈H(W), the zero locus of t is open: if t_ṽ=0, some étale neighbourhood of ṽ kills t, its image is open, and separatedness forces t to vanish there. Hence supports of sections are closed in the object itself.

4. Stalks of j_! and adjunction. For a geometric point x̄ of X with image x, (j_!H)_x̄=0 if x∉U: any section has closed support not containing x, so its germ at x̄ is zero. If x∈U, the restriction map (j_!H)_x̄→H_x̄ is an isomorphism: surjectivity uses that a section over an étale neighbourhood in U has closed support in that neighbourhood; injectivity uses that a section with zero germ at x̄ vanishes on the open neighbourhood V minus Supp(s) of x̄. These identifications are functorial. The unit H→j^*j_!H is an isomorphism. The adjunction j_!⊣j^* is obtained by restricting a map j_!H→G to U, and conversely by extending a map H→j^*G by zero outside the closed support of a section. Since j^* and j_! have the above stalk descriptions, both are exact; exactness is checked on geometric stalks. The pullback j^* is strictly monoidal: j^*(A⊗_ΛB)≅j^*A⊗_Λj^*B, because restriction to U_et commutes with sheafification and with the colimits defining tensor products.

5. Definition of θ_{F,G}. Since j_! and j^* are exact, their derived functors are computed degreewise, and the exact adjunction induces a triangulated adjunction (j_!,j^*) between D(U_et,Λ) and D(X_et,Λ). Let η_F:F→j^*j_!F be the unit. Tensoring η_F with j^*G and using strict monoidality gives α_{F,G}:F⊗^L_Λj^*G→j^*j_!F⊗^L_Λj^*G→j^*(j_!F⊗^L_ΛG). Let θ_{F,G}:j_!(F⊗^L_Λj^*G)→j_!F⊗^L_ΛG be the adjoint of α_{F,G}.

6. Stalkwise check. Fix a geometric point x̄ of X. Write S_x for the stalk functor at x̄. Because S_x is exact and monoidal, and because derived tensors are computed termwise, S_x commutes with all derived tensor products used below. If x∉U, then S_x(j_!K)=0 for every K∈D(U_et,Λ) by the stalk formula. Hence S_x(j_!(F⊗^L j^*G))=0, while S_x(j_!F⊗^L G)≅S_x(j_!F)⊗^L S_x(G)=0. Thus θ_{x̄} is the unique map 0→0, an isomorphism.

Assume x∈U. There are canonical identifications S_x^X(j_!K)≅S_x^U(K) for K∈D(U_et,Λ), S_x^X(j^*G)≅S_x^U(G), and S_x^X∘j^*≅S_x^U. Under these identifications the stalk of the unit η_F is the identity on S_x^U(F). Therefore, under the canonical identifications
S_x(j_!(F⊗^L j^*G))≅S_x^U(F)⊗^L_ΛS_x^X(G),
S_x(j_!F⊗^L G)≅S_x^U(F)⊗^L_ΛS_x^X(G),
the stalk S_x(α_{F,G}) is the identity. The adjunction equation for θ_{F,G} is j^*θ_{F,G}∘η_{F⊗^L j^*G}=α_{F,G}. Applying S_x, identifying S_x(j^*θ_{F,G}) with S_x(θ_{F,G}) under the same canonical isomorphisms, and using that the stalk of η_{F⊗^L j^*G} is the identity gives S_x(θ_{F,G})=S_x(α_{F,G})=id. Thus θ_{x̄} is an isomorphism.

7. Conclusion. Every geometric stalk of θ_{F,G} is an isomorphism, and geometric stalks are conservative, so θ_{F,G} is an isomorphism in D(X_et,Λ). If X is empty the statement is vacuous; if U is empty then j_! is the zero functor and both sides are zero; if U=X then j_!=id and θ is the identity. These cases are also contained in the stalk computation."

lemma_393.statement: Let \(S\) be a connected noetherian scheme, let \(\ell\) be a prime invertible on \(S\), and let \(f:\mathcal X\to S\) be a smooth proper morphism whose fibres are geometrically connected. For every integer \(i\ge0\), the function \(s\mapsto \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\mathcal X_{\overline{s}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is constant on \(S\).
lemma_393.proof:
Proof. If S is empty the assertion is vacuous, so assume S is nonempty. Fix an integer i >= 0. For a point s of S, choose an algebraic closure kbar(s) of the residue field k(s), and write d_i(s) = dim_{Q_l} H^i_et(Xcal_{kbar(s)}, Q_l). First, this number does not depend on the chosen algebraic closure: if k1 and k2 are two algebraic closures of k(s), choose a k(s)-isomorphism phi:k1->k2. It induces an equivalence of the etale sites of Xcal_{k1} and Xcal_{k2}, hence an isomorphism of their etale cohomology groups with Q_l coefficients; in particular the dimensions are equal.

We use the declared standard smooth proper base change theorem. It says that, since f:Xcal->S is smooth and proper and l is invertible on S, the etale sheaf F_i := R^i f_* Q_l on S_et is a lisse Q_l-sheaf of finite rank, and for every geometric point sbar:Spec Omega -> S the natural base-change map (F_i)_sbar -> H^i_et(Xcal_sbar, Q_l) is an isomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces. Here lisse is used in the following etale-local form: for every point s of S there exists an etale morphism u:U->S and a point u0 in U lying over s such that u^*F_i is the constant sheaf V_U attached to a finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space V. The hypothesis that the fibres are geometrically connected is not needed for this constancy argument; it is simply part of the given hypotheses.

We now prove that d_i is locally constant. Fix s in S. Choose u:U->S and V as above with u0 over s. Let W = u(U), regarded with the induced open subscheme structure. Since etale morphisms are open, W is a Zariski open neighbourhood of s. The restriction u_W:U->W is surjective. Let t be any point of W, and choose a geometric point tbar:Spec Omega -> W over t. Base changing the surjective morphism u_W to tbar gives the morphism U_tbar := U x_W Spec Omega -> Spec Omega. This morphism is surjective, hence U_tbar is nonempty. Choose a point v of U_tbar. Let Omega' be an algebraic closure of the residue field kappa(v); the structure map Omega -> kappa(v) followed by the chosen embedding kappa(v) -> Omega' gives a geometric point ubar:Spec Omega' -> U_tbar. Composing with the projection U_tbar -> U gives a geometric point of U whose image in W is tbar. By the stalk formula for the inverse image of a sheaf on the etale site, (F_i)_tbar is canonically isomorphic to (u_W^*F_i)_ubar. This stalk formula is part of the definition of inverse image sheaves; no finiteness, quasi-finiteness, or affineness of the fibre U_tbar is used. Since u_W^*F_i is the constant sheaf V_U, its stalk at ubar is V. Therefore (F_i)_tbar is isomorphic to V. Applying the base-change isomorphism of the standard theorem gives H^i_et(Xcal_tbar, Q_l) isomorphic to V. Thus d_i(t) = dim_{Q_l} V for every t in W. Hence d_i is constant on the Zariski open neighbourhood W of s. Since s was arbitrary, d_i is locally constant on S.

Finally, for each integer m >= 0 let A_m = {s in S : d_i(s) = m}. The local constancy just proved shows that each A_m is open. The sets A_m are pairwise disjoint and cover S. For fixed m, the complement of A_m in S is the union of the open sets A_n with n != m, hence is open; therefore each A_m is also closed. Since S is connected, at most one A_m can be nonempty. Because S is nonempty, exactly one A_m is nonempty, so d_i is constant on S. This proves the lemma for the fixed i, and since i was arbitrary, the lemma follows. QED.

lemma_396.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(Y\) be a proper variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(F_Y:Y_k\to Y_k\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism. Let \(K\) be a semisimple perverse \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaf on \(Y_k\) for the middle perversity and let \(\varphi:F_Y^*K\xrightarrow{\sim}K\) be an isomorphism. Then the set of isomorphism classes of simple perverse \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subsheaves of \(K\) is finite and stable under \(P\mapsto F_Y^*P\), and there is a decomposition \(K\cong\bigoplus_{O}K_O\), indexed by the orbits \(O\) of this action, such that each \(K_O\) is a perverse subsheaf of \(K\) equal to the sum of the simple subsheaves of \(K\) whose isomorphism class lies in \(O\), and \(\varphi\) induces an isomorphism \(F_Y^*K_O\xrightarrow{\sim}K_O\) for every \(O\).
lemma_396.proof:
Let A = Perv(Y_k, Q_l) be the abelian category of middle-perversity perverse Q_l-sheaves on Y_k. If K = 0, then there are no simple subobjects, the set of isomorphism classes is empty, and the decomposition is the empty direct sum; hence assume K ≠ 0.

Step 1. Frobenius pullback is an autoequivalence of the perverse category. The q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism F_Y = id_Y × Spec σ is an automorphism of the scheme Y_k, because σ is an automorphism of k and the inverse is id_Y × Spec σ^{-1}. Pullback by a scheme automorphism is an exact equivalence of étale sheaves and preserves constructibility. The middle-perversity perverse t-structure on D^b_c(Y_k, Q_l) is characterized by the usual support and cosupport dimension conditions. Since F_Y is a homeomorphism preserving dimensions of irreducible closed subsets and preserving stalks up to isomorphism, it preserves these conditions. Therefore F_Y^* is an exact autoequivalence of A. In particular it sends simple objects to simple objects, preserves monomorphisms, and preserves finite length.

Step 2. K is a finite direct sum of simple perverse sheaves. A perverse sheaf is by definition an object of D^b_c(Y_k, Q_l). Since K is equipped with the arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism φ:F_Y^*K → K, the proved lemma eoinm lemma_7 gives that Ext^n_{D^b_c(Y_k,Q_l)}(K,K) is finite-dimensional over Q_l for every n. In particular End_A(K) = Ext^0_{D^b_c(Y_k,Q_l)}(K,K) is finite-dimensional over Q_l.

We use the following elementary fact. If M is a semisimple object of an abelian category and End(M) is finite-dimensional over Q_l, then M is a finite direct sum of simple objects. First note that a subobject of a semisimple object is semisimple: if M ⊂ K and N ⊂ M, then N ⊂ K, so K = N ⊕ C for some subobject C. If p:K → N is the projection, then M = N ⊕ (M ∩ ker p), because m = p(m) + (m - p(m)) with p(m) ∈ N ⊂ M.

Now construct a sequence of semisimple subobjects K_0 ⊃ K_1 ⊃ ... of K. Put K_0 = K. Given K_n, if K_n = 0 or K_n is simple, stop. If K_n is not simple and has a simple subobject, choose a simple subobject A_n ⊂ K_n. Since K_n is semisimple, A_n is a direct summand, so K_n = A_n ⊕ B_n with B_n ≠ 0. If K_n is not simple and has no simple subobject, choose any nonzero proper subobject A_n ⊂ K_n; semisimplicity gives K_n = A_n ⊕ B_n, and B_n is nonzero and has no simple subobject, since a simple subobject of B_n would also be a simple subobject of K_n. In both cases set K_{n+1} = B_n.

If this construction were infinite, then for every n we would have K ≅ A_0 ⊕ ... ⊕ A_{n-1} ⊕ K_n, with the A_i nonzero and pairwise intersecting trivially. For each i define e_i:K → K to be the projection onto A_i along the complementary direct sum. These are mutually orthogonal idempotents. They are linearly independent over Q_l: if Σ_{i∈F} c_i e_i = 0, choose n larger than all indices in F and let u_j:A_j → K be the inclusion. Then e_i u_j = 0 for i ≠ j and e_j u_j = u_j; applying the relation to u_j gives c_j u_j = 0, hence c_j = 0. This contradicts finite-dimensionality of End(K). Therefore the construction stops.

It cannot stop after a step in which K_n had no simple subobject, because then all subsequent K_m would have no simple subobject and could never be simple or zero. Hence the stop occurs with K_N simple and with every chosen A_i simple. Consequently K is a finite direct sum of simple objects. Applying this to K, choose simple perverse sheaves S_1, ..., S_N such that K ≅ S_1 ⊕ ... ⊕ S_N.

Step 3. Finiteness and Frobenius stability of the set of simple subobjects. Let Σ be the set of isomorphism classes of simple subobjects of K. If P ⊂ K is simple, consider the projections p_j:K → S_j. If all p_j ∘ i_P were zero, then i_P = 0, impossible. Thus some p_j ∘ i_P:P → S_j is nonzero. Since P and S_j are simple, this morphism is an isomorphism, so [P] = [S_j]. Hence Σ ⊂ {[S_1], ..., [S_N]}, so Σ is finite.

For stability, let P ⊂ K be simple. Since F_Y^* is exact, it sends the monomorphism P ↪ K to a monomorphism F_Y^*P ↪ F_Y^*K. Composing with φ:F_Y^*K ≅ K gives a monomorphism F_Y^*P ↪ K whose image is isomorphic to F_Y^*P and hence is a simple subobject of K. This defines an action [P] ↦ [F_Y^*P] on Σ. The action is bijective because F_Y^* is an autoequivalence and φ is an isomorphism; the inverse is obtained by applying (F_Y^*)^{-1} to subobjects transported by φ^{-1}. Thus Σ is stable under P ↦ F_Y^*P.

Step 4. Orbit decomposition. For an orbit O ⊂ Σ, let K_O be the sum in A of all simple subobjects P ⊂ K with [P] ∈ O. We identify this sum with a direct sum of the chosen summands. Put L_O = ⊕_{j:[S_j] ∈ O} S_j ⊂ K. If P ⊂ K is simple with [P] ∈ O, then P ≅ S_i for some i with [S_i] ∈ O. For every j with [S_j] ∉ O, Hom(P,S_j) = 0, because a nonzero morphism between simple objects is an isomorphism. Hence the projection of P to the direct sum of the S_j with [S_j] ∉ O is zero, so P factors through L_O and P ⊂ L_O. Therefore the sum of all simple subobjects whose class lies in O is contained in L_O. Conversely each S_j with [S_j] ∈ O is itself a simple subobject of K in O, so S_j ⊂ K_O. Thus K_O = L_O. Since the orbits partition the finite set of classes [S_j], we obtain K ≅ ⊕_O K_O, and K_O is precisely the sum of the simple subsheaves whose isomorphism class lies in O.

Step 5. Frobenius stability of each K_O. Let i_O:K_O → K be the inclusion and define α_O:F_Y^*K_O → K by α_O = φ ∘ F_Y^*(i_O). Exactness of F_Y^* makes α_O a monomorphism. If P ⊂ K_O is simple, then [P] ∈ O. The image of φ ∘ F_Y^*(P ↪ K) is a simple subobject of K whose class is F_Y^*([P]), which lies in O; hence it is contained in K_O. Therefore im(α_O) ⊂ K_O. The object K_O has finite length, and F_Y^* preserves length because it is an exact autoequivalence sending simple objects to simple objects. Hence length(F_Y^*K_O) = length(K_O). Since α_O identifies F_Y^*K_O with im(α_O), the subobject im(α_O) of K_O has the same length as K_O. A subobject of a finite-length object with the same length is the whole object. Thus im(α_O) = K_O, and α_O is an isomorphism F_Y^*K_O ≅ K_O.

This proves all the required assertions.

lemma_399.statement: Let ℓ be a prime, let V be a finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector space, let T∈GL(V), and let m≥1 be an integer. Then T is semisimple on V, equivalently diagonalizable over overline(Q_ℓ), if and only if T^m is semisimple on V.
lemma_399.proof:
Let $K:=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, let $\overline V:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$, and write $\overline T:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}_K\in\mathrm{GL}(\overline V)$. Note $\overline{\mathcal V}$ is a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space and $(\overline T)^m=\overline{T^m}$, since tensoring the identity $T\circ\cdots\circ T=T^m$ with $\mathrm{id}_K$ gives $(T\otimes\mathrm{id})^m=T^m\otimes\mathrm{id}$.

**Step 0 (reduction to the algebraically closed field $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$).** By eoinm's lemma_5 applied to the pair $(V,T)$, $T$ is semisimple on $V$ if and only if $\overline T$ is diagonalizable over $K$; applying the same lemma to the pair $(V,T^m)$ (note $T^m\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ because $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$), $T^m$ is semisimple on $V$ if and only if $\overline{T^m}=(\overline T)^m$ is diagonalizable over $K$. Hence the desired equivalence for $V$ over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ follows from the same statement for the single finite-dimensional vector space $\overline V$ over the algebraically closed field $K$. In the rest of the proof we therefore work over $K$ and write $T$ for $\overline T$; $K$ has characteristic $0$.

We shall use the following standard criterion, which we prove in full.

**Criterion.** Let $F$ be any field, $W$ a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space, $S\in\mathrm{End}_F(W)$, and $\mu_S\in F[X]$ the minimal polynomial of $S$. Then $S$ is diagonalizable over $F$ if and only if $\mu_S$ is a product of pairwise distinct monic linear factors in $F[X]$.

*Proof of the criterion.* ($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\mu_S=\prod_{i=1}^{s}(X-a_i)$ with the $a_i\in F$ pairwise distinct. For each $i$ put $Q_i:=\mu_S/(X-a_i)\in F[X]$. The polynomials $Q_1,\dots,Q_s$ have no common irreducible factor (the $X-a_i$ are distinct primes and $Q_i$ is divisible by $X-a_j$ for every $j\neq i$ but not by $X-a_i$), so their gcd is $1$; by B\'ezout there exist $c_1,\dots,c_s\in F[X]$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{s}c_iQ_i=1$. Define $\pi_i:=c_i(S)Q_i(S)\in\mathrm{End}_F(W)$. Then:
(i) $\sum_i\pi_i=\mathrm{id}_W$, by applying $\sum c_iQ_i=1$ to $S$;
(ii) for $i\neq j$, $Q_iQ_j$ is divisible by $\mu_S$ (it contains the factor $X-a_i$ from $Q_j$ and $X-a_j$ from $Q_i$, and all remaining factors), so $\pi_i\pi_j=c_i(S)c_j(S)(Q_iQ_j)(S)=0$;
(iii) $(S-a_i\,\mathrm{id})\pi_i=c_i(S)\,(X-a_i)Q_i(S)=c_i(S)\mu_S(S)=0$, so $\pi_i(W)\subseteq\ker(S-a_i\,\mathrm{id})$.
Given $w\in W$, (i) gives $w=\sum_i\pi_iw$ with each $\pi_iw\in\ker(S-a_i\,\mathrm{id})$ by (iii); hence $W=\sum_{i=1}^s\ker(S-a_i\,\mathrm{id})$. The sum of eigenspaces belonging to pairwise distinct eigenvalues is direct (a standard induction: if $v_1+\cdots+v_r=0$ with $v_j$ an eigenvector of eigenvalue $a_j$, applying $\prod_{j\ge2}(S-a_j\,\mathrm{id})$ kills $v_2,\dots,v_r$ and leaves $\big(\prod_{j\ge2}(a_1-a_j)\big)v_1=0$, forcing $v_1=0$, using that the $a_j$ are distinct and $F$ is a field). Thus $W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^s\ker(S-a_i\,\mathrm{id})$, and choosing a basis of each summand yields a basis of $W$ consisting of eigenvectors of $S$, i.e. $S$ is diagonalizable over $F$.
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $S$ is diagonalizable and let $a_1,\dots,a_s$ be its pairwise distinct eigenvalues, each occurring. Put $P:=\prod_{i=1}^s(X-a_i)$. For $w\in W$ write $w=\sum_i w_i$ with $Sw_i=a_iw_i$; then $P(S)w=\sum_iP(a_i)w_i=0$, so $P(S)=0$. Conversely, if $Q\in F[X]$ satisfies $Q(S)=0$, then for each $i$ choose $0\neq v_i\in\ker(S-a_i\,\mathrm{id})$; $0=Q(S)v_i=Q(a_i)v_i$ gives $Q(a_i)=0$, so $X-a_i$ divides $Q$. Hence every annihilating polynomial is divisible by $P$, and since $P$ itself annihilates $S$, the minimal polynomial is $\mu_S=P$, a product of distinct linear factors. This proves the criterion. $\square$

We now prove the two implications over $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

**Step 1 ($T$ semisimple $\Rightarrow$ $T^m$ semisimple).** Assume $T$ is diagonalizable over $K$. Choose a basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $V$ with $Te_i=\lambda_ie_i$ for some $\lambda_i\in K$. Then, by induction on $j$, $T^je_i=\lambda_i^je_i$: the case $j=1$ is the definition, and $T^{j+1}e_i=T^j(\lambda_ie_i)=\lambda_iT^je_i=\lambda_i^{j+1}e_i$ since $T^j$ is $K$-linear. Taking $j=m$ gives $T^me_i=\lambda_i^me_i$, so the same basis diagonalises $T^m$. Thus $T^m$ is diagonalizable over $K$, hence semisimple on $V$ by lemma_5.

**Step 2 ($T^m$ semisimple $\Rightarrow$ $T$ semisimple).** Assume $T^m$ is diagonalizable over $K$, and let $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r\in K$ be its pairwise distinct eigenvalues. By the criterion applied to $S=T^m$ (direction $\Rightarrow$), the minimal polynomial of $T^m$ is
$$\mu_{T^m}(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(X-\mu_i),$$
a product of distinct linear factors.

*The $\mu_i$ are nonzero.* If some $\mu_i=0$, then $0$ is an eigenvalue of $T^m$, so $T^m$ has a nonzero kernel and is not invertible, contradicting $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ (whence $T^m\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ with inverse $(T^{-1})^m$). Thus $\mu_i\neq0$ for all $i$.

*An annihilating polynomial for $T$ with distinct roots.* Consider
$$M(X):=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\bigl(X^m-\mu_i\bigr)\in K[X].$$
Evaluating at $T$ and using that each factor $T^m-\mu_i\,\mathrm{id}$ is a polynomial in $T$ (hence they commute),
$$M(T)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\bigl(T^m-\mu_i\,\mathrm{id}\bigr)=\mu_{T^m}(T^m)=0,$$
the last equality being the defining property of the minimal polynomial of $T^m$. So $M$ annihilates $T$, and consequently the minimal polynomial $\mu_T$ divides $M$ in $K[X]$ (indeed $\mu_T$ generates the ideal of polynomials annihilating $T$: dividing $M$ by $\mu_T$ gives $M=A\mu_T+B$ with $\deg B<\deg\mu_T$, and $0=M(T)=B(T)$ forces $B=0$).

We check that $M$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors over $K$. Fix $i$. Since $K$ is algebraically closed and $\mu_i\neq0$, choose $\alpha_i\in K^\times$ with $\alpha_i^m=\mu_i$, and let $\zeta\in K$ be a primitive $m$-th root of unity (exists: $K^\times$ is divisible, or take a root of $X^m-1$ that is not a root of any $X^d-1$ with $d\mid m$, $d<m$; such exists because $X^m-1$ has $m$ distinct roots in $K$ as $\gcd(m,\,mX^{m-1})=1$ in characteristic $0$). Then
$$X^m-\mu_i=X^m-\alpha_i^m=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\bigl(X-\zeta^{j}\alpha_i\bigr).$$
The $m$ roots $\zeta^0\alpha_i,\dots,\zeta^{m-1}\alpha_i$ are pairwise distinct: $\zeta^j\alpha_i=\zeta^k\alpha_i$ with $0\le j<k\le m-1$ implies $\zeta^{k-j}=1$ (as $\alpha_i\ne0$ and $K$ is a field), contradicting that $\zeta$ has order $m$ and $0<k-j<m$. Finally, if $i\neq i'$, no root of $X^m-\mu_i$ is a root of $X^m-\mu_{i'}$, since $\beta^m=\mu_i$ and $\beta^m=\mu_{i'}$ would give $\mu_i=\mu_{i'}$, contradicting the choice of distinct eigenvalues. Hence all $rm$ roots of $M$ are pairwise distinct, i.e.
$$M(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\bigl(X-\zeta^{j}\alpha_i\bigr)\quad\text{with all } \zeta^j\alpha_i\in K \text{ pairwise distinct.}$$

*Conclusion.* Since $\mu_T\mid M$, the polynomial $\mu_T$ is itself a product of pairwise distinct monic linear factors over $K$. By the criterion (direction $\Leftarrow$) applied to $S=T$, $T$ is diagonalizable over $K$, and by lemma_5 applied to $(V,T)$, $T$ is semisimple on $V$.

**Step 3 (assembling).** Steps 1 and 2 show, over $K=\overline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, that $\overline T$ is diagonalizable if and only if $(\overline T)^m$ is diagonalizable. Transporting this back through the two applications of lemma_5 in Step 0 gives: $T$ is semisimple on $V$ $\iff$ $\overline T$ diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ $\iff$ $(\overline T)^m=\overline{T^m}$ diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ $\iff$ $T^m$ is semisimple on $V$. This is exactly the required equivalence, and it also exhibits the announced "equivalently, diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$" reformulation for both $T$ and $T^m$.

(The case $m=1$ is covered by the same argument: then $M(X)=\prod_i(X-\mu_i)=\mu_{T^m}(X)$ and the two sides of the equivalence coincide.) $\blacksquare$

lemma_397.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(r\ge1\) be an integer, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space written as a direct sum \(V=V_0\oplus V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{r-1}\), and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) be a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism with \(T(V_i)=V_{i+1}\) for \(0\le i\le r-2\) and \(T(V_{r-1})=V_0\). Then \(T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) if and only if the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism \(T^r\) of \(V_0\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_397.proof:
We write $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ for a fixed algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and for a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $E$ we write $\overline E:=E\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and $\overline S:=S\otimes\mathrm{id}$ for the scalar extension of a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism $S$ of $E$. By definition, "$S$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$" means that $\overline S$ is diagonalizable as an $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linear automorphism of $\overline E$.

=====================================================================
PART I. THREE LINEAR-ALGEBRA FACTS.

Fact A (spectral decomposition criterion). Let $K$ be a field, let $W$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, and let $N\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)$.
(a) If $N$ is diagonalizable, then its minimal polynomial $\nu_N\in K[X]$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors of $K[X]$.
(b) Conversely, if $\nu_N=\prod_{t=1}^{u}(X-\beta_t)$ with the $\beta_t\in K$ pairwise distinct, then $W=\bigoplus_{t=1}^{u}\ker(N-\beta_t\,\mathrm{id})$; in particular $N$ is diagonalizable.

Proof of (a). If $N$ is diagonalizable, $W$ has a basis of eigenvectors of $N$. Let $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_u$ be the distinct eigenvalues of $N$ occurring, and put $g(X):=\prod_{t=1}^{u}(X-\beta_t)$. For $w$ an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\beta_{t_0}$, one of the factors $N-\beta_{t_0}\,\mathrm{id}$ occurring in $g(N)$ annihilates $w$; since the factors commute, $g(N)w=0$. As the eigenvectors span $W$, $g(N)=0$. Hence $\nu_N\mid g$ in $K[X]$, so $\nu_N$ is a product of distinct linear factors. $\square$

Proof of (b). For each $t$ put $q_t(X):=\prod_{v\ne t}(X-\beta_v)$ and $f_t(X):=q_t(X)/q_t(\beta_t)$. This is legitimate: the $\beta_v$ are pairwise distinct, so $q_t(\beta_t)=\prod_{v\ne t}(\beta_t-\beta_v)$ is a product of nonzero elements of the field $K$, hence is nonzero and invertible in $K$. By construction $f_t(\beta_t)=1$ and $f_t(\beta_v)=0$ for $v\ne t$.
Consider $h(X):=1-\sum_{t=1}^{u}f_t(X)\in K[X]$. For each fixed $v$, $h(\beta_v)=1-\sum_t f_t(\beta_v)=1-1=0$, so by the factor theorem $(X-\beta_v)\mid h$ in $K[X]$. The polynomials $X-\beta_1,\dots,X-\beta_u$ are pairwise non-associate irreducibles of the UFD $K[X]$, hence pairwise coprime; since each divides $h$, their product $\nu_N$ divides $h$ (apply Euclid's lemma inductively). Write $h=\nu_N\cdot r$ with $r\in K[X]$. Evaluating at $N$ and using $\nu_N(N)=0$ gives $\mathrm{id}_W-\sum_t f_t(N)=0$, i.e.
$$\sum_{t=1}^{u} f_t(N)=\mathrm{id}_W. \tag{A1}$$
Next, $(N-\beta_t\,\mathrm{id})\,q_t(N)=\nu_N(N)=0$, so $\mathrm{Im}\,f_t(N)\subseteq \ker(N-\beta_t\,\mathrm{id})=:E_t$. Also, on $E_t$ the operator $N$ acts as $\beta_t\,\mathrm{id}$, hence $q_t(N)|_{E_t}=q_t(\beta_t)\,\mathrm{id}$ and $f_t(N)|_{E_t}=\mathrm{id}_{E_t}$; and for $v\ne t$, $f_t(N)|_{E_v}=f_t(\beta_v)\,\mathrm{id}_{E_v}=0$.
Now every $w\in W$ equals $\sum_t f_t(N)w$ by (A1), with $f_t(N)w\in E_t$; thus $W=\sum_t E_t$. The sum is direct: if $w\in E_{t_0}\cap\sum_{v\ne t_0}E_v$, then $f_{t_0}(N)w=w$ because $w\in E_{t_0}$, while $f_{t_0}(N)w=0$ because $w$ is a sum of elements of the $E_v$ with $v\ne t_0$; hence $w=0$. So $W=\bigoplus_t E_t$ and $N$ is diagonalizable. $\square$

Fact B (powers). Let $K$ be a field, $W$ a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, $N\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)$ and $m\ge1$. If $N$ is diagonalizable, then $N^{m}$ is diagonalizable.
Proof. If $W=0$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise choose a basis of $W$ consisting of eigenvectors of $N$, say $Nw_i=\alpha_i w_i$. Then $N^{m}w_i=\alpha_i^{m}w_i$, so the same basis diagonalises $N^{m}$. $\square$

Fact C (root extraction for invertible operators). Let $K$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, let $W$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, let $M\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ and let $m\ge1$. If $M^{m}$ is diagonalizable over $K$, then $M$ is diagonalizable over $K$.
Proof. If $W=0$, then $M$ is the identity of the zero space and the empty family is a basis of eigenvectors, so $M$ is diagonalizable; assume henceforth $W\ne0$, so that the set of eigenvalues of $M^{m}$ is nonempty (the characteristic polynomial of $M^{m}$ has a root in the algebraically closed field $K$).

Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s\in K^{\times}$ be the pairwise distinct eigenvalues of $M^{m}$; they are nonzero because $M^{m}\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$, so $0$ is not an eigenvalue. By Fact A(a) applied to $N=M^{m}$, the minimal polynomial $\nu$ of $M^{m}$ is a product of distinct linear factors; its roots are exactly the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s$ (a linear factor $X-\beta$ divides $\nu$ iff $\beta$ is an eigenvalue), hence
$$\nu(X)=\prod_{j=1}^{s}(X-\lambda_j). \tag{C1}$$
For each $j$ set $p_j(X):=\prod_{k\ne j}(X-\lambda_k)$ and, following Lagrange interpolation,
$$e_j(X):=\frac{p_j(X)}{p_j(\lambda_j)},\qquad p_j(\lambda_j)=\prod_{k\ne j}(\lambda_j-\lambda_k).$$
The denominator is a product of nonzero elements of the field $K$ (the $\lambda_k$ are pairwise distinct), hence nonzero and invertible, so $e_j\in K[X]$ is well defined, with $e_j(\lambda_j)=1$ and $e_j(\lambda_k)=0$ for $k\ne j$. Put $E_j:=\ker(M^{m}-\lambda_j\,\mathrm{id})$.

Step C1: $\sum_{j=1}^{s}e_j(M^{m})=\mathrm{id}_W$. Indeed $1-\sum_j e_j(X)$ vanishes at each $\lambda_j$, so each $X-\lambda_j$ divides it (factor theorem); the $X-\lambda_j$ are pairwise coprime irreducibles in the UFD $K[X]$, so their product $\nu$ divides $1-\sum_j e_j$. Evaluating at $M^{m}$ and using $\nu(M^{m})=0$ gives the claim.

Step C2: $\mathrm{Im}\,e_j(M^{m})\subseteq E_j$ and $e_j(M^{m})|_{E_j}=\mathrm{id}_{E_j}$. For the first, $(M^{m}-\lambda_j\,\mathrm{id})p_j(M^{m})=\nu(M^{m})=0$, so $(M^{m}-\lambda_j\,\mathrm{id})e_j(M^{m})=0$. For the second, $p_j$ is a product of factors $X-\lambda_k$ with $k\ne j$ only, and $M^{m}$ acts on $E_j$ as $\lambda_j\,\mathrm{id}$, so $p_j(M^{m})|_{E_j}=p_j(\lambda_j)\,\mathrm{id}$ and therefore $e_j(M^{m})|_{E_j}=\mathrm{id}_{E_j}$.

Step C3: $W=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{s}E_j$, and each $E_j$ is $M$-stable. That $W=\sum_j E_j$ follows from Step C1 and Step C2 (write $w=\sum_j e_j(M^{m})w$). The sum is direct: if $w\in E_{j_0}\cap\sum_{j\ne j_0}E_j$, then $e_{j_0}(M^{m})w=w$ by Step C2, while $e_{j_0}(M^{m})|_{E_j}=e_{j_0}(\lambda_j)\mathrm{id}=0$ for $j\ne j_0$, so $w=0$. For stability, if $w\in E_j$ then $M^{m}(Mw)=M(M^{m}w)=M(\lambda_j w)=\lambda_j (Mw)$, so $Mw\in E_j$.

Step C4: $M|_{E_j}$ is diagonalizable for each $j$. On $E_j$ we have $M^{m}=\lambda_j\,\mathrm{id}$, so the minimal polynomial $\mu_j$ of $M|_{E_j}$ divides $X^{m}-\lambda_j$. Since $K$ is algebraically closed and $\lambda_j\ne0$, choose $\alpha\in K$ with $\alpha^{m}=\lambda_j$; then $X^{m}-\lambda_j=\prod_{\zeta}(X-\alpha\zeta)$, where $\zeta$ runs over the $m$-th roots of unity in $K$. There are exactly $m$ of them and they are distinct: $X^{m}-1$ has derivative $mX^{m-1}$, whose only root is $0$, which is not a root of $X^{m}-1$; hence $\gcd(X^{m}-1,\,mX^{m-1})=1$ and $X^{m}-1$ has $m$ distinct roots (this is where characteristic $0$ is used). Consequently $X^{m}-\lambda_j$ is a product of $m$ pairwise distinct linear factors of $K[X]$, so its divisor $\mu_j$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors. If $E_j=0$ there is nothing to prove; otherwise Fact A(b) applied to $M|_{E_j}$ shows $M|_{E_j}$ is diagonalizable.
(We remark explicitly that the invertibility of $M$ is essential here: it is exactly what forces $\lambda_j\ne0$ and hence the separability of $X^{m}-\lambda_j$. Without it the statement is false: a nonzero nilpotent $J$ with $J^{2}=0$ has $J^{2}=0$ diagonalizable while $J$ is not.)

Step C5: conclusion. By Step C3, $W=\bigoplus_j E_j$ with each $E_j$ $M$-stable and $M|_{E_j}$ diagonalizable; concatenating eigenbases of the $M|_{E_j}$ gives a basis of $W$ of eigenvectors of $M$. Hence $M$ is diagonalizable. $\square$

=====================================================================
PART II. STRUCTURAL CONSEQUENCES OF THE CYCLIC GRADING.

Let $V=V_0\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{r-1}$ and $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ with $T(V_i)=V_{i+1}$ for $0\le i\le r-2$ and $T(V_{r-1})=V_0$.

(a) If $V=0$ then every $V_i=0$, $T$ is the identity of the zero space (diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$) and $T^{r}|_{V_0}$ is the identity of the zero space (also diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$); both sides of the claimed equivalence are then true. In what follows we argue in a way that also covers this case, but we note it for the invocation of Fact C.

(b) For $0\le i\le r-1$ we have $T^{i}(V_0)=V_i$, by induction on $i$: for $i=0$ it is clear, and if $T^{i}(V_0)=V_i$ with $i\le r-2$, then $T^{i+1}(V_0)=T(T^{i}(V_0))=T(V_i)=V_{i+1}$.

(c) For each $i$, the map $\varphi_i:V_0\xrightarrow{\sim}V_i$, $w\mapsto T^{i}w$, is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism: it is surjective onto $V_i$ by (b) and injective because $T$ (hence $T^{i}$) is injective.

(d) $T^{r}(V_i)=V_i$ for every $i$. Indeed, for $0\le i\le r-1$, iterating as in (b) gives $T^{r-1-i}(V_i)=V_{r-1}$, then $T(V_{r-1})=V_0$, so $T^{r-i}(V_i)=V_0=T^{i}(V_0)$; applying $T^{i}$ (which is injective, and $T^{i}(V_0)=V_i$) yields $T^{r}(V_i)=T^{i}\bigl(T^{r-i}(V_i)\bigr)=T^{i}(V_0)=V_i$. In particular each $V_i$ is $T^{r}$-stable and $A_i:=T^{r}|_{V_i}\in\mathrm{GL}(V_i)$; write $A:=A_0=T^{r}|_{V_0}\in\mathrm{GL}(V_0)$.

(e) The isomorphisms $\varphi_i$ intertwine $A$ with $A_i$: for $w\in V_0$,
$$\varphi_i(Aw)=T^{i}T^{r}w=T^{r}T^{i}w=A_i(\varphi_i(w)),$$
since powers of $T$ commute. Thus $\varphi_i\circ A=A_i\circ\varphi_i$.

(f) As an operator on $V$, $T^{r}=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-1}A_i$, because $V$ is the direct sum of the $T^{r}$-stable subspaces $V_i$.

=====================================================================
PART III. PROOF OF THE "$\Rightarrow$" DIRECTION.

Assume $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, i.e. $\overline T\in\mathrm{GL}(\overline V)$ is diagonalizable.

1. By eoinm/lemma_5 (applied to $V$ and $T$), $T$ is semisimple on $V$; equivalently, by the same lemma, $\overline T$ is diagonalizable, which is our hypothesis. Applying Fact B over the field $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ to $N=\overline T$ and $m=r$, the operator $\overline T^{\,r}=\overline{T^{r}}$ is diagonalizable on $\overline V$. Using eoinm/lemma_5 again (in the reverse direction), $T^{r}$ is semisimple on $V$.

2. $V_0$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear subspace of $V$ with $T^{r}(V_0)\subseteq V_0$ (by (d), with equality), and $T^{r}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is invertible and semisimple on $V$. By eoinm/lemma_358 applied to $V$, $T:=T^{r}$ and $W:=V_0$, the restriction $T^{r}|_{V_0}=A$ is semisimple on $V_0$.

3. By eoinm/lemma_5 (applied to $V_0$ and $A$), $A$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. This is exactly the desired conclusion.

=====================================================================
PART IV. PROOF OF THE "$\Leftarrow$" DIRECTION.

Assume $A=T^{r}|_{V_0}\in\mathrm{GL}(V_0)$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

1. First, $A$ is semisimple on $V_0$: this is eoinm/lemma_5 applied to $V_0$ and $A$ (the diagonalizability over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ being the hypothesis).

2. Fix $i\in\{0,\dots,r-1\}$. The $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\varphi_i:V_0\xrightarrow{\sim}V_i$ satisfies $\varphi_i\circ A=A_i\circ\varphi_i$ by (e), and both $A\in\mathrm{GL}(V_0)$ and $A_i\in\mathrm{GL}(V_i)$ are invertible. By eoinm/lemma_8 applied to $V=V_0$, $W=V_i$, $T_V=A$, $T_W=A_i$, $\alpha=\varphi_i$, the operator $A_i$ is semisimple on $V_i$.

3. By eoinm/lemma_9 applied to the spaces $V_0,\dots,V_{r-1}$ and the invertible operators $A_0,\dots,A_{r-1}$, the direct-sum operator $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-1}A_i$ on $V=\bigoplus_i V_i$ is semisimple. By (f) this operator is $T^{r}$; hence $T^{r}$ is semisimple on $V$.

4. By eoinm/lemma_5 applied to $V$ and $T^{r}$, the scalar extension $\overline{T^{r}}=\overline T^{\,r}$ is diagonalizable on $\overline V$ (a finite-dimensional $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-vector space).

5. We now apply Fact C with $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (which is algebraically closed of characteristic $0$), $W=\overline V$, $M=\overline T$ and $m=r$. The operator $M=\overline T$ lies in $\mathrm{GL}(\overline V)$ because $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, so $\overline T\,\overline{T^{-1}}=\overline{T\,T^{-1}}=\mathrm{id}$; this invertibility is precisely the hypothesis of Fact C that rules out nilpotent counterexamples (e.g. a nonzero $J$ with $J^{2}=0$, for which $J^{2}$ is diagonalizable but $J$ is not). The hypothesis of Fact C, that $M^{m}=\overline T^{\,r}$ be diagonalizable, is Step 4. Fact C yields that $\overline T$ is diagonalizable on $\overline V$, i.e. that $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

(If $V=0$ this step is vacuous and the conclusion was already noted in (a).)

=====================================================================
PART V. CONCLUSION.

Part III proves that diagonalizability of $T$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ implies diagonalizability of $T^{r}|_{V_0}$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and Part IV proves the converse. Together they establish the claimed equivalence, completing the proof of the lemma.

Dependencies used: eoinm/lemma_5 (translation between semisimplicity over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and diagonalizability over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$), eoinm/lemma_358 (restriction of a semisimple operator to a stable subspace), eoinm/lemma_8 (conjugate operators are simultaneously semisimple), eoinm/lemma_9 (semisimplicity of a direct sum). The auxiliary Facts A, B, C were proved in full above.

lemma_402.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(w\) and \(k\) be integers with \(k\neq 0\), let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) be diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) with every eigenvalue \(\alpha\) satisfying \(|\sigma(\alpha)|=q^{w/2}\) for every field embedding \(\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\), and let \(N\) be a nilpotent \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear endomorphism of \(V\) with \(T\,N\,T^{-1}=q^{k}N\). Then \(N=0\).
lemma_402.proof:
We prove the statement by a weight/eigenvalue argument; note in passing that the nilpotence of $N$ will not even be needed — diagonalisability of $T$ together with the equimodulus condition on its eigenvalues already forces $N=0$ when $k\neq 0$.

**Step 0 (trivial case).** If $V=0$ then $N=0$ holds trivially. Assume henceforth $V\neq 0$.

**Step 1 (choice of an archimedean absolute value).** Since $q=p^a$ is a prime power, $p$ is a prime and $a\ge 1$, so $q\ge 2$; in particular the map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R_{>0}$, $k\mapsto q^k$, is injective, and $q^{w/2}$ denotes the positive real square root of $q^w$, which is $>0$.

We need one field embedding $\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$. Such embeddings exist: the elements of $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ form an algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb Q}\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ embeds in $\mathbb C$, $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ has transcendence degree $\le 2^{\aleph_0}$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ (because $|\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell|=2^{\aleph_0}$), $\mathbb C$ has transcendence degree $2^{\aleph_0}$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$, so a transcendence basis of $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell/\overline{\mathbb Q}$ can be sent to algebraically independent elements of $\mathbb C$, and the resulting embedding $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ extends to the algebraic extension $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell/\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$ because $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed. Fix such a $\sigma$. Being a field embedding of a characteristic-$0$ field, $\sigma$ fixes the prime field $\mathbb Q$ elementwise; in particular $\sigma(q^k)=q^k$ (viewed as the positive real number $q^k$, also when $k<0$, where $q^k=1/q^{|k|}$), and $\sigma$ is multiplicative.

**Step 2 (extension of scalars).** Put $W:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, $T_W:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ and $N_W:=N\otimes\mathrm{id}$; these are $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-vector space $W$. The assignment $M\mapsto M\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is an injective $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebra homomorphism $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}(W)$ (check on a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis of $V$, which remains a basis of $W$); consequently $N_W=0\Rightarrow N=0$, so it suffices to prove $N_W=0$.

Since $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $T_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$. From the hypothesis $T\,N\,T^{-1}=q^kN$ we obtain, after right multiplication by $T$, the identity $T\,N=q^k\,N\,T$ in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$; applying the above homomorphism gives
\[
T_W\,N_W=q^k\,N_W\,T_W .
\tag{1}
\]

**Step 3 (eigenspace decomposition).** By hypothesis $T$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, i.e. $T_W$ is diagonalisable: $W$ admits a basis of eigenvectors of $T_W$. Let $S\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ be the finite set of eigenvalues of $T_W$ (the roots in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ of the characteristic polynomial of $T$, which lies in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$); $S$ does not contain $0$ because $T_W$ is invertible. Grouping the basis eigenvectors by eigenvalue, $W$ is spanned by the subspaces $W_\alpha:=\ker(T_W-\alpha\,\mathrm{id}_W)$, $\alpha\in S$. The sum $\sum_{\alpha\in S}W_\alpha$ is direct: indeed, if $v_1+\cdots+v_m=0$ with $v_i\in W_{\alpha_i}$ for pairwise distinct $\alpha_i$ and $m$ minimal, applying $T_W$ gives $\alpha_1v_1+\cdots+\alpha_mv_m=0$, and subtracting $\alpha_m(v_1+\cdots+v_m)=0$ yields $\sum_{i<m}(\alpha_i-\alpha_m)v_i=0$, a shorter relation, hence all $v_i=0$ by minimality. Thus
\[
W=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in S}W_\alpha ,
\tag{2}
\]
and each nonzero $v\in W_\alpha$ is an eigenvector of $T_W$ with eigenvalue $\alpha\in S$.

**Step 4 ($N_W$ shifts eigenspaces by $q^k$).** Let $\alpha\in S$ and $v\in W_\alpha$. Using (1),
\[
T_W(N_Wv)=q^k\,N_W(T_Wv)=q^k\,N_W(\alpha v)=q^k\alpha\,(N_Wv),
\]
so $N_Wv\in W_{q^k\alpha}$, where $W_{q^k\alpha}:=\ker(T_W-q^k\alpha\,\mathrm{id})$ (this space is $0$ if $q^k\alpha\notin S$). Hence
\[
N_W(W_\alpha)\subseteq W_{q^k\alpha}\qquad\text{for every }\alpha\in S .
\tag{3}
\]

**Step 5 ($N_W$ vanishes on each eigenspace).** Fix $\alpha\in S$ and suppose $N_W|_{W_\alpha}\neq 0$. Choose $v\in W_\alpha$ with $N_Wv\neq 0$. By (3), $N_Wv\in W_{q^k\alpha}$ is a nonzero eigenvector of $T_W$ with eigenvalue $q^k\alpha$; therefore $q^k\alpha$ is an eigenvalue of $T_W$, i.e. $q^k\alpha\in S$. Applying the hypothesis on eigenvalue moduli to the two eigenvalues $\alpha$ and $q^k\alpha$ for the fixed embedding $\sigma$ of Step 1 gives
\[
|\sigma(\alpha)|=q^{w/2},\qquad |\sigma(q^k\alpha)|=q^{w/2} .
\]
On the other hand, by multiplicativity and $\sigma(q^k)=q^k\in\mathbb R_{>0}$,
\[
|\sigma(q^k\alpha)|=|\sigma(q^k)|\,|\sigma(\alpha)|=q^k\,|\sigma(\alpha)|=q^k\,q^{w/2} .
\]\nComparing the two expressions for $|\sigma(q^k\alpha)|$ yields $q^k\,q^{w/2}=q^{w/2}$. Since $q^{w/2}>0$ we may divide by it and obtain $q^k=1$. As $q\ge 2$, the map $k\mapsto q^k$ is injective on $\mathbb Z$, so $k=0$, contradicting the hypothesis $k\neq 0$. Hence $N_W|_{W_\alpha}=0$ for every $\alpha\in S$.

(Notice that the case $q^k\alpha=\alpha$ is not an exception: then $q^k\alpha\in S$ holds automatically and the same computation still forces $q^k=1$.)

**Step 6 (conclusion).** By (2), $W$ is spanned by the subspaces $W_\alpha$, $\alpha\in S$, and $N_W$ vanishes on each of them by Step 5. Hence $N_W=0$, and by the injectivity noted in Step 2, $N=0$. This completes the proof. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Remark.** The nilpotence of $N$ was not used: the argument shows more generally that if $T$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ with all eigenvalues of a single archimedean absolute value and $k\neq 0$, then any $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear $N$ with $TNT^{-1}=q^kN$ is zero.

lemma_401.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime. Then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is semisimple, equivalently diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_401.proof:
Fix data as in the statement: q = p^a a prime power, X a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_q, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, and \ell \neq p a prime. Write \sigma:k\to k for \sigma(c)=c^q, let F_X := \mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma : X_k \to X_k be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism (a morphism over F_q), and put
\[ V := H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad T := F_X^{*} = (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* \in \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V). \]
We must show T is semisimple (equivalently diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell).

Step 0 (V is finite dimensional and T \in GL(V)). X is proper over \mathbb F_q because it is projective. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) to the proper \mathbb F_q-variety X, with K = \mathbb Q_\ell the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \psi:F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell; it gives that H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V is finite dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell. Applying lemma_6a (eoinm) to X, with i=1, gives that F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{*}=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* and F_{\mathrm{geo}}^{*}=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^* are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphisms of V with F_{\mathrm{geo}}^{*}=(F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{*})^{-1}; in particular T = F_X^* \in GL(V). (Concretely, (\mathrm{id}\times\sigma)\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\sigma^{-1}) = \mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{id}_k = \mathrm{id}_{X_k} and likewise in the other order, so taking pullbacks gives T\circ T^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_V=T^{-1}\circ T.)

Step 1 (the empty case). If X = \emptyset then X_k = \emptyset and V = H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\emptyset,\mathbb Q_\ell) = 0. The zero operator on the zero vector space is semisimple (its minimal polynomial is 1, which is separable; equivalently the zero space is a direct sum of the empty family of eigenspaces). Hence the lemma holds in this case. In the sequel assume X \neq \emptyset.

Step 2 (a closed point of X). Since X is a non-empty scheme of finite type over the field \mathbb F_q, it has a closed point: take any non-empty affine open U = \operatorname{Spec} A \subseteq X (possible since X is covered by affine opens and X\neq\emptyset); A is a non-zero finitely generated \mathbb F_q-algebra, hence has a maximal ideal \mathfrak m by Zorn's lemma, and by Zariski's lemma \kappa(\mathfrak m) is a finite field extension of \mathbb F_q; the corresponding point x \in U is closed in U, hence closed in X. Thus \kappa(x) is a finite extension of \mathbb F_q, so there is a unique integer r \ge 1 and an \mathbb F_q-isomorphism \kappa(x) \simeq \mathbb F_{q^r}; the point x, viewed as an \operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x) \to X, gives, by transport of structure along this isomorphism, a point x \in X(\mathbb F_{q^r}) = X'(\mathbb F_{q^r}).

Step 3 (base change to the field of definition of x). Set
\[ X' := X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}, \]
a variety over \mathbb F_{q^r}. We verify the hypotheses needed for lemma_366 (Spark) with \mathbb F_q replaced by \mathbb F_{q^r}:
(a) X' is smooth over \mathbb F_{q^r}: smoothness is stable under arbitrary base change, and X \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q is smooth.
(b) X' is projective over \mathbb F_{q^r}: projectivity is stable under base change.
(c) X' is geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q^r}: since \mathbb F_{q^r}\subseteq k and k is algebraically closed and algebraic over \mathbb F_{q^r}, k is an algebraic closure of \mathbb F_{q^r}. Hence, by associativity of the fibre product,
\[ X'\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\operatorname{Spec}k \;=\; \bigl(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}\bigr)\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}}\operatorname{Spec}k \;\cong\; X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k \;=\; X_k, \]
and X_k is connected (and non-empty) because X is geometrically connected over \mathbb F_q. So X' is geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q^r}.
(d) X'(\mathbb F_{q^r}) \neq \emptyset, as noted at the end of Step 2.
Thus X' is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \mathbb F_{q^r} admitting an \mathbb F_{q^r}-rational point, and \ell\neq p, so lemma_366 (Spark) applies to (X',\mathbb F_{q^r},k,\ell): the q^r-power arithmetic Frobenius
\[ T' := (\mathrm{id}_{X'_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_r)^*,\qquad \sigma_r(c)=c^{q^r}, \]
is semisimple on H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Step 4 (identifying T' with T^r). Transport the group H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) to V along the canonical isomorphism \theta: X'_k \xrightarrow{\sim} X_k of Step 3(c); thus T' becomes a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of V. We claim that, under this identification, T' = T^{r}, the r-fold composition of T with itself.

First we show by induction on n \ge 1 that F_X^{\,n} = \mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{n} as F_q-morphisms X_k\to X_k. Recall X_k = X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k, so an F_q-morphism into X_k is the same as a pair of F_q-morphisms into X and into \operatorname{Spec}k. The morphism F_X = \mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma is the pair (p_X,\ \sigma\circ p_k), where p_X:X_k\to X and p_k:X_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k are the projections. For n=1 this is the definition. Assuming it for n, the (n+1)-st iterate F_X^{\,n+1} = F_X\circ F_X^{\,n} has first component p_X\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{n}) = p_X (because \mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{n} is over the identity of X), and second component (\sigma\circ p_k)\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{n}) = \sigma\circ\sigma^{n}\circ p_k = \sigma^{n+1}\circ p_k.
