Hence F_X^{\,n+1} = (p_X,\sigma^{n+1}\circ p_k) = \mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{n+1}. Taking n=r and using \sigma^{r}(c)=c^{q^r}=\sigma_r(c) for all c\in k, we obtain
\[ F_X^{\,r} \;=\; \mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{r} \;=\; \mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_r. \]
Under \theta:X'_k\xrightarrow{\sim}X_k the morphism \mathrm{id}_{X'_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_r corresponds exactly to \mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_r, since \theta is induced by the identity on the X-factor and the inclusion \mathbb F_{q^r}\hookrightarrow k on the second factor, and \sigma_r restricts to \sigma_r on \mathbb F_{q^r}. Therefore, using (g\circ f)^{*}=f^{*}\circ g^{*},
\[ \theta^{*}\circ T'\circ (\theta^{*})^{-1} \;=\; \theta^{*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{X'_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_r)^{*}\circ(\theta^{*})^{-1} \;=\; \bigl(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_r\bigr)^{*} \;=\; (F_X^{\,r})^{*} \;=\; (F_X^{*})^{r} \;=\; T^{r}. \]
Since conjugation by the isomorphism \theta^{*} preserves semisimplicity (it identifies T' with T^r as operators on the same space), T^{r} is semisimple on V.

Step 5 (descent from T^r to T). We have V a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space (Step 0), T\in GL(V) (Step 0), and the integer r\ge 1 (Step 2). By lemma_399 (Spark), T is semisimple on V if and only if T^{r} is semisimple on V. Since T^{r} is semisimple by Step 4, T is semisimple on V = H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Step 6 (the equivalent formulation). Finally, by lemma_5 (eoinm), a linear operator on a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space is semisimple if and only if it is diagonalisable after extending scalars to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. Applying this to T on V, the semisimplicity just proved is equivalent to diagonalisability of T on H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.

Combining Steps 1 and 5 we conclude that the q-power arithmetic Frobenius (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^q, is semisimple, equivalently diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, on H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). This completes the proof.

lemma_405.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\), and let \(U\) be an affine scheme of finite type over \(k\) of Krull dimension \(d\ge 0\). Then \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(n>d\), where \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) denotes the constant sheaf on the small \'etale site of \(U\).
lemma_405.proof:
We prove the vanishing by verifying that the constant sheaf Q_\ell[0] satisfies every hypothesis of the already proved lemma_288 (Spark), which is the affine cohomological-dimension bound for constructible Q_\ell-complexes, and then identifying the hypercohomology of that complex with the étale cohomology of the constant sheaf.

STEP 0 (The empty case). If U = \varnothing, then the small étale site U_{\acute et} is the trivial topos, R\Gamma(U_{\acute et},-) is the zero functor on abelian groups, and H^n_{\acute et}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every integer n; the required vanishing for n>d holds trivially. Henceforth assume U\neq\varnothing, and write d=\dim U for the Krull dimension, which by hypothesis is an integer \ge 0.

STEP 1 (Reduction to a statement about R\Gamma of a complex). Since U is of finite type over the field k, it is noetherian; write U=\operatorname{Spec} A with A a finitely generated k-algebra. Because char(k)\neq\ell, the prime \ell is invertible in \mathcal O_U, so the constant sheaves \mathbb Z/\ell^m on U_{\acute et} are torsion sheaves of order prime to the residue characteristics. For a sheaf \mathcal F of \mathbb Q_\ell-modules on U_{\acute et}, the étale cohomology groups H^n_{\acute et}(U,\mathcal F) of the statement are, by definition of derived functor cohomology, the cohomology groups of the derived global-sections functor applied to \mathcal F placed in degree 0:
  H^n_{\acute et}(U,\mathcal F) \;=\; R^n\Gamma(U_{\acute et},\mathcal F) \;=\; H^n\bigl(R\Gamma(U_{\acute et},\mathcal F[0])\bigr).
Thus, taking \mathcal F = \mathbb Q_\ell to be the constant sheaf, it suffices to prove
  H^q\bigl(R\Gamma(U_{\acute et},\,\mathbb Q_\ell[0])\bigr)=0 \quad\text{for every } q>d.   (\ast)

STEP 2 (The complex \mathbb Q_\ell[0] is constructible, i.e. is an object of D^b_c(U_{\acute et},\mathbb Q_\ell)). We check this from the definitions, in three substeps.

(2a) Finite stratification by normal strata. U is noetherian, so it admits a finite stratification U = \bigsqcup_{\alpha} S_\alpha into locally closed integral normal subschemes. Indeed, argue by noetherian induction on the closed subsets Z\subseteq U: for a non-empty integral closed subscheme Z (replace Z by Z_{\mathrm{red}}; this does not change the underlying topological space, hence not the étale topos), the normalisation \nu:\widetilde Z\to Z is finite because Z is of finite type over the field k (k is excellent, hence Japanese, so the integral closure of \mathcal O_Z/\mathrm{torsion} in its function field is finite); the locus where \nu is an isomorphism is open and dense in \widetilde Z (it contains the normal points, in particular the generic point), so its image is a dense open subset of Z on which Z is normal; remove it and repeat on the strictly smaller closed complement. Noetherianity makes this process terminate after finitely many steps, and the pieces obtained are locally closed, integral and normal.

(2b) Constructibility of \mathbb Z/\ell^m. Fix m\ge 1 and a stratum S_\alpha. Since S_\alpha is integral (hence connected) and normal noetherian, the constant sheaf \underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m} on (S_\alpha)_{\acute et} is locally constant for the étale topology with the single finite stalk \mathbb Z/\ell^m: the trivial covering {S_\alpha\to S_\alpha} is an étale cover on which the sheaf becomes constant with finite stalk. A sheaf of \Lambda-modules (\Lambda=\mathbb Z/\ell^m, with \ell invertible on S_\alpha) which is locally constant with finite stalks on a noetherian scheme is constructible, by the very definition of constructibility (a finite stratification by locally closed noetherian subschemes on each of which the sheaf is of finite type/locally constant of finite type, here the one-piece stratification). Hence \underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}|_{S_\alpha} is constructible for every \alpha. Since the S_\alpha form a finite stratification of U by locally closed noetherian subschemes, the defining criterion for constructible sheaves on a noetherian scheme (stability of constructibility under gluing along a finite stratification) shows that the constant sheaf \underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m} on U_{\acute et} is constructible. Concretely: a section of a quotient of \underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m} is determined by its finitely many values on the finitely many strata, so the sheaf is of finite type, and its restriction to each stratum is constructible by the previous sentence.

(2c) Passage to \mathbb Q_\ell. The transition maps \underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^{m+1}}\twoheadrightarrow\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m} exhibit (\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m})_{m\ge1} as a constructible \mathbb Z_\ell-sheaf (a projective system with constructible terms and surjective transition maps); its generic fibre
   \bigl(\varprojlim_m \underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}\bigr)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell \;=\; \underline{\mathbb Z_\ell}\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell \;=\; \underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}
is then, by the definition of a constructible \mathbb Q_\ell-sheaf, a constructible \mathbb Q_\ell-sheaf on U_{\acute et}. The complex \mathbb Q_\ell[0] has exactly one non-zero cohomology sheaf, namely \mathcal H^0(\mathbb Q_\ell[0])=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}, which is constructible, and all other cohomology sheaves zero; hence \mathbb Q_\ell[0]\in D^b_c(U_{\acute et},\mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 3 (Verification of the positivity hypothesis). The cohomology sheaves of K:=\mathbb Q_\ell[0] are \mathcal H^0(K)=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell} and \mathcal H^q(K)=0 for q\neq 0; in particular \mathcal H^q(K)=0 for every q>0. Thus K satisfies the exact positivity hypothesis of lemma_288.

STEP 4 (Application of lemma_288). We now check the hypotheses of lemma_288 (Spark) one by one for U and K=\mathbb Q_\ell[0]:
 - k is algebraically closed (hypothesis of the target, hence of the lemma);
 - \ell is a prime different from char(k) (hypothesis of the target);
 - U is an affine scheme of finite type over k (hypothesis of the target), of Krull dimension d;
 - K\in D^b_c(U_{\acute et},\mathbb Q_\ell) (Step 2c) and \mathcal H^q(K)=0 for q>0 (Step 3).
Lemma_288, applied with its integer n equal to our d, yields
   H^q\bigl(R\Gamma(U_{\acute et},\mathbb Q_\ell[0])\bigr)=0 \qquad\text{for every integer } q>d,
which is precisely (\ast).

STEP 5 (Conclusion). By the identification of Step 1, (\ast) reads H^q_{\acute et}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every integer q>d, where \mathbb Q_\ell is the constant sheaf on the small étale site of U. Renaming q as n gives exactly the required statement. (For n<0 the groups vanish as well, being negative derived functors of a left-exact functor; and the case U=\varnothing was settled in Step 0.) This completes the proof.

Remark on the logical content. Lemma_288 is the statement that on an affine k-scheme of finite type of dimension d the functor R\Gamma on constructible Q_\ell-complexes with no positive cohomology sheaves vanishes above degree d; the present lemma is the case of that statement where the complex is the constant sheaf in degree 0, and all the work needed beyond it — noetherianity of U, invertibility of \ell on U, and the constructibility of the constant Q_\ell-sheaf — was verified explicitly in Steps 1–3.

lemma_406.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\), and let \(U\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(k\) such that \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\) is a finite abelian group for every \(n\ge0\) and every \(r\ge1\). Then \(R^1\varprojlim_r H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)=0\) for every \(n\), and for every \(n\ge0\) the canonical comparison homomorphism \(\bigl(\varprojlim_r H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\bigr)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces.
lemma_406.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_406",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "PROOF.

CONVENTION. For a separated scheme of finite type over a field, $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ denotes \emph{\'{e}tale $\ell$-adic cohomology}, defined by the derived-limit formula (SGA 5, Exp. VIII, \S 1; Milne, \emph{Lectures on \'{e}tale cohomology}, VI.2):
\[ H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\;:=\;H^n\Bigl(\mathbf R\varprojlim_{r\ge 1} R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\Bigr)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell ,\]
where $\mathbb Z_\ell=\varprojlim_r\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbf R\varprojlim$ is the derived functor of the inverse limit of towers, taken in the derived category $D(\mathbf{Ab})$ (which has countable products). The comparison homomorphism in the statement is the one induced by the canonical map of the Milnor sequence (Step 3 below). (This is the standard definition; it cannot be replaced by the cohomology of the constant \emph{discrete} sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$: e.g. for a smooth projective curve $C$ one has $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C,\mathbb Q_\ell\text{-constant})=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(\pi_1(C),\mathbb Q_\ell^{\mathrm{disc}})=0$ since a continuous homomorphism from a profinite group to a discrete torsion-free group is trivial, whereas

a continuous homomorphism from a profinite group to a discrete torsion-free group is trivial, whereas \(\varprojlim_r H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\) is nonzero for a curve of positive genus. Thus the statement is to be read with this standard \(\ell\)-adic convention.)

STEP 1. NOTATION AND THE TOWER.
Fix \(n\). Put
\[
A_r=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z),\qquad r\ge1,
\]
and let \(\pi_r:A_{r+1}\to A_r\) be the map induced by reduction \(\mathbb Z/\ell^{r+1}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z\). The hypothesis says that every \(A_r\) is a finite abelian group. For \(n<0\) all \(A_r=0\), all cohomology groups under consideration vanish, and both assertions are immediate; hence assume \(n\ge0\) in the sequel.

STEP 2. THE FIRST DERIVED LIMIT VANISHES.
For a tower \(A=(A_r,\pi_r)\) of abelian groups define
\[
\Delta_A:\prod_{r\ge1}A_r\longrightarrow\prod_{r\ge1}A_r,
\qquad
\Delta_A((a_r))=(a_r-\pi_r(a_{r+1})).
\]
We use the standard elementary computation of the derived functors of \(\varprojlim\) on towers indexed by \(\mathbb N\): the sequence
\[
0\to\varprojlim A_r\to\prod_{r\ge1}A_r\xrightarrow{\Delta_A}\prod_{r\ge1}A_r\to\operatorname{coker}\Delta_A\to0
\]
is exact, and \(\operatorname{coker}\Delta_A\) is canonically \(R^1\varprojlim A_r\); moreover \(R^i\varprojlim A_r=0\) for \(i\ge2\). For completeness, one proves this by the Eilenberg--Moore replacement: embed \(A\) into the tower \(QA_r=\prod_{s=1}^r A_s\) (with the reverse diagonal embedding and the projection transitions), whose transitions are surjective and whose quotient also has surjective transitions; for a tower with surjective transitions \(\Delta\) is surjective by choosing the \(a_r\) recursively from left to right, and dimension shifting gives the stated identification.

Now take \(A_r=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\). We prove directly that \(\Delta_A\) is surjective. Let \(b=(b_r)\in\prod A_r\). For each \(N\ge1\), let \(S_N\) be the set of tuples \((a_1,\dots,a_{N+1})\in\prod_{r=1}^{N+1}A_r\) satisfying
\[
a_r-\pi_r(a_{r+1})=b_r\qquad(1\le r\le N).
\]
Each \(S_N\) is finite. It is nonempty: choose \(a_{N+1}=0\) and define recursively, for \(r=N,N-1,\dots,1\),
\[
a_r=b_r+\pi_r(a_{r+1}).
\]
The restriction map \(S_{N+1}\to S_N\) forgets the last coordinate, so \((S_N)\) is a tower of finite sets. A tower of finite nonempty sets satisfies the Mittag-Leffler condition; if \(T_N=\bigcap_{M\ge N}\operatorname{im}(S_M\to S_N)\), then \(T_N\) is nonempty finite and the maps \(T_{N+1}\to T_N\) are surjective. Choosing successively compatible elements in the \(T_N\) gives an element of \(\varprojlim_N S_N\). Such an element is a sequence \((a_r)_{r\ge1}\) satisfying \(a_r-\pi_r(a_{r+1})=b_r\) for every \(r\). Hence \(\Delta_A\) is surjective, so \(\operatorname{coker}\Delta_A=0\). By the identification above,
\[
R^1\varprojlim_r H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)=0.
\]
This proves the first assertion for every \(n\) (negative \(n\) having been handled above).

STEP 3. MILNOR SEQUENCE FOR A TOWER OF COMPLEXES.
Let \(C_\bullet=(C_r^\bullet,\pi_r)\) be a tower of cochain complexes of abelian groups. In the derived category of abelian groups, the derived limit is represented by
\[
\mathbf R\varprojlim_r C_r^\bullet\simeq \operatorname{Cone}\Bigl(\Delta_C:\prod_{r\ge1}C_r^\bullet\longrightarrow\prod_{r\ge1}C_r^\bullet\Bigr)[-1],
\]
where \(\Delta_C((x_r))=(x_r-\pi_r(x_{r+1}))\). This is the usual homotopy-limit model for a countable tower.

Taking the long exact sequence in cohomology of the distinguished triangle
\[
\prod C_r^\bullet\xrightarrow{\Delta_C}\prod C_r^\bullet\longrightarrow\mathbf R\varprojlim C_r^\bullet\longrightarrow
\]
gives, for each \(m\), an exact sequence
\[
0\to\operatorname{coker}\bigl(\Delta_C:H^{m-1}(\prod C_r^\bullet)\to H^{m-1}(\prod C_r^\bullet)\bigr)
\to H^m(\mathbf R\varprojlim C_r^\bullet)
\to\ker\bigl(\Delta_C:H^m(\prod C_r^\bullet)\to H^m(\prod C_r^\bullet)\bigr)
\to0.
\]
Products are exact in \(\mathbf{Ab}\), and boundaries in a product complex are computed componentwise; hence
\[
H^m\Bigl(\prod_{r\ge1}C_r^\bullet\Bigr)=\prod_{r\ge1}H^m(C_r^\bullet).
\]
Under this identification, the kernel of \(\Delta_C\) on \(H^m(\prod C_r^\bullet)\) is exactly \(\varprojlim_r H^m(C_r^\bullet)\), and its cokernel on \(H^{m-1}(\prod C_r^\bullet)\) is \(R^1\varprojlim_r H^{m-1}(C_r^\bullet)\) by the computation in Step 2. Therefore there is a natural short exact sequence (the Milnor sequence)
\[
0\to R^1\varprojlim_r H^{m-1}(C_r^\bullet)
\to H^m(\mathbf R\varprojlim_r C_r^\bullet)
\to\varprojlim_r H^m(C_r^\bullet)
\to0.
\]

STEP 4. APPLICATION TO \(\ell\)-ADIC COHOMOLOGY.
Apply Step 3 to the tower
\[
C_r^\bullet=R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z),
\]
with transitions induced by the reductions \(\mathbb Z/\ell^{r+1}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z\). For every \(m\),
\[
H^m(C_r^\bullet)=H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z),
\]
which is finite by hypothesis. Step 2 applied to the tower \(H^{m-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\) gives
\[
R^1\varprojlim_r H^{m-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)=0.
\]
Thus the Milnor sequence becomes a canonical isomorphism
\[
\theta_m:H^m\Bigl(\mathbf R\varprojlim_r R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\Bigr)
\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}
\varprojlim_r H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z).
\]
All groups here are naturally \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-modules: each \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\) is a \(\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z\)-module, hence a \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module via \(\mathbb Z_\ell\to\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z\), and the inverse limit and the derived-limit cohomology inherit the compatible \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-action. The map \(\theta_m\) is \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-linear because it is induced by the natural maps of the tower and by \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-linear constructions.

By the convention stated at the beginning,
\[
H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)
:=
H^m\Bigl(\mathbf R\varprojlim_r R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\Bigr)
\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell.
\]
The canonical comparison homomorphism in the lemma is
\[
\bigl(\varprojlim_r H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)\bigr)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell
\longrightarrow
H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell),
\]
and it is defined as \(\theta_n^{-1}\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\). Since \(\theta_n\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-modules, tensoring with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) gives an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces. (Equivalently, \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) is flat over \(\mathbb Z_\ell\), so tensoring the Milnor short exact sequence with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) kills the already-zero \(R^1\varprojlim\) term and identifies the two sides.)

This completes the proof."
}

lemma_ell_power_coefficient_reduction.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\), and let \(U\) be an affine scheme of finite type over \(k\) of Krull dimension \(d\ge 0\). Suppose \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell\mathbb Z)=0\) for every integer \(n>d\), where \(\mathbb Z/\ell\mathbb Z\) denotes the constant sheaf on the small étale site of \(U\). Then \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)=0\) for every integer \(r\ge 1\) and every integer \(n>d\).
lemma_ell_power_coefficient_reduction.proof:
We prove: if $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $n>d$, then $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $r\ge1$ and every $n>d$. The whole content is a formal induction on $r$ driven by the short exact sequence of constant sheaves $0\to\mathbb Z/\ell\to\mathbb Z/\ell^r\to\mathbb Z/\ell^{r-1}\to0$; no input beyond the stated hypothesis is used. (Note in particular that the argument uses neither affineness, nor the dimension bound, nor $\ell\ne\mathrm{char}(k)$ except through the single assumed vanishing; those hypotheses enter only insofar as they are what makes the assumed $r=1$ case true.)

Notation. For $s\ge1$ write $\Lambda_s$ for the constant sheaf $\mathbb Z/\ell^s\mathbb Z$ on the small \`etale site $U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, and $H^n(U,\Lambda_s):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^s\mathbb Z)=R^n\Gamma(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\Lambda_s)$, the derived functors of the global-sections functor on the abelian category $\mathrm{Sh}(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$ of abelian sheaves.

Step 0 (the empty scheme). If $U=\varnothing$, the small \`etale site of $U$ has a single object, namely $\varnothing\to\varnothing$, and the empty family is an \`etale cover of $\varnothing$ (the union of the empty family of images is $\varnothing$). The sheaf axiom for that empty cover forces $F(\varnothing)$ to be a singleton for every sheaf of sets $F$; hence $\mathrm{Sh}(\varnothing_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$ is the terminal category, and the category of abelian sheaves on it has exactly one object, the zero group. Thus $\Gamma(\varnothing,-)$ is trivially exact and $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\varnothing,-)=0$ for all $n\ge1$. Since $d\ge0$, every integer $n>d$ satisfies $n\ge1$, so all groups $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\varnothing,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)$ vanish and the conclusion holds. In the rest of the proof $U$ is non-empty.

Step 1 (stalks of constant sheaves). Let $\bar u:\mathrm{Spec}(\Omega)\to U$ be a geometric point. We compute the stalk of the constant sheaf associated to an abelian group $A$. By definition $A_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the sheafification of the constant presheaf $V\mapsto A$, and the stalk is
$$(A_{\mathrm{sh}})_{\bar u}=\varinjlop_{(V,\bar v)}A_{\mathrm{sh}}(V),$$
the filtered colimit over \`etale neighbourhoods $(V,\bar v)$ of $\bar u$. Since $V$ is \`etale over the field $k$, it is locally noetherian, so its connected components are open and $A_{\mathrm{sh}}(V)=\mathrm{Map}(\pi_0(V),A)$ (the sections of the constant sheaf over a locally noetherian, locally connected space are exactly the locally constant functions to the discrete group $A$; this is the standard description of the constant sheaf, and it is immediate from the fact that such a $V$ is covered by its components, which are open, disjoint and form a covering family). The connected \`etale neighbourhoods are cofinal among all \`etale neighbourhoods: given $(V,\bar v)$, the connected component $V_{\bar v}$ containing $\bar v$ is open in $V$, hence the open immersion $V_{\bar v}\hookrightarrow V$ is \`etale and $(V_{\bar v},\bar v)\to(V,\bar v)$ is a morphism of \`etale neighbourhoods. For a connected $(V,\bar v)$ we have $\pi_0(V)=\{*\}$, so $A_{\mathrm{sh}}(V)=\mathrm{Map}(\{*\},A)\cong A$, and for an inclusion of connected neighbourhoods $V'\subset V$ the restriction map $\mathrm{Map}(\pi_0V,A)\to\mathrm{Map}(\pi_0V',A)$ sends a constant function to the same constant function, i.e. it is the identity of $A$ under the above identifications. Hence the filtered colimit is $A$, and the resulting isomorphism
$$\theta_A:\;A\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;(A_{\mathrm{sh}})_{\bar u},\qquad a\longmapsto\text{germ at }\bar u\text{ of the constant section }a,$$
is natural in $A$ (post-composition with a homomorphism $f:A\to B$ on both sides gives $\theta_B\circ f=(f_{\mathrm{sh}})_{\bar u}\circ\theta_A$).

Step 2 (the short exact sequence of sheaves). Fix $r\ge2$. Consider the homomorphisms of abelian groups
$$\alpha_1:\mathbb Z/\ell\longrightarrow \mathbb Z/\ell^r,\qquad \bar a\longmapsto \overline{\ell^{\,r-1}a},\qquad\qquad \beta_1:\mathbb Z/\ell^r\longrightarrow \mathbb Z/\ell^{r-1},\qquad \bar a\longmapsto \bar a\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \ell^{r-1}).$$
We check exactness of $0\to\mathbb Z/\ell\xrightarrow{\alpha_1}\mathbb Z/\ell^r\xrightarrow{\beta_1}\mathbb Z/\ell^{r-1}\to0$ directly:
\emph{$\alpha_1$ is well defined:} if $a\equiv a'\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \ell)$, then $a-a'=\ell b$ and $\ell^{r-1}(a-a')=\ell^r b\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \ell^r)$. 
\emph{$\alpha_1$ is injective:} if $\overline{\ell^{r-1}a}=0$ in $\mathbb Z/\ell^r$, then $\ell^r\mid\ell^{r-1}a$, hence $\ell\mid a$ (cancelling $\ell^{r-1}$ in $\mathbb Z$), so $\bar a=0$ in $\mathbb Z/\ell$. 
\emph{$\beta_1$ is surjective:} any class $\bar a\in\mathbb Z/\ell^{r-1}$ is the image of $\bar a\in\mathbb Z/\ell^r$. 
\emph{$\ker\beta_1=\mathrm{im}\,\alpha_1$:} $\beta_1(\bar a)=0\iff\ell^{r-1}\mid a\iff a\in\ell^{r-1}\mathbb Z\iff\bar a=\overline{\ell^{r-1}a'}$ with $a'$ the quotient $a/\ell^{r-1}$; and $\overline{\ell^{r-1}a'}=\alpha_1(\bar a')$. Note that $\beta_1$ is a well-defined ring (hence group) homomorphism.

Sheafify: the group homomorphisms $\alpha_1,\beta_1$ induce morphisms of sheaves $\alpha:\Lambda_1\to\Lambda_r$ and $\beta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_{r-1}$, described concretely on sections over $V$ by post-composition of locally constant functions, $\mathrm{Map}(\pi_0V,\mathbb Z/\ell)\to\mathrm{Map}(\pi_0V,\mathbb Z/\ell^r)$, $\varphi\mapsto\alpha_1\circ\varphi$, and similarly for $\beta_1$. We claim
$$0\longrightarrow\Lambda_1\xrightarrow{\;\alpha\;}\Lambda_r\xrightarrow{\;\beta\;}\Lambda_{r-1}\longrightarrow0\tag{SES$_r$}$$
is exact in $\mathrm{Sh}(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$. Exactness of a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups is equivalent to exactness of the sequence of stalks at every geometric point. By the naturality established in Step 1, the stalk of (SES$_r$) at any geometric point $\bar u$ identifies, via the isomorphisms $\theta_{\mathbb Z/\ell},\theta_{\mathbb Z/\ell^r},\theta_{\mathbb Z/\ell^{r-1}}$, with the sequence of abelian groups $0\to\mathbb Z/\ell\xrightarrow{\alpha_1}\mathbb Z/\ell^r\xrightarrow{\beta_1}\mathbb Z/\ell^{r-1}\to0$, which is exact. Hence (SES$_r$) is exact. (This is the justification demanded rather than an appeal to exactness of the constant-sheafification functor as a black box; the point is that the stalk functor at a geometric point sends $A_{\mathrm{sh}}$ to $A$ naturally, so it transports the exactness of the sequence of groups to exactness of the sequence of sheaves.)

Step 3 (the long exact cohomology sequence). The abelian category $\mathrm{Sh}(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$ has enough injectives, and $\Gamma(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},-)$ is left exact with right derived functors $H^n(U,-)$. Applying the standard long exact sequence of derived functors to (SES$_r$) yields, for every integer $n$,
$$\cdots\to H^n(U,\Lambda_1)\xrightarrow{\alpha_*}H^n(U,\Lambda_r)\xrightarrow{\beta_*}H^n(U,\Lambda_{r-1})\xrightarrow{\ \delta_n\ }H^{n+1}(U,\Lambda_1)\to\cdots,\tag{LES$_r$}$$
exact at every term. For completeness of the justification of this standard machinery: take an injective resolution of (SES$_r$) (the horseshoe lemma upgrades the monomorphism $\Lambda_1\hookrightarrow\Lambda_r$ to a short exact sequence of complexes of injectives $0\to I^\bullet\to J^\bullet\to K^\bullet\to0$ resolving (SES$_r$)); applying the left exact functor $\Gamma$ gives again a short exact sequence of cochain complexes, and the snake lemma applied to the truncations of that short exact sequence of complexes produces exactly (LES$_r$), with $\delta_n$ the connecting homomorphism.

Step 4 (induction on $r$). For $r\ge1$ let $P(r)$ be the statement: $H^n(U,\Lambda_r)=0$ for all integers $n>d$.

\emph{Base case $r=1$.} $P(1)$ is precisely the hypothesis of the lemma.

\emph{Inductive step.} Let $r\ge2$ and assume $P(r-1)$. Let $n>d$ be an integer. Then $n\ge d+1>d$ and also $n+1>d$, so by $P(1)$ the two outer groups in the piece
$$H^n(U,\Lambda_1)\xrightarrow{\alpha_*}H^n(U,\Lambda_r)\xrightarrow{\beta_*}H^n(U,\Lambda_{r-1})\xrightarrow{\delta_n}H^{n+1}(U,\Lambda_1)$$
of (LES$_r$) are zero: $H^n(U,\Lambda_1)=0$ and $H^{n+1}(U,\Lambda_1)=0$. Moreover $H^n(U,\Lambda_{r-1})=0$ by $P(r-1)$. Exactness at $H^n(U,\Lambda_r)$ says $\mathrm{im}(\alpha_*)=\ker(\beta_*)$; since $H^n(U,\Lambda_1)=0$, we get $\ker\beta_*=0$, i.e. $\beta_*$ is injective. Exactness at $H^n(U,\Lambda_{r-1})$ says $\mathrm{im}(\beta_*)=\ker(\delta_n)$; since $H^n(U,\Lambda_{r-1})=0$ its only element maps to $0$, so $\mathrm{im}(\beta_*)=0$. An injective map with zero image has zero source, hence $H^n(U,\Lambda_r)=0$. This proves $P(r)$.

By induction on $r$, $P(r)$ holds for all $r\ge1$. (Concretely, for $r=2$ the relevant sequence is $0\to\Lambda_1\xrightarrow{\alpha}\Lambda_2\xrightarrow{\beta}\Lambda_1\to0$, whose exactness is Step 2 with $r=2$, and the argument above is exactly the case $r=2$ of the inductive step.)

Step 5 (conclusion). Combining Step 0 (empty $U$) with Step 4 (non-empty $U$), we obtain $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z)=0$ for every integer $r\ge1$ and every integer $n>d$, which is the desired conclusion. $\blacksquare$

Remark on the scope of the lemma. The reduction proved here is only in the exponent $r$: it shows the prime-exponent case $r=1$ implies all $r$. It supplies no information about the case $r=1$ itself, and it cannot be obtained from any vanishing theorem with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ coefficients, since $\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Z/\ell^r=0$, so $\mathbb Q_\ell$-cohomological vanishing is blind to $\ell$-primary torsion. The remaining gap for applications (e.g. to lemma_404) is precisely the prime-exponent vanishing $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell\mathbb Z)=0$ for $n>d$, which must be established as a separate result.

lemma_408.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), let \(\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) be a field embedding, and let \(c\in\mathbb R_{>0}\). Suppose there exists a positive definite Hermitian form \(h\) on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C\) such that \(h(T_\sigma x, T_\sigma y)=c\,h(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C\), where \(T_\sigma=T\otimes\mathrm{id}\). Then \(T_\sigma\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb C\) if and only if \(T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\); in particular \(T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_408.proof:
We write ι := σ|_{\mathbb Q_\ell} : \mathbb Q_\ell \hookrightarrow \mathbb C for the induced field embedding, W := V \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\,\iota} \mathbb C (a \mathbb C-vector space of dimension n := \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} V), and T_\sigma := T \otimes \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C} \in \mathrm{GL}(W). "T is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell" means that \bar T := T \otimes \mathrm{id}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} is diagonalizable on V \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. The proof has two independent parts: Part I proves the equivalence for an arbitrary T (no use of the Hermitian form), and Part II uses the Hermitian form to prove that T_\sigma is diagonalizable, whence the "in particular".

=== Part I: the equivalence, for every T \in \mathrm{GL}(V) ===

I.1 (Minimal polynomial under scalar extension). Let m_T \in \mathbb Q_\ell[x] be the monic minimal polynomial of T. Claim: the monic minimal polynomial \mu of T_\sigma over \mathbb C is \iota(m_T) (the polynomial obtained by applying \iota to the coefficients).

Proof. Let \varphi: \mathbb Q_\ell[x] \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V), x \mapsto T. Its kernel is the ideal (m_T): indeed (m_T) is contained in the kernel, and if f = q m_T + r with \deg r < \deg m_T and f in the kernel then r(T) = 0, so r = 0 by minimality of m_T. Hence \varphi induces an injective \mathbb Q_\ell-algebra homomorphism \bar\varphi: \mathbb Q_\ell[x]/(m_T) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V).

Now \mathbb C is a \mathbb Q_\ell-algebra via \iota; being a vector space over the field \mathbb Q_\ell it is free, hence flat. Tensoring the injection with \mathbb C over \mathbb Q_\ell therefore gives an injection of \mathbb C-algebras
  \mathbb C[x]/(\iota(m_T)) \;\cong\; \bigl(\mathbb Q_\ell[x]/(m_T)\bigr) \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} \mathbb C \;\hookrightarrow\; \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb C,
using the canonical \mathbb C-algebra isomorphism \mathbb Q_\ell[x]\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb C \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb C[x], \ \sum_i p_i(x)\otimes\lambda_i \mapsto \sum_i \iota(\lambda_i) p_i(x), under which the ideal (m_T)\otimes\mathbb C maps to (\iota(m_T)).
Choose a \mathbb Q_\ell-basis e_1,\dots,e_n of V; then e_i\otimes 1 is a \mathbb C-basis of W. If A \in M_n(\mathbb Q_\ell) is the matrix of T in this basis, the matrix of T_\sigma in the \mathbb C-basis is \iota(A). The map \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb C \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb C}(W), B\otimes\lambda \mapsto (\text{C-linear map with matrix }\iota(\lambda)\iota(B)), is a \mathbb C-algebra isomorphism (both sides are M_n(-) in these bases), and under it the composite \mathbb C[x] \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb C}(W) is exactly x \mapsto T_\sigma. Hence the kernel of \mathbb C[x] \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb C}(W), x\mapsto T_\sigma, is precisely (\iota(m_T)), so \mu = \iota(m_T). \qed

The identical argument with \mathbb C replaced by \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell shows that the minimal polynomial of \bar T over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is m_T itself.

I.2 (Diagonalizability over an algebraically closed field). Let K be algebraically closed and S an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional K-vector space with minimal polynomial \nu. Then S is diagonalizable if and only if \nu has no repeated root in K.

(\Longleftarrow) Write \nu(x) = \prod_{j=1}^{r}(x-\lambda_j) with the \lambda_j \in K distinct. Put p_j(x) := \prod_{k\neq j}(x-\lambda_k) and d_j := p_j(\lambda_j) \neq 0, e_j := p_j/d_j \in K[x]. The polynomial \sum_j e_j - 1 has degree \le r-1 and vanishes at each of the r distinct points \lambda_j, hence is zero: \sum_j e_j = 1 in K[x]. Also (x-\lambda_j)e_j vanishes at every \lambda_k and has degree r, so (x-\lambda_j)e_j is divisible by \nu. For any vector v, v = \sum_j e_j(S)v, and (S-\lambda_j)\bigl(e_j(S)v\bigr) = \bigl((x-\lambda_j)e_j\bigr)(S)v = 0 since \nu(S) = 0. Thus v lies in \sum_j \ker(S-\lambda_j), so S is diagonalizable.

(\Longrightarrow) If S is diagonalizable with distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r, the space is spanned by eigenvectors and P(x) := \prod_j (x-\lambda_j) annihilates each eigenspace, hence P(S) = 0. Thus \nu \mid P, so \nu is a product of distinct linear factors. \qed

I.3 (Squarefreeness is preserved by \iota). We claim m_T has no repeated root in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell if and only if \iota(m_T) has no repeated root in \mathbb C.

First, for any field F of characteristic 0 and any monic f \in F[x] with F algebraically closed, f has a repeated root in F iff \gcd(f,f') is nonconstant in F[x]: writing f = (x-\alpha)^k s with k \ge 1, s(\alpha)\neq 0, one gets f' = k(x-\alpha)^{k-1}s + (x-\alpha)^k s', so (x-\alpha) \mid f' iff k \ge 2, i.e. iff \alpha is a repeated root of f.

Second, let g := \gcd(m_T, m_T') \in \mathbb Q_\ell[x] be the monic gcd. The Euclidean algorithm on the pair (m_T, m_T') in \mathbb Q_\ell[x] produces a sequence of divisions with uniquely determined quotients and remainders; the same equalities hold in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[x] and (applying \iota) in \mathbb C[x], and uniqueness of quotient and remainder in the larger polynomial rings shows these sequences are exactly the Euclidean algorithms there. Hence \gcd(m_T,m_T') computed in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[x] is g, and \gcd(\iota(m_T), \iota(m_T)') computed in \mathbb C[x] is \iota(g) (note (\iota(m_T))' = \iota(m_T'), since \iota fixes the prime field \mathbb Q and differentiation is given by integer polynomial formulas in the coefficients). Therefore
  m_T has a repeated root in \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \iff \deg g \ge 1 \iff \deg \iota(g) \ge 1 \iff \iota(m_T) has a repeated root in \mathbb C.

I.4 (Conclusion of Part I). Since \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell and \mathbb C are algebraically closed, I.2, I.1 and I.3 give
  T diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell
  \iff m_T \text{ has no repeated root in } \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell
  \iff \iota(m_T) = \mu \text{ has no repeated root in } \mathbb C
  \iff T_\sigma \text{ is diagonalizable over } \mathbb C.
This is the claimed equivalence; no metric hypothesis was used.

=== Part II: the Hermitian hypothesis forces T_\sigma to be diagonalizable ===

We use the convention that a Hermitian form is conjugate-linear in the first variable and linear in the second, so h(y,x) = \overline{h(x,y)}; the hypothesis is unchanged under this convention (the other convention is obtained by complex-conjugating h). Positive definiteness means h(x,x) \in \mathbb R_{>0} for x \neq 0 (it is real because h(x,x) = \overline{h(x,x)}); in particular h is nondegenerate.

II.1 (Rescaling to an isometry). Let \sqrt c > 0 be the positive real square root of c, and set U := c^{-1/2} T_\sigma \in \mathrm{GL}(W). Then for all x,y \in W,
  h(Ux, Uy) = c^{-1} h(T_\sigma x, T_\sigma y) = c^{-1}\cdot c\, h(x,y) = h(x,y).

II.2 (The adjoint, and normality). Since h is nondegenerate and W is finite dimensional, for each z \in W the map y \mapsto \overline{h(z,y)}... more directly: the map W \to W^{\vee},\ z \mapsto h(z,\cdot) is a C-antilinear bijection, so for every U' \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb C}(W) there is a unique U'^{*} \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb C}(W) with h(U'x, y) = h(x, U'^{*}y) for all x,y; explicitly, U'^{*} = (z \mapsto h(z,\cdot))^{-1} \circ (y \mapsto \overline{h(U'\,\cdot\,,y)})... To avoid convention issues we define the adjoint by the requirement
  h(x, U'y) = h(U'^{*}x, y) \qquad \forall x,y \in W,
which determines U'^{*} uniquely and C-linearly (with our convention: h(x,U'(\alpha y)) = \alpha h(x,U'y) = \alpha h(U'^*x,y) = h(x, U'^*(\alpha y)) is consistent with U'^* being C-linear). Applying this with U' = U and y replaced by Uy gives h(Ux,Uy) = h(U^{*}Ux, y) for all x,y; by II.1 this equals h(x,y) = h(Ix,y), and nondegeneracy yields
  U^{*}U = I. \quad (\ast)
From (\ast), U is injective, hence bijective as W is finite dimensional, and (\ast) gives U^{*} = U^{-1}; consequently UU^{*} = I as well, i.e.
  UU^{*} = U^{*}U,
so U is normal. Also U^{*} is normal, since U^{*}U^{**} = U^{*}U = UU^{*} = U^{**}U^{*}.

II.3 (Kernel identity). For \lambda \in \mathbb C we have (U-\lambda)^{*} = U^{*} - \bar\lambda, because h(x,(U-\lambda)y) = h(x,Uy) - \lambda h(x,y) = h(U^{*}x,y) - h(\bar\lambda x,y) = h((U^{*}-\bar\lambda)x,y) (using conjugate-linearity in the first variable: h(\bar\lambda x, y) = \lambda h(x,y)). Hence, writing \|v\|^2 := h(v,v),
  \|(U-\lambda)v\|^2 = h(v, (U^{*}-\bar\lambda)(U-\lambda)v), \qquad
  \|(U^{*}-\bar\lambda)v\|^2 = h(v, (U-\lambda)(U^{*}-\bar\lambda)v),
where the second identity uses (U^{*}-\bar\lambda)^{*} = U - \lambda. Expanding both products,
  (U^{*}-\bar\lambda)(U-\lambda) = U^{*}U - \lambda U^{*} - \bar\lambda U + |\lambda|^2 = (U-\lambda)(U^{*}-\bar\lambda),
the two being equal because UU^{*} = U^{*}U. Therefore
  \|(U-\lambda)v\| = \|(U^{*}-\bar\lambda)v\| \quad\text{for all } v, \quad\text{so}\quad \ker(U-\lambda) = \ker(U^{*}-\bar\lambda). \quad (\dagger)

II.4 (Reduction). We prove by induction on n = \dim_{\mathbb C} W that every normal operator is diagonalizable. For n = 0 there is nothing to prove. Let n \ge 1 and let U be normal. The characteristic polynomial of U is a nonconstant polynomial with coefficients in \mathbb C, which is algebraically closed; hence U has an eigenvalue \lambda with a nonzero eigenvector v. By (\dagger), U^{*}v = \bar\lambda v. Consider v^{\perp} := \{w : h(v,w) = 0\}. The map y \mapsto h(v,y) is a nonzero \mathbb C-linear functional (linear in the second variable, and h(v,v) \neq 0), so \dim v^{\perp} = n-1. If w \in v^{\perp}, then h(v,Uw) = h(U^{*}v,w) = h(\bar\lambda v, w) = \lambda h(v,w) = 0, so v^{\perp} is U-invariant; the same argument with U and U^{*} interchanged (both are normal) shows v^{\perp} is U^{*}-invariant. Also \mathbb Cv \cap v^{\perp} = 0, since h(v,\alpha v) = \bar\alpha h(v,v) = 0 forces \alpha = 0; hence W = \mathbb Cv \oplus v^{\perp}.
The restriction h|_{v^{\perp}\times v^{\perp}} is a positive definite Hermitian form, and for x,y \in v^{\perp} we have h(x, U|_{v^{\perp}}y) = h(U^{*}x,y) with U^{*}x \in v^{\perp}; so the adjoint of U|_{v^{\perp}} for the restricted form is U^{*}|_{v^{\perp}}, which is again the restriction of an operator commuting with U|_{v^{\perp}}. Thus U|_{v^{\perp}} is normal. By the induction hypothesis v^{\perp} has a \mathbb C-basis of eigenvectors of U|_{v^{\perp}}, hence of U; adjoining v gives a \mathbb C-basis of W of eigenvectors of U. So U is diagonalizable over \mathbb C.

II.5. Since T_\sigma = \sqrt c\, U with \sqrt c \in \mathbb R_{>0}, T_\sigma has exactly the same eigenvectors as U, and is therefore diagonalizable over \mathbb C.

=== Part III: conclusion ===

Part II shows the left-hand side of the equivalence of Part I holds for our T; by the equivalence, T is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. Together with Part I this gives exactly the statement: T_\sigma is diagonalizable over \mathbb C if and only if T is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, and in particular T is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. \qed

lemma_409.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), let \(\langle-,-\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) be a perfect bilinear pairing and let \(a\mapsto a^\dagger\) be the associated adjoint, let \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\), and let \(\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) be a field embedding such that \(\sigma(c)\in\mathbb R_{>0}\). Suppose \(T^\dagger=c\,T^{-1}\) and that there exists a positive definite Hermitian form \(h\) on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C\) with \(h(T_\sigma x,T_\sigma y)=\sigma(c)\,h(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\), where \(T_\sigma=T\otimes\mathrm{id}\). Then \(T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_409.proof:
We prove that $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Note at the outset that the perfect pairing $\langle-,-\rangle$, its adjoint $a\mapsto a^\dagger$, and the relation $T^\dagger=c\,T^{-1}$ play no role in the argument: the conclusion already follows from the existence of the Hermitian form $h$, i.e. from the displayed similarity-to-a-scalar-times-unitary condition. (That extra data is consistent with, but logically independent of, what is used below.)

Step 1: The numerical input required by the cited criterion.
By hypothesis $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ and the embedding $\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ satisfies $\sigma(c)\in\mathbb R_{>0}$. Put
$$c_\infty:=\sigma(c)\in\mathbb R_{>0}.$$
Thus $c_\infty$ is a strictly positive real number, and $c_\infty\neq0$, so $c_\infty^{-1/2}\in\mathbb R_{>0}$ is defined. The hypothesis on $h$ reads, verbatim,
$$h(T_\sigma x,T_\sigma y)=c_\infty\,h(x,y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in V_\sigma:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C,$$
with $h$ a positive definite Hermitian form on the finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space $V_\sigma$ (finite-dimensional because $\dim_{\mathbb C}V_\sigma=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V<\infty$; the assumption $V\neq0$ is stronger than anything needed).

Step 2: $T_\sigma$ is a positive real scalar times a unitary operator, hence diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$.
Define the $\mathbb C$-linear operator $U:=c_\infty^{-1/2}T_\sigma\in\mathrm{GL}(V_\sigma)$. Using that $h$ is Hermitian (linear in the first slot, conjugate-linear in the second) and that $c_\infty^{-1/2}$ is a positive real number, hence equal to its own complex conjugate, we compute for all $x,y\in V_\sigma$:
$$h(Ux,Uy)=h\bigl(c_\infty^{-1/2}T_\sigma x,\,c_\infty^{-1/2}T_\sigma y\bigr)=c_\infty^{-1/2}\overline{c_\infty^{-1/2}}\;h(T_\sigma x,T_\sigma y)=c_\infty^{-1}\cdot c_\infty\, h(x,y)=h(x,y).$$
So $U$ is unitary for the positive definite Hermitian form $h$. Let $U^*$ denote the $h$-adjoint of $U$; the identity $h(Ux,Uy)=h(x,y)$ says exactly that $U^*U=\mathrm{id}$. Since $U$ is invertible, $U^*$ is then a two-sided inverse of $U$, so also $UU^*=\mathrm{id}$; hence $U$ is normal ($U^*U=UU^*$). By the spectral theorem for normal operators on a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $U$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$ (and its eigenvalues $\lambda$ satisfy $|\lambda|^2=1$, because for an $h$-orthonormal eigenline $\mathbb C v$ one has $h(v,v)=h(Uv,Uv)=|\lambda|^2h(v,v)$ with $h(v,v)>0$). Since $T_\sigma=c_\infty^{1/2}U$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of a diagonalizable operator, $T_\sigma$ is itself diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$.

Step 3: Descent of diagonalizability from $\mathbb C$ to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.
We now invoke the cited lemma (Spark, lemma_408) with the inputs $\ell$, the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $V$, the operator $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, the embedding $\sigma$, and the positive real number $c_\infty$. Its hypotheses are exactly what Steps 1--2 verify: $h$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C$ with $h(T_\sigma x,T_\sigma y)=c_\infty h(x,y)$ for all $x,y$. Its conclusion is that $T_\sigma$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$ if and only if $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and in particular that $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Applying the ($\Rightarrow$) direction to the diagonalizability of $T_\sigma$ obtained in Step 2 yields the claim.

For completeness we spell out the content of the descent direction used, so that no step is left unverified. Let $\mu_T\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ be the minimal polynomial of $T$. The evaluation homomorphism $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$, $t\mapsto T$, has kernel $(\mu_T)$; since $\mathbb C$ is flat over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ via $\sigma$, tensoring gives $\mathbb C[t]\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_\sigma)$, $t\mapsto T_\sigma$, with kernel $\sigma(\mu_T)\,\mathbb C[t]$. Hence the minimal polynomial of $T_\sigma$ is $\sigma(\mu_T)$ (the monic generator). As $T_\sigma$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$, $\sigma(\mu_T)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(t-\alpha_i)$ with pairwise distinct $\alpha_i\in\mathbb C$. Each $\alpha_i$ is algebraic over $\sigma(\mathbb Q_\ell)$; since $\sigma(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$ is an algebraic closure of $\sigma(\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (field-isomorphic to the algebraically closed field $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and algebraic over $\sigma(\mathbb Q_\ell)$), we have $\alpha_i\in\sigma(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$, say $\alpha_i=\sigma(\beta_i)$ with $\beta_i\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ distinct. Then $\sigma(\mu_T)=\prod_i(t-\sigma(\beta_i))=\sigma\!\bigl(\prod_i(t-\beta_i)\bigr)$ inside $\sigma(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)[t]$, and injectivity of $\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]\hookrightarrow\mathbb C[t]$ gives $\mu_T=\prod_i(t-\beta_i)$, a product of distinct linear factors over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Therefore $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ decomposes as the direct sum of the eigenspaces $\ker(T-\beta_i)$, i.e. $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. This is precisely the required conclusion.

Thus $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, completing the proof. (Equivalently, by the standard equivalence between diagonalizability over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and semisimplicity on $V$, $T$ acts semisimply on $V$.)

lemma_poincare_duality_smooth_projective.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(Y\) be a smooth projective variety of pure dimension \(e\ge0\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Then there exists a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map \(\operatorname{tr}_Y:H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-e)\) such that for every integer \(n\) the pairing \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^{2e-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-e)\), \((x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup y)\), is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces.
lemma_poincare_duality_smooth_projective.proof:
Write H^n(Z) := H^n_{\acute et}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell) for a scheme Z over k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, and recall that \mathbb Q_\ell(-e) is a one-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space, so a pairing with that target is simply a \mathbb Q_\ell-bilinear map.

If Y = \emptyset then every H^n(Y_k) = 0 and the zero map tr_Y = 0 satisfies the requirement. Assume henceforth Y \neq \emptyset.

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality). Y is projective, hence proper, over \mathbb F_q. The constant sheaf \mathbb Q_\ell on (Y_k)_{\acute et} is an object of D^b_c(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) (Y_k is of finite type over the field k), and the q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism F_Y : Y_k \to Y_k carries the canonical isomorphism \psi : F_Y^*\mathbb Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell (F_Y is the identity on the underlying topological space and acts as c \mapsto c^q on k, hence pulls the constant sheaf back to itself). Applying eoinm:lemma_45_finite_frob with X = Y, K = \mathbb Q_\ell and \varphi = \psi, we obtain
\[ \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^n(Y_k) < \infty \quad \text{for every } n\ge 0. \]

Step 2 (vanishing outside [0,2e]). Y_k is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field k, of pure dimension e. By Spark:lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing, H^n(Y_k) = 0 for every n > 2e; and H^n(Y_k) = 0 for n < 0 by definition of cohomology. Hence if n \notin [0,2e], both H^n(Y_k) and H^{2e-n}(Y_k) vanish, and the pairing 0 \times 0 \to \mathbb Q_\ell(-e) is trivially perfect. It remains to construct tr_Y and to prove perfectness for 0 \le n \le 2e.

Step 3 (the connected components of Y_k and their descent). 
(3a) The ring A := H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y) is a finite-dimensional \mathbb F_q-algebra because Y is proper over \mathbb F_q. Y is smooth over \mathbb F_q, hence regular, hence reduced; since Y is noetherian and reduced, restriction to the set Y^{(0)} of generic points embeds A into \prod_{y\in Y^{(0)}} \mathcal O_{Y,y}, a product of fields, so A is reduced. As \mathbb F_q is perfect, A \cong \prod_{j=1}^{s} L_j with each L_j a finite separable (equivalently finite) field extension of \mathbb F_q; i.e. A is finite \'etale over \mathbb F_q. Let N := \dim_{\mathbb F_q} A \ge 1.

(3b) Let r \ge 1 be the least common multiple of the degrees [L_j:\mathbb F_q], put K := \mathbb F_{q^r} and Y_K := Y \times_{\mathbb F_q} K. Each L_j/\mathbb F_q is cyclic of degree dividing r, so L_j \otimes_{\mathbb F_q} K \cong \prod_{[L_j:\mathbb F_q]} K; consequently A_K := A \otimes_{\mathbb F_q} K \cong K^N.

(3c) For every field extension K'/\mathbb F_q the canonical map H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\otimes_{\mathbb F_q} K' \to H^0(Y_{K'},\mathcal O) is an isomorphism: this is flat base change for cohomology of the proper flat \mathbb F_q-morphism Y \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q (every \mathbb F_q-vector space is free, so the cohomology-and-base-change theorem applies). In particular
\[ H^0(Y_K,\mathcal O) \cong A_K \cong K^N, \qquad H^0(Y_k,\mathcal O) \cong A\otimes_{\mathbb F_q} k \cong k^N. \]

(3d) Let \varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_N be the primitive idempotents of A_K \cong K^N. An idempotent of H^0(Y_K,\mathcal O) cuts out an open-and-closed subscheme, so the \varepsilon_i give a decomposition Y_K = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^N Y_i with Y_i := V(1-\varepsilon_i) open and closed in Y_K. Base changing to k, the elements \varepsilon_i\otimes 1 are exactly the primitive idempotents of A\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k = A_K\otimes_K k \cong k^N, so Y_k = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^N Y_{i,k} with Y_{i,k} := Y_i\times_K k = V(1-\varepsilon_i\otimes 1). Each Y_{i,k} is nonempty (otherwise \varepsilon_i\otimes 1 = 0 in k^N, impossible for a primitive idempotent), and by (3c) applied to the summand \varepsilon_i A_K we get H^0(Y_{i,k},\mathcal O) = (\varepsilon_i A)\otimes_{\mathbb F_q} k = k, a field. A noetherian scheme whose ring of global functions is a field is connected (a nontrivial disjoint-union decomposition would yield a nontrivial idempotent in H^0). Thus the Y_{i,k} are precisely the connected components of Y_k; in particular Y_k has finitely (N) many components, each open and closed.

(3e) Each Y_i is smooth over K (open subscheme of the smooth K-scheme Y_K), projective over K (closed subscheme of the K-projective Y_K), of finite type, nonempty, and of pure dimension e: an open-and-closed subscheme of a noetherian pure-dimensional scheme is pure of the same dimension, since its irreducible components are irreducible components of Y_K.

(3f) Each Y_i is geometrically connected over K. Indeed Y_i is proper and geometrically reduced over K (smooth over the perfect field K), and (Y_i)_{\bar K} = Y_{i,k} is connected with H^0 = k, so by (3c) H^0(Y_i,\mathcal O) = K. If for some extension K'/K the scheme Y_{i,K'} were a disjoint union of two nonempty open-and-closed pieces, then H^0(Y_{i,K'},\mathcal O) would be a product of two nonzero rings, of K'-dimension \ge 2; but (3c) gives H^0(Y_{i,K'},\mathcal O) = H^0(Y_i,\mathcal O)\otimes_K K' = K', a contradiction. Hence Y_i is geometrically connected. Moreover Y_i is regular, noetherian and connected, and a connected noetherian normal scheme is irreducible; so Y_i is a (geometrically integral) variety over K.

Step 4 (Poincar\'e traces on the components). Fix i. Apply eoinm:lemma_77 to the smooth projective geometrically connected K-variety Y_i of pure dimension e, with the integer m := r \ge 1 (so q^m = q^r and K = \mathbb F_{q^m}), with k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q = \overline K, and with the prime \ell \neq p. Part (a) of that lemma provides a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear trace
\[ \operatorname{tr}_i : H^{2e}(Y_{i,k}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell(-e) \]
(the cycle-class/Gysin isomorphism), and part (b) asserts that for every 0 \le n \le 2e the pairing
\[ H^n(Y_{i,k}) \times H^{2e-n}(Y_{i,k}) \longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-e), \qquad (x,y) \longmapsto \operatorname{tr}_i(x\cup y), \]
is perfect.

Step 5 (cohomology of a disjoint union). Each Y_{i,k} is open and closed in the separated k-scheme Y_k of finite type. Iterating Spark:lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum (applied to U = Y_k, V = Y_{1,k}, W = \bigsqcup_{i\ge 2} Y_{i,k}, and then to W, and so on; the base case of one piece is trivial) we obtain, for every n, a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism given by restriction
\[ \operatorname{res} : H^n(Y_k) \xrightarrow{\sim} \bigoplus_{i=1}^N H^n(Y_{i,k}), \qquad x \longmapsto (x_i), \quad x_i := x|_{Y_{i,k}}, \]
and, under these identifications, the cup product is computed componentwise: (x\cup y)_i = x_i \cup y_i for all x,y. (Concretely, the lemma gives the assertion for a decomposition into two open-and-closed pieces and states that the cup-product pairing is the direct sum of the two pieces' pairings; the induction on the number of pieces is immediate.) Each H^n(Y_{i,k}) is finite-dimensional, being a direct summand of the finite-dimensional space H^n(Y_k) of Step 1.

Step 6 (definition of tr_Y and perfectness). Define
\[ \operatorname{tr}_Y := \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{tr}_i \circ \operatorname{res}_i \;:\; H^{2e}(Y_k) \longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-e), \]
a finite sum of \mathbb Q_\ell-linear maps, hence \mathbb Q_\ell-linear. For x \in H^n(Y_k) and y \in H^{2e-n}(Y_k), using that each restriction map is a morphism of ringed topoi (hence \operatorname{res}_i(x\cup y) = x_i\cup y_i) and Step 5,
\[ \operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup y) = \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{tr}_i\bigl((x\cup y)_i\bigr) = \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{tr}_i(x_i\cup y_i). \]
Suppose 0 \le n \le 2e. The right-hand side is exactly the orthogonal direct sum of the perfect pairings of Step 4. We check nondegeneracy on the left: if x \neq 0 then x_i \neq 0 for some i; by perfectness of the pairing on Y_{i,k} there exists w \in H^{2e-n}(Y_{i,k}) with \operatorname{tr}_i(x_i\cup w) \neq 0; choosing y with y_i = w and y_j = 0 for j \neq i (possible since res is an isomorphism) gives \operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup y) = \operatorname{tr}_i(x_i\cup w) \neq 0. Nondegeneracy on the right is identical, with the roles of x and y interchanged. Since both H^n(Y_k) and H^{2e-n}(Y_k) are finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell (Step 1), nondegeneracy on both sides is equivalent to the two induced maps H^n(Y_k) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{2e-n}(Y_k),\mathbb Q_\ell(-e)) and H^{2e-n}(Y_k) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^n(Y_k),\mathbb Q_\ell(-e)) being isomorphisms, i.e. to the pairing being perfect. Together with Step 2 (which handles n \notin [0,2e]) this proves perfectness for every integer n.

Step 7 (the case e = 0, spelled out). The argument above covers e = 0: then each Y_i is smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension 0 over K, hence Y_i \cong \operatorname{Spec} K, Y_{i,k} \cong \operatorname{Spec} k, H^0(Y_{i,k}) = \mathbb Q_\ell with higher groups zero, and lemma_77 with d = 0 gives \operatorname{tr}_i : \mathbb Q_\ell \to \mathbb Q_\ell(0) = \mathbb Q_\ell nonzero, so (x,y)\mapsto \operatorname{tr}_i(xy) is perfect. Equivalently, arguing directly: Y is quasi-finite and proper over \mathbb F_q, hence finite, and smooth, hence finite \'etale; so Y_k \cong \bigsqcup_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{Spec} k, H^0(Y_k) = \{\text{locally constant functions } \pi_0(Y_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\} \cong \mathbb Q_\ell^N with H^n = 0 for n > 0, cup product is coordinatewise multiplication, and the sum-of-coordinates trace gives the perfect pairing (x,y)\mapsto\sum_j x_j y_j.

Thus in all cases there exists a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear map \operatorname{tr}_Y : H^{2e}_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \mathbb Q_\ell(-e) such that for every integer n the pairing (x,y)\mapsto \operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup y) is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces.

lemma_410.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be its cycle class via a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and let \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace. For each \(m\in\mathbb Z\) let \(\Lambda_m:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{m+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map (with \(H^r=0\) for \(r<0\) and \(r>2d\)) such that \(\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda_m y)\) for all \(x\in H^{2d-m-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(y\in H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(F_m=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(u)=u^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F_{m+2}\circ\Lambda_m=q\,(\Lambda_m\circ F_m)\) for every integer \(m\).
lemma_410.proof:
Write $H^r:=H^r_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $r\in\mathbb Z$, with the convention $H^r=0$ for $r<0$ and $r>2d$, and write $F_r$ for the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(u)=u^q$, acting on $H^r$. Write $\langle a,b\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}_X(a\cup b)$ whenever the degrees add up to $2d$; this is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear pairing with values in $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, on which the scalar $q^d$ (a positive rational number, hence a non-zero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell$) acts by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear multiplication.

STEP 0 (Preliminaries: vanishing and finite-dimensionality). Since $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ is algebraically closed and $X_k$ is projective of pure dimension $d$, Spark/lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing gives $H^r=0$ for every $r>2d$; for $r<0$ the group is $0$ by definition of cohomological degree. Thus the convention $H^r=0$ for $r\notin[0,2d]$ is legitimate. Since $X$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, eoinm/lemma_45_finite_frob applied to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ (with its natural Frobenius structure) shows each $H^r$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and eoinm/lemma_6a shows each $F_r$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^r$ (with inverse the geometric Frobenius). In particular, for $r\notin[0,2d]$, $H^r=0$ and $F_r$ is the identity of the zero space.

STEP 1 (The pairing is perfect and $q^d$-semi-invariant under Frobenius). Apply eoinm/lemma_77 with the extension degree equal to $1$ (so the ground field is $\mathbb F_q$ and $q^m=q$) and $Y=X$: part (a) provides a canonical $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ (the one normalised by closed points) which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ as multiplication by $q^d$; part (b) asserts that for every $n$ with $0\le n\le 2d$ the pairing $H^n\times H^{2d-n}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(a\cup b)$, is perfect, and that $\langle F_na,F_{2d-n}b\rangle_{\mathrm{tr}}=q^d\langle a,b\rangle_{\mathrm{tr}}$, where we subscript to indicate the pairing built from $\operatorname{tr}$.

The trace $\operatorname{tr}_X$ of the present statement is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $H^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$. Hence $\lambda:=\operatorname{tr}_X\circ\operatorname{tr}^{-1}\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d))\cong\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, and $\operatorname{tr}_X=\lambda\circ\operatorname{tr}$, i.e.
$$\langle a,b\rangle=\lambda\,\langle a,b\rangle_{\mathrm{tr}}\qquad\text{for all }a,b\text{ of complementary degrees.}\tag{1.1}$$
Since $\lambda\neq0$, (1.1) shows that $\langle-,-\rangle$ is perfect on $H^n\times H^{2d-n}$ for every $0\le n\le 2d$: non-degeneracy on each side is unchanged after multiplying the values by a non-zero scalar. (Equivalently, (1.1) identifies $H^{2d-n}$ with the full $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear dual of $H^n$.) Moreover, since $\lambda$ is a scalar and $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ as the scalar $q^d$, the same identity gives, for all $0\le n\le 2d$,
$$\langle F_na,F_{2d-n}b\rangle=\lambda\,q^d\langle a,b\rangle_{\mathrm{tr}}=q^d\langle a,b\rangle.\tag{1.2}$$
We shall use (1.2) twice, for the pairs of degrees $(2d-m,\,m)$ and $(2d-m-2,\,m+2)$.

STEP 2 (Existence and uniqueness of $\Lambda_m$). Spark/lemma_385 applies verbatim to the present data ($d\ge1$, $H$ very ample over $\mathbb F_q$, $\xi=\mathrm{cl}(H)$, $L$ cup product with $\xi$, $\operatorname{tr}_X$ the Poincar\'e duality trace): it yields a unique $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism $\Lambda$ of $\bigoplus_{n=0}^{2d}H^n$ with $\Lambda(H^m)\subseteq H^{m+2)$ for every $m$ and
$$\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y)\qquad(x\in H^{2d-m-2},\ y\in H^m)\tag{2.1}$$
for every $m\ge0$ (with $H^r=0$ for $r<0$ and $r>2d$). Set $\Lambda_m:=\Lambda|_{H^m}:H^m\to H^{m+2}$; for $m<0$ or $m>2d$ the domain is $0$ and $\Lambda_m$ is the unique map from the zero space. Thus a map $H^m\to H^{m+2}$ satisfying the required identity exists for every $m\in\mathbb Z$.

For uniqueness, let $T_1,T_2:H^m\to H^{m+2}$ both satisfy the identity, and fix $y\in H^m$. Then $\langle x,T_1y-T_2y\rangle=\langle Lx,y\rangle-\langle Lx,y\rangle=0$ for all $x\in H^{2d-m-2}$. If $0\le2d-m-2\le2d$, the pairing $H^{2d-m-2}\times H^{m+2}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is perfect by Step 1, so non-degeneracy on the right forces $T_1y=T_2y$. If $2d-m-2<0$ then $m\ge2d-1$, hence $m+2\ge2d+1>2d$ and $H^{m+2}=0$ by Step 0, so again $T_1y=T_2y=0$. Hence $\Lambda_m$ is the unique map appearing in the statement, and it is precisely the restriction to $H^m$ of the operator of Spark/lemma_385. Note also that in the case $2d-m-2<0$ both sides of the desired relation are automatically the zero map $H^m\to H^{m+2}=0$; these cases are recorded explicitly in Step 5.

STEP 3 (Frobenius commutes with $L$ up to the factor $q$). eoinm/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable applies to $X$ (smooth projective of pure dimension $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$), the divisor $H$ and $\xi=\mathrm{cl}(H)$, and states that $F\circ L=q\,L\circ F$ on every $H^m$. Concretely, for every $r\in\mathbb Z$ and every $z\in H^r$,
$$F_{r+2}(Lz)=q\,L(F_rz).\tag{3.1}$$
(For $r\notin[0,2d]$ both sides are zero because $H^r=0$; for $r>2d-2$ the target $H^{r+2}=0$ and both sides vanish, so (3.1) holds for all $r$.)

STEP 4 (The main computation, in the range $0\le m\le 2d-2$). Fix $m$ with $0\le m\le 2d-2$, and let $y\in H^m$ and $x\in H^{2d-m-2}$ be arbitrary. Note first that all pairings below are meaningful: $x\in H^{2d-m-2}$, $Lx\in H^{2d-m}$, $y\in H^m$, $\Lambda_my\in H^{m+2}$, $F_{2d-m-2}x\in H^{2d-m-2}$ (by Step 0/lemma_6a), $F_my\in H^m$, $\Lambda_mF_my\in H^{m+2}$ and $F_{m+2}\Lambda_my\in H^{m+2}$; in each pairing the two degrees add to $2d$.

Applying the defining identity (2.1) to $x$ and $y$ gives
$$\langle x,\Lambda_my\rangle=\langle Lx,y\rangle.\tag{4.1}$$
Apply (1.2) with $n=2d-m$ to the pair $(Lx,\,y)$, where $Lx\in H^{2d-m}$ and $y\in H^m$:
$$\langle F_{2d-m}(Lx),\,F_my\rangle=q^d\langle Lx,y\rangle,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \langle Lx,y\rangle=q^{-d}\langle F_{2d-m}(Lx),\,F_my\rangle.\tag{4.2}$$
By (3.1) with $r=2d-m-2$ and $z=x$, $F_{2d-m}(Lx)=q\,L(F_{2d-m-2}x)$; substituting into (4.2) and using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of the pairing in the first argument,
$$\langle Lx,y\rangle=q^{-d}\langle q\,L(F_{2d-m-2}x),\,F_my\rangle=q^{1-d}\langle L(F_{2d-m-2}x),\,F_my\rangle.\tag{4.3}$$
Now apply the defining identity (2.1) to the class $x':=F_{2d-m-2}x\in H^{2d-m-2}$ and $y':=F_my\in H^m$:
$$\langle L(F_{2d-m-2}x),\,F_my\rangle=\langle F_{2d-m-2}x,\,\Lambda_mF_my\rangle.\tag{4.4}$$
Combining (4.1)--(4.4),
$$\langle x,\Lambda_my\rangle=q^{1-d}\,\langle F_{2d-m-2}x,\,\Lambda_mF_my\rangle.\tag{4.5}$$
On the other hand, apply (1.2) with $n=2d-m-2$ to the pair $(x,\Lambda_my)$, where $x\in H^{2d-m-2}$ and $\Lambda_my\in H^{m+2}$:
$$\langle F_{2d-m-2}x,\,F_{m+2}\Lambda_my\rangle=q^d\langle x,\Lambda_my\rangle,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \langle x,\Lambda_my\rangle=q^{-d}\langle F_{2d-m-2}x,\,F_{m+2}\Lambda_my\rangle.\tag{4.6}$$
Equating the right-hand sides of (4.5) and (4.6) and multiplying by $q^d$ (which is legitimate since $q^d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$) yields
$$\langle F_{2d-m-2}x,\,F_{m+2}\Lambda_my\rangle=q\,\langle F_{2d-m-2}x,\,\Lambda_mF_my\rangle=\langle F_{2d-m-2}x,\,q\,\Lambda_mF_my\rangle,\tag{4.7}$$
the last equality by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity in the second argument. Thus for every $x\in H^{2d-m-2}$,
$$\bigl\langle F_{2d-m-2}x,\;F_{m+2}\Lambda_my-q\,\Lambda_mF_my\bigr\rangle=0.\tag{4.8}$$
The element $F_{m+2}\Lambda_my-q\,\Lambda_mF_my$ lies in $H^{m+2}$. Since $F_{2d-m-2}$ is an automorphism of $H^{2d-m-2}$ (eoinm/lemma_6a), the set $\{F_{2d-m-2}x:x\in H^{2d-m-2}\}$ is all of $H^{2d-m-2}$; and since $0\le m\le 2d-2$ we have $0\le 2d-m-2\le 2d$, so the pairing $H^{2d-m-2}\times H^{m+2}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is perfect by Step 1. Non-degeneracy on the right applied to (4.8) gives
$$F_{m+2}(\Lambda_my)=q\,\Lambda_m(F_my).\tag{4.9}$$
As $y\in H^m$ was arbitrary, $F_{m+2}\circ\Lambda_m=q\,(\Lambda_m\circ F_m)$ as maps $H^m\to H^{m+2}$, for every $m$ with $0\le m\le 2d-2$.

STEP 5 (Remaining values of $m$).
(a) $m\ge2d-1$ (equivalently $2d-m-2<0$). Then $m+2\ge2d+1>2d$, so $H^{m+2}=0$ by Step 0. Both $F_{m+2}\circ\Lambda_m$ and $q\,(\Lambda_m\circ F_m)$ are maps $H^m\to H^{m+2}=0$, hence both are the zero map and are equal.
(b) $m<0$. Then $H^m=0$ by convention, so both sides are maps from the zero space $0$ to $H^{m+2}$ (if $m=-1$ the target is $H^1$, and $\Lambda_{-1}:0\to H^1$ is the zero map); the two composite maps $0\to H^{m+2}$ coincide.
(c) $m>2d$. Then $H^m=0$, and the same argument as in (b) applies: both sides are the zero map $0\to H^{m+2}$ (and $H^{m+2}=0$ as well, since $m+2>2d$).
These exhaust all $m\in\mathbb Z$ together with Step 4.

STEP 6 (Conclusion). Steps 4 and 5 establish $F_{m+2}\circ\Lambda_m=q\,(\Lambda_m\circ F_m)$ for every integer $m$, where $\Lambda_m:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{m+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the unique map characterised by $\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda_my)$ for all $x\in H^{2d-m-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $y\in H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (existence from Spark/lemma_385, uniqueness from the perfectness in Step 1, both established in Step 2). This is exactly the required statement. $\blacksquare$

lemma_finite_over_strictly_henselian_exa.statement: Let \(R\) be a strictly henselian local ring and let \(f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) be a finite morphism. Then the global sections functor \(G\mapsto\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},G)\) from abelian sheaves on the small étale site of \(X\) to abelian groups is exact.
lemma_finite_over_strictly_henselian_exa.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_finite_over_strictly_henselian_exact",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "PROOF. Throughout, (R,m,k) is a strictly henselian local ring: by definition its residue field k is separably closed and R is henselian, where we take henselianity to mean the FACTORIZATION FORM of Hensel's lemma: for every monic P \in R[T] and every factorization \bar P=\bar F\bar G in k[T] with \bar F,\bar G monic and coprime, there are monic F,G\in R[T] lifting \bar F,\bar G with P=FG. (This form is equivalent to each of the usual definitions of a henselian local ring; cf. SGA 1 Exp. VIII, Stacks Project, Tags 04GH, 09X7. We use only this form, applied to the ring R, which is henselian by hypothesis.)

A finite morphism is affine, so X=\operatorname{Spec}B with B a finite R-algebra. We prove that \Gamma(X_{\acute et},-) is exact.

===============================================================
PART I. A FIELD FACT.

Proposition 1. Let k be a separably closed field and K/k a FINITE purely inseparable extension. Then K is separably closed.
Proof. Let L/K be a finite separable extension. Since K/k is finite by hypothesis, L/k is finite. Let M=\{x\in L: x \text{ is separable algebraic over } k\} be the maximal separable subextension of L/k; M/k is finite separable, hence M=k (k separably closed). Thus every x\in L is purely inseparable over k. If char(k)=0 this means x\in k\subset K. If char(k)=p>0 there is n\ge 0 with x^{p^{n}}\in k\subset K, so x is purely inseparable over K. But L/K is separable, and an element which is both separable and purely inseparable over K lies in K; hence x\in K. Thus L=K, so K has no nontrivial finite separable extensions, i.e. K is separably closed. \square

Corollary 1b. Every finite field extension of a separably closed field is purely inseparable (same maximal-separable-subextension argument), hence, by Proposition 1, separably closed. \square

===============================================================
PART II. LIFTING IDEMPOTENTS ACROSS FINITE ALGEBRAS OVER A HENSELIAN LOCAL RING.

We fix a henselian local ring (A,\mathfrak m) with residue field \kappa, and finite A-algebras C.

Lemma 2.1 (the maximal ideal of A lands in the Jacobson radical). If C is a finite A-algebra, then \mathfrak m C\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(C).
Proof. Let M\subset C be maximal. Then C/M is a field which is a finite A-module, hence a finite A/(M\cap A)-module; put D:=A/(M\cap A), a domain, and K:=C/M, a field containing D with K finite as D-module. For 0\ne d\in D, the element d^{-1}\in K satisfies d^{-1}K\subseteq K; since K is a finite D-module, the determinant trick (Cayley--Hamilton applied to multiplication by d^{-1} on the finite D-module K) gives d^{-n}+c_1d^{-(n-1)}+\cdots+c_n=0 with c_i\in D; multiplying by d^{n-1} gives d^{-1}=-(c_1+\cdots+c_nd^{n-1})\in D. So D is a field, M\cap A is maximal in A, hence M\cap A=\mathfrak m. Thus \mathfrak m\subseteq M for every maximal M, i.e. \mathfrak mC\subseteq\bigcap_M M=\operatorname{Jac}(C). \square

Lemma 2.2 (monogenic lifting). Let P\in A[T] be monic of degree n and let \tilde e\in (A/\mathfrak m)[T]/(\bar P)=\kappa[T]/(\bar P) be an idempotent. Then \tilde e is the reduction of an idempotent e\in A[T]/(P).
Proof. Write \bar P=\prod_{i=1}^{s}\bar Q_i^{e_i} in \kappa[T] with the \bar Q_i distinct monic irreducibles. By the Chinese remainder theorem \kappa[T]/(\bar P)\cong\prod_i\kappa[T]/(\bar Q_i^{e_i}), and \tilde

{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_finite_over_strictly_henselian_exact",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "PROOF. Let (R,m,k) be strictly henselian local. We take henselianity in the factorization form of Hensel's lemma: if P in R[T] is monic and bar P = bar F bar G in k[T] with bar F, bar G monic and coprime, then P = F G for monic lifts F,G. A finite morphism is affine, so X = Spec B with B a finite R-algebra. If B=0 then X is empty and Gamma(empty_et,-)=0 is exact. Assume B nonzero.

PART I. Field fact. If k is separably closed and K/k is finite purely inseparable, then K is separably closed. Let L/K be finite separable. Since K/k is finite, L/k is finite. Let M be the maximal separable subextension of L/k. Then M/k is finite separable, hence M=k. Thus every x in L is purely inseparable over k. If char k=0 this means x in k subset K. If char k=p>0, then x^{p^n} in k subset K for some n, so x is purely inseparable over K. But L/K is separable, hence x in K. Thus L=K. Consequently every finite extension of a separably closed field is separably closed.

PART II. Idempotent lifting. Let (A,m,kappa) be henselian local and C a finite A-algebra.
Lemma 2.1. mC subset Jac(C). Proof: Let M be a maximal ideal of C. Then C/M is a field which is finite as an A-module. Put D=A/(M cap A). Then D is a domain and K=C/M is a field finite as a D-module. For 0 neq d in D, multiplication by d^{-1} is a D-linear endomorphism of the finite D-module K. Cayley-Hamilton gives (d^{-1})^n + c_1(d^{-1})^{n-1}+...+c_n=0 with c_i in D. Multiplying by d^{n-1} gives d^{-1}=-(c_1+...+c_n d^{n-1}) in D. Hence D is a field, so M cap A is maximal in A and equals m. Thus m is contained in every maximal ideal of C, i.e. mC subset Jac(C).

Lemma 2.2 (Artinian surjection). If pi:S->T is a surjection of Artinian rings, every idempotent of T lifts to S. Proof: Decompose S=prod_{j=1}^r S_j and T=prod_{l=1}^t T_l into local Artinian rings, with primitive idempotents e_j in S. The images f_j=pi(e_j) are pairwise orthogonal idempotents of T summing to 1. In T, idempotents correspond to subsets of {1,...,t}; let L_j be the support of f_j. The sets L_j form a partition of {1,...,t}. If |L_j|>=2, then since all other factors S_{j'} with j' neq j have zero support on L_j, the projection pi(S_j)->prod_{l in L_j} T_l is surjective: for any tuple (a_l), choose s in S with pi(s)_l=a_l on L_j, then pi(e_j s) has the desired tuple on L_j and zero outside. But pi(S_j) is a quotient of the local ring S_j, hence local, whereas a product of two or more nonzero local rings is not local. Contradiction. Thus every nonzero f_j is primitive. The nonzero f_j are exactly the primitive idempotents of T. Any idempotent e of T is a sum of some f_j, and the sum of the corresponding e_j lifts it.

Lemma 2.3 (monogenic lifting). Let P in A[T] be monic and let tilde e be an idempotent in kappa[T]/(bar P). Then tilde e lifts to an idempotent e in A[T]/(P). Proof: If tilde e=0 or 1, lift by 0 or 1. Factor bar P=prod_i bar Q_i^{a_i} in kappa[T] with the bar Q_i distinct monic irreducibles. By the Chinese remainder theorem, kappa[T]/(bar P)=prod_i kappa[T]/(bar Q_i^{a_i}); each factor is local, so the component of tilde e is 0 or 1. Let I be the set of indices with component 1, and set bar F=prod_{i notin I} bar Q_i^{a_i}, bar G=prod_{i in I} bar Q_i^{a_i}, with empty products equal to 1. Then bar F, bar G are monic, coprime, bar F bar G=bar P, and tilde e is 0 modulo bar F and 1 modulo bar G. Hensel's factorization form gives monic F,G in A[T] lifting bar F,bar G with P=FG. We show F and G are comaximal. The module M=A[T]/(F) is finite free over A. Modulo m, M/mM=kappa[T]/(bar F), and multiplication by G is invertible there because bar F and bar G are coprime. By Nakayama, multiplication by G on M is surjective. Since M is finite free, a surjective endomorphism is bijective: choose a right inverse matrix and take determinants. Hence 1 lies in the image, so there exist U,V in A[T] with U F+V G=1. Put e=U F mod P. Then e^2-e=U F(UF-1)=U F(-V G)=-U V P=0 in A[T]/(P). Reducing U F+V G=1 modulo m and evaluating in kappa[T]/(bar F) x kappa[T]/(bar G) shows U F maps to (0,1), so e reduces to tilde e. If the convention for tilde e is reversed, replace e by 1-e.

Lemma 2.4 (general idempotent lifting). For a finite A-algebra C, the map Idem(C)->Idem(C/mC) is bijective. Injectivity: by Lemma 2.1, mC subset Jac(C). If e,f have the same image modulo m, then e(1-f) and (1-e)f are idempotents lying in Jac(C), hence are zero; therefore e=ef=f. Surjectivity: take bar e in C/mC. Choose b in C lifting bar e and set C'=A[b]. Since C is finite over A, b satisfies a monic polynomial P in A[T] by Cayley-Hamilton, so C' is finite over A and A[T]/(P)->C' is surjective. The ring C'/mC' is finite-dimensional over kappa, hence Artinian. Its image D in C/mC is an Artinian subring containing bar e. By Lemma 2.2, bar e lifts to an idempotent bar e' in C'/mC'. Again by Lemma 2.2, bar e' lifts to an idempotent bar e'' in kappa[T]/(bar P). Lemma 2.3 lifts bar e'' to an idempotent e'' in A[T]/(P), whose image in C' and then in C lifts bar e.

PART III. Decompose B. Since B/mB is finite-dimensional over k, it is Artinian. Write B/mB=prod_{i=1}^r D_i with D_i Artin local. Lift the factor idempotents bar e_i to idempotents e_i in B using Lemma 2.4. They are pairwise orthogonal and sum to 1. Put B_i=e_i B. Each B_i is local: an idempotent f of B_i, viewed as an idempotent of B, reduces to an idempotent of D_i, hence to 0 or 1. If it reduces to 0, then f is an idempotent in mB_i subset Jac(B_i), so f=0. If it reduces to 1, then e_i-f reduces to 0, so f=e_i. Thus B=prod_i B_i with each B_i finite local over R. Let n_i be the maximal ideal of B_i. Since mB_i subset Jac(B_i)=n_i, the residue field kappa_i=B_i/n_i is a quotient of B_i/mB_i=D_i, hence is finite over k. By Part I, kappa_i is separably closed.

PART IV. Sections over local factors. We prove: if (B,n) is a finite local R-algebra whose residue field kappa_B is separably closed, then for every etale morphism p:E->Spec B and every point e in E over n there is a unique section sigma:Spec B->E with sigma(n)=e.
Existence. Choose an affine open neighbourhood V=Spec C of e. By the standard etale local form, after shrinking V to an open neighbourhood E_0 of e, there are a monic P in B[T] and h in B[T] such that E_0=Spec((B[T]/(P))_h), and e corresponds to a prime q over n with h(q) neq 0 and P'(q) invertible. Let C_0=B[T]/(P), finite free over B, and let q_0 be the contraction of q to C_0. Because p is etale, kappa(q)/kappa_B is finite separable; since kappa_B is separably closed, kappa(q)=kappa_B. The finite kappa_B-algebra C_0/nC_0 is Artinian. The point q_0 is isolated in its spectrum; let bar e_0 be the idempotent of C_0/nC_0 which is 1 on the local factor at q_0 and 0 on the other factors. Since h is invertible at q_0 and the fibre of an etale morphism is etale, this local factor is the field kappa_B. Lift bar e_0 to an idempotent e_0 in C_0: first lift from C_0/nC_0 to C_0/mC_0 using Lemma 2.2 (both are Artinian and n contains mB), then lift from C_0/mC_0 to C_0 using Lemma 2.4 applied to the finite R-algebra C_0. Let C=e_0 C_0. It is a direct summand of the finite free B-module C_0, hence finite free over B.
