Its reduction modulo n is the local factor just described, so C/nC is isomorphic to kappa_B as a B/n-algebra. The structural map B->C induces an isomorphism B/n -> C/nC. Hence C = image(B)+nC, and Nakayama implies B->C is surjective. Since C is finite free and C/nC has dimension 1, C has rank 1; a surjective B-linear map B->B is an isomorphism. Thus C is B as a B-algebra. Composing C_0 -> e_0 C_0 = C with the inverse C -> B gives a B-algebra homomorphism alpha:C_0->B. Let t=alpha(T). The reduction of t is the root corresponding to q_0, and h(t) is a unit because its reduction is nonzero. Hence alpha factors through (C_0)_h, giving a section Spec B -> E_0 subset E through e.
Uniqueness. If sigma_1,sigma_2:Spec B->E are two sections agreeing at n, their equalizer is the inverse image of the diagonal Delta:E->E x_B E under (sigma_1,sigma_2). The diagonal of an etale morphism is an open immersion, so the equalizer is an open subset of Spec B containing the closed point n. In a local scheme every open set containing the closed point is the whole scheme. Hence sigma_1=sigma_2.

PART V. Exactness. Fix one local factor B_i and write B for it. The functor Gamma(Spec B_et,-) is left exact: in the abelian category of sheaves it is Hom(Z,-), or equivalently exactness of a short exact sequence can be checked on the final object Spec B. Let F->G be an epimorphism of etale sheaves and let s in G(Spec B). Epimorphisms of sheaves are locally surjective, so there is an etale cover {U_j->Spec B} and sections s_j in F(U_j) mapping to s|_{U_j}. Some U_j has a point u over the closed point n. By Part IV there is a section sigma:Spec B->U_j with sigma(n)=u. Then sigma^* s_j in F(Spec B) maps to sigma^*(s|_{U_j})=s. Thus Gamma(Spec B,F)->Gamma(Spec B,G) is surjective. Therefore Gamma(Spec B_i_et,-) is exact for every i.
Finally X=Spec B is the disjoint union of the open and closed subschemes Spec B_i. The open cover {Spec B_i->X} is an etale cover with empty intersections, so the sheaf condition gives Gamma(X_et,G)=prod_i Gamma((Spec B_i)_et,G|_{Spec B_i}) functorially in G. Finite products are exact in abelian groups. Hence Gamma(X_et,-) is exact. QED."
}

lemma_hc_zero_smooth_affine_positive_dim.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of k, and let U be a smooth affine scheme of finite type over k of pure dimension \(d\ge 1\). Then \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\), where \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) denotes the constant sheaf on the small etale site of U.
lemma_hc_zero_smooth_affine_positive_dim.proof:
Let f:U -> Spec k be the structure morphism. If U is empty the assertion is trivial, so assume U is nonempty. Since U is affine of finite type over k, f is separated of finite type. By the definition of compactly supported cohomology in degree 0, H^0_{et,c}(U,Q_l) is the group of global sections s of the constant sheaf Q_l on U_et whose support supp(s) is proper over k.

U is noetherian. Hence it has finitely many irreducible components. Each connected component is a union of irreducible components, so U has finitely many connected components C_1,...,C_r. Each C_i is closed, and because there are finitely many components its complement is a finite union of closed subsets, hence closed; thus each C_i is open and closed.

By repeated application of lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum (with a=0), the open-and-closed decomposition U = C_1 disjoint union ... disjoint union C_r identifies H^0_{et,c}(U,Q_l) with the direct sum over i of H^0_{et,c}(C_i,Q_l). Therefore it suffices to prove the assertion for a connected component C.

Fix such C. It is open and closed in the affine scheme U, hence affine: if U=Spec A, clopen subsets correspond to idempotents e in A, and C is Spec(A/(1-e)). It is smooth over k, hence reduced and of finite type. Since U is pure of dimension d, every irreducible component of C is an irreducible component of U (an irreducible component is connected, so if it meets the connected component C it is contained in C); consequently dim C=d>=1.

Now take s in H^0_{et,c}(C,Q_l). Then s is a global section of the constant sheaf Q_l with proper support. Since C is connected, every global section of the constant sheaf is constant; equivalently, it is a morphism from the connected scheme C to the discrete scheme given by a disjoint union of copies of Spec k. Thus s is given by an element lambda in Q_l. If lambda is nonzero, then every stalk of s is nonzero, so supp(s)=C as a set. Because C is smooth, hence reduced, the reduced induced structure on supp(s) is C itself. The hypothesis that s has compact support therefore says that C -> Spec k is proper.

We now show that this is impossible. Write C=Spec B, with B a reduced finitely generated k-algebra. If dim C>=1, then B is not equal to k. Choose b in B not in k. Since B is reduced noetherian, it has finitely many minimal primes p_1,...,p_s. If the image of b in each residue field kappa(p_j) were algebraic over k, then because k is algebraically closed it would lie in k for each j. The regular function b would then be constant on each irreducible component. As there are finitely many components and C is connected, these constants must all be equal; otherwise the preimages of two different values would be nonempty disjoint open-and-closed subsets. Hence b would equal a scalar on every minimal prime, and reducedness would imply b in k, contradiction. Thus for some minimal prime p, the image t of b in L=kappa(p) is transcendental over k. Let Z be the corresponding irreducible component and eta its generic point. Choose a valuation ring V of L containing k but not t (extend the valuation on k(t) with v(t)=-1). The generic point eta gives a k-morphism Spec L -> C. Since C is proper over k, the valuative criterion extends this morphism to a k-morphism Spec V -> C. The corresponding ring map B -> V sends b to an element of V whose image in L is t, contradicting t not in V. Hence dim C=0, contradiction. Thus lambda=0 and s=0.

Thus H^0_{et,c}(C,Q_l)=0 for every connected component C, and the direct-sum decomposition gives H^0_{et,c}(U,Q_l)=0.

lemma_415.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\) and \(r\ge1\) be integers, let \(C_1,\dots,C_r\) be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(X=C_1\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}C_r\), and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Then the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple, equivalently diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\).
lemma_415.proof:
Fix a prime power q = p^a, a prime \ell \neq p, integers m \ge 1 and r \ge 1, and smooth projective geometrically connected curves C_1,\dots,C_r over \mathbb F_{q^m}. Write
\[ Q := q^m = p^{am},\qquad K := \mathbb F_{q^m} = \mathbb F_Q,\qquad X := C_1\times_K\cdots\times_K C_r,\qquad k := \overline{\mathbb F}_q .\]
Since Q = p^{am} is again a prime power with the same residue characteristic p, we have k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q = \overline{\mathbb F}_{Q} (the algebraic closure of \mathbb F_q in a fixed algebraic closure of k is the same as that of \mathbb F_Q, because \mathbb F_q \subset \mathbb F_Q \subset \overline{\mathbb F}_q and both finite fields have the same algebraic closure inside \overline{\mathbb F}_q). Also \ell \neq p = \operatorname{char} K, so \ell is invertible on Spec K.

For a smooth projective K-variety W and n \ge 0 we write
\[ F_{W,n} := (\mathrm{id}_{W_k}\times \operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* : H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad \sigma(c)=c^{Q}=c^{q^m},\]
the Q-power (= q^m-power) arithmetic Frobenius. The claim to be proved is: for every n \ge 0, F_{X,n} is semisimple, equivalently diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.

Step 0 (finite-dimensionality). X is proper over K (see Step 1), so by lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm), applied to the proper K-variety X with the constant sheaf \mathbb Q_\ell on X_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, each H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell and carries a canonical \mathbb Q_\ell-linear arithmetic Frobenius automorphism, which is precisely F_{X,n}. Thus the notions "semisimple" and "diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell" used below are the usual ones for automorphisms of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces; by lemma_5 (eoinm) they are equivalent.

Step 1 (X is a smooth projective K-variety). Each structure morphism C_i \to Spec K is smooth and projective, hence of finite type, separated and proper. The product X = \prod_{i=1}^r C_i over K is of finite type over K (finite products of finite-type morphisms are of finite type), and the structure morphism X \to Spec K is the composite X \to \coprod-free product (\operatorname{Spec} K)^r = \operatorname{Spec} K, i.e. the composition of the projection X \to C_1 (a base change of \prod_{i\ge2}C_i \to Spec K, hence proper/smooth by stability of properness and smoothness under base change) with C_1 \to Spec K (proper and smooth). Since properness and smoothness are stable under base change and under composition, X \to Spec K is proper and smooth; projectivity of a product of projective K-schemes follows by embedding X into a product of projective spaces and composing with the Segre embedding \mathbb P^N\times\mathbb P^N\to\mathbb P^{N'}, so X is projective over K. In particular X is a smooth projective K-variety, so all the cited lemmas apply to it. (Geometric connectedness of X is not needed anywhere in the argument.)

Step 2 (three pieces of elementary linear algebra, proved explicitly).
(a) Direct sums. Let V_1,\dots,V_s be finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces and T_j \in \mathrm{GL}(V_j) operators each diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. Then \bigoplus_j T_j on \bigoplus_j V_j is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell: after extending scalars to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, choose for each j a basis B_j of V_j\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell consisting of eigenvectors of T_j\otimes\mathrm{id}; the disjoint union \bigsqcup_j B_j is a basis of (\bigoplus_j V_j)\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell (the sum is direct, so the inclusions V_j\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \hookrightarrow (\bigoplus_j V_j)\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell identify the summands with mutually complementary subspaces) and consists of eigenvectors of \bigoplus_j (T_j\otimes\mathrm{id}).
(b) Tensor products. If T \in \mathrm{GL}(V) and S \in \mathrm{GL}(W) are diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, so is T\otimes S on V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W. Indeed, choose \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell-bases (e_i)_i of V_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}:=V\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell with T_\sigma e_i = \alpha_i e_i and (f_j)_j of W_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} with S_\sigma f_j = \beta_j f_j. Then (e_i\otimes f_j)_{i,j} is a basis of (V\otimes W)\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \cong V_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}\otimes_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}W_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} (explicitly: e_i\otimes f_j = \sum_{i',j'} c_{i,i'}d_{j,j'} e_{i'}\otimes f_{j'} forces, by linear independence of the pure tensors in the tensor product of two bases, c_{i,i'}d_{j,j'}=0 unless i'=i and j'=j), and
\[ (T\otimes S)_\sigma(e_i\otimes f_j) = (T_\sigma e_i)\otimes(S_\sigma f_j) = (\alpha_i\beta_j)\,(e_i\otimes f_j), \]
so (e_i\otimes f_j) is an eigenbasis.
(c) Conjugation. If \varphi:V\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }W is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism with \varphi\circ T = S\circ\varphi, then T is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell if and only if S is: \varphi\otimes\mathrm{id} is an isomorphism V\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim\ } W\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell intertwining T_\sigma with S_\sigma, and it maps an eigenbasis of T_\sigma bijectively onto an eigenbasis of S_\sigma (eigenvectors are preserved because \varphi is bijective, and it preserves \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell-linear independence).

Step 3 (base case r=1). Here X = C_1, which is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \mathbb F_{q^m} = \mathbb F_{q^m}. Lemma_364 (Spark), applied with the given q and m, says exactly that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (\mathrm{id}_{C_{1,k}}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple, i.e. diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_{1,k},\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n \ge 0. This is the desired statement for r=1.

Step 4 (induction step). Let r \ge 2 and assume the statement proved for products of r-1 smooth projective geometrically connected curves over K = \mathbb F_{q^m} (with the same q and m). Put X' := C_1\times_K\cdots\times_K C_{r-1}; by Step 1 (applied to r-1 in place of r) X' is a smooth projective K-variety, and X = X'\times_K C_r. The induction hypothesis says that F_{X',a} is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell on H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every a \ge 0, and Step 3 says that F_{C_r,b} is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell on H^b_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_{r,k},\mathbb Q_\ell) for every b \ge 0.

We now apply lemma_81 (eoinm) with the prime power Q = p^{am} in the role of its "q", with K = \mathbb F_Q as the ground field, with X := X' and Y := C_r (both smooth projective over K, and \ell \neq p = \operatorname{char}K). Its conclusion for the given n is that the K\unneth map
\[ \kappa_n : \bigoplus_{a+b=n} H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^b_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_{r,k},\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\bigl((X'\times_K C_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr) = H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \]
is an isomorphism which carries the operator F_{X',a}\otimes F_{C_r,b} on the (a,b)-summand to the Q-power (= q^m-power) arithmetic Frobenius on the target; that is,
\[ \kappa_n\circ\Bigl(\bigoplus_{a+b=n} F_{X',a}\otimes F_{C_r,b}\Bigr) = F_{X,n}\circ\kappa_n . \]
By Step 2(b), each summand operator F_{X',a}\otimes F_{C_r,b} is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell (the sum over a+b=n is finite, since H^a = 0 for a > 2(r-1) and H^b = 0 for b > 2, so the direct sum is a finite direct sum); by Step 2(a), the direct sum \bigoplus_{a+b=n}(F_{X',a}\otimes F_{C_r,b}) is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell; and by Step 2(c), applied to the intertwiner \kappa_n, F_{X,n} is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. Equivalently, by lemma_5, F_{X,n} is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

(One may also reach the same conclusion directly from the "Hence" clause of lemma_81, which asserts precisely that semisimplicity on all H^a(X'_k) and all H^b(C_{r,k}) implies semisimplicity on all H^n((X'\times_K C_r)_k); the computation in Steps 2(a)-(c) is the explicit linear-algebra content of that clause, reproduced here so that no step is left implicit.)

Step 5 (assembly and edge cases). By induction on r \ge 1, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F_{X,n} is semisimple, equivalently diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n \ge 0. The argument treats every n \ge 0 uniformly (including n = 0, where \kappa_0 identifies H^0(X_k) with H^0(X'_k)\otimes H^0(C_{r,k}) and the Frobenius is the tensor product of the two degree-zero Frobenius operators, and including arbitrarily large n, where the finite direct sum in Step 4 is simply empty/zero whenever no pair (a,b) with a+b=n contributes, in which case H^n(X_k)=0 and the zero operator is trivially diagonalisable). The hypotheses that each C_i is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q^m} were used only to invoke lemma_364 in the base case and to ensure the K\unneth isomorphism of lemma_81 applies; no genus restriction is needed (genus 0 curves are covered by lemma_364 as stated). This completes the proof.\n\nRemark on the role of the base change q \mapsto q^m: every cited lemma was stated for an arbitrary prime power in the role of "q"; substituting the prime power Q = q^m = p^{am} (with ground field \mathbb F_Q = \mathbb F_{q^m} and algebraic closure k = \overline{\mathbb F}_Q = \overline{\mathbb F}_q) is legitimate and produces exactly the operator (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, appearing in the statement.

lemma_proj_principal_open_affine.statement: Let \(S=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}S_n\) be a commutative \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)-graded ring, let \(d\ge1\), and let \(F\in S_d\) be homogeneous. Equip \(\operatorname{Proj}S\) with its usual scheme structure and \(D_+(F)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Proj}S : F\notin\mathfrak p\}\) with the induced open subscheme structure. Then \(D_+(F)\) is canonically isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Spec} S_{(F)}\), where \(S_{(F)}:=(S_F)_0\) is the degree-zero part of the localisation of \(S\) at the multiplicative set \(\{1,F,F^2,\dots\}\).
lemma_proj_principal_open_affine.proof:
Proof. Let S_+ = ⊕_{n>0} S_n. Recall that Proj S is the set of homogeneous prime ideals p with S_+ not contained in p, with the Zariski topology generated by the closed sets V(I) for homogeneous ideals I, and that for a homogeneous element H the basic open D_+(H) has structure sheaf O(D_+(H)) = (S_H)_0. We prove the assertion in several steps.

1. Nilpotent case. If F is nilpotent, say F^r=0, then every prime ideal of S contains F, hence D_+(F)=∅. In the localization S_F one has 1 = F^r/F^r = 0, so S_F is the zero ring and therefore S_{(F)}=(S_F)_0 is the zero ring. Its spectrum is empty. Thus D_+(F) and Spec S_{(F)} are both empty, and the unique map between them is a canonical isomorphism of schemes. Henceforth assume F is not nilpotent.

2. Reduction to degree one by the Veronese subring. Put d=deg F and let R=S^{(d)}=⊕_{n≥0} S_{nd} be the d-th Veronese subring, graded by R_n=S_{nd}. Define c:Proj S→Proj R by c(p)=p∩R. This is well defined: if c(p) contained R_+, then every element of S_{nd} for n>0 lies in p; for any a∈S_m with m>0, a^d∈S_{dm}⊂p, and since p is prime, a∈p, so S_+⊂p, contradiction. Define e:Proj R→Proj S by e(q)=q^* = ⊕_{m≥0}{a∈S_m | a^d∈q}. We check q^* is a homogeneous prime ideal. First it is an ideal: if a∈q^* is homogeneous of degree m and s∈S_n is homogeneous, then (sa)^d=s^d a^d∈q because s^d∈R_n and q is an ideal of R. For homogeneous a,b∈S_m with a^d,b^d∈q, each term a^i b^{d-i} lies in S_{dm}=R_m and its d-th power is (a^d)^i(b^d)^{d-i}∈q; since q is prime, a^i b^{d-i}∈q. Hence (a+b)^d∈q, so a+b∈q^*. For homogeneous a∈S_m,b∈S_n, if ab∈q^*, then (ab)^d=a^d b^d∈q, so a^d∈q or b^d∈q. Thus q^* is prime. It does not contain S_+: if S_+⊂q^*, then for every b∈R_m=S_{dm} with m>0 we have b∈q^*, hence b^d∈q and therefore b∈q, contradicting q∈Proj R. The maps c and e are inverse: c(e(q))=q^*∩R={b∈R_m | b^d∈q}=q because q is prime, and e(c(p))={a∈S_m | a^d∈p}=p because p is prime.

The map c is a homeomorphism. For homogeneous H∈S_e, D_+(H)=D_+(H^d), and H^d∈R_e; hence c(D_+(H))=D_+(H^d) in Proj R. The same identity for inverse images shows continuity of c and of e.

It remains to compare structure sheaves on the basis of opens D_+(H^d) with H homogeneous. On D_+(H^d)⊂Proj S we have O=(S_{H^d})_0, while on the corresponding open of Proj R we have O=(R_{H^d})_0. These two rings are canonically equal: an element of (S_{H^d})_0 is a fraction a/(H^d)^n with deg a=n deg(H^d)=nde, hence a∈S_{nde}=R_{ne}; conversely every such fraction is already in (R_{H^d})_0. The identifications are compatible with restrictions, so c is an isomorphism of schemes. Under c, the element F∈S_d becomes an element of R_1, and (S_F)_0=(R_F)_0 because a fraction a/F^n has degree zero exactly when deg a=nd, i.e. a∈R_n. Therefore it suffices to prove the theorem when deg F=1.

3. The case deg F=1: the topological bijection. Assume deg F=1 and put A=S_F and R=A_0=(S_F)_0. The map Φ:R[T,T^{-1}]→A, rT^n↦rF^n, is an isomorphism of Z-graded rings, where deg T=1. It is a homomorphism by construction. Surjectivity: if a/F^m∈A is homogeneous of degree n, then deg a=m+n, so m+n≥0 and r=a/F^{m+n}∈R; then a/F^m=rF^n=Φ(rT^n). Injectivity: a sum Σ r_iT^i maps to Σ r_iF^i; the summands have distinct degrees, so each r_iF^i=0; since F is a unit in A, r_i=0 in A, hence in R.

For p∈D_+(F), the localization p_F={a/F^m | ∃t, F^t a∈p} is a homogeneous prime ideal of A. Define ψ(p)=p_F∩R. For q∈Spec R, define p_q=Φ(qR[T,T^{-1}])∩S explicitly as p_q=⊕_{m≥0}{a∈S_m | a/F^m∈q}. Because Φ is a graded isomorphism, qR[T,T^{-1}] is a homogeneous prime of A and p_q is a homogeneous prime of S. Moreover F∉p_q since F/F=1∉q, and S_+ is not contained in p_q because F∈S_+. Thus p_q∈D_+(F). The maps ψ and q↦p_q are inverse. If p∈D_+(F), then under Φ the homogeneous prime p_F is generated by its degree-zero part p_F∩R, so p_{ψ(p)}=p. If q∈Spec R, then ψ(p_q)=q by the explicit description of p_q. Hence ψ:D_+(F)→Spec R is a bijection.

For homogeneous G∈S_e, set g=G/F^e∈R. For p∈D_+(F), G∈p iff G/1∈p_F iff gF^e∈p_F. Since F^e is a unit in A, this is equivalent to g∈p_F∩R=ψ(p). Therefore ψ(D_+(G)∩D_+(F))=D(g). The sets D_+(G)∩D_+(F) form a basis of D_+(F), and the sets D(g) form a basis of Spec R, so ψ is a homeomorphism.

4. The case deg F=1: the sheaf isomorphism. We first record a simple graded localization fact. If B is a Z-graded ring and t∈B is homogeneous of degree 0, then the natural map (B_0)_t→(B_t)_0 is an isomorphism. Surjectivity: take x∈(B_t)_0 and write x=b/t^N with b=Σ b_i homogeneous. Since x has degree 0, each nonzero homogeneous component b_i with i≠0 becomes zero in B_t; hence t^{M_i}b_i=0 for some M_i. Let M be their maximum. Then x=t^M b/t^{M+N}=t^M b_0/t^{M+N}, with t^M b_0∈B_0. Injectivity is the same localization relation inside B_0.

Now let G∈S_e be homogeneous and set g=G/F^e∈R. Let B=A=S_F and u=G/1∈B, a homogeneous element of degree e. There is a canonical graded isomorphism B_u≅S_{FG}, since localizing S_F at G/1 is the same as localizing S at FG. Also u=F^e g in B. In B_g the element u maps to the unit F^e g, so the universal property of localization gives a unique B-algebra isomorphism α:B_u→B_g with α(u^{-1})=(F^e g)^{-1}; its inverse sends g^{-1} to F^e u^{-1}. This isomorphism is homogeneous of degree 0. Combining with the graded localization fact gives a canonical ring isomorphism
θ_G:(S_{FG})_0=(B_u)_0≅(B_g)_0=(B_0)_g=R_g.
Explicitly, for a homogeneous element a∈S_{ν(e+1)},
θ_G(a/(FG)^ν)=(a/F^{ν(e+1)})/g^ν.
The exponent ν(e+1) is necessary: deg(a/F^{ν(e+1)})=ν(e+1)-ν(e+1)=0, so the numerator lies in R.

We check compatibility with restrictions. Let K∈S_k be homogeneous and let k'=K/F^k∈R. The restriction (S_{FG})_0→(S_{FGK})_0 sends a/(FG)^ν to aK^ν/(FGK)^ν. Applying θ_{GK} gives (aK^ν/F^{ν(e+1+k)})/((GK)/F^{e+k})^ν. On the other hand, applying θ_G first gives (a/F^{ν(e+1)})/g^ν, and the localization map R_g→R_{gk'} sends this to (a/F^{ν(e+1)})(k')^ν/(gk')^ν, which is the same element. Thus the θ_G are compatible with the restriction maps between the basic opens D_+(FG). Since any inclusion of these basic opens becomes of this form after replacing a generator by a power (which does not change the open), the compatible family {θ_G} glues to an isomorphism of sheaves O_{D_+(F)}≅ψ^{-1}O_{Spec R}; equivalently, the inverses θ_G^{-1}:R_g→(S_{FG})_0 are compatible and define the morphism of sheaves ψ^#:O_{Spec R}→ψ_*O_{D_+(F)}.

Together with the homeomorphism ψ, this is an isomorphism of locally ringed spaces, hence an isomorphism of schemes, in the case deg F=1.

5. End of proof. For arbitrary d=deg F, compose the canonical Veronese isomorphism c:D_+(F)⊂Proj S→D_+(F)⊂Proj S^{(d)} with the degree-one isomorphism D_+(F)≅Spec((S^{(d)}_F)_0). Since (S^{(d)}_F)_0=(S_F)_0=S_{(F)}, this gives the required canonical isomorphism D_+(F)≅Spec S_{(F)}. All maps are defined by universal properties of localization and by the canonical Veronese contraction, so no choices are involved. QED.

lemma_418.statement: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_K(V)\) have Jordan decomposition \(T=T_sT_n\) with \(T_s\) semisimple, \(T_n\) unipotent and \(T_sT_n=T_nT_s\), let \(c\in K^{\times}\), and let \(A\in\operatorname{End}_K(V)\) satisfy \(TAT^{-1}=cA\). Then \(T_nA=AT_n\).
lemma_418.proof:
We write Ad(g) for the conjugation action of g \in GL_K(V) on End_K(V): Ad(g)(B)=gBg^{-1}. The map g\mapsto Ad(g) is a group homomorphism GL_K(V)\to GL_K(End_K V). In this notation the hypothesis is Ad(T)(A)=cA and the conclusion T_nA=AT_n is equivalent to Ad(T_n)(A)=A.

STEP 1 (Reduction to K algebraically closed).
Claim 1.1. Let S\in End_K(V), let m_S\in K[t] be its minimal polynomial, and let L/K be any field extension with S_L:=id\otimes S on V_L:=L\otimes_K V. Then m_{S_L}=m_S.
Proof of claim. The evaluation map ev_S:K[t]\to End_K(V), p\mapsto p(S), has kernel (m_S), so K[S]:=im(ev_S)\cong K[t]/(m_S). Since L/K is flat, L\otimes_K ev_S:L[t]=L\otimes_K K[t]\to L\otimes_K End_K(V)\cong End_L(V_L) (V is finite free over K, so this last identification holds) is injective on L\otimes_K K[S]\cong L[t]/(m_S) and its image is L[S_L]. Hence L[t]/(m_S)\cong L[S_L], so the kernel of L[t]\to L[S_L] is exactly (m_S); as m_S is monic it is the minimal polynomial of S_L. \square

Claim 1.2. If S is semisimple (i.e. its minimal polynomial over K is a product of pairwise distinct irreducible polynomials; in particular if S is diagonalisable over K), then S_{\bar K} is diagonalisable over an algebraic closure \bar K.
Proof of claim. Since char K=0 every irreducible polynomial is separable, so m_S is squarefree. By Claim 1.1, m_{S_{\bar K}}=m_S, and over \bar K it factors as a product of distinct linear factors \prod_i(t-a_i) with the a_i distinct. By the Chinese remainder theorem \bar K[t]/(m_{S_{\bar K}})\cong\prod_i\bar K, so V_{\bar K}=\bigoplus_i\ker(S_{\bar K}-a_i) is a direct sum of eigenspaces; hence S_{\bar K} is diagonalisable. \square

Now form \bar V:=\bar K\otimes_K V and denote by \bar B the base change id\otimes B of any K-linear map B. The identities T=T_sT_n=T_nT_s, the nilpotence of T_n-I, and the relation TAT^{-1}=cA are polynomial identities in the structure constants of these maps, so they base-change to \bar T=\bar T_s\bar T_n=\bar T_n\bar T_s, (\bar T_n-I) nilpotent, and \bar T\bar A\bar T^{-1}=c\bar A (c\in K^\times\subset\bar K^\times). By Claim 1.2, \bar T_s is \bar K-diagonalisable. Suppose the theorem is known over algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0; then \bar T_n\bar A=\bar A\bar T_n, i.e. the base change to \bar K of B:=T_nA-AT_n\in End_K(V) is zero. Choosing a K-basis of V, the matrix of \bar B in the induced \bar K-basis is the matrix of B with entries viewed in \bar K; it is zero, hence B=0. So it suffices to prove the theorem with K algebraically closed.

Henceforth assume K algebraically closed, char K=0. Write S:=T_s and U:=T_n. Both are invertible: U=I+(U-I) with U-I nilpotent is invertible (inverse \sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j(U-I)^j), and S=TU^{-1}. Moreover SU=US=T.

STEP 2 (Ad(U) is unipotent on End(V)).
Put N:=U-I, so N^m=0 for some m\ge1. For X\in End(V) let L_X,R_X\in End_K(End V) be left and right multiplication by X. Then L_XL_Y=L_{XY}, R_XR_Y=R_{YX}, and L_XR_Y=R_YL_X for all X,Y. Since Ad(U)=L_UR_{U^{-1}},
  Ad(U)-I_{End V} = L_UR_{U^{-1}}-L_IR_I = (L_I+L_N)R_{U^{-1}}-L_IR_I = L_NR_{U^{-1}} + R_{U^{-1}-I}.
Set X_0:=L_NR_{U^{-1}} and Y_0:=R_{U^{-1}-I}. Then X_0^{k}=L_{N^k}R_{U^{-k}}, so X_0^m=0. Also U^{-1}-I=-NU^{-1}, and N commutes with U^{-1} (N is a polynomial in U), so (U^{-1}-I)^m=(-1)^mN^mU^{-m}=0; hence Y_0^m=R_{(U^{-1}-I)^m}=0. Finally X_0Y_0=Y_0X_0 since left and right multiplications commute. Therefore
  (Ad(U)-I)^{2m-1}=\sum_{i+j=2m-1}\binom{2m-1}{i}X_0^{\,i}Y_0^{\,j}=0,\nbecause in each summand i\ge m or j\ge m. Thus Ad(U) is unipotent.

STEP 3 (Ad(S)-eigenspace decomposition of End(V), and its Ad(U)-stability).
Since S is diagonalisable and invertible, V=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}V_\lambda with V_\lambda=\ker(S-\lambda)\ne0 and \Lambda\subset K^\times. For \lambda,\mu\in\Lambda let
  H_{\lambda,\mu}=\{f\in End(V): f(V_\mu)\subset V_\lambda,\ f(V_\nu)=0\ (\nu\ne\mu)\}\cong Hom_K(V_\mu,V_\lambda).
Every f\in End(V) decomposes uniquely as f=\sum_{\lambda,\mu}f_{\lambda,\mu} with f_{\lambda,\mu}\in H_{\lambda,\mu}, namely f_{\lambda,\mu} is V\xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}_\mu}V_\mu\xrightarrow{f}V\hookrightarrow V_\lambda (the projections exist because the V_\nu are S-stable and S is diagonalisable). Hence End(V)=\bigoplus_{\lambda,\mu}H_{\lambda,\mu}.
For f\in H_{\lambda,\mu} and v\in V_\nu: since S is diagonalisable with nonzero eigenvalues, S^{-1}(V_\nu)=V_\nu and S^{-1}|_{V_\nu}=\nu^{-1}; thus Ad(S)(f)(v)=S f(\nu^{-1}v), which is 0 for \nu\ne\mu and equals \mu^{-1}\lambda f(v) for \nu=\mu. Hence Ad(S)(f)=\lambda\mu^{-1}f, i.e. Ad(S) acts on H_{\lambda,\mu} as the scalar \lambda\mu^{-1}.
For \alpha\in\Sigma:=\{\lambda\mu^{-1}:\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda\}\subset K^\times put W_\alpha:=\bigoplus_{\lambda\mu^{-1}=\alpha}H_{\lambda,\mu}. Then
  End(V)=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Sigma}W_\alpha \quad\text{and}\quad Ad(S)|_{W_\alpha}=\alpha\cdot id.   (3.1)
We claim each W_\alpha is Ad(U)-stable. Indeed, for v\in V_\lambda we have S(Uv)=U(Sv)=\lambda Uv, so U(V_\lambda)\subset V_\lambda; applying the same to U^{-1} gives U(V_\lambda)=V_\lambda. Hence for f\in H_{\lambda,\mu}, Ad(U)(f)=UfU^{-1} maps V_\mu into V_\lambda and kills V_\nu for \nu\ne\mu, i.e. Ad(U)(H_{\lambda,\mu})\subset H_{\lambda,\mu}. Consequently Ad(U)(W_\alpha)\subset W_\alpha, and since Ad(U)^{-1}=Ad(U^{-1}) has the same form, Ad(U)|_{W_\alpha}\in GL(W_\alpha); denote it by U_\alpha. By Step 2, (U_\alpha-I)^{2m-1}=0, so each U_\alpha is unipotent and its only eigenvalue is 1.

STEP 4 (Conclusion).
Write A=\sum_{\alpha\in\Sigma}A_\alpha with A_\alpha\in W_\alpha (if A=0 there is nothing to prove, and the argument below still applies).
Since T=SU, Ad(T)=Ad(S)\circ Ad(U); both factors preserve each W_\alpha (Step 3 and (3.1)), hence so does Ad(T). The hypothesis Ad(T)(A)=cA becomes
  \sum_{\alpha\in\Sigma}Ad(T)(A_\alpha)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Sigma}cA_\alpha,\nwith Ad(T)(A_\alpha)\in W_\alpha and cA_\alpha\in W_\alpha for every \alpha. By uniqueness of the components in the direct sum (3.1),
  Ad(T)(A_\alpha)=cA_\alpha \quad\text{for every }\alpha\in\Sigma.   (4.1)
Fix \alpha. Using (3.1) again, Ad(T)|_{W_\alpha}=Ad(S)|_{W_\alpha}\circ Ad(U)|_{W_\alpha}=\alpha\,U_\alpha, so (4.1) gives \alpha\,U_\alpha(A_\alpha)=cA_\alpha, i.e.
  U_\alpha(A_\alpha)=(c\alpha^{-1})A_\alpha,\nwhich is legitimate since \alpha\in\Sigma\subset K^\times (and c\in K^\times).
If A_\alpha\ne0, then c\alpha^{-1} is an eigenvalue of U_\alpha with eigenvector A_\alpha. As (U_\alpha-I)^{2m-1}=0 we get (c\alpha^{-1}-1)^{2m-1}A_\alpha=(U_\alpha-I)^{2m-1}(A_\alpha)=0, and A_\alpha\ne0 forces c\alpha^{-1}=1. Thus U_\alpha(A_\alpha)=A_\alpha. If A_\alpha=0 then trivially U_\alpha(A_\alpha)=A_\alpha. Hence U_\alpha(A_\alpha)=A_\alpha for all \alpha\in\Sigma, and summing,
  Ad(U)(A)=\sum_\alpha U_\alpha(A_\alpha)=\sum_\alpha A_\alpha=A.
That is, UAU^{-1}=A, equivalently UA=AU. Returning to the original notation, T_nA=AT_n, which is the desired conclusion. (By Step 1 the result over \bar K implies the result over K.) \qedsymbol

lemma_cohom_abelian_variety_hopf_algebra.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let A be an abelian variety over F_q with group law m:A x A -> A, inversion [-1]:A -> A and origin e:Spec F_q -> A, and let k=overline(F_q). Give H = direct sum_{n in Z} H^n_et(A_k,Q_ell) the product given by cup product, the unit Q_ell = H^0_et(A_k,Q_ell) -> H, the counit epsilon = (e_k)^*, the antipode S = ([-1]_k)^*, and the comultiplication Delta:H -> H tensor_{Q_ell} H characterised by the requirement that, under the Kunneth isomorphism H tensor_{Q_ell} H -> H^*_{et}((A x A)_k,Q_ell), Delta equals (m_k)^*. Then H is a graded-commutative, graded-cocommutative Hopf algebra over Q_ell, and every element of H^1_et(A_k,Q_ell) is primitive for Delta.
lemma_cohom_abelian_variety_hopf_algebra.proof:
Proof. Put H^n=H^n_et(A_k,Q_l) and H=direct sum_{n in Z}H^n, with H^n=0 for n<0. The product on H is cup product. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the proper F_q-variety A and the constant sheaf Q_l with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure, each H^n is finite-dimensional over Q_l. Since an abelian variety is geometrically connected, H^0=Q_l. The étale cohomology of Spec k is Q_l in degree 0 and 0 in positive degrees. Let eta:Q_l=H^0(A_k,Q_l)->H be the inclusion of degree zero, let epsilon=e_k^*:H->H^0(Spec k)=Q_l, and let S=([-1]_k)^*:H->H. All group identities below are used after base change to k.

1. Kunneth and graded tensor product. For smooth projective X,Y over F_q, lemma_146 gives an isomorphism from direct sum_{i+j=n}H^i_et(X_k,Q_l) otimes H^j_et(Y_k,Q_l) to H^n_et((X x Y)_k,Q_l), a otimes b maps to pr_1^*a cup pr_2^*b. In particular define kappa:H otimes H -> H^*((A x A)_k,Q_l) by kappa(a otimes b)=pr_1^*a cup pr_2^*b for homogeneous a,b. This is a degree-preserving isomorphism. Give H otimes H the graded tensor product algebra structure (a otimes b)(c otimes d)=(-1)^{|b||c|}ac otimes bd. Then kappa is an algebra isomorphism: for homogeneous a,b,c,d, kappa((a otimes b)(c otimes d))=(-1)^{|b||c|}pr_1^*a cup pr_1^*c cup pr_2^*b cup pr_2^*d = pr_1^*a cup pr_2^*b cup pr_1^*c cup pr_2^*d = kappa(a otimes b)kappa(c otimes d), where the middle equality uses graded commutativity to move pr_2^*b past pr_1^*c. Also kappa(1 otimes 1)=1. The same construction applied twice gives kappa_3:H otimes H otimes H -> H^*((A x A x A)_k,Q_l), kappa_3(a otimes b otimes c)=p_1^*a cup p_2^*b cup p_3^*c.

2. The coalgebra maps. Define Delta= kappa^{-1} circ m_k^*, so kappa circ Delta=m_k^*. It is homogeneous of degree 0. Since m_k^* is a ring map and kappa is an algebra isomorphism, Delta is a graded algebra map: for homogeneous x,y, kappa(Delta(xy))=m_k^*x cup m_k^*y=kappa(Delta x)kappa(Delta y)=kappa(Delta x Delta y), hence Delta(xy)=Delta x Delta y. Also Delta(1)=1 otimes 1. The map epsilon is an algebra map because it is pullback along e_k; epsilon(1)=1. The unit eta is the algebra inclusion of constants. Moreover epsilon circ eta=id_{Q_l} because pi_k circ e_k=id_{Spec k}, and Delta circ eta=eta otimes eta because Delta(1)=1 otimes 1.

3. Counit. Write Delta x=sum_i a_i otimes b_i with homogeneous terms. Then (epsilon otimes id)Delta x=sum_i epsilon(a_i)b_i. Interpreting e_k times id as (e_k circ pi_k,id_{A_k}), we have (e_k times id)^*m_k^*x=(e_k times id)^*kappa(Delta x)=sum_i (e_k times id)^*(pr_1^*a_i cup pr_2^*b_i)=sum_i pi_k^*e_k^*a_i cup b_i. Since pi_k^*e_k^*a_i is the constant class epsilon(a_i), this sum is exactly (epsilon otimes id)Delta x. But (e_k times id)^*m_k^*x=(m_k circ (e_k times id))^*x=x because m_k circ (e_k times id)=id_{A_k}. Hence (epsilon otimes id)Delta x=x. Similarly (id otimes epsilon)Delta x=x using m_k circ (id times e_k)=id_{A_k}.

4. Coassociativity. For x, write Delta x=sum_i a_i otimes b_i and Delta a_i=sum_j a_{ij} otimes b_{ij}. Then kappa_3((Delta otimes id)Delta x)=sum_{i,j}p_1^*a_{ij} cup p_2^*b_{ij} cup p_3^*b_i. Also m_k^*x=sum_i p_1^*a_i cup p_2^*b_i. Pulling back by m_k times id, which is (m_k,p_3), gives (m_k times id)^*m_k^*x=sum_i (m_k circ (p_1,p_2))^*a_i cup p_3^*b_i=sum_{i,j}p_1^*a_{ij} cup p_2^*b_{ij} cup p_3^*b_i. Hence kappa_3((Delta otimes id)Delta x)=(m_k times id)^*m_k^*x. Similarly kappa_3((id otimes Delta)Delta x)=(id times m_k)^*m_k^*x. Associativity of the group law gives m_k circ (m_k times id)=m_k circ (id times m_k), so the two sides are equal; kappa_3 is injective, hence (Delta otimes id)Delta=(id otimes Delta)Delta.

5. Graded cocommutativity. Let tau_k be the swap of the two factors and tau_H the graded flip tau_H(a otimes b)=(-1)^{|a||b|}b otimes a. For homogeneous a,b, kappa(tau_H(a otimes b))=(-1)^{|a||b|}pr_1^*b cup pr_2^*a=pr_2^*a cup pr_1^*b=tau_k^*kappa(a otimes b). Therefore kappa(tau_H Delta x)=tau_k^*m_k^*x=(m_k circ tau_k)^*x. Since the group law on an abelian variety is commutative, m_k circ tau_k=m_k, so this equals kappa(Delta x). Hence tau_H Delta=Delta.

6. Antipode. Let mu:H otimes H->H be the multiplication mu(a otimes b)=a cup b, and let delta_k:A_k->A_k x A_k be the diagonal. For homogeneous a,b, mu(a otimes b)=delta_k^*kappa(a otimes b). For Delta x=sum_i a_i otimes b_i, we have mu((id otimes S)Delta x)=sum_i a_i cup S(b_i)=delta_k^*sum_i p_1^*a_i cup p_2^*S(b_i). But sum_i p_1^*a_i cup p_2^*S(b_i)=(id times [-1]_k)^*sum_i p_1^*a_i cup p_2^*b_i=(id times [-1]_k)^*m_k^*x. Hence mu((id otimes S)Delta x)=delta_k^*(id times [-1]_k)^*m_k^*x=(m_k circ (id times [-1]_k) circ delta_k)^*x. The identity a+(-a)=0 for the group law gives m_k circ (id times [-1]_k) circ delta_k=e_k circ pi_k, so this is pi_k^*e_k^*x=eta circ epsilon(x). The identity m_k circ ([-1]_k times id) circ delta_k=e_k circ pi_k gives mu((S otimes id)Delta x)=eta circ epsilon(x). Thus S is the antipode.

7. Primitive classes in degree 1. Let x in H^1. Since kappa(Delta x)=m_k^*x lies in H^1((A x A)_k,Q_l), the Kunneth decomposition gives Delta x=u otimes 1+1 otimes v with u,v in H^1. Applying the counit identities and using epsilon=0 on positive degrees gives x=(epsilon otimes id)Delta x=epsilon(u)1+epsilon(1)v=v and x=(id otimes epsilon)Delta x=u. Therefore Delta x=x otimes 1+1 otimes x.

We have shown that H is an associative unital graded-commutative algebra, a coassociative counital graded-cocommutative coalgebra, that Delta and epsilon are algebra maps, that eta and epsilon satisfy the bialgebra compatibility, and that S satisfies the antipode identities. Hence H is a graded-commutative graded-cocommutative Hopf algebra over Q_l, and every element of H^1 is primitive.

lemma_421.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) be semisimple, equivalently diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), and let \(m\ge0\) be an integer. Then the induced automorphism of \(\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\) is semisimple.
lemma_421.proof:
We prove that the exterior power of a semisimple operator is semisimple. Throughout, write $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and $n=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$.

**Step 0: The induced map on $\textstyle\bigwedge^m$.** For $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ the map
$$V^m\longrightarrow \textstyle\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V,\qquad (v_1,\dots,v_m)\longmapsto Tv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tv_m$$
is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-multilinear and alternating, so by the universal property of the exterior power it factors uniquely through a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $\bigwedge^m T:\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\to\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$ with $(\bigwedge^m T)(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m)=Tv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tv_m$. By the same universal property, $\bigwedge^m(\mathrm{id}_V)=\mathrm{id}$ and $\bigwedge^m(S\circ T)=(\bigwedge^m S)\circ(\bigwedge^m T)$ whenever the composites make sense (both sides are the unique linear map sending $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$ to $STv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge STv_m$). Applying this to $T$ and $T^{-1}$ gives $(\bigwedge^m T)\circ(\bigwedge^m T^{-1})=\bigwedge^m(TT^{-1})=\mathrm{id}$ and similarly the other way, so $\bigwedge^m T\in\mathrm{GL}(\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V)$; this is "the induced automorphism".

**Step 1: Edge cases.** If $m=0$, then $\bigwedge^0_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\bigwedge^0T=\mathrm{id}$, which is diagonalizable. If $m>n$, every elementary wedge $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$ vanishes: writing each $v_k$ in a basis of the $n$-dimensional space $V$ and expanding by multilinearity, every resulting wedge of basis vectors has a repeated index and hence is $0$ in the exterior power (which is the quotient of the tensor power by the subspace generated by tensors with two equal adjacent factors). Thus $\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=0$, and the identity of the zero space is diagonalizable (empty eigenbasis). Henceforth assume $1\le m\le n$.

**Step 2: A basis fact for exterior powers (proved in full).** Let $F$ be a field, $E$ an $F$-vector space with basis $b_1,\dots,b_n$, and $0\le m\le n$. Then $\mathcal B_m:=\{b_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{i_m}:1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\}$ is an $F$-basis of $\bigwedge^m_F E$.

*Spanning.* $\bigwedge^m_F E$ is by definition generated (as an $F$-vector space) by elementary wedges $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$. Write $v_k=\sum_{j}a_{kj}b_j$; by $m$-linearity,
$$v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m=\sum_{j_1,\dots,j_m}a_{1j_1}\cdots a_{mj_m}\; b_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{j_m}.$$
Any term with two equal indices is $0$ (the defining quotient of the exterior power kills tensors with a repeated factor, since the relation $w\otimes\cdots\otimes w\otimes\cdots\sim -(w\otimes\cdots\otimes w\otimes\cdots)$ together with additivity forces $2$-torsion-freeness-independent vanishing: explicitly the exterior power is the quotient of $E^{\otimes m}$ by the span of tensors with two equal adjacent entries, and transposing equal entries shows every tensor with a repeated entry lies in that span). Terms with pairwise distinct indices are, after reordering, $\pm b_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{i_m}$ with $i_1<\cdots<i_m$, using anticommutativity $u\wedge w=-\,w\wedge u$. Hence $\mathcal B_m$ spans.

*Independence.* Let $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n\in E^\vee$ be the dual basis. For $I=\{i_1<\dots<i_m\}$ define $\Delta_I:E^m\to F$ by $\Delta_I(w_1,\dots,w_m)=\det\big(\varepsilon_{i_s}(w_t)\big)_{1\le s,t\le m}$. This map is $m$-linear and alternating (the determinant is multilinear and alternating in the columns, and the columns are $w_1,\dots,w_m$), so it factors uniquely through a linear form, again denoted $\Delta_I$, on $\bigwedge^m_F E$. For $J=\{j_1<\dots<j_m\}$ we have $\Delta_I(b_J)=\det(\varepsilon_{i_s}(b_{j_t}))=\det(\delta_{i_s,j_t})=\delta_{I,J}$. If $\sum_J c_J b_J=0$ with $b_J:=b_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{j_m}$, applying $\Delta_I$ yields $c_I=0$ for every $I$. $\square$

**Step 3: Compatibility of exterior powers with extension of scalars.** Put $W=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$ and $S=T\otimes\mathrm{id}_K\in\mathrm{GL}_K(W)$. Consider the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-multilinear alternating map
$$\beta:V^m\longrightarrow \textstyle\bigwedge^m_K W,\qquad \beta(v_1,\dots,v_m)=(v_1\otimes 1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(v_m\otimes 1).$$
It induces a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear $\widetilde\beta:\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\to\bigwedge^m_K W$, and since the target is a $K$-vector space, the universal property of extension of scalars gives a $K$-linear map
$$\theta:\Big(\textstyle\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\Big)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\longrightarrow \textstyle\bigwedge^m_K W,\qquad \theta\big((v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m)\otimes\lambda\big)=\lambda\,(v_1\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(v_m\otimes1).$$
Choose a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $V$. By Step 2, $\{e_I\}$ (with $e_I=e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_m}$) is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis of $\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$, so $\{e_I\otimes1\}$ is a $K$-basis of the source. Since $\{e_j\otimes1\}$ is a $K$-basis of $W$, Step 2 applied over $K$ says $\{(e_{i_1}\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(e_{i_m}\otimes1)\}$ is a $K$-basis of $\bigwedge^m_K W$. As $\theta(e_I\otimes1)$ is exactly the corresponding basis element, $\theta$ sends a basis bijectively to a basis, hence is a $K$-linear isomorphism.

Moreover $\theta$ intertwines $\bigwedge^m T$ and $\bigwedge^m_K S$: for a basis element and $\lambda\in K$,
$$\theta\big((\textstyle\bigwedge^m T)(e_I)\otimes\lambda\big)=\lambda\,(Te_{i_1}\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(Te_{i_m}\otimes1)=\lambda\,(S(e_{i_1}\otimes1))\wedge\cdots\wedge(S(e_{i_m}\otimes1))=(\textstyle\bigwedge^m_K S)\,\theta(e_I\otimes\lambda),$$
using $S(e_j\otimes1)=Te_j\otimes1$. Thus
$$\theta\circ\big((\textstyle\bigwedge^m T)\otimes\mathrm{id}_K\big)=\big(\textstyle\bigwedge^m_K S\big)\circ\theta.\tag{$\ast$}$$

**Step 4: Diagonalising $\bigwedge^m_K S$ over $K$.** By hypothesis $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; by lemma_5 (eoinm) this is equivalent to $S$ being semisimple/diagonalizable on $W$. Choose a $K$-basis $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $W$ with $Sf_j=\alpha_j f_j$. Since $S$ is invertible, each $\alpha_j\in K^\times$ (indeed $Sf_j=\alpha_jf_j$ and $f_j\ne0$; if $\alpha_j=0$ then $Sf_j=0$, contradicting injectivity of $S$). By Step 2, $\{f_I:=f_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge f_{i_m}\}_{I}$ is a $K$-basis of $\bigwedge^m_K W$, and by the defining formula of the induced map,
$$\big(\textstyle\bigwedge^m_K S\big)(f_I)=Sf_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge Sf_{i_m}=\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_m}\; f_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge f_{i_m}=(\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_m})\,f_I.$$
Since each $\alpha_{i_s}\in K^\times$, the scalar $\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_m}$ is a nonzero element of $K$. Hence $\bigwedge^m_K S$ is diagonal with respect to the basis $\{f_I\}$; in particular it is diagonalizable over $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

**Step 5: Descent to $\mathbb Q_\ell$.** By $(\ast)$ and Step 3, the operator $(\bigwedge^m T)\otimes\mathrm{id}_K$ on $\big(\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\big)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$ is conjugate (via the isomorphism $\theta$) to the diagonalizable operator $\bigwedge^m_K S$; conjugate operators have the same Jordan form, so $(\bigwedge^m T)\otimes\mathrm{id}_K$ is itself diagonalizable over $K$. Now apply lemma_5 (eoinm) to the finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$ and the operator $\bigwedge^m T$: it states that an operator on a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space is semisimple if and only if it is semisimple, equivalently diagonalizable, after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Since the base change is diagonalizable, $\bigwedge^m T$ is semisimple on $\bigwedge^m_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$.

Together with the edge cases of Step 1 this covers every $m\ge0$ and completes the proof.

lemma_422.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) and \(S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\) be automorphisms that are diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). Then the automorphism \(T\otimes S\) of \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_422.proof:
Write K = \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). For a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space \(U\) and \(A\in\mathrm{GL}(U)\) we write \(U_K := U\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\) and \(A_K := A\otimes\mathrm{id}_K\). By definition, \(A\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) precisely when the \(K\)-linear automorphism \(A_K\) of \(U_K\) is diagonalizable, i.e. when \(U_K\) is the direct sum of the eigenspaces \(\ker(A_K-\lambda)\), \(\lambda\in K\).

**Reduction to the case \(V,W\neq 0\).** If \(V=0\) or \(W=0\) then \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W=0\); the unique automorphism of the zero space is diagonal (it is represented by the empty diagonal matrix in the empty basis), so the claim holds. Assume henceforth \(V\neq0\) and \(W\neq0\).

**Step 1: the canonical identification.** Define a map
\[
\Phi:(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W)_K\longrightarrow V_K\otimes_K W_K,\qquad \Phi\bigl((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\bigr)=(v\otimes\lambda)\otimes(w\otimes 1).
\]
Well-definedness: the map \(V\times W\times K\to V_K\otimes_K W_K\), \((v,w,\lambda)\mapsto (v\otimes\lambda)\otimes(w\otimes1)\), is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-trilinear (each of the three slots is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear by construction, and \(\mathbb Q_\ell\subset K\)), hence by the universal property of the tensor product induces a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear \(\widetilde\Phi:(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\to V_K\otimes_KW_K\), which is the displayed \(\Phi\). It is \(K\)-linear because for \(\mu\in K\),
\[
\Phi\bigl(((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda)\mu\bigr)=\Phi((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\mu)=(v\otimes\lambda\mu)\otimes(w\otimes1)=\mu\bigl((v\otimes\lambda)\otimes(w\otimes1)\bigr)=\mu\,\Phi((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda),
\]
where in the middle equality we used that \(K\)-scalars may be moved between the two factors of a tensor product over \(K\). Since the elements \((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\) generate the source, \(\Phi\) is \(K\)-linear.

Define \(\Psi:V_K\otimes_KW_K\to (V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W)_K\) on pure tensors by \(\Psi\bigl((v\otimes\lambda)\otimes(w\otimes\mu)\bigr)=(v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\mu\). This is well defined: the map \(V_K\times W_K\to (V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W)_K\), \(((v\otimes\lambda),(w\otimes\mu))\mapsto (v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\mu\) is \(K\)-bilinear (clearly \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear, and \(\Psi_K\)-balanced since \(\Psi((v\otimes\lambda)\kappa,\,w\otimes\mu)=(v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\kappa\mu=\Psi(v\otimes\lambda,(w\otimes\mu)\kappa)\)), so it factors through \(V_K\otimes_KW_K\). Finally,
\[
\Psi\Phi((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda)=\Psi((v\otimes\lambda)\otimes(w\otimes1))=(v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda,
\]
\[
\Phi\Psi((v\otimes\lambda)\otimes(w\otimes\mu))=\Phi((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\mu)=(v\otimes\lambda\mu)\otimes(w\otimes1)=(v\otimes\lambda)\otimes\mu(w\otimes1)=(v\otimes\lambda)\otimes(w\otimes\mu),
\]
so \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\) are mutually inverse \(K\)-linear isomorphisms.

**Step 2: \(\Phi\) conjugates \((T\otimes S)_K\) to \(T_K\otimes S_K\).** For generators,
\[
\Phi\bigl((T\otimes S)_K((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda)\bigr)=\Phi((Tv\otimes Sw)\otimes\lambda)=(Tv\otimes\lambda)\otimes(Sw\otimes1),
\]
while
\[
(T_K\otimes S_K)\Phi((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda)=(T_K\otimes S_K)\bigl((v\otimes\lambda)\otimes(w\otimes1)\bigr)=(Tv\otimes\lambda)\otimes(Sw\otimes1),
\]
because \(T_K(v\otimes\lambda)=Tv\otimes\lambda\) and \(S_K(w\otimes1)=Sw\otimes1\). Since such generators span the source, \((T_K\otimes S_K)\circ\Phi=\Phi\circ (T\otimes S)_K\). Consequently \((T\otimes S)_K\) is diagonalizable if and only if \(T_K\otimes S_K\) is: a \(K\)-basis of eigenvectors of one pushes through \(\Phi\) (resp. \(\Phi^{-1}\)) to a \(K\)-basis of eigenvectors of the other, using the intertwining relation just proved. It therefore suffices to prove \(T_K\otimes S_K\) diagonalizable.

**Step 3: eigenspace decompositions of \(T_K\) and \(S_K\).** By hypothesis \(T_K\) and \(S_K\) are diagonalizable. Let \(A\subset K\) (resp. \(B\subset K\)) be the finite set of eigenvalues of \(T_K\) (resp. \(S_K\)), and put
\[
V_\alpha:=\ker(T_K-\alpha),\quad \alpha\in A,\qquad W_\beta:=\ker(S_K-\beta),\quad\beta\in B.
\]
Finiteness of \(A,B\) holds because they are subsets of the roots of the characteristic polynomials of \(T_K,S_K\). Diagonalizability says exactly that
\[
V_K=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in A}V_\alpha,\qquad W_K=\bigoplus_{\beta\in B}W_\beta,
\]
with all \(V_\alpha,W_\beta\neq0\). Note also \(\alpha,\beta\neq0\) since \(T_K,S_K\) are invertible.

**Step 4: the sum \(\bigoplus_{\alpha,\beta}V_\alpha\otimes_KW_\beta\) is the whole space, and is direct.** The natural \(K\)-linear map
\[
\bigoplus_{(\alpha,\beta)\in A\times B}V_\alpha\otimes_K W_\beta\longrightarrow V_K\otimes_KW_K
\]
is an isomorphism. Surjectivity: since \(\bigoplus_\alpha V_\alpha\xrightarrow{\sim}V_K\) and \(\bigoplus_\beta W_\beta\xrightarrow{\sim}W_K\) are isomorphisms, so is their tensor product \((\bigoplus_\alpha V_\alpha)\otimes_K(\bigoplus_\beta W_\beta)\to V_K\otimes_KW_K\), and the canonical map \(\bigoplus_{\alpha,\beta}V_\alpha\otimes W_\beta\to(\bigoplus_\alpha V_\alpha)\otimes(\bigoplus_\beta W_\beta)\) is an isomorphism (both sides represent the same universal object for families of bilinear maps out of the \(V_\alpha\times W_\beta\); explicitly, \(\sum_{\alpha,\beta}v_{\alpha,\beta}\otimes w_{\alpha,\beta}\mapsto\sum_{\alpha,\beta}(v_{\alpha,\beta})_\alpha\otimes(w_{\alpha,\beta})_\beta\) with inverse given by the inclusions).

Injectivity (directness inside \(V_K\otimes W_K\)): let \(p_\alpha:V_K\to V_\alpha\) be the \(K\)-linear projection along \(\bigoplus_{\alpha'\neq\alpha}V_{\alpha'}\), and \(q_\beta:W_K\to W_\beta\) the analogous projection. For \(x_{\alpha',\beta'}\in V_{\alpha'}\otimes W_{\beta'}\) and a pure tensor \(x_{\alpha',\beta'}=\sum_i v_i\otimes w_i\) with \(v_i\in V_{\alpha'},w_i\in W_{\beta'}\), we have \((p_\alpha\otimes q_\beta)(x_{\alpha',\beta'})=\sum_i p_\alpha(v_i)\otimes q_\beta(w_i)=0\) unless \(\alpha'=\alpha\) and \(\beta'=\beta\), in which case it equals \(x_{\alpha,\beta}\). Hence if \(\sum_{\alpha,\beta}x_{\alpha,\beta}=0\) with \(x_{\alpha,\beta}\in V_\alpha\otimes W_\beta\), applying \(p_\alpha\otimes q_\beta\) gives \(x_{\alpha,\beta}=0\) for every \((\alpha,\beta)\).

**Step 5: grouping by the product \(\alpha\beta\).** For \(\gamma\in K\) set
\[
E_\gamma:=\bigoplus_{\substack{(\alpha,\beta)\in A\times B\\ \alpha\beta=\gamma}}V_\alpha\otimes_K W_\beta\qquad(\text{empty sum }=0).
\]
Only finitely many \(\gamma\) give \(E_\gamma\neq0\). Grouping the direct sum of Step 4 along the fibres of the map \(A\times B\to K\), \((\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\alpha\beta\), gives
\[
V_K\otimes_KW_K=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in K}E_\gamma .
\]
For \(v\otimes w\in V_\alpha\otimes W_\beta\) with \(\alpha\beta=\gamma\),
\[
(T_K\otimes S_K)(v\otimes w)=T_Kv\otimes S_Kw=(\alpha v)\otimes(\beta w)=\alpha\beta\,(v\otimes w)=\gamma(v\otimes w),
\]
so by linearity \((T_K\otimes S_K)|_{E_\gamma}=\gamma\,\mathrm{id}_{E_\gamma}\); in particular \(E_\gamma\subseteq\ker(T_K\otimes S_K-\gamma)\).

**Step 6: the \(E_\gamma\) are exactly the eigenspaces.** Let \(x\in\ker(T_K\otimes S_K-\gamma)\). Write \(x=\sum_{\gamma'}x_{\gamma'}\) with \(x_{\gamma'}\in E_{\gamma'}\) (finite sum, by Step 5). Then
\[
0=(T_K\otimes S_K-\gamma)x=\sum_{\gamma'}(\gamma'-\gamma)x_{\gamma'},
\]
and each \((\gamma'-\gamma)x_{\gamma'}\in E_{\gamma'}\); by directness of \(\bigoplus_{\gamma'}E_{\gamma'}\) we get \((\gamma'-\gamma)x_{\gamma'}=0\) for all \(\gamma'\), hence \(x_{\gamma'}=0\) for \(\gamma'\neq\gamma\) and \(x=x_\gamma\in E_\gamma\). Thus \(E_\gamma=\ker(T_K\otimes S_K-\gamma)\) for every \(\gamma\), and
\[
V_K\otimes_KW_K=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in K}\ker\bigl((T_K\otimes S_K)-\gamma\bigr),
\]
which is precisely the statement that \(T_K\otimes S_K\) is diagonalizable over \(K\). (Equivalently: choosing a \(K\)-basis of each \(E_\gamma\) and concatenating over the finitely many non-zero \(E_\gamma\) yields a \(K\)-basis of \(V_K\otimes_KW_K\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(T_K\otimes S_K\); the matrix of \(T_K\otimes S_K\) in this basis is diagonal with diagonal entries the products \(\alpha\beta\).)

**Step 7: conclusion.** By Step 2, \((T\otimes S)_K\) is conjugate over \(K\) to the diagonalizable automorphism \(T_K\otimes S_K\), hence \((T\otimes S)_K\) is itself diagonalizable: if \(\{e_i\}_i\) is a \(K\)-basis of \(V_K\otimes_KW_K\) with \((T_K\otimes S_K)e_i=\gamma_i e_i\), then \(\{\Phi^{-1}(e_i)\}_i\) is a \(K\)-basis of \((V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W)_K\) and
\[
(T\otimes S)_K\Phi^{-1}(e_i)=\Phi^{-1}(T_K\otimes S_K)e_i=\gamma_i\Phi^{-1}(e_i).
\]
By the definition recalled at the start, this means exactly that \(T\otimes S\in\mathrm{GL}(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W)\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). \(
\blacksquare\)

lemma_416.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(\mathcal L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\). Then there exist integers \(m\ge1\) and \(n\ge1\) and \(d+1\) sections \(s_0,\dots,s_d\in H^0(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}},\mathcal L^{\otimes n})\) with no common zero, such that the induced morphism \(f:X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\to\mathbb P^d_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) is surjective and generically finite, and such that there is a nonempty open subscheme \(V\subseteq\mathbb P^d_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) over which \(f\) is finite étale.
lemma_416.proof:
Proof. Let k=overline(F_q). We first work over k and then descend to a finite extension.

Choose an integer n>=1 such that M=L^{otimes n} is very ample and, for some closed point x in X(k), the evaluation map on 1-jets
H^0(X_k,M_k) -> M_k tensor (O_{X_k}/m_x^2)
is surjective. This is a standard consequence of ampleness: some power of an ample line bundle is very ample, and Serre vanishing applied to the coherent sheaf M_k tensor (O/m_x^2) gives the surjectivity for all sufficiently large powers.

Let V=H^0(X,M) as an F_q-vector space and let A=V^{d+1} over F_q. For any field extension K/F_q we identify A(K) with H^0(X_K,M_K)^{d+1}. For a=(s_0,...,s_d) in A(K) write Z(a)=intersection of zero loci of s_i in X_K.

1. The basepoint-free locus.
Define I_base subset A x X by (a,y) in I_base iff all s_i vanish at y. This is closed because it is the common zero locus of the universal sections. Let p:A x X -> A be projection. Since X is proper over F_q, p is closed. Hence A_base=A\p(I_base) is open.

We show A_base is nonempty. It suffices to work over k. If dim V=d+1, the complete very ample linear system embeds X_k into P^d_k. Its image is a closed irreducible subset of dimension d, hence all of P^d_k; the complete system has no common zero. If dim V=N>d+1, consider G=Gr(d+1,V_k). For y in X_k, evaluation at y is a nonzero linear functional V_k -> M_k(y), with kernel H_y a hyperplane. Let J={(W,y) in G x X_k : W subset H_y}. For fixed y, the fiber J_y=Gr(d+1,H_y) has dimension (d+1)(N-d-2), while dim G=(d+1)(N-d-1). Hence dim J <= d + dim G - (d+1) = dim G - 1. Therefore the projection J->G has proper image. Choose W outside this image. Then W is not contained in H_y for any y, so the sections in W have no common zero. A basis of W gives a point of A_base(k). Thus A_base is nonempty.

2. The locus where the induced map is etale somewhere.
Let D=(A x X)\I_base. On D the universal tuple of sections generates p_X^*M, hence defines a universal morphism F:D -> P^d_A. Let E be the locus in D where F is etale. The etale locus of a morphism locally of finite presentation is open, so E is open. The projection p:D->A is smooth: it is the composition of the smooth projection A x X -> A (base change of X->Spec F_q) with the open immersion D->A x X. Smooth morphisms are open, so A_sep=p(E) is open in A.

We show A_sep is nonempty. Work over k. By the choice of x and n, the 1-jet evaluation map is surjective. Choose sections t_0,...,t_d in H^0(X_k,M_k) whose 1-jets at x satisfy t_0(x)=1, dt_0(x)=0, t_i(x)=0 for i=1,...,d, and dt_1(x),...,dt_d(x) form a basis of the cotangent space m_x/m_x^2. Since t_0(x) is nonzero, the tuple defines a morphism in a neighborhood of x. In the affine chart t_0 != 0 of P^d_k, the coordinates of the induced map are u_i=t_i/t_0. At x we have du_i(x)=dt_i(x), because t_0(x)=1 and dt_0(x)=0. Thus the differential of the induced map X_k -> P^d_k at x is an isomorphism. By the Jacobian criterion for smooth varieties, the map is etale at x. Therefore the corresponding point of A(k) lies in A_sep. Hence A_sep is nonempty.

3. Descent to a finite extension.
The intersection A_good=A_base cap A_sep is a nonempty open subscheme of A. Indeed, after base change to k, A_k is irreducible affine space, so the two nonempty open subsets A_base_k and A_sep_k meet. Since A is of finite type over the finite field F_q, A_good has a closed point. Its residue field is a finite extension F_{q^m} of F_q. The corresponding tuple gives sections s_0,...,s_d in H^0(X_{F_{q^m}},M)=H^0(X_{F_{q^m}},L^{otimes n}) with no common zero and such that the induced morphism f:X_{F_{q^m}} -> P^d_{F_{q^m}} is etale at some point.

4. The morphism is finite and surjective.
Because the sections generate M, f^*O(1) is isomorphic to M. We claim that any morphism from a projective variety to P^d whose pullback of O(1) is ample is finite. To prove the claim, take the Stein factorization of f: X -> Y -> P^d, where X->Y is proper with connected fibers and g:Y->P^d is finite. Since g is finite, g^*O(1) is ample on Y. If X->Y had a positive-dimensional fiber C, then f^*O(1)|_C would be trivial, because C is contracted to a point. But f^*O(1) is ample on X, and the restriction of an ample line bundle to a closed subscheme is ample; the trivial line bundle on a positive-dimensional proper scheme is not ample. Contradiction. Thus X->Y is quasi-finite. A proper quasi-finite morphism is finite, so f is finite.

Since f is finite, its image is closed. The variety X_{F_{q^m}} is integral of dimension d: it is smooth over a field and geometrically connected. Finite morphisms preserve dimension of closed subsets, so the image of f has dimension d. The only closed subset of P^d_{F_{q^m}} of dimension d is the whole space. Hence f is surjective.

5. A nonempty open over which f is finite etale.
Let E_X be the etale locus of f in X_{F_{q^m}}. By construction E_X is nonempty open. Since X_{F_{q^m}} is integral, E_X contains the generic point. Let Z=X_{F_{q^m}}\E_X. Then Z is a proper closed subset, so dim Z<d. Since f is finite, f(Z) is closed and dim f(Z)<=dim Z<d. Therefore
V=P^d_{F_{q^m}}\f(Z)
is a nonempty open subscheme. The restriction f^{-1}(V)->V is finite because it is a restriction of the finite morphism f, and it is etale because f^{-1}(V) is contained in the etale locus E_X.

This gives the required integers m,n and sections s_0,...,s_d. QED.

lemma_417.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(H\) be an \(\mathbb F_q\)-rational very ample divisor on \(X\), and, after fixing a trivialisation of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), let \(L\) be cup product with the cycle class of \(H\). Suppose \(L^{d-m}:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-m}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le m\le d\). Put \(P^m=\ker(L^{d-m+1}:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-m+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\) for \(0\le m\le d\) and \(P^m=0\) for \(m<0\) and \(m>d\). Then for every \(n\ge0\) the map \(\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,n-d)}P^{n-2r}\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \((x_r)\mapsto\sum_r L^r x_r\), is an isomorphism, and each subspace \(L^r(P^{n-2r})\subseteq H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is stable under the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius.
lemma_417.proof:
Proof. Write V^n = H^n_et(X_k, Q_l), with V^n = 0 for n < 0 or n > 2d, and let F_n denote the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of V^n. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant sheaf Q_l on X_k, each V^n is finite-dimensional over Q_l and F_n is an automorphism. By lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing, V^n = 0 for n > 2d. By lemma_77 with m = 1, there is a trace map tr_X : V^{2d} -> Q_l(-d) such that for every n the pairing <x,y>_n = tr_X(x cup y) on V^n x V^{2d-n} is perfect; in particular dim V^n = dim V^{2d-n}.

We first record the Frobenius weight of L. Since H is very ample, choose a closed immersion i : X -> P^N over F_q such that O_X(H) = i^*O(1). Let eta in H^2_et(P^N_k, Q_l) be the cycle class of a hyperplane and let xi be the cycle class of H. Under the fixed trivialization of Q_l(1), xi = i^*eta. Let j : P^{N-1} -> P^N be the inclusion of that hyperplane. Under the usual identification of eta with the Gysin image j_!(1), lemma_gysin_frobenius_weight with c = 1 gives F_P(eta) = q eta, because the q-power arithmetic Frobenius acts as the identity on H^0_et(P^{N-1}_k, Q_l). Since i is defined over F_q, we have F_X^* i^* = i^* F_P^*. Hence F_2(xi) = q xi. Pullback on etale cohomology is compatible with cup products, so for every n and every x in V^n,
F_{n+2}(Lx) = F_{n+2}(xi cup x) = F_2(xi) cup F_n(x) = q xi cup F_n(x) = q L(F_n x).
Thus F_{n+2} L = q L F_n for all n.

For k >= 0 and any a, consider T = L^k : V^a -> V^{a+2k}. With respect to the perfect Poincare pairings, its adjoint is T^dagger = L^k : V^{2d-a-2k} -> V^{2d-a}. Indeed, for x in V^a and y in V^{2d-a-2k},
<L^k x, y> = tr_X(xi^k cup x cup y) = tr_X(x cup xi^k cup y) = <x, L^k y>,
where the middle equality uses graded commutativity and the fact that xi has degree 2. A linear map and its adjoint under perfect pairings have the same rank: if T : U -> W, then ker(T^dagger) is the annihilator of Im(T) in W^*, so rank(T^dagger) = dim W - dim ker(T^dagger) = dim W - (dim W - rank(T)) = rank(T).

From the hard Lefschetz hypothesis we deduce two standard consequences.
(i) If 0 <= a <= d and 0 <= k <= d-a, then L^k : V^a -> V^{a+2k} is injective. Indeed, L^{d-a} = L^{d-a-k} o L^k and L^{d-a} is an isomorphism by hypothesis.
(ii) If a+k >= d, then L^k : V^a -> V^{a+2k} is surjective (if a+2k > 2d the target is zero). Put b = 2d-a-2k. If b < 0, then a+2k > 2d and the target is zero. Assume b >= 0. The inequality a+k >= d implies b <= d, and since d-b = a+2k-d, it also implies k <= d-b. By (i), L^k : V^b -> V^{b+2k} = V^{2d-a} is injective. This map is the adjoint of T, so rank(T) = rank(T^dagger) = dim V^b. By Poincare duality, dim V^b = dim V^{a+2k}; hence T is surjective.

Now fix 0 <= m <= d. We prove V^m = P^m direct sum L(V^{m-2}). First L : V^{m-2} -> V^m is injective by (i) with a = m-2 and k = 1 (for m < 2 the source is zero). If z lies in P^m cap L(V^{m-2}), write z = Lx with x in V^{m-2}. Since z in P^m, L^{d-m+1}z = 0, i.e. L^{d-m+2}x = 0. By (i) with a = m-2 and k = d-m+2 (when m >= 2; otherwise x = 0), this map is injective, so x = 0 and z = 0. Thus the intersection is zero.
Next compute the rank of L^{d-m+1} : V^m -> V^{2d-m+2}. If m = 0 or m = 1, the target is V^{>2d} = 0 and the rank is 0 = dim V^{m-2}. If 2 <= m <= d, factor L^{d-m+1} = L o L^{d-m}. The map L^{d-m} : V^m -> V^{2d-m} is an isomorphism by hypothesis, and L : V^{2d-m} -> V^{2d-m+2} is surjective by (ii) with a = 2d-m and k = 1. Hence rank(L^{d-m+1}) = dim V^{2d-m+2} = dim V^{m-2} by Poincare duality. Therefore dim P^m = dim V^m - dim V^{m-2}. Since L(V^{m-2}) has dimension dim V^{m-2} and intersects P^m trivially, the sum P^m + L(V^{m-2}) has dimension dim V^m, so V^m = P^m direct sum L(V^{m-2}).

We prove the asserted isomorphism for Phi_n. Let r_0(n) = max(0, n-d). We first prove surjectivity by induction on n.
For n = 0, r_0(0) = 0 and Phi_0 is the identity P^0 = V^0 -> V^0, because P^0 = ker(L^{d+1} : V^0 -> V^{2d+2} = 0) = V^0.
Assume n > 0.
If n > 2d, then V^n = 0 by top-degree vanishing. Also r_0(n) = n-d > d, so for r >= r_0(n) we have n-2r <= 2d-n < 0; hence every P^{n-2r} = 0 and Phi_n is the zero map from 0 to 0.
If 1 <= n <= d, then r_0(n) = 0. The primitive decomposition gives V^n = P^n + L(V^{n-2}). If n-2 < 0 the second summand is zero; otherwise the induction hypothesis applied to n-2 gives V^{n-2} = sum_{r >= 0} L^r P^{n-2-2r}. Applying L yields L(V^{n-2}) = sum_{s >= 1} L^s P^{n-2s}. Together with P^n (the term s = 0) this gives surjectivity of Phi_n.
If d < n <= 2d, then r_0(n) = n-d. The map L : V^{n-2} -> V^n is surjective by (ii) with a = n-2 and k = 1. By the induction hypothesis applied to n-2,
V^{n-2} = sum_{r >= r_0(n-2)} L^r P^{n-2-2r}.
Applying L gives
V^n = sum_{s >= r_0(n-2)+1} L^s P^{n-2s}.
If n = d+1, then r_0(n-2)+1 = n-d, so the required lower bound is obtained. If n >= d+2, then r_0(n-2)+1 = n-d-1, and the only extra summand is s = n-d-1. Its primitive degree is n-2s = 2d-n+2. By definition,
P^{2d-n+2} = ker(L^{d-(2d-n+2)+1} : V^{2d-n+2} -> V^{2d-(2d-n+2)+2}) = ker(L^{n-d-1} : V^{2d-n+2} -> V^{n+2}),
so L^{n-d-1}P^{2d-n+2} = 0. Hence the sum over s >= r_0(n-2)+1 coincides with the sum over s >= n-d = r_0(n). This proves surjectivity in all cases.

For injectivity, let r >= r_0(n) and put m = n-2r. If P^m is nonzero then 0 <= m <= d: if n <= d this is clear, and if n > d then r >= n-d gives m <= 2d-n < d. Also r <= d-m, because r <= d-m is equivalent to r >= n-d. By (i), L^r : V^m -> V^n is injective, hence its restriction to P^m is injective. Thus the image of P^{n-2r} in V^n has dimension dim P^{n-2r}.
Let R = floor(n/2). For n > 2d the map is already the zero map from 0 to 0. Assume 0 <= n <= 2d. Using dim P^m = dim V^m - dim V^{m-2} for 0 <= m <= d, the sum of the dimensions of the images is
sum_{r = r_0(n)}^R (dim V^{n-2r} - dim V^{n-2r-2})
= dim V^{n-2r_0(n)} - dim V^{n-2R-2}.
The last index is -1 or -2, so the second term is 0. If n <= d, r_0(n) = 0 and the sum is dim V^n. If n > d, r_0(n) = n-d and the sum is dim V^{2d-n} = dim V^n by Poincare duality. Since the images already sum to V^n and their dimensions add to dim V^n, the sum is direct. Therefore Phi_n is injective, hence an isomorphism.

It remains to check Frobenius stability. From F_{n+2}L = q L F_n and the invertibility of q in Q_l, we have L^N F_m = q^{-N} F_{m+2N} L^N for all N >= 0. Let 0 <= m <= d and x in P^m. With N = d-m+1,
L^N(F_m x) = q^{-N} F_{2d-m+2}(L^N x) = 0,
because L^N x = 0 by definition of P^m. Thus F_m x in P^m, so F_m(P^m) subset P^m; equality follows since F_m is an automorphism and P^m is finite-dimensional. For y in L^r(P^m), write y = L^r x with x in P^m. Then
F_{m+2r}(y) = q^r L^r(F_m x) in L^r(P^m),
again using F_{m+2r}L^r = q^r L^r F_m. Hence each L^r(P^m) is stable under arithmetic Frobenius. This completes the proof.

lemma_420.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(k\), let \(Y\subsetneq X\) be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor that is smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(k\), and let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the closed immersion. Then \(i^*:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(m<d-1\) and is injective for \(m=d-1\).
lemma_420.proof:
Proof. Let U be the open complement of Y in X, with open immersion j: U -> X and closed immersion i: Y -> X. We first prove that U is affine. Since Y is an effective Cartier divisor, there is a line bundle L = O_X(Y) and a section s in H^0(X,L) whose zero scheme is Y. Since Y is ample, L is ample. Choose n >= 1 such that L^n is very ample. The section s^n has zero scheme nY, whose underlying closed subset is Y; hence X minus V(s^n) equals U. Let phi: X -> P^N be the closed immersion associated to the complete linear system of L^n, so L^n = phi^* O_{P^N}(1) and H^0(P^N,O(1)) maps onto H^0(X,L^n). The section s^n is therefore the pullback of a nonzero homogeneous linear form F on P^N. Thus U = phi^{-1}(D_+(F)). By lemma_proj_principal_open_affine, D_+(F) is affine. Since phi is a closed immersion, U is a closed subscheme of an affine scheme, hence affine. Because Y is a proper closed subset of the pure d-dimensional scheme X, U is nonempty and pure of dimension d.

Since U is affine of finite type over the algebraically closed field k and has Krull dimension d, lemma_405 gives H^r_et(U,Q_l) = 0 for every integer r > d.

We use the standard Poincare duality theorem for smooth separated finite type schemes over an algebraically closed field: for U smooth separated finite type of pure dimension d, for every integer q there is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional Q_l-vector spaces H_c^q(U,Q_l) x H^{2d-q}(U,Q_l) -> Q_l(-d). For q < 0 the groups are zero by convention. For 0 <= q < d, the second factor is H^{2d-q}(U,Q_l), and 2d-q > d, so it is zero by lemma_405. Perfectness then forces H_c^q(U,Q_l) = 0 for every q < d.

Now consider the localization long exact sequence for the pair (X,Y), equivalently obtained from the triangle j_! Q_l -> Q_l -> i_* Q_l -> by taking R Gamma(X,-). It is
... -> H_c^m(U,Q_l) -> H^m(X,Q_l) -> H^m(Y,Q_l) -> H_c^{m+1}(U,Q_l) -> ...
for every integer m, with negative cohomology groups interpreted as zero.

Let m be an integer with m < d-1. Then m <= d-2, so m < d and m+1 < d. The vanishing just proved gives H_c^m(U,Q_l) = 0 and H_c^{m+1}(U,Q_l) = 0. Exactness of the displayed sequence gives an isomorphism H^m(X,Q_l) -> H^m(Y,Q_l).

For m = d-1, the same sequence contains 0 -> H^{d-1}(X,Q_l) -> H^{d-1}(Y,Q_l) -> H_c^d(U,Q_l), because H_c^{d-1}(U,Q_l) = 0. Hence the restriction map is injective.

This proves the assertion for every integer m < d-1 and for m = d-1. Negative m are included in the first case, since all negative cohomology groups vanish. QED.

lemma_423.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(F\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(X_k\). Let the set of geometrically connected components of \(X_k\) be acted on by \(F\), and for each orbit choose a component \(C\) and let \(m\ge1\) be minimal with \(F^m(C)=C\). Then for every integer \(i\ge0\), \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if for every orbit the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \(F^m\) is semisimple on \(H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_423.proof:
Proof. Write k=overline(F_q) and let sigma:k->k be sigma(u)=u^q. Let Phi=(id_X x Spec sigma):X_k->X_k be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism. We write F for the induced Q_ell-linear automorphism Phi^* of H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell). If X is empty, all cohomology groups are zero and the assertion is trivial, so assume X non-empty.

1. Components and finite-dimensionality. Since X is of finite type over F_q, X_k is noetherian. A noetherian space has finitely many irreducible components, hence finitely many connected components; each connected component is closed, and because there are finitely many, each is also open. Since k is algebraically closed, the geometrically connected components of X_k are precisely its connected components. Thus the components form a finite partition of X_k into open-and-closed subschemes.

The variety X is proper over F_q. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant sheaf Q_ell with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure, H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell) is finite-dimensional over Q_ell.

2. Decomposition into components. Let pi_0 be the finite set of components. For C in pi_0 let i_C:C->X_k be the inclusion and res_C=i_C^*. Iterating lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum over the finite open-and-closed partition gives an isomorphism
res: H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> direct sum_{C in pi_0} H^i_et(C,Q_ell), alpha |-> (res_C alpha)_C.
For each C let V_C be the inverse image under res of the summand H^i_et(C,Q_ell). Then H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell)=direct sum_C V_C, and each V_C is finite-dimensional.

3. Action of Frobenius on the summands. Since sigma is an automorphism of k, Phi is an automorphism of X_k with inverse id_X x Spec sigma^{-1}. Hence Phi permutes pi_0. For C in pi_0 let Phi_C=Phi|_C:C->Phi(C). This is an isomorphism. Functoriality of pullback gives, for every alpha,
res_C(F alpha) = Phi_C^*(res_{Phi(C)} alpha).   (1)
Indeed i_C o Phi_C = Phi o i_C, and taking pullbacks yields i_C^* Phi^* = Phi_C^* i_{Phi(C)}^*.

If alpha lies in V_D, then res_E(alpha)=0 unless E=D. By (1), res_E(F alpha)=0 unless Phi(E)=D, i.e. E=Phi^{-1}(D). Thus F(V_D)=V_{Phi^{-1}(D)}, and the map V_D -> V_{Phi^{-1}(D)} is the isomorphism Phi_{Phi^{-1}(D)}^*:H^i_et(D,Q_ell)->H^i_et(Phi^{-1}(D),Q_ell). In particular F preserves the sum V_O=direct sum_{C in O} V_C attached to each orbit O of Phi on pi_0.

4. Reduction to orbits. By lemma_6a, F is an invertible Q_ell-linear operator on H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell). Therefore its restrictions to the F-stable subspaces V_O are invertible. Since the whole space is the direct sum of the V_O, lemma_9 gives:
F is semisimple on H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell) iff F is semisimple on V_O for every orbit O.

5. A single orbit. Fix an orbit O and choose C_0 in O. Let m>=1 be minimal with Phi^m(C_0)=C_0. Index the orbit by C_j=Phi^{-j}(C_0) for j modulo m. Then Phi^{-1}(C_j)=C_{j+1}. Put V_j=V_{C_j}. The formula from step 3 gives F(V_j)=V_{j+1} (indices mod m). Let T=F|_{V_O}. Then T is in GL(V_O) and T(V_j)=V_{j+1}.

If V_0=0, then all V_j=0 because T gives isomorphisms V_j -> V_{j+1}; both sides of the desired equivalence for this orbit are trivially true. Assume V_0 nonzero. Apply lemma_397 to the cyclic decomposition V_O=V_0 oplus ... oplus V_{m-1} and the operator T. It says that T is diagonalizable over Q_ell_bar iff T^m is diagonalizable on V_0. By lemma_5, diagonalizability over Q_ell_bar is equivalent to semisimplicity, so
T is semisimple on V_O iff T^m is semisimple on V_0.

6. Identification of T^m on V_0. Since F=Phi^*, we have F^m=(Phi^m)^*. The morphism Phi^m is id_X x Spec sigma^m, where sigma^m(u)=u^{q^m}; it is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on X_k. Because Phi^m(C_0)=C_0, its restriction Phi^m_{C_0}:C_0->C_0 is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on the component C_0 (in the sense induced from X_k). For alpha in V_0, using (1) iterated, or simply functoriality,
res_{C_0}(T^m alpha) = (Phi^m_{C_0})^*(res_{C_0} alpha).
Thus the operator T^m on V_0 is conjugate via the isomorphism res_{C_0}:V_0 -> H^i_et(C_0,Q_ell) to the pullback by Phi^m_{C_0}. By lemma_8, conjugate operators have the same semisimplicity. Hence T^m is semisimple on V_0 iff the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^i_et(C_0,Q_ell) is semisimple.

7. Conclusion. Combining the equivalences from steps 4 and 5-6, for every i>=0,
F is semisimple on H^i_et(X_k,Q_ell)
iff for every orbit O the restriction T^m on V_0 is semisimple
iff for every chosen representative C in O the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^i_et(C,Q_ell).
The choice of representative in an orbit is immaterial: if C_j is another representative, T^m on V_j is conjugate to T^m on V_0 by T^j, so semisimplicity is the same (lemma_8). This proves the lemma.

lemma_compatible_tower_finite_generation.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime. For each integer \(r\ge1\) let \(A_r\) be a finite \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module annihilated by \(\ell^r\), and let \(\rho_{r+1,r}:A_{r+1}\to A_r\) and \(\mu_r:A_r\to A_{r+1}\) be \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-linear maps. Write \(\rho_{r,1}=\rho_{r,r-1}\circ\cdots\circ\rho_{2,1}\). Suppose that \(\ker(\rho_{r,1})=\operatorname{im}(\mu_{r-1})\) for every \(r\ge2\), that \(\rho_{r+1,r}\circ\mu_r\) is multiplication by \(\ell\) on \(A_r\) for every \(r\ge1\), and that \(\mu_{r-1}\circ\rho_{r,r-1}\) is multiplication by \(\ell\) on \(A_r\) for every \(r\ge2\). Then the inverse limit \(\varprojlim_r A_r\) with respect to the maps \(\rho_{r+1,r}\) is a finitely generated \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module.
lemma_compatible_tower_finite_generation.proof:
We prove the statement purely algebraically; no geometry and no external lemma is needed.

NOTATION AND FIRST REMARKS. For each r >= 1 the module A_r is a finite set (finite Z_ell-module) with ell^r A_r = 0; in particular the Z_ell-action on A_r factors through Z/ell^r Z. Put
    A := lim_r A_r = { (a_r)_{r>=1} in prod_{r>=1} A_r : rho_{r+1,r}(a_{r+1}) = a_r for all r >= 1 },
with coordinatewise addition and scalar multiplication. Because every rho_{r+1,r} is Z_ell-linear, A is a Z_ell-submodule of prod_r A_r: if a in A and lambda in Z_ell then rho_{r+1,r}(lambda a_{r+1}) = lambda rho_{r+1,r}(a_{r+1}) = lambda a_r. For r >= s >= 1 write rho_{r,s} := rho_{r,r-1} circ ... circ rho_{s+1,s}, and let pi_r : A -> A_r be the r-th projection; thus pi_r = rho_{r,s} circ pi_r for s <= r, i.e. rho_{r,s}(x_r) = x_s for every x = (x_t) in A. We write K := ker(pi_1) = { x in A : x_1 = 0 } and I := im(pi_1) subset A_1.
