(Side remark, not used below: each A_r is finite discrete, hence compact; A is the equaliser of the two continuous maps prod_r A_r => prod_r A_r given by (a_r) |-> (rho_{r+1,r}(a_{r+1})) and (a_r) |-> (a_r), so A is a closed subgroup of a compact product and is therefore a compact Hausdorff topological group.)

We shall use three times the following elementary fact about inverse systems of finite sets.

CLAIM 1 (Koenig). Let (S_t)_{t>=2} be nonempty finite sets with maps f_t : S_{t+1} -> S_t for t >= 2. Then lim_t S_t = { (y_t)_{t>=2} : f_t(y_{t+1}) = y_t for all t >= 2 } is nonempty.
Proof of Claim 1. For t >= 2 and N >= t let E_{t,N} subset S_t be the set of elements y_t in S_t which occur as the t-th entry of some tuple (y_2,...,y_N) with y_i in S_i and f_i(y_{i+1}) = y_i for 2 <= i <= N-1. Each E_{t,N} is nonempty: given any element of S_N, its successive f-images give such a tuple. Also E_{t,N+1} subset E_{t,N}, since a compatible tuple of length N+1 restricts to one of length N. As S_t is finite, a decreasing sequence of nonempty subsets stabilises, so E_{t,infty} := cap_{N>=t} E_{t,N} is nonempty.
We now build a compatible sequence inductively. Choose y_2 in E_{2,infty}. Suppose y_2,...,y_{t-1} have been chosen with f_i(y_{i+1}) = y_i and y_i in E_{i,infty}. For N >= t the set E'_{t,N} := { y_t in S_t : f_{t-1}(y_t) = y_{t-1} and y_t occurs in a compatible tuple of length N whose (t-1)-st entry is y_{t-1} } is nonempty, because y_{t-1} in E_{t-1,N} supplies such a tuple. The E'_{t,N} are nested subsets of the finite set S_t, so cap_{N>=t} E'_{t,N} is nonempty; choose y_t in it. This yields, for every t >= 2, an element y_t with f_t(y_{t+1}) = y_t. QED (Claim 1).

STEP 2 (the key claim: K subset ell A). Fix x in A with x_1 = 0. For each t >= 2 set
    S_t := { y in A_{t-1} : mu_{t-1}(y) = x_t }.
Each S_t is finite, being a subset of the finite set A_{t-1}.

S_t is nonempty: since x in A we have rho_{t,1}(x_t) = x_1 = 0, so x_t in ker(rho_{t,1}) = im(mu_{t-1}) by hypothesis (a) applied at r = t (valid since t >= 2). Hence some y in A_{t-1} satisfies mu_{t-1}(y) = x_t.

The reduction maps send S_t into S_{t-1} for t >= 3. Indeed, let y in S_t, so mu_{t-1}(y) = x_t. Hypothesis (c) at r = t-1 (valid since t-1 >= 2) says mu_{t-2} circ rho_{t-1,t-2} = (multiplication by ell) on A_{t-1}, and hypothesis (b) at r = t-1 says rho_{t,t-1} circ mu_{t-1} = (multiplication by ell) on A_{t-1}. Therefore
    mu_{t-2}( rho_{t-1,t-2}(y) ) = ell y = rho_{t,t-1}( mu_{t-1}(y) ) = rho_{t,t-1}(x_t) = x_{t-1},
where the last equality is the compatibility of x. Thus rho_{t-1,t-2}(y) in S_{t-1}.

Applying Claim 1 to the system (S_t)_{t>=2} with bonding maps f_t = rho_{t-1,t-2} : S_{t+1} -> S_t (t >= 2), we obtain elements y_t in S_t with rho_{t-1,t-2}(y_t) = y_{t-1} for all t >= 3. Define w = (w_s)_{s>=1} in prod_s A_s by w_s := y_{s+1} (note y_{s+1} in S_{s+1} subset A_s, so this is well typed). Then w in A: for s >= 1,
    rho_{s+1,s}(w_{s+1}) = rho_{s+1,s}(y_{s+2}) = y_{s+1} = w_s
(the bonding relation with t = s+2). Finally, for each t >= 1, using hypothesis (b) at r = t, namely rho_{t+1,t} circ mu_t = (multiplication by ell) on A_t, and y_{t+1} in S_{t+1} so that mu_t(y_{t+1}) = x_{t+1},
    (ell w)_t = ell w_t = ell y_{t+1} = rho_{t+1,t}( mu_t(y_{t+1}) ) = rho_{t+1,t}(x_{t+1}) = x_t.
Hence ell w = x, i.e. x in ell A. This proves K subset ell A.

STEP 3 (A/ell A is a finite F_ell-vector space). Consider the Z_ell-linear surjection pi_1 : A -> I; it induces a surjection of F_ell-vector spaces phi : A/ell A -> I/ell I. We compute its kernel. Clearly phi^{-1}(0) = pi_1^{-1}(ell I)/ell A. We show pi_1^{-1}(ell I) = ell A. The inclusion "supset" holds because pi_1(ell a) = ell pi_1(a) in ell I. Conversely, take x in A with x_1 = pi_1(x) in ell I; write x_1 = ell z with z in I, choose a' in A with pi_1(a') = z, and put x' := x - ell a'. Then pi_1(x') = x_1 - ell z = 0, so x' in K subset ell A by Step 2; hence x = x' + ell a' in ell A. Thus ker(phi) = 0 and phi is an isomorphism A/ell A ~-> I/ell I. Since I is a submodule of the finite module A_1, I is finite, so I/ell I is a finite F_ell-vector space. Hence A/ell A is a finite F_ell-vector space; say dim_{F_ell} A/ell A = k with basis the classes of n_1,...,n_k in A (k = 0 allowed, meaning A/ell A = 0). Let N := Z_ell n_1 + ... + Z_ell n_k subset A, a finitely generated Z_ell-submodule. By construction A = N + ell A.  (If k = 0 this reads A = ell A.)

STEP 4 (the quotients A/ell^n A are finite, and A = N + ell^n A for all n). By induction on n: n = 1 is Step 3. If A = N + ell^n A then ell^n A = ell^n N + ell^{n+1} A subset N + ell^{n+1} A, so A = N + ell^{n+1} A. Thus A = N + ell^n A for all n >= 1.
Now fix n >= 1 and a in A. Write a = nu + ell^n a' with nu in N, say nu = sum_i c_i n_i, c_i in Z_ell. Reduction Z_ell -> Z/ell^n Z is surjective (Z_ell = lim_m Z/ell^m), so c_i = sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_{ij} ell^j + ell^n d_i with c_{ij} in {0,1,...,ell-1} and d_i in Z_ell. Then nu - sum_{i,j} c_{ij} ell^j n_i = ell^n sum_i d_i n_i in ell^n N subset ell^n A, so a is congruent modulo ell^n A to an element of the finite set { sum_{i,j} c_{ij} ell^j n_i : c_{ij} in {0,...,ell-1} }. Hence A/ell^n A is a finite abelian group (of order at most ell^{nk}).

STEP 5 (separatedness: cap_{n>=1} ell^n A = 0). For n >= 1 and a in A we have (ell^n a)_n = ell^n a_n = 0, because A_n is annihilated by ell^n. Hence ell^n A subset ker(pi_n) for every n, and therefore cap_{n>=1} ell^n A subset cap_{n>=1} ker(pi_n) = 0, the last equality holding because an element of prod_r A_r all of whose components vanish is zero.

STEP 6 (N is compact in its ell-adic topology). Choose a Z_ell-linear surjection Z_ell^k -> N, e_i |-> n_i (for k = 0 take N = 0). Endow Z_ell^k and N with their ell-adic topologies (fundamental neighbourhoods of 0 given by ell^m Z_ell^k and ell^m N). The map is a quotient map for these topologies, since the image of ell^m Z_ell^k is exactly ell^m N. Now Z_ell = lim_m Z/ell^m Z is a closed subgroup of the compact product prod_m Z/ell^m Z, hence compact; so Z_ell^k is compact, and its continuous image N is compact.

STEP 7 (N is closed under taking the required limits; conclusion). Fix a in A. For n >= 1 set
    C_n := { nu in N : a - nu in ell^n A }.
Each C_n is nonempty by Step 4 (A = N + ell^n A). If nu_0 in C_n then C_n = nu_0 + (N cap ell^n A): indeed nu in C_n iff (a - nu_0) - (a - nu) = nu - nu_0 lies in ell^n A. The subgroup N cap ell^n A of N has finite index, because N/(N cap ell^n A) ~ (N + ell^n A)/ell^n A = A/ell^n A, which is finite by Step 4. A finite-index subgroup L of the finitely generated Z_ell-module N contains ell^m N for some m: N/L is a finite Z_ell-module, and the annihilator of each of its elements is an ideal of Z_ell of finite index, hence of the form (ell^{m_x}); taking m the maximum over the finitely many generators of N/L gives ell^m N subset L. Hence L is a union of cosets of the open subgroup ell^m N, so L is open and therefore closed in N. Consequently each C_n is closed in N. The C_n are nested, since ell^{n+1} A subset ell^n A. As N is compact (Step 6), the nested family of nonempty closed subsets C_n has nonempty intersection; choose nu in cap_{n>=1} C_n. Then a - nu in cap_{n>=1} ell^n A = 0 by Step 5, so a = nu in N.

Since a was arbitrary, A = N. Thus A is generated over Z_ell by the finitely many elements n_1,...,n_k, i.e. lim_r A_r is a finitely generated Z_ell-module. This completes the proof.

lemma_428.statement: Let q = p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m >= 1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_{q^m}. Put k = bar F_q. If the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_l) for some integer n with 0 <= n < d, then it is semisimple on H^{2d-n}_et(X_k, Q_l).
lemma_428.proof:
Write \(Q:=q^m\). Then \(Q\) is a prime power, \(X\) is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\ge 1\) over \(\mathbb F_Q\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q\), and the operator whose semisimplicity is at stake is the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius
\[
F:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times \operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*,\qquad \sigma(u)=u^{Q}=u^{q^m}.
\]
We must show: if \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for some \(0\le n<d\), then \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^{2d-n}:=H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

Step 1 (finite dimensionality and invertibility). Since \(X\) is projective over \(\mathbb F_Q\) it is proper. The constant sheaf \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) on \(X_k\) is an object of \(D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \(\psi:F_X^*\mathbb Q_\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\). Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm), with the prime power \(Q\) in the role of its \(q\), to \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\) and \(\varphi=\psi\), we obtain that \(H^i\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) for every \(i\). By lemma_6a (eoinm), applied to the \(\mathbb F_Q\)-scheme \(X\) and the automorphism \(\sigma\), the pullback \((\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of \(H^i\) for every \(i\) (its inverse being \((\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*\)). Thus
\[
T:=F|_{H^n}\in \mathrm{GL}(H^n),\qquad S:=F|_{H^{2d-n}}\in \mathrm{GL}(H^{2d-n})
\]
are well-defined invertible operators, and both spaces are finite-dimensional.

Step 2 (Frobenius-equivariant Poincaré duality). Because \(0\le n<d\le 2d\), we may apply lemma_77 (eoinm) with \(Y=X\) (smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)), with the same \(q,m,\ell,k\) and with \(F\) the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Its part (b) gives:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] the pairing \(\langle-,-\rangle:H^n\times H^{2d-n}\to \mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\), \((x,y)\mapsto \operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)\), is a PERFECT pairing of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces;
\item[(ii)] \(\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=q^{md}\langle x,y\rangle\) for all \(x\in H^n\), \(y\in H^{2d-n}\).
\end{itemize}
Its part (a) tells us that \(F\) acts on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) as multiplication by the positive rational number \(c:=q^{md}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\). Put \(L:=\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\); then \(F_L:=F|_L=c\,\mathrm{id}_L\), and \(L\) is one-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\).

Step 3 (the adjoint identification is Frobenius-equivariant). Set \(V:=H^n\) and \(W:=H^{2d-n}\). Define
\[
\phi:W\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L),\qquad \phi(y)(x):=\langle x,y\rangle .
\]
This is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear, and it is an isomorphism precisely because the pairing is perfect: non-degeneracy in the second variable says \(\phi\) is injective, non-degeneracy in the first says it is surjective (and \(\dim V=\dim W<\infty\)).

Give \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L)\) the natural conjugate Frobenius action
\[
F_{\mathrm{Hom}}(f):=F_L\circ f\circ T^{-1},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad (F_{\mathrm{Hom}}f)(x)=c\,f(T^{-1}x).
\]
We claim \(\phi\circ S=F_{\mathrm{Hom}}\circ\phi\). Indeed, for \(x\in V\) and \(y\in W\), apply (ii) to the pair \((T^{-1}x,\,y)\):
\[
\langle x,Sy\rangle=\langle T(T^{-1}x),\,S(y)\rangle=c\,\langle T^{-1}x,\,y\rangle .
\]
Therefore
\[
(\phi(Sy))(x)=\langle x,Sy\rangle=c\,\langle T^{-1}x,y\rangle=c\,\phi(y)(T^{-1}x)=(F_{\mathrm{Hom}}(\phi(y)))(x),
\]
for every \(x\), hence \(\phi(Sy)=F_{\mathrm{Hom}}(\phi(y))\) for every \(y\), proving the claim.

Step 4 (identifying \(F_{\mathrm{Hom}}\) with a tensor product). Since \(L\) is a free \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-module of rank \(1\), the canonical map
\[
V^{\vee}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}L\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L),\qquad \xi\otimes\lambda\longmapsto \bigl(x\mapsto \xi(x)\lambda\bigr)
\]
is an isomorphism. Let \(T^{\vee}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})\) be the contragredient, \((T^{\vee}\xi)(x):=\xi(T^{-1}x)\). Then for \(\xi\in V^{\vee}\), \(\lambda\in L\) and \(x\in V\),
\[
\bigl(F_{\mathrm{Hom}}(\xi\otimes\lambda)\bigr)(x)=c\,(\xi\otimes\lambda)(T^{-1}x)=c\,\xi(T^{-1}x)\,\lambda=(T^{\vee}\xi)(x)\cdot(c\lambda)=\bigl(T^{\vee}\xi\otimes c\lambda\bigr)(x).
\]
Hence, under this isomorphism, \(F_{\mathrm{Hom}}\) corresponds exactly to \(T^{\vee}\otimes F_L=T^{\vee}\otimes(c\,\mathrm{id}_L)\).

Step 5 (the dual of a semisimple operator is semisimple). By hypothesis \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\); by lemma_5 (eoinm) the operator \(T\otimes\mathrm{id}\) is diagonalizable on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). Choose a \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-basis \(e_1,\dots,e_N\) with \((T\otimes\mathrm{id})e_j=\alpha_j e_j\), \(\alpha_j\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\); each \(\alpha_j\neq0\) because \(T\) is invertible. Since \(V\) is finite-dimensional, the natural map \(V^{\vee}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)^{\vee}\) is an isomorphism, so the dual basis \(\varepsilon^1,\dots,\varepsilon^N\) is a basis of \(V^{\vee}\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). For all \(j\),
\[
\bigl((T^{\vee}\otimes\mathrm{id})\varepsilon^i\bigr)(e_j)=\varepsilon^i\bigl((T^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id})e_j\bigr)=\varepsilon^i(\alpha_j^{-1}e_j)=\alpha_j^{-1}\delta_{ij}=\alpha_i^{-1}\delta_{ij}=\bigl(\alpha_i^{-1}\varepsilon^i\bigr)(e_j),
\]
so \((T^{\vee}\otimes\mathrm{id})\varepsilon^i=\alpha_i^{-1}\varepsilon^i\). Thus \(T^{\vee}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).

Step 6 (tensoring with the Tate twist). The automorphism \(c\,\mathrm{id}_L\) of the one-dimensional space \(L\) is represented, over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), by the \(1\times1\) diagonal matrix \((c)\); it is therefore diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). Applying lemma_422 (Spark) to \((V^{\vee},T^{\vee})\) and \((L,c\,\mathrm{id}_L)\), the automorphism \(T^{\vee}\otimes(c\,\mathrm{id}_L)\) of \(V^{\vee}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}L\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). By the identification of Step 4, the operator \(F_{\mathrm{Hom}}\) on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L)\) is conjugate to a diagonalizable operator, hence is itself diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).

Step 7 (transfer back to \(H^{2d-n}\)). By Step 3, \(\phi:W\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L)\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism with \(\phi\circ S=F_{\mathrm{Hom}}\circ\phi\). Lemma_8 (eoinm), applied with \(T_V=S\), \(T_W=F_{\mathrm{Hom}}\) and \(\alpha=\phi\), yields that \(S\) is semisimple if and only if \(F_{\mathrm{Hom}}\) is. By Step 6 and lemma_5 (eoinm), \(F_{\mathrm{Hom}}\) is semisimple; hence \(S=F|_{H^{2d-n}}\) is semisimple, equivalently diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) by lemma_5 again.

This is exactly the required conclusion: the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). (The argument used only \(0\le n\le 2d\); the hypothesis \(n<d\) is more than needed, and no edge case arises for \(n=0\), where the same reasoning applies verbatim since \(H^0\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\) and \(H^{2d}\cong\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) with \(F\) acting as \(q^{md}\).) \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_p1_factor_semisimplicity.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\) be an integer, let \(V\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(n\ge0\). If the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple, equivalently diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((V\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_{q^m}})_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then it is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_p1_factor_semisimplicity.proof:
Write Q := q^m, so Q is a power of p and the ground field in question is F_Q = F_{q^m}. Put

  W := V \times_{\mathbb F_Q} \mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_Q},

and for T \in \{V, W\} write T_k := T \times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q}\operatorname{Spec} k for the base change to k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q. Let \sigma:k\to k, \sigma(c)=c^{Q}, and denote by

  \Phi_T := (\mathrm{id}_T \times \operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* \;\in\; \mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^n_{\acute et}(T_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)

the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius of T_k, which is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism by lemma_6a (eoinm, applied with the base field \mathbb F_{q^m} in the role of the field called \mathbb F_q there, and with \sigma the Q-power automorphism).

Step 0 (finite dimensionality). V is smooth projective over \mathbb F_Q, hence proper; W is a product of the proper \mathbb F_Q-scheme V with the proper \mathbb F_Q-scheme \mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_Q}, hence proper. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) to the proper \mathbb F_Q-schemes V and W with K = \mathbb Q_\ell the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \psi:\mathrm{Frob}^*\mathbb Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell, we obtain that H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and H^n_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces. (Thus the hypothesis of the lemma, and the conclusion, are statements about operators on finite-dimensional spaces, and the zero space, if it occurs, poses no problem: the identity of the zero space is diagonalisable.)

Step 1 (the projection and the section). Let

  p : W = V \times_{\mathbb F_Q}\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_Q} \longrightarrow V, \qquad p(v,t)=v,

be the first projection, and let [1:0] \in \mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_Q) be the \mathbb F_Q-rational point corresponding to the homogeneous prime ideal (X_0) \subset \mathbb F_Q[X_0,X_1] (so X_0 \mapsto 1, X_1 \mapsto 0). Define

  s : V \longrightarrow W, \qquad s(v) = (v,[1:0]);

equivalently s = (\mathrm{id}_V, c) where c:\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q \to \mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_Q} is the morphism defining the point [1:0]. Both s and p are morphisms of \mathbb F_Q-schemes, and

  p \circ s = \mathrm{id}_V \tag{1}

holds by direct evaluation: p(s(v)) = p(v,[1:0]) = v for every v.

Step 2 (functoriality of the Frobenius action for morphisms over the ground field). We record the general fact we apply. Let f:X\to Y be a morphism of \mathbb F_Q-schemes, and let f_k:X_k\to Y_k be its base change to k. Both \mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma and \mathrm{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma are defined because \sigma fixes \mathbb F_Q pointwise (indeed \sigma(a)=a^{q^m}=a for a\in\mathbb F_{q^m}), so they are endomorphisms of X_k and Y_k as \mathbb F_Q-schemes. We claim

  (\mathrm{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ f_k \;=\; f_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma) \tag{2}

as morphisms X_k \to Y_k. Indeed, Y_k = Y\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q}\operatorname{Spec}k is a fibre product, so a morphism T\to Y_k is uniquely determined by the pair of its composites with the two projections, i.e. by a pair (a:T\to Y,\; b:T\to\operatorname{Spec}k) whose structure maps to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q agree. Taking T = X_k, the left-hand side of (2) gives a = p\circ\mathrm{pr}_X = f\circ\mathrm{pr}_X and b = (\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\mathrm{pr}_k, while the right-hand side gives a = f\circ\mathrm{pr}_X\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma) = f\circ\mathrm{pr}_X and b = (\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\mathrm{pr}_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma) = (\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\mathrm{pr}_k. The two pairs coincide, so (2) holds.

Pullback on étale cohomology with constant \mathbb Q_\ell-coefficients is contravariant: for g:X\to Y one has g^*:H^n_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) (induced by the inverse-image functor of the morphism of small étale topoi, using g_{\acute et}^{-1}\mathbb Q_{\ell,Y_k}=\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}), and (g\circ h)^* = h^*\circ g^*. Applying this to (2) gives

  f_k^* \circ \Phi_Y \;=\; \Phi_X\circ f_k^*. \tag{3}

That is: for every morphism f over \mathbb F_Q, the pullback f_k^* is a morphism of \mathbb Q_\ell[\Phi]-modules.

Step 3 (the image of p^* is a Frobenius-stable direct summand). Apply Step 2 to f=p and f=s. We obtain \mathbb Q_\ell-linear maps

  p^* : H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow H^n_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad
  s^* : H^n_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),

satisfying, by (3),

  p^*\circ\Phi_V = \Phi_W\circ p^*, \qquad s^*\circ\Phi_W = \Phi_V\circ s^*. \tag{4}

By (1) and contravariance,

  s^*\circ p^* \;=\; (p\circ s)^* \;=\; \mathrm{id}_V^* \;=\; \mathrm{id}_{H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)}. \tag{5}

Put U := \mathrm{im}(p^*) \subseteq H^n_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). From (5), p^* is injective, so p^*:H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim} U is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism. Moreover, by the first relation in (4),

  \Phi_W(U) = \Phi_W(p^* H^n(V_k)) = p^*(\Phi_V H^n(V_k)) = p^* H^n(V_k) = U,

so U is a \Phi_W-stable \mathbb Q_\ell-linear subspace. (For later reference we note that U is in fact a direct summand: by (5), every x\in H^n(W_k) decomposes as x = p^*s^*x + (x - p^*s^*x) with s^*(x-p^*s^*x)=s^*x-s^*p^*s^*x=0, and U\cap\ker s^* = 0 because x=p^*y\in\ker s^* forces y=s^*p^*y=0. We shall not need this.)

Step 4 (restriction of a semisimple operator to a stable subspace). By hypothesis, \Phi_W is semisimple on the finite-dimensional space H^n_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Since U is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear subspace with \Phi_W(U)\subseteq U, lemma_358 (eoinm) applies and yields that the restricted operator

  \Phi_W|_U \;\in\; \mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(U)

is semisimple on U.

Step 5 (transport along the Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism). The isomorphism p^*:H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}U intertwines \Phi_V with \Phi_W|_U by the first relation in (4). Both operators are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphisms of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces (for \Phi_W|_U this is the content of lemma_358, which asserts \Phi_W|_U\in\mathrm{GL}(U); for \Phi_V it is lemma_6a). Hence lemma_8 (eoinm) applies with (V,T_V) = (H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\Phi_V) and (W,T_W) = (U,\Phi_W|_U), and gives that \Phi_V is semisimple on H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Step 6 (the diagonalisability formulation). By lemma_5 (eoinm), an operator on a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space is semisimple if and only if its scalar extension to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is diagonalisable. Thus the semisimplicity of \Phi_V just obtained is exactly the statement that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell on H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

This is precisely the desired conclusion. Note that the argument used only the existence of the \mathbb F_{q^m}-rational point [1:0]\in\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_{q^m}) and functoriality of the Frobenius action; in particular no Künneth decomposition was needed, and no statement about H^{n-2}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) or about other degrees was invoked, so the argument is non-circular.

QED.

lemma_426.statement: Let q = p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let X and Y be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over F_q, and let f: Y -> X be a finite locally free surjective morphism of degree N >= 1. Let k be an algebraic closure of F_q. For every integer n >= 0, the pullback f^*: H^n_et(X_k, Q_l) -> H^n_et(Y_k, Q_l) is a split monomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces that commutes with the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms.
lemma_426.proof:
Let sigma:k->k be sigma(c)=c^q. For a smooth projective F_q-variety Z and integer i, write H^i(Z)=H^i_et(Z_k,Q_l) and let F_{Z,i} be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of H^i(Z) induced by pullback along F_{Z,k}=id_{Z_k} x Spec sigma. By lemma_6a, F_{Z,i} is a Q_l-linear automorphism.

Since f is a morphism of F_q-varieties, after base change to k the square f_k o F_{Y,k}=F_{X,k} o f_k commutes. Pullback is contravariant, so for every n>=0 we have F_{Y,n} o f^* = f^* o F_{X,n}. This proves the Frobenius-commutation assertion for all n.

It remains to prove that f^* is split. First note that X and Y are integral: smoothness over a field implies regularity, hence local integrality, and geometric connectedness implies connectedness; a connected locally integral scheme of finite type over a field is integral. The morphism f is finite, hence proper. It is surjective, hence dominant. Since f is finite locally free of degree N, its generic fiber is finite locally free of rank N over kappa(X). Because Y is integral and f is dominant, the generic fiber is integral, hence isomorphic to Spec L for a finite field extension L/kappa(X). Its length as a kappa(X)-vector space is N, so [L:kappa(X)]=N. Thus f is generically finite of degree N. Also a finite dominant morphism of integral finite type schemes preserves dimension, so dim X=dim Y. Put d=dim X=dim Y.

If d=0, then X and Y are smooth projective geometrically connected 0-dimensional F_q-schemes. Hence they are finite etale over F_q. A finite etale F_q-scheme is a disjoint union of spectra of finite extensions of F_q. Geometric connectedness forces a single factor of degree 1: Spec F_{q^r} tensor_{F_q} k is a disjoint union of r copies of Spec k, so it is connected only when r=1. Therefore X=Y=Spec F_q and f is the identity, so N=1. Since k is algebraically closed, H^0_et(Spec k,Q_l)=Q_l and H^i_et(Spec k,Q_l)=0 for i>0. Thus f^* is the identity on Q_l in degree 0 and the zero map 0->0 in positive degree; both are split monomorphisms. Frobenius commutation was already proved.

Now assume d>=1. If n>2d, then X_k and Y_k are projective schemes over k of pure dimension d. By lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing, H^n(X)=0 and H^n(Y)=0. Hence f^*:0->0 is a split monomorphism, and Frobenius commutation was already proved.

It remains to treat 0<=n<=2d. Apply lemma_77 with m=1 to X and to Y. It gives trace isomorphisms tr_X:H^{2d}(X)->Q_l(-d) and tr_Y:H^{2d}(Y)->Q_l(-d), normalised on closed points by residue-field degrees, and perfect pairings H^r(Z) x H^{2d-r}(Z)->Q_l(-d), (u,v)->tr_Z(u cup v), for Z in {X,Y}. The same normalisation is used in lemma_top_trace_generically_finite.

For each a in H^n(Y), the assignment b->tr_Y(a cup f^*b) is a Q_l-linear functional on H^{2d-n}(X). By perfection of the pairing on X, the canonical map H^n(X)->Hom(H^{2d-n}(X),Q_l(-d)) is an isomorphism, so there is a unique element f_*a in H^n(X) satisfying tr_X(f_*a cup b)=tr_Y(a cup f^*b) for all b in H^{2d-n}(X). This defines a Q_l-linear auxiliary map f_*:H^n(Y)->H^n(X), defined by adjunction through Poincare duality.

We claim f_* o f^* = N id on H^n(X). Let x in H^n(X) and b in H^{2d-n}(X). Then
tr_X((f_* f^* x) cup b)
= tr_Y(f^*x cup f^*b)
= tr_Y(f^*(x cup b))
= N tr_X(x cup b)
= tr_X((N x) cup b).
The first equality is the defining property of f_*, the second uses functoriality of cup product under pullback, and the third is lemma_top_trace_generically_finite applied to the proper surjective generically finite degree N morphism f:Y->X between smooth projective geometrically connected pure d-dimensional varieties. Since the pairing on X is perfect, equality against every b implies f_* f^* x = N x.

Because N is a positive integer, N is nonzero and hence invertible in Q_l. Define s=(1/N)f_*:H^n(Y)->H^n(X). Then s is Q_l-linear and s o f^*=id. Hence f^* is a split monomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces.

In fact the splitting can be chosen Frobenius-equivariant. Lemma_77 also gives tr_Z(F_{Z,r}u cup F_{Z,s}v)=q^d tr_Z(u cup v) for Z=X,Y. For a in H^n(Y) and b in H^{2d-n}(X),
tr_X(F_{X,n}(f_*a) cup F_{X,2d-n}b)
= q^d tr_X(f_*a cup b)
= q^d tr_Y(a cup f^*b)
= tr_Y(F_{Y,n}a cup F_{Y,2d-n}(f^*b))
= tr_Y(F_{Y,n}a cup f^*F_{X,2d-n}b)
= tr_X(f_*(F_{Y,n}a) cup F_{X,2d-n}b).
The penultimate equality uses the already proved commutation F_{Y,2d-n} o f^* = f^* o F_{X,2d-n}. By lemma_6a, F_{X,2d-n} is an automorphism of H^{2d-n}(X), so as b varies, F_{X,2d-n}b varies through all of H^{2d-n}(X). Perfectness gives F_{X,n} f_* = f_* F_{Y,n}. Since 1/N is a scalar in Q_l fixed by Frobenius, F_{X,n}s=sF_{Y,n}. This stronger equivariance is not needed for the statement but shows the chosen splitting is compatible with arithmetic Frobenius.

Combining the cases d=0, n>2d, and 0<=n<=2d proves that for every integer n>=0 the pullback f^*:H^n(X)->H^n(Y) is a split monomorphism and satisfies F_{Y,n} o f^* = f^* o F_{X,n}.

lemma_ample_complement_pairing.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field and let \ell \neq \operatorname{char}(k) be prime. Let X be a smooth projective connected variety of pure dimension d \ge 1 over k, let Y \subsetneq X be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor that is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over k, and put U=X\setminus Y. Then for every integer a with 0\le a\le 2d the cup-product pairing H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^{2d-a}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell) is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces, where \mathbb Q_\ell denotes the constant sheaf.
lemma_ample_complement_pairing.proof: Let s be the canonical section of O_X(Y). Its zero scheme is Y, and on U=X minus Y it generates O_X(Y). Since Y is an ample Cartier divisor, O_X(Y) is ample. Applying lemma_308 to the projective k-scheme X, the ample line bundle O_X(Y), n=1, and s shows that U is affine. In particular U is separated and of finite type over k. Also X is smooth and connected over the algebraically closed field k; hence X is regular and locally irreducible, and a connected locally irreducible noetherian scheme is irreducible. Since Y is a proper nonempty closed subset, U is a nonempty open subset of an irreducible scheme, hence U is irreducible. As an open subscheme of the smooth pure d-fold X, U is smooth of pure dimension d. We use the standard Poincare duality theorem for smooth irreducible separated varieties over an algebraically closed field: if V is smooth irreducible of pure dimension d over k and l != char(k), then H^i_c(V,Q_l) and H^i(V,Q_l) are finite-dimensional Q_l-vector spaces, there is an isomorphism tr_V: H^{2d}_c(V,Q_l(d)) -> Q_l, and for every r the cup-product pairing H^r_c(V,Q_l) x H^{2d-r}(V,Q_l(d)) -> Q_l, (u,v) -> tr_V(u cup v), is perfect. Apply this theorem to V=U. Fix a nonzero element tau in Q_l(d). For x in H^a_c(U,Q_l) and y in H^{2d-a}(U,Q_l), let mu_a(x,y)=x cup y in H^{2d}_c(U,Q_l). Define B_a(x,y)=tr_U(x cup (y tensor tau)). The map y -> y tensor tau is an isomorphism H^{2d-a}(U,Q_l) -> H^{2d-a}(U,Q_l(d)), and the standard duality pairing with r=a is perfect; hence B_a is perfect. The map psi: H^{2d}_c(U,Q_l) -> Q_l given by psi(z)=tr_U(z tensor tau) is an isomorphism, since tensoring with tau is an isomorphism and tr_U is an isomorphism. Moreover psi o mu_a = B_a. For finite-dimensional vector spaces V,W and a one-dimensional target T, a bilinear pairing V x W -> T is perfect if and only if its composite with any isomorphism T -> Q_l is perfect: the left and right adjoints differ by the isomorphisms induced on Hom spaces by that isomorphism. Applying this with V=H^a_c(U,Q_l), W=H^{2d-a}(U,Q_l), T=H^{2d}_c(U,Q_l), and psi, the perfectness of B_a implies the perfectness of mu_a. The finite-dimensionality of H^a_c(U,Q_l) and H^{2d-a}(U,Q_l) is part of the standard duality theorem. This completes the proof.

lemma_431.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(m\ge1\), let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let H be a very ample divisor on X defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(\xi=\mathrm{cl}(H)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) under a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), let L be cup product with \(\xi\), and put \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\). Suppose cup product with \(\xi^{\,d-n}\) is an isomorphism \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(0\le n\le d\), let \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace and set \(B(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)\). Suppose there exist a field embedding \(\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) and \(\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}\) such that \((x,y)\mapsto\varepsilon\,\sigma(B(x,y))\) is a positive definite Hermitian form on \(P^d\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C\). Then the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(P^d\).
lemma_431.proof:
Write $Q:=q^{m}=p^{ma}$, a prime power, so that $X$ is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension $d\ge 1$ over $\mathbb F_{Q}$, and let $F:=F_d=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^{Q}$ denote the $Q$-power (equivalently, $q^m$-power) arithmetic Frobenius $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

STEP 1 (finite dimensionality). $X$ is projective over $\mathbb F_{Q}$, hence proper. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) with $\mathbb F_q:=\mathbb F_Q$, $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ the constant sheaf (an object of $D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$) equipped with its natural arithmetic-Frobenius isomorphism, we obtain that $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space for every $n$. In particular $H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite dimensional, and since $P^d=\ker(L)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear subspace of it, $P^d$ is finite dimensional.

STEP 2 ($P^d$ is stable under $F$ and $F^{-1}$; $T:=F|_{P^d}\in\mathrm{GL}(P^d)$). Apply lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable (eoinm) with its ground field $\mathbb F_q$ taken to be $\mathbb F_{Q}$: it gives $F\circ L=Q\,L\circ F$ on every $H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and that for $0\le j\le d$ the space $\ker\!\bigl(L^{\,d-j+1}:H^j\to H^{2d-j+2}\bigr)$ is stable under both $F$ and $F^{-1}$. For $j=d$ this kernel is exactly $\ker(L:H^d\to H^{d+2})=P^d$. Hence $F(P^d)=P^d=F^{-1}(P^d)$, and $T:=F|_{P^d}$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $P^d$ with inverse $F^{-1}|_{P^d}$. (One may also check this directly: $Lx=0\iff LF x=Q^{-1}F Lx=0$, and similarly with $F$ replaced by $F^{-1}$.)

If $P^d=0$, then $T$ is the identity of the zero space; its characteristic polynomial is $1$, which is square-free, so $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and the lemma holds. Assume from now on that $P^d\ne 0$.

STEP 3 (the pairing $B$ is perfect). By hypothesis, $L^{d-n}:H^n\to H^{2d-n}$ is an isomorphism for every $0\le n\le d$. Therefore lemma_primitive_middle_pairing_perfect (Spark), applied over $\mathbb F_Q$, says that $P^d\times P^d\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, $(x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)$, is a perfect pairing. Via the fixed trivialisation $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell$ appearing in the statement, $B(x,y):=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)$ is thus a perfect $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear pairing $P^d\times P^d\to\mathbb Q_\ell$. (We take $\operatorname{tr}_X$ to be the standard Poincar\'e duality trace used in that lemma and in lemma_77(a), normalised by $\operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_Q]$ on closed points. Any other choice of "the Poincar\'e duality trace" differs from this one by a fixed scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, i.e. replaces $B$ by $\lambda B$; every property of $B$ used below is either a hypothesis of the present lemma (perfectness, positive definiteness of $\varepsilon\,\sigma B$) or homogeneous of degree one in $B$ (the identity $B(Fx,Fy)=Q^{d}B(x,y)$ and the resulting adjoint relation), so the argument is unaffected by that normalisation choice.)

STEP 4 ($F$ scales $B$ by $Q^{d}=q^{md}$). Let $x,y\in P^d$. First, Frobenius pullback commutes with cup product: the cup product on $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is induced, in the derived category of the small \'etale topos, by the canonical isomorphism $\mathbb Q_\ell\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbb Q_\ell$ together with the derived tensor product, and for any morphism $f$ the functor $\mathbf L f^*$ is symmetric monoidal, $\mathbf Lf^*(\mathcal K\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathcal L)\simeq\mathbf Lf^*\mathcal K\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbf Lf^*\mathcal L$, with $\mathbf Lf^*\mathbb Q_\ell=\mathbb Q_\ell$; the induced map on $\mathrm{Hom}$ groups therefore satisfies $f^*(\alpha\cup\beta)=f^*\alpha\cup f^*\beta$. Applying this to $f=F_{X_k}=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ gives $F(x\cup y)=Fx\cup Fy$. Second, by lemma_77(a) (eoinm), applied to $Y=X$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ with the $q^m$-power Frobenius, the trace $\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ as multiplication by the positive rational number $q^{md}=Q^{d}$. Under the chosen $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear identification $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell$, the transported operator is $\varphi\circ(Q^{d}\,\mathrm{id})\circ\varphi^{-1}=Q^{d}\,\mathrm{id}$, i.e. $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell$ as multiplication by $Q^{d}$. Combining, with $c:=Q^{d}=q^{md}\in\mathbb Q^{\times}\subset\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$,
\[
B(Fx,Fy)=\operatorname{tr}_X(Fx\cup Fy)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F(x\cup y)\bigr)=c\,\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup y)=c\,B(x,y).
\]
Note $F x, F y\in P^d$ by Step 2, so both sides are defined.

STEP 5 (the adjoint relation $T^{\dagger}=c\,T^{-1}$). Let $a\mapsto a^{\dagger}$ be the adjoint anti-automorphism of $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(P^d)$ attached to the perfect pairing $B$, defined by $B(au,w)=B(u,a^{\dagger}w)$ for all $u,w$ (existence and uniqueness of $a^{\dagger}$ follow from perfectness, e.g. via $\theta:w\mapsto B(-,w)$, $a^{\dagger}=\theta^{-1}\circ a^{t}\circ\theta$). For all $x,y\in P^d$, substituting $F^{-1}y$ for $y$ in Step 4 gives
\[
B(Fx,y)=B\bigl(Fx,F(F^{-1}y)\bigr)=c\,B(x,F^{-1}y)=B\bigl(x,(cT^{-1})y\bigr),
\]
while by definition of the adjoint $B(Fx,y)=B(x,T^{\dagger}y)$. Hence $B\bigl(x,(T^{\dagger}-cT^{-1})y\bigr)=0$ for every $x\in P^d$; perfectness (non-degeneracy in the first variable) forces $(T^{\dagger}-cT^{-1})y=0$. As $y$ was arbitrary, $T^{\dagger}=c\,T^{-1}$.

STEP 6 (positivity hypothesis in the form needed). By hypothesis there is an embedding $\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ such that
\[
h(x,y):=\varepsilon\,\sigma\bigl(B(x,y)\bigr),\qquad x,y\in P^d\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C,
\]
is a positive definite Hermitian form. Since $c=q^{md}$ is a positive rational number, $\sigma(c)=q^{md}\in\mathbb R_{>0}$. We verify the covariance identity of $h$ with respect to $T_\sigma:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. For $\mathbb Q_\ell$-rational vectors $u,v\in P^d$ (viewed inside $P^d\otimes\mathbb C$),
\[
h(T_\sigma u,T_\sigma v)=\varepsilon\,\sigma\bigl(B(Tu,Tv)\bigr)=\varepsilon\,\sigma\bigl(c\,B(u,v)\bigr)=\sigma(c)\,\varepsilon\,\sigma\bigl(B(u,v)\bigr)=\sigma(c)\,h(u,v),
\]
using that $\sigma$ fixes $\mathbb Q$, hence $c$. Now take arbitrary $x,y\in P^d\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C$; write $x=\sum_i\lambda_i u_i$ and $y=\sum_j\mu_j v_j$ with $\lambda_i,\mu_j\in\mathbb C$ and $u_i,v_j\in P^d$. Since $T_\sigma$ is $\mathbb C$-linear and $h$ is sesquilinear,
\[
h(T_\sigma x,T_\sigma y)=\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\overline{\mu_j}\,h(T_\sigma u_i,T_\sigma v_j)=\sigma(c)\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\overline{\mu_j}\,h(u_i,v_j)=\sigma(c)\,h(x,y)
\]
(with the analogous computation under the opposite sesquilinearity convention). Thus $h(T_\sigma x,T_\sigma y)=\sigma(c)\,h(x,y)$ for all $x,y$.

STEP 7 (conclusion). We have assembled exactly the hypotheses of lemma_409 (Spark) with $V=P^d$ (a nonzero finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space), $T=F|_{P^d}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $\langle-,-\rangle=B$ (perfect, Step 3), $a\mapsto a^{\dagger}$ its adjoint, $c=q^{md}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ with $\sigma(c)\in\mathbb R_{>0}$ (Step 6), the relation $T^{\dagger}=cT^{-1}$ (Step 5), and the positive definite Hermitian form $h$ with $h(T_\sigma x,T_\sigma y)=\sigma(c)h(x,y)$ (Step 6). Lemma 409 yields that $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. By Step 2, $T$ is precisely the restriction to $P^d$ of the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius, which therefore is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ on $P^d$. This completes the proof.

lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power and let l != p be prime, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d >= 2 over F_q, let Y subsetneq X be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor defined over F_q which is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over F_q, let j:U = X \ Y hookrightarrow X be the open immersion, and let k = overline(F_q). Then H^j_et,c(U_k, Q_l) = 0 for every integer j < d.
lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement.proof: Let i:Y -> X denote the closed immersion and j:U -> X the open immersion. Write i_k:Y_k -> X_k and j_k:U_k -> X_k for the base changes to k = overline F_q. Since base change commutes with complements of closed subschemes, U_k = X_k \ Y_k. First, for every finite type k-scheme V and every integer n<0, H^n_et,c(V,Q_l)=0. Indeed compactly supported cohomology is defined as the right derived functor R^n Gamma_c(V,Q_l) of the left exact functor Gamma_c(V,-), and right derived functors vanish in negative degrees. This proves the assertion for j<0. Now fix an integer j with 0 <= j <= d-1. We use the localisation long exact sequence supplied by lemma_283. Its hypotheses are satisfied because X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=1 over F_q and Y is an effective ample Cartier divisor defined over F_q and smooth of pure dimension d-1. Thus for every integer n the localisation sequence contains an exact piece H^n_et,c(U_k,Q_l) -> H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) -> H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) -> H^{n+1}_et,c(U_k,Q_l), where the first map is extension by zero j_{k,!} and the second is pullback i_k^*. We also need the affine Lefschetz theorem lemma_420 over k. The base change X_k is smooth projective and connected of pure dimension d over k: smoothness, projectivity, connectedness of a geometrically connected variety, and purity of dimension are stable under base change from F_q to k. The base change Y_k is nonempty, smooth of pure dimension d-1, and is an effective ample Cartier divisor on X_k: nonemptiness, smoothness, purity of dimension, and the Cartier and ampleness properties are stable under the flat base change Spec k -> Spec F_q; strict inclusion Y_k subsetneq X_k is preserved because this base change is faithfully flat. Therefore lemma_420 applies to X_k and Y_k. It says that for every integer m<d-1 the pullback i_k^*:H^m_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^m_et(Y_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism, and for m=d-1 it is injective. Apply the long exact sequence in the degrees j-1 and j. It gives an exact sequence H^{j-1}_et(X_k,Q_l) --alpha--> H^{j-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l) --delta--> H^j_et,c(U_k,Q_l) --beta--> H^j_et(X_k,Q_l) --gamma--> H^j_et(Y_k,Q_l), where alpha and gamma are the pullbacks i_k^* and beta is the extension-by-zero map j_{k,!}. If j=0, then H^{-1}_et(X_k,Q_l)=H^{-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l)=0 by the same negative-degree vanishing for ordinary cohomology. We claim alpha is surjective. If j=0 this is clear because both groups are zero. If j>=1, then j-1 <= d-2 < d-1, so by lemma_420 alpha is an isomorphism, hence surjective. We claim gamma is injective. Since j <= d-1, either j<d-1 and lemma_420 says gamma is an isomorphism, or j=d-1 and lemma_420 says gamma is injective. Now use exactness. Exactness at H^{j-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l) gives ker(delta)=im(alpha). Since alpha is surjective, im(alpha)=H^{j-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l), hence ker(delta)=H^{j-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l), so delta=0. Exactness at H^j_et,c(U_k,Q_l) gives ker(beta)=im(delta). Since delta=0, ker(beta)=0; hence beta is injective. Exactness at H^j_et(X_k,Q_l) gives im(beta)=ker(gamma). Since gamma is injective, ker(gamma)=0; hence im(beta)=0, so beta is the zero map. A linear map which is both injective and zero has zero domain. Therefore H^j_et,c(U_k,Q_l)=0. Combining this with the negative-degree case proves H^j_et,c(U_k,Q_l)=0 for every integer j<d.

lemma_429_middle_degree.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime and \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be its cycle class under a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), and let \(L\) denote cup product with \(\xi\). Suppose that \(L^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\), that the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\), and that it is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n<d\). Then it is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_429_middle_degree.proof: Proof. Put H^n = H^n_et(X_k,Q_l), and let F denote the q-power arithmetic Frobenius on the total cohomology. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant sheaf Q_l on X_k with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure, each H^n is finite-dimensional over Q_l. By lemma_6a, F is a Q_l-linear automorphism of each H^n. By lemma_5 we identify semisimple Q_l-linear operators with operators diagonalizable over bar Q_l; hence the hypotheses and the desired conclusion are statements about semisimplicity. Define P^m = ker(L^{d-m+1}:H^m -> H^{2d-m+2}) for 0<=m<=d and P^m=0 for m<0 or m>d, as in lemma_417. The assumed hard Lefschetz isomorphisms are exactly the hypothesis of lemma_417. Therefore lemma_417 gives an isomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces Phi: direct sum_{r>=0} P^{d-2r} -> H^d, (x_r) -> sum_r L^r x_r. Thus H^d is the finite direct sum of the subspaces S_r = L^r(P^{d-2r}) for 0<=r<=floor(d/2); the sum is direct because Phi is injective, and lemma_417 also says that each S_r is stable under F. We first prove a Frobenius scaling relation. The class xi is the cycle class of the F_q-rational divisor H under the fixed nonzero element of Q_l(1). By lemma_78 with j=1, F(xi)=q xi. Pullback on etale cohomology is a graded ring homomorphism for the cup product; this follows from the definition of cup product via derived tensor product and the symmetric monoidal nature of pullback. Applying this to the Frobenius morphism gives F(alpha cup beta)=F(alpha) cup F(beta) for homogeneous classes alpha and beta. Hence, since F(1)=1, induction gives F(xi^s)=q^s xi^s for every s>=0. For every homogeneous y in H^m, F(L^s y)=F(xi^s cup y)=F(xi^s) cup F(y)=q^s xi^s cup F(y)=q^s L^s F(y). Thus F L^s = q^s L^s F for all s>=0. Now fix m with 0<=m<=d. If y in P^m, then L^{d-m+1}y=0. Applying F and using the scaling relation with s=d-m+1 gives 0=F(L^{d-m+1}y)=q^{d-m+1}L^{d-m+1}F(y). Since l != p, q^{d-m+1} is nonzero in Q_l, so L^{d-m+1}F(y)=0. Hence F(P^m) subset P^m. Because F is an automorphism and P^m is finite-dimensional, F restricts to an automorphism of P^m. For r=0, S_0=P^d=ker(L:H^d -> H^{d+2}); if S_0=0 it is semisimple trivially, and otherwise the hypothesis says that F is semisimple on S_0. Now let r>=1 and put m=d-2r. If P^m=0, then S_r=0 and there is nothing to prove. Assume P^m nonzero. Then m<d, so by hypothesis F is semisimple on H^m. Since P^m is F-stable, lemma_358 implies that F|P^m is semisimple. The map alpha=L^r:P^m -> S_r is an isomorphism: it is surjective by definition of S_r, and injective because Phi is injective and alpha is the restriction of Phi to the r-th summand. In particular S_r is nonzero. Let T_P=F|P^m and let T_S=F|S_r. Both are automorphisms, since P^m is F-stable as proved above, S_r is F-stable by lemma_417, and F is an automorphism of H^d. The relation F L^r = q^r L^r F gives, for x in P^m, alpha(T_P x)=L^r(Fx)=q^{-r}F(L^r x)=q^{-r}T_S(alpha x), where q^{-r} exists in Q_l because l != p. Thus alpha T_P = T' alpha with T'=q^{-r}T_S. The operator T' is invertible because T_S is invertible and q^{-r} is nonzero. By lemma_8, T_P is semisimple if and only if T' is semisimple. Since T_P is semisimple, T' is semisimple. Multiplication by a nonzero scalar preserves diagonalizability over bar Q_l: if an operator is diagonalizable, multiplying it by a nonzero scalar leaves the same eigenbasis unchanged and only rescales the eigenvalues. Applying this with scalar q^r shows that T_S is semisimple. Therefore F is semisimple on every summand S_r. Finally, if all S_r are zero, then H^d=0 and the conclusion is trivial. Otherwise, the nonzero S_r form a finite F-stable direct-sum decomposition of H^d, and each restriction F|S_r is an automorphism. By lemma_9, the direct-sum operator F on H^d is semisimple if and only if its restriction to each nonzero S_r is semisimple. We have proved the latter for all r. Therefore F is semisimple on H^d. By lemma_5 this is exactly diagonalizable over bar Q_l. QED.

lemma_hard_lefschetz_reduces_to_injectiv.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(\mathcal A\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be its cycle class under a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), and for each integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d\) let \(L^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) denote cup product with \(\xi^{\,d-n}\). Then for each integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d\), the map \(L^{d-n}\) is injective if and only if it is an isomorphism.
lemma_hard_lefschetz_reduces_to_injectiv.proof:
Fix integers q = p^a, ℓ ≠ p, a smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of pure dimension d ≥ 1 over F_q, k = \bar{F}_q, an F_q-rational ample line bundle 𝒜 with cycle class ξ ∈ H^2_et(X_k, Q_ℓ), and an integer n with 0 ≤ n ≤ d. Write

  V := H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ),   W := H^{2d-n}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ),   T := Q_ℓ(-d),

and let φ := L^{d-n}: V → W denote x ↦ x ∪ ξ^{d-n}.

**Step 1: φ is a well-defined Q_ℓ-linear map.** Cup product on H^•_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) is Q_ℓ-bilinear, so for a fixed element ξ^{d-n} ∈ H^{2(d-n)}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) the map x ↦ x ∪ ξ^{d-n} is Q_ℓ-linear. Since deg ξ = 2, an element of H^n is sent to H^{n+2(d-n)} = H^{2d-n} = W. For n = d this is cup product with ξ^0 = 1, i.e. the identity of H^d. Thus φ ∈ Hom_{Q_ℓ}(V, W).

**Step 2: V and W are finite-dimensional.** The constant sheaf Q_ℓ lies in D^b_c(X_k, Q_ℓ): X_k is Noetherian (of finite type over the field k), and Q_ℓ is locally constant with stalk Q_ℓ of finite rank for the one-stratum stratification {X_k}. Equip Q_ℓ with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism ψ: F_X^* Q_ℓ → Q_ℓ. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) with K = Q_ℓ and φ = ψ, we obtain that H^i_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) is finite-dimensional over Q_ℓ for every integer i. In particular dim_{Q_ℓ} V < ∞ and dim_{Q_ℓ} W < ∞.

**Step 3: a perfect pairing V × W → T.** Apply lemma_77 (eoinm) with m = 1 and Y = X; its hypotheses are satisfied because X is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^1} = F_q. Part (a) supplies the trace isomorphism tr := tr_X: H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) ~→ Q_ℓ(-d), and part (b) asserts that for every integer r with 0 ≤ r ≤ 2d the pairing

  H^r_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) × H^{2d-r}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → Q_ℓ(-d),   (x, y) ↦ tr(x ∪ y),

is a perfect pairing of Q_ℓ-vector spaces. Since 0 ≤ n ≤ d ≤ 2d and 0 ≤ 2d − n ≤ 2d, taking r = n yields a perfect pairing ⟨−,−⟩: V × W → T. By definition of perfectness, the two induced Q_ℓ-linear maps

  V → Hom_{Q_ℓ}(W, T),  x ↦ (y ↦ ⟨x, y⟩),      W → Hom_{Q_ℓ}(V, T),  y ↦ (x ↦ ⟨x, y⟩)

are isomorphisms.

**Step 4: dim V = dim W.** First note that T = Q_ℓ(-d) is a finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector space, of dimension 1: indeed k = \bar F_q contains all ℓ-power roots of unity, μ_{ℓ^r}(k) is a finite subgroup of the multiplicative group k^×, hence is cyclic (a finite subgroup G of k^× of exponent m satisfies |G| ≤ m because X^m − 1 has at most m roots, while m ≤ |G| always; thus |G| = m and a finite abelian group whose exponent equals its order is cyclic), so choosing generators ζ_{ℓ^r} with ζ_{ℓ^{r+1}}^ℓ = ζ_{ℓ^r} identifies lim←_r μ_{ℓ^r} with Z_ℓ; therefore Q_ℓ(1) = (lim←_r μ_{ℓ^r}) ⊗_{Z_ℓ} Q_ℓ has Q_ℓ-dimension 1, and so does its d-th tensor power Q_ℓ(d) and its Q_ℓ-linear dual Q_ℓ(-d) = Hom_{Q_ℓ}(Q_ℓ(d), Q_ℓ). (Equivalently, the nonzero element of Q_ℓ(1) fixed in the statement identifies Q_ℓ(1) with Q_ℓ.)

Taking Q_ℓ-dimensions in the two isomorphisms of Step 3 and using dim Hom_{Q_ℓ}(U, T) = dim U · dim T for finite-dimensional U gives

  dim V = dim W · dim T,     dim W = dim V · dim T.

If dim V and dim W are both ≥ 1, substituting the first equality into the second gives dim W = dim W · (dim T)^2, hence (dim T)^2 = 1, so dim T = 1 and then dim V = dim W. If dim W = 0 then the first equality gives dim V = 0, and if dim V = 0 the second gives dim W = 0; in these cases dim V = dim W = 0 as well. In every case,

  dim_{Q_ℓ} H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) = dim_{Q_ℓ} H^{2d-n}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) < ∞.   (∗)

(Notice that this dimension count uses only perfectness of the trace pairing; no adjointness statement about φ, no Gysin map, and no operator Λ is involved.)

**Step 5: isomorphism ⇒ injective.** If φ is an isomorphism of Q_ℓ-vector spaces then it is bijective, hence injective. This direction is immediate.

**Step 6: injective ⇒ isomorphism.** Suppose φ is injective. By the rank–nullity theorem applied to the Q_ℓ-linear map φ: V → W,

  dim V = dim ker φ + dim im φ = 0 + dim im φ,

so dim im φ = dim V. By (∗), dim im φ = dim W. Since im φ is a Q_ℓ-linear subspace of the finite-dimensional space W and has the same dimension as W, im φ = W; that is, φ is surjective. A bijective Q_ℓ-linear map is an isomorphism of Q_ℓ-vector spaces. This proves the nontrivial direction.

**Step 7: edge cases.** The argument is uniform in n, but we record the endpoints explicitly. For n = d, φ = L^0 = id_{H^d}, which is both injective and an isomorphism, so both sides of the equivalence hold. For n = 0, (∗) reads dim H^0 = dim H^{2d}; indeed H^0_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) ≅ Q_ℓ because X is geometrically connected, and H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) ≅ Q_ℓ(-d) by the trace isomorphism of lemma_77(a), so both sides are 1-dimensional and the equivalence holds by Step 6 (the map Q_ℓ → Q_ℓ(-d) sends 1 to tr(ξ^d), and is injective exactly when it is nonzero, hence an isomorphism). No separate treatment is needed, since Steps 2–6 already cover 0 ≤ n ≤ d.

Combining Steps 5 and 6, for each integer n with 0 ≤ n ≤ d the Lefschetz map L^{d-n}: H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{2d-n}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) is injective if and only if it is an isomorphism. ∎

lemma_432.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, m>=1, l!=p prime, X a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d>=1 over F_{q^m}, k=overline(F_q). Let H be a very ample divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, let xi in H^2_et(X_k,Q_l) be its cycle class via a fixed nonzero element of Q_l(1), let L be cup product with xi, and put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_l)). Let tr_X:H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_l)->Q_l(-d) be the Poincare duality trace and B(x,y)=tr_X(x cup y). Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F restricts to an automorphism of P^d such that B(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}B(x,y) for all x,y in P^d.
lemma_432.proof:
Write Q := q^m. Then F_{q^m} is the finite field with Q elements and k = \overline{F}_q = \overline{F}_{q^m}. Let \sigma:k\to k, \sigma(u)=u^Q, and for each i\ge 0 put H^i := H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and F_i := (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*:H^i\to H^i, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. In the statement, F denotes this operator on H^d (and on H^{2d} inside the trace computation).

Step 0 (finite dimensionality and invertibility of F). The variety X is proper over F_{q^m}. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm/lemma_45_finite_frob) with base field F_{q^m}, with K = \mathbb Q_\ell the constant complex equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism: each H^i is a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space carrying a canonical \mathbb Q_\ell-linear arithmetic-Frobenius automorphism. By lemma_6a (eoinm/lemma_6a) this canonical operator is exactly F_i = (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, and its inverse is the geometric Frobenius (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*. Hence F_i\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^i) for every i; in particular H^d and H^{d+2} are finite-dimensional, so P^d := \ker(L:H^d\to H^{d+2}) is a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space.

Step 1 (Frobenius commutes with L up to the scalar Q). The divisor H is very ample and defined over F_{q^m}, and \xi = \mathrm{cl}(H)\in H^2 is its cycle class obtained through the fixed nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell(1); L:H^i\to H^{i+2} is x\mapsto \xi\cup x. Apply lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable (eoinm/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable) to the smooth projective pure-dimensional variety X over the finite field F_{q^m} (so that the field denoted \mathbb F_q and the prime power denoted q in that lemma are F_{q^m} and Q = q^m, and its Frobenius F is our F). Its first assertion gives, for every i\ge 0,
   (\ast)\qquad F_{i+2}\circ L = Q\,(L\circ F_i)\quad\text{on }H^i,
and its second assertion, applied at m=d (where d-m+1 = 1 and 2d-m+2 = d+2, so that the lemma's P^d is precisely the kernel of L:H^d\to H^{d+2} appearing in the present statement), gives that P^d is stable under both F_d and F_d^{-1}.

Step 2 (F restricts to an automorphism of P^d). First, for the reader's convenience we spell out the one-line verification of stability from (\ast): if x\in P^d, i.e. Lx = 0, then by (\ast) with i=d,
   L(F_d x) = Q^{-1}F_{d+2}(Lx) = Q^{-1}F_{d+2}(0) = 0,
so F_d x\in P^d. Conjugating (\ast) by F_d (which is invertible by Step 0) gives L\circ F_d^{-1} = Q\,(F_d^{-1}\circ L); hence for x\in P^d,
   L(F_d^{-1}x) = Q\,F_d^{-1}(Lx) = 0,
so F_d^{-1}x\in P^d as well. (These are exactly the conclusions of the cited lemma in Step 1.) Thus F_d(P^d)\subseteq P^d and F_d^{-1}(P^d)\subseteq P^d. The restriction \varphi := F_d|_{P^d}:P^d\to P^d is then bijective: injectivity is inherited from F_d\in\mathrm{GL}(H^d); surjectivity holds because for x\in P^d one has F_d^{-1}x\in P^d and \varphi(F_d^{-1}x) = x. Hence F restricts to an element of \mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(P^d), with inverse F_d^{-1}|_{P^d}. (If P^d = 0 there is nothing to check and the same conclusion holds vacuously.)

Step 3 (the trace isomorphism and its Frobenius equivariance). Apply lemma_77 (eoinm/lemma_77) to Y = X, regarded as a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, with F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Part (a) supplies the canonical Poincar\'e duality trace isomorphism \operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d) and states that it is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where F acts on \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) as multiplication by the positive rational number q^{md} = Q^d. In formulas,
   (\dagger)\qquad \operatorname{tr}\bigl(F_{2d}(z)\bigr) = q^{md}\,\operatorname{tr}(z)\quad\text{for all }z\in H^{2d}.
Part (b) of the same lemma asserts that (x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y) is a perfect pairing on H^d\times H^{2d-n}|_{n=d} = H^d\times H^d; we only need the equivariance (\dagger) below, so (b) is not used as a black box.

The map \operatorname{tr}_X in the statement is "the Poincar\'e duality trace". Since \operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d) is an isomorphism, H^{2d} is 1-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell; hence any \mathbb Q_\ell-linear map \operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d) (in particular one making the pairing B perfect) is of the form \operatorname{tr}_X = \lambda\,\operatorname{tr} for a unique \lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell. The identity to be proved, B(Fx,Fy) = q^{md}B(x,y), is linear in the trace map: replacing \operatorname{tr}_X by \lambda\operatorname{tr} multiplies both sides by \lambda. Therefore it suffices to prove it for the normalised trace \operatorname{tr} of lemma_77(a); the general case follows (with \lambda = 1 if \operatorname{tr}_X is that normalised trace).

Step 4 (the computation for x,y\in P^d). Let x,y\in P^d\subseteq H^d. We use functoriality of the cup product with respect to pullback: for any morphism g:Z\to W of k-schemes and classes a\in H^p(W,\mathbb Q_\ell), b\in H^q(W,\mathbb Q_\ell) one has g^*(a\cup b) = g^*a\cup g^*b. Indeed, the cup product is the map on cohomology induced by the natural pairing of the derived global-sections functors, R\Gamma(W,\mathcal F)\otimes R\Gamma(W,\mathcal G)\to R\Gamma(W,\mathcal F\otimes^{\mathbb L}\mathcal G), and pullback g^* is symmetric monoidal on the derived category of \ell-adic sheaves (the inverse-image functor g^{-1} is strictly symmetric monoidal and g^* = \mathcal O_Z\otimes_{g^{-1}\mathcal O_W}g^{-1}(-) is lax symmetric monoidal via the canonical map g^*\mathcal O_W\to\mathcal O_Z), so the square
  R\Gamma(W,\mathcal F)\otimes R\Gamma(W,\mathcal G) \to R\Gamma(W,\mathcal F\otimes^{\mathbb L}\mathcal G)
  \ \ \downarrow g^*\otimes g^* \qquad\qquad\quad \downarrow g^*
  R\Gamma(Z,g^*\mathcal F)\otimes R\Gamma(Z,g^*\mathcal G) \to R\Gamma(Z,g^*\mathcal F\otimes^{\mathbb L}g^*\mathcal G)
commutes; taking \mathcal F = \mathcal G = \mathbb Q_{\ell,W} the constant sheaf, g = (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma):X_k\to X_k, and the (d,d)\to(2d) component yields
   F_{2d}(x\cup y) = (F_d x)\cup(F_d y).
Therefore, using (\dagger),
   B(Fx,Fy) = \operatorname{tr}\bigl((F_d x)\cup(F_d y)\bigr) = \operatorname{tr}\bigl(F_{2d}(x\cup y)\bigr) = q^{md}\,\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y) = q^{md}\,B(x,y),
where x\cup y\in H^{2d} because x,y\in H^d and \dim X = d, so that the trace applies. Since Q^d = (q^m)^d = q^{md}, this is precisely the required identity.

Step 5 (conclusion). Steps 2 and 4 together say exactly that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F restricts to a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of P^d = \ker(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)) and that B(Fx,Fy) = q^{md}B(x,y) for all x,y\in P^d. This completes the proof.

lemma_437.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(\mathcal L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\). Then there exist integers \(m\ge1\), \(r\ge1\) and a section \(s\in H^0(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}},\mathcal L^{\otimes r})\) whose zero scheme \(Y=V(s)\), with its induced closed subscheme structure, is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\).
lemma_437.proof:
Let k = overline(F_q). Fix a prime ell != p.

Step 1. Apply lemma_bertini_finite_extension to X and L. It gives integers a >= 1 and b >= 1 and a section s0 in H^0(X_{F_{q^b}}, L^{tensor a}) such that Y0 = V(s0) is an effective Cartier divisor on X_{F_{q^b}}, smooth over F_{q^b}, and of pure dimension d - 1. Rename m = b, r = a, s = s0, and Y = Y0.

Step 2. We show Y is nonempty. Put Z = X_{F_{q^m}}. Since X is geometrically connected over F_q, Z is connected. Indeed, if Z were a disjoint union of two nonempty open and closed subschemes, then after base change to k it would be a disjoint union of two nonempty open and closed subschemes, because faithfully flat base change of a nonempty finite type scheme over a field is nonempty; this would contradict connectedness of X_k. Also dim Z = d >= 2.

Assume for contradiction that Y is empty. Then s is nowhere vanishing, hence gives an isomorphism O_Z -> M := L^{tensor r}; thus M is trivial. Since L is ample, M is ample. If a trivial line bundle on a positive-dimensional connected projective scheme were ample, then some positive power of it would be trivial and very ample. Hence O_Z would be very ample. Therefore there would be a closed immersion f: Z -> P^N_E, with E = F_{q^m}, such that f^*O(1) is isomorphic to O_Z. Choose a trivialization of O_Z. The pullbacks of the homogeneous coordinates are global sections t_0,...,t_N in H^0(Z,O_Z) which generate O_Z and define f.

Because Z is smooth, connected, and proper over E, H^0(Z,O_Z) is a finite field extension of E: properness gives finite-dimensionality over E, smoothness gives reducedness, and connectedness excludes nontrivial idempotents. Hence every t_j is a constant element of this field. Since the t_j generate the trivial bundle, they are not all zero. Thus f sends every point of Z to the single point [t_0:...:t_N] in P^N_E. A closed immersion whose image is a point has dimension 0, contradicting dim Z = d >= 2. Therefore Y is nonempty.

Step 3. We show Y is ample. For an effective Cartier divisor defined by a regular section of a line bundle M, the associated invertible sheaf is O_Z(Y) = M. Here M = L^{tensor r}. Since L is ample, M is ample. Thus Y is an ample effective Cartier divisor on Z. It is a proper closed subscheme because it has pure dimension d - 1 while Z has pure dimension d.

Step 4. We show Y is geometrically connected. Base change to k. Let Z_k = X_k and Y_k = Y x_{F_{q^m}} k. The morphism Spec k -> Spec F_{q^m} is faithfully flat, so smoothness, being an effective Cartier divisor, nonemptiness, pure dimension d - 1, and ampleness are preserved under this base change. Thus Y_k is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor on X_k, smooth of pure dimension d - 1 over k.

Apply lemma_420 to X_k and Y_k. Since d >= 2, we have 0 < d - 1, so the degree 0 case gives an isomorphism i^*: H^0_et(X_k, Q_l) -> H^0_et(Y_k, Q_l), where i: Y_k -> X_k is the closed immersion.

Because X_k is connected and of finite type over k, H^0_et(X_k, Q_l) = Q_l. Indeed, for a connected locally connected noetherian scheme, global sections of the constant sheaf Q_l are exactly the constant Q_l-valued functions. Hence H^0_et(Y_k, Q_l) = Q_l.

For any finite type scheme W over a field, the connected components are open and closed and there are finitely many. Therefore H^0_et(W, Q_l) is the Q_l-vector space of functions on the finite set pi_0(W), so its dimension is the number of connected components of W. Applying this to W = Y_k, the fact that H^0_et(Y_k, Q_l) is one-dimensional implies that Y_k has exactly one connected component. Since Y_k is nonempty, it is connected. Thus Y is geometrically connected over F_{q^m}.

Combining Steps 1-4, the integers m,r and the section s satisfy all the required properties.

lemma_438.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Let \(Y\subset X\) be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the closed immersion. Put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and for each integer \(j\) let \(F_{X,j}\) and \(F_{Y,j}\) denote the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of \(H^j_{\acute{\mathrm{et}}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^j_{\acute{\mathrm{et}}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(i^*\circ F_{X,j}=F_{Y,j}\circ i^*\) for every \(j\), \(i^*\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(j<d-1\), and \(i^*\) is injective for \(j=d-1\).
lemma_438.proof:
Write K := \mathbb F_{q^m}; thus K is a finite field of characteristic p containing \mathbb F_q, k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{K}, and X (resp. Y) is a scheme over K. We prove the three claims (Frobenius equivariance of i^*, the isomorphism statement for j<d-1, and injectivity for j=d-1) in Steps 1-3 and Steps 4-5.

Step 1 (the Frobenius morphisms as base-change morphisms). Let \sigma:k\to k, \sigma(u)=u^{q^m}. This is a field automorphism of k (the q^m-power map is the inverse of the q^m-power map composed with the appropriate power of the q-power Frobenius; concretely \sigma = (u\mapsto u^q)^m is an automorphism since u\mapsto u^q generates Gal(k/\mathbb F_q)). Since every element of K=\mathbb F_{q^m} satisfies u^{q^m}=u, the automorphism \sigma fixes K pointwise; hence \operatorname{Spec}\sigma:\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k is a K-morphism. Therefore the fibre products
  \Phi_X := \mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma : X_k=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k \longrightarrow X_k,
  \Phi_Y := \mathrm{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma : Y_k=Y\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k \longrightarrow Y_k
are well-defined morphisms of k-schemes. Applying lemma_6a (eoinm) with the prime power q^m in place of its q (which is legitimate: K=\mathbb F_{q^m} is a finite field of characteristic p and k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^m}), to the K-schemes X and Y, we obtain that for every j\ge 0 the pullbacks (\Phi_X)^* and (\Phi_Y)^* are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphisms of H^j_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and H^j_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) respectively, and that these are exactly the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms. Hence
  F_{X,j}=(\Phi_X)^*,\qquad F_{Y,j}=(\Phi_Y)^* \qquad (j\ge 0),
and for j<0 both cohomology groups are 0 (sheaf cohomology vanishes in negative degrees), so the asserted equivariance is then the trivial identity 0\to 0. In what follows all cohomology groups are with \mathbb Q_\ell-coefficients on the small étale site, and we write i^* for the pullback (i_k)^*:H^j(X_k)\to H^j(Y_k) induced by the base-changed closed immersion i_k:=i\times\mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}k}:Y_k\to X_k.

Step 2 (the square with Frobenius commutes). Denote by q_X:X_k\to X and \pi_X:X_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k (resp. q_Y,\pi_Y) the two projections of the fibre products, and by \Sigma:=\operatorname{Spec}\sigma. By definition of the fibre-product projections,
  q_X\circ\Phi_X=q_X,\qquad \pi_X\circ\Phi_X=\Sigma\circ\pi_X,\qquad q_Y\circ\Phi_Y=q_Y,\qquad \pi_Y\circ\Phi_Y=\Sigma\circ\pi_Y, \tag{2.1}
and by definition of the base change i_k of i,
  q_X\circ i_k = i\circ q_Y,\qquad \pi_X\circ i_k=\pi_Y. \tag{2.2}
We compare the two morphisms \Phi_X\circ i_k and i_k\circ\Phi_Y from Y_k to X_k by composing with the two projections of X_k=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k. First,
  q_X\circ(\Phi_X\circ i_k)=(q_X\circ\Phi_X)\circ i_k \overset{(2.1)}{=} q_X\circ i_k \overset{(2.2)}{=} i\circ q_Y \overset{(2.1)}{=} i\circ(q_Y\circ\Phi_Y)=(i\circ q_Y)\circ\Phi_Y \overset{(2.2)}{=} (q_X\circ i_k)\circ\Phi_Y=q_X\circ(i_k\circ\Phi_Y).
Second,
  \pi_X\circ(\Phi_X\circ i_k)=(\pi_X\circ\Phi_X)\circ i_k \overset{(2.1)}{=} \Sigma\circ\pi_X\circ i_k \overset{(2.2)}{=} \Sigma\circ\pi_Y \overset{(2.1)}{=} \pi_Y\circ\Phi_Y=(\pi_X\circ i_k)\circ\Phi_Y=\pi_X\circ(i_k\circ\Phi_Y).
Since X_k is the fibre product over \operatorname{Spec}K, the pair (q_X,\pi_X):X_k\to X\times\operatorname{Spec}k is a monomorphism onto the fibre product, i.e. two morphisms into X_k that agree after composition with both q_X and \pi_X are equal (universal property of the fibre product). Hence
  \Phi_X\circ i_k = i_k\circ\Phi_Y \quad\text{as morphisms } Y_k\to X_k. \tag{2.3}

Step 3 (equivariance of i^*). Étale cohomology is contravariantly functorial for morphisms of schemes, so from (2.3), for every integer j,
  F_{Y,j}\circ i^* = (\Phi_Y)^*\circ(i_k)^* = (i_k\circ\Phi_Y)^* = (\Phi_X\circ i_k)^* = (i_k)^*\circ(\Phi_X)^* = i^*\circ F_{X,j},
where for j\ge0 we used Step 1 and for j<0 the statement is the trivial identity on the zero groups. This is exactly i^*\circ F_{X,j}=F_{Y,j}\circ i^* for every j.

Step 4 (verification of the hypotheses of lemma_420 for X_k, Y_k, i_k over k). We check each hypothesis of lemma_420 (Spark) with k in place of its k, X_k in place of its X, Y_k in place of its Y, and i_k in place of its i.

(a) k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q is algebraically closed of characteristic p, and \ell\neq p by hypothesis.

(b) X_k is smooth, projective and of pure dimension d over k. Indeed X\to\operatorname{Spec}K is smooth of pure relative dimension d (X is smooth of pure dimension d over K), and smoothness together with relative dimension is preserved by arbitrary base change, so X_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k is smooth of pure relative dimension d; being non-empty (X is non-empty, as it contains the non-empty Y, and X_k\to X is surjective by (d) below) it has pure dimension d\ge 2. Projectivity is preserved by base change (a closed immersion X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_K base-changes to a closed immersion X_k\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_k), and separatedness and finite type are likewise preserved, so X_k is a variety over k; it is reduced because smooth k-schemes are geometrically regular.

(b') X_k is geometrically connected over k. Let L/k be any field extension. Then
  X_k\times_k L \;\simeq\; (X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k)\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}\operatorname{Spec}L \;\simeq\; X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}L,
using associativity of the fibre product and k\times_k L\simeq L. The composite K\hookrightarrow k\hookrightarrow L exhibits L as a field extension of K, and since X is geometrically connected over K the K-scheme X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}L is connected (this is the standard characterisation of geometric connectedness for a finite-type scheme over a field: X is geometrically connected over K iff X_{K'} is connected for every field extension K'/K). Hence X_k\times_k L is connected for every field extension L/k, i.e. X_k is geometrically connected over k. (Equivalently: X_k is connected — take L=k — and smooth over k, hence geometrically reduced; a connected, geometrically reduced scheme of finite type over a field is geometrically connected.)

(c) Y_k is non-empty. Consider the projection p:Y_k=Y\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}k\to Y. It is the base change of the morphism \operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}K. A field extension is faithfully flat: k is a free (hence flat) K-module, and for every K-vector space M one has k\otimes_K M\simeq\bigoplus_{b\in\mathcal B}M for any K-basis \mathcal B of k containing 1, so k\otimes_K M=0 forces M=0; equivalently \operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}K is surjective and k is faithfully flat over K. Faithfully flat morphisms are stable under base change, so p is faithfully flat, in particular surjective. Since Y\neq\emptyset by hypothesis, surjectivity of p gives Y_k\neq\emptyset.

(d) Y_k\subsetneq X_k. The same argument shows the projection X_k\to X is faithfully flat, hence surjective, so X_k\neq\emptyset; as in (b), X_k has pure dimension d. By (c), Y_k is non-empty, and since Y\to\operatorname{Spec}K is smooth of pure relative dimension d-1, base change shows Y_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k is smooth of pure relative dimension d-1, so the non-empty scheme Y_k has pure dimension d-1. If Y_k equalled X_k as closed subschemes of X_k, then the two schemes would have the same dimension, forcing d-1=d, a contradiction since d\ge 2. Thus Y_k is a proper closed subscheme of X_k.

(e) Y_k\hookrightarrow X_k is an effective Cartier divisor. The closed immersion i:Y\hookrightarrow X is an effective Cartier divisor, so there is an open affine cover \{U=\operatorname{Spec}A\} of X with Y\cap U=\operatorname{Spec}(A/fA) for some non-zero-divisor f\in A. Since X_k\to X is flat (base change of the flat morphism \operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}K), pr^{-1}U=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_K k) and flat base change identifies Y_k\cap\mathrm{pr}^{-1}U with \operatorname{Spec}\big((A\otimes_K k)/(f\otimes 1)\big); moreover f\otimes 1 is a non-zero-divisor in A\otimes_K k, because 0\to A\xrightarrow{\cdot f}A is exact and A\otimes_K k- is exact. Hence Y_k is locally cut out by a non-zero-divisor, i.e. i_k is an effective Cartier divisor. (Equivalently: regular immersions are preserved by flat base change.)

(f) \mathcal O_{X_k}(Y_k) is ample. By construction of the base-changed divisor, \mathcal O_{X_k}(Y_k)\simeq\mathrm{pr}_X^*\mathcal O_X(Y), where \mathrm{pr}_X:X_k\to X is the projection. Ampleness is preserved under arbitrary base change (EGA II, 4.5.2.3: the pullback of an f-ample invertible sheaf along any base change is f'-ample; here X\to\operatorname{Spec}K and X_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k are projective, so relative and absolute ampleness coincide). Since \mathcal O_X(Y) is ample on X by hypothesis, \mathcal O_{X_k}(Y_k) is ample on X_k.

(g) Y_k is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over k: proved in (d) (smoothness and pure relative dimension are preserved by base change).

Thus all hypotheses of lemma_420 are satisfied for the algebraically closed field k, the smooth projective geometrically connected k-variety X_k of pure dimension d\ge 2, the non-empty effective ample Cartier divisor Y_k\subsetneq X_k which is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over k, and the closed immersion i_k:Y_k\hookrightarrow X_k.

Step 5 (conclusion). Applying lemma_420 yields that (i_k)^*:H^m_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^m_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is an isomorphism for every integer m<d-1 and is injective for m=d-1. For m<0 both groups are 0, so (i_k)^* is the zero map 0\to 0, hence an isomorphism, which covers the remaining integers m<d-1. Recalling from Step 3 that i^* denotes (i_k)^*, this gives exactly: i^* is an isomorphism for every integer j<d-1, and i^* is injective for j=d-1. Together with the equivariance i^*\circ F_{X,j}=F_{Y,j}\circ i^* established in Step 3 for every integer j, this completes the proof of the lemma.

lemma_439.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(k\), let \(Y\subsetneq X\) be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor that is smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(k\), let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the closed immersion and \(U=X\setminus Y\). Suppose \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\), and that the groups \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for \(j\in\mathbb Z\) are connected by homomorphisms forming a long exact sequence in which the arrow \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is \(i^*\). If \(i^*\) is an isomorphism for every \(j<d-1\) and injective for \(j=d-1\), then \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(j<d\).
lemma_439.proof:
