We write, for brevity, H^j_c := H^j_{\acute et,c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell), H^j(X) := H^j_{\acute et}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell) and H^j(Y) := H^j_{\acute et}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 0 (Unpacking the long-exact-sequence hypothesis). By hypothesis the three \(\mathbb Z\)-indexed families of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces are connected by homomorphisms so as to form a long exact sequence in which the arrow \(H^j(X)\to H^j(Y)\) is the restriction \(i^*\). Concretely, this is the excision long exact sequence of the triple \(U=X\setminus Y\subset X\supset Y\): there exist homomorphisms
\[\alpha_j:H^j_c\longrightarrow H^j(X),\qquad \delta_j:H^j(Y)\longrightarrow H^{j+1}_c\qquad (j\in\mathbb Z)\]
such that for every \(j\in\mathbb Z\) the segment
\[H^j_c\xrightarrow{\ \alpha_j\ }H^j(X)\xrightarrow{\ i^*\ }H^j(Y)\xrightarrow{\ \delta_j\ }H^{j+1}_c\xrightarrow{\ \alpha_{j+1}\ }H^{j+1}(X)\]
is exact. Equivalently, for every \(j\in\mathbb Z\) we have the three exactness identities
\[(E1_j)\quad \operatorname{im}\alpha_j=\ker\bigl(i^*:H^j(X)\to H^j(Y)\bigr),\]
\[(E2_j)\quad \operatorname{im} i^*=\ker\delta_j,\]
\[(E3_j)\quad \operatorname{im}\delta_{j-1}=\ker\alpha_j.\]
(Only these formal consequences of the hypothesis are used below; no property of the actual construction of the sequence, and no finiteness, smoothness, projectivity, geometric connectedness or ampleness statement beyond what is packaged in the hypotheses, enters the argument.)

STEP 1 (The key claim). We claim that \(H^j_c=0\) for every integer \(j\le d-1\). Fix such a \(j\) and argue in three steps.

(1a) The map \(\alpha_j\) is zero. Indeed, either \(j\le d-2<d-1\), in which case the hypothesis says \(i^*:H^j(X)\to H^j(Y)\) is an isomorphism, or \(j=d-1\), in which case the hypothesis says \(i^*:H^j(X)\to H^j(Y)\) is injective. In both cases \(\ker(i^*:H^j(X)\to H^j(Y))=0\). By \((E1_j)\), \(\operatorname{im}\alpha_j=0\); hence \(\alpha_j=0\), and consequently \(\ker\alpha_j=H^j_c\).

(1b) The map \(\delta_{j-1}\) is zero. Since \(j\le d-1\) we have \(j-1\le d-2<d-1\), so by hypothesis \(i^*:H^{j-1}(X)\to H^{j-1}(Y)\) is an isomorphism; in particular it is surjective, i.e. \(\operatorname{im} i^*=H^{j-1}(Y)\). By \((E2_{j-1})\), \(\ker\delta_{j-1}=H^{j-1}(Y)\), so \(\delta_{j-1}=0\) and hence \(\operatorname{im}\delta_{j-1}=0\).

(1c) Conclusion for this \(j\). Applying \((E3_j)\) and then (1a) and (1b),
\[H^j_c=\ker\alpha_j=\operatorname{im}\delta_{j-1}=0.\]
This proves the claim.

STEP 2 (Negative and low degrees are covered). The claim of Step 1 was proved for every integer \(j\le d-1\) without any restriction on the sign of \(j\): the argument at \(j\le 0\) is identical, using that \(i^*\) is an isomorphism in all degrees \(<d-1\) (for instance at \(j=0\) one uses that \(0<d-1\), which holds because \(d\ge2\), so that \(\alpha_0=0\) by \((E1_0)\), and that \(-1<d-1\), so that \(\delta_{-1}=0\) by \((E2_{-1})\)). Since for integers one has \(j<d\iff j\le d-1\), Step 1 yields exactly
\[H^j_{\acute et,c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\qquad\text{for every integer }j<d,\]
which is the desired conclusion. In particular the conclusion holds a fortiori for \(j<0\); no separate input about negative-degree cohomology is required.

STEP 3 (Consistency of the extra hypothesis, and remarks). The assumed vanishing \(H^0_{\acute et,c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) is not needed for the deduction (Step 1 with \(j=0\) already gives it), but it is consistent with it; in the geometric situation at hand it is the standard vanishing of \(H^0\) of compactly supported cohomology of a smooth affine variety of positive dimension (\(U=X\setminus Y\) is affine because \(Y\) is an effective ample Cartier divisor, and nonempty and of dimension \(d\ge2\)), and the hypotheses on \(i^*\) are the Lefschetz-type statements valid for an ample smooth divisor. Since both facts are assumed as hypotheses of the present lemma, the proof above is complete and self-contained: it is a formal diagram chase in the excision long exact sequence, using exactness at the three terms \(H^j_c\), \(H^j(X)\), \(H^j(Y)\) for the two consecutive degrees \(j-1\) and \(j\), together with the stated injectivity/surjectivity properties of \(i^*\).

lemma_440.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\) be diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), and let \(W\subseteq V\) be a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear subspace with \(T(W)=W\). Then the restricted automorphism \(T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W)\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_440.proof:
Write $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\overline K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Recall the convention used in the statement (and in eoinm/lemma_5): an automorphism $S\in\mathrm{GL}_K(U)$ of a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space is called *diagonalizable over $\overline K$* precisely when $S\otimes 1$ is diagonalizable on $U\otimes_K\overline K$.

**Reduction to the two cited lemmas.**

Step 1 (from diagonalizable to semisimple). Apply eoinm/lemma_5 to the pair $(V,T)$. Its hypothesis is satisfied because $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline K$ by assumption; the lemma yields that $T$ is *semisimple* on $V$, i.e. that $V$ is a semisimple $K[t]$-module with $t$ acting as $T$.

Step 2 (restriction to an invariant subspace). Since $T(W)=W$, certainly $T(W)\subseteq W$. Moreover $T|_W:W\to W$ is an automorphism: it is injective because $T$ is injective on $V$, and it is surjective because $T(W)=W$. Thus $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}_K(W)$, as the statement requires. Applying eoinm/lemma_358 to the semisimple operator $T\in\mathrm{GL}_K(V)$ and the $T$-stable subspace $W$ gives that $T|_W$ is semisimple on $W$.

Step 3 (from semisimple to diagonalizable). Apply eoinm/lemma_5 to the pair $(W,T|_W)$ (which is legitimate since $W$ is finite-dimensional over $K$, being a subspace of the finite-dimensional $V$). Semisimplicity of $T|_W$ on $W$ implies that $T|_W\otimes 1$ is diagonalizable on $W\otimes_K\overline K$, which is exactly the assertion that $T|_W$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

If $W=0$ the operator $T|_W=\mathrm{id}_0$ has the empty matrix, which is diagonal; the conclusion is then immediate, and Steps 1--3 above also apply verbatim since lemma_5 and lemma_358 are valid for the zero space. Henceforth assume nothing about $W$ beyond the hypotheses.

**Direct verification of the key step (so that the argument is self-contained).** We spell out the content of Steps 1--3 in elementary linear algebra, proving the required diagonalizability without appealing to the vocabulary of semisimple modules.

(1) Base change is faithful on subspaces. $\overline K$ is a free (hence flat) $K$-module, because every vector space has a basis. Therefore the natural map
$$W\otimes_K\overline K\longrightarrow V\otimes_K\overline K,\qquad w\otimes\alpha\longmapsto w\otimes\alpha,$$
is injective; we identify $\overline W:=W\otimes_K\overline K$ with its image inside $\overline V:=V\otimes_K\overline K$. Put $\overline T:=T\otimes 1\in\mathrm{GL}_{\overline K}(\overline V)$.

(2) $\overline W$ is $\overline T$-stable. Every element of $\overline W$ is a finite sum $\sum_i w_i\otimes\alpha_i$ with $w_i\in W$, $\alpha_i\in\overline K$, and $\overline T(\sum_i w_i\otimes\alpha_i)=\sum_i T(w_i)\otimes\alpha_i\in\overline W$, since $T(W)\subseteq W$.

(3) The eigenspace decomposition of $\overline T$. By hypothesis $\overline T$ is diagonalizable, so $\overline V$ has a basis of eigenvectors. Let $\Lambda\subset\overline K$ be the (finite) set of eigenvalues and $E_\lambda:=\ker(\overline T-\lambda\,\mathrm{id})$. Then $\overline V=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}E_\lambda$. The sum is direct: if $\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}v_\lambda=0$ with $v_\lambda\in E_\lambda$ is a relation with the minimal number of nonzero terms, applying $(\overline T-\mu)$ for an eigenvalue $\mu$ occurring in the relation sends it to $\sum_{\lambda}(\lambda-\mu)v_\lambda$, in which the $\mu$-term vanishes, contradicting minimality unless only one term was nonzero, in which case that term is $0$. Hence
$$\overline V=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}E_\lambda.$$

(4) The spectral projections preserve $\overline W$. For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ define the Lagrange interpolation polynomial
$$P_\lambda(t):=\prod_{\mu\in\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}}\frac{t-\mu}{\lambda-\mu}\;\in\overline K[t].$$
This is well defined because $\lambda-\mu\neq0$ for $\mu\neq\lambda$. For $\mu,\nu\in\Lambda$ we have $P_\lambda(\mu)=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$ (the value is $1$ when $\mu=\lambda$, and $0$ because the factor $t-\mu$ occurs in the product when $\mu\neq\lambda$). Consequently, for $v=\sum_{\mu}v_\mu\in\bigoplus_\mu E_\mu$,
$$P_\lambda(\overline T)v=\sum_{\mu}P_\lambda(\mu)v_\mu=v_\lambda,$$
so $\pi_\lambda:=P_\lambda(\overline T)$ is exactly the projection of $\overline V$ onto $E_\lambda$ along the decomposition of (3).

Now $\pi_\lambda$ is a polynomial in $\overline T$ with coefficients in $\overline K$. Since $\overline T(\overline W)\subseteq\overline W$, every polynomial in $\overline T$ preserves $\overline W$; hence $\pi_\lambda(\overline W)\subseteq\overline W$.

(5) $\overline W$ is a direct sum of eigenspace pieces. For $w\in\overline W$ write $w=\sum_{\lambda}\pi_\lambda(w)$; by Step 4 each $\pi_\lambda(w)\in\overline W$, and $\pi_\lambda(w)\in E_\lambda$. Thus $\overline W=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\overline W\cap E_\lambda)$, and the sum is direct because it is a sub-sum of the direct sum (3). Moreover, for $w\in\overline W\cap E_\lambda$ we have $\overline T|_{\overline W}(w)=\lambda w$, so $\overline W\cap E_\lambda\subseteq\ker(\overline T|_{\overline W}-\lambda\,\mathrm{id}_{\overline W})$. Therefore
$$\overline W=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\bigl(\overline W\cap E_\lambda\bigr)\subseteq\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\ker\bigl(\overline T|_{\overline W}-\lambda\,\mathrm{id}_{\overline W}\bigr),$$
which says that $\overline W$ is spanned by eigenvectors of $\overline T|_{\overline W}$; equivalently, $\overline T|_{\overline W}$ is diagonalizable.

(6) Identification with the base change of the restriction. The inclusion $W\hookrightarrow V$ induces $W\otimes_K\overline K\to V\otimes_K\overline K$ whose image is $\overline W$, and under this identification $\overline T|_{\overline W}$ corresponds to $(T|_W)\otimes 1\in\mathrm{GL}_{\overline K}(W\otimes_K\overline K)$, since both act by $w\otimes\alpha\mapsto T(w)\otimes\alpha$. Step 5 therefore says that $(T|_W)\otimes 1$ is diagonalizable on $W\otimes_K\overline K$.

By the definition recalled at the beginning, this is exactly the statement that $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}_K(W)$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. This completes the proof. (Steps 3--6 reproduce the content of eoinm/lemma_358 together with eoinm/lemma_5, which were the lemmas invoked in the first part of the argument.)

lemma_436.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Suppose that for every integer \(e\ge1\), every integer \(t\ge1\), and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(V\) of pure dimension \(e\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), the \(q^t\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^t}\), is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^e_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then for every integer \(t\ge1\), every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(W\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), and every integer \(n\ge0\), the \(q^t\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_436.proof: Proof. Fix q=p^a, ell != p, and k=overline(F_q). For each t>=1 let sigma_t(c)=c^{q^t} and write F_t(X)=(id_X times Spec(sigma_t))^* on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l). We first make two uniform observations. Since q^t is again a prime power, lemma_45_finite_frob, applied over F_{q^t} with K the constant sheaf Q_l equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, shows that H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) is finite-dimensional over Q_l for every proper X over F_{q^t}; in particular this holds for every smooth projective X. Then lemma_6a, applied over F_{q^t}, identifies the pullback (id_X times Spec(sigma_t))^* with the arithmetic Frobenius automorphism and shows it is Q_l-linear. By lemma_5, for these finite-dimensional Q_l-vector spaces semisimplicity of F_t(X) is equivalent to diagonalizability over Qbar_l. Hence it suffices to prove semisimplicity. We also note that any smooth projective geometrically connected variety over a finite field has a well-defined pure dimension. Indeed, smoothness over a field makes the local dimension locally constant on the scheme, and geometric connectedness makes the underlying scheme connected; hence the local dimension is constant. If varieties are taken irreducible by definition this is immediate. Verify the compact-support vanishing hypothesis (HC) required by lemma_below_middle_induction. Let m>=1, let e'>=2, let X' be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension e' over F_{q^m}, and let Y' subset X' be an effective ample divisor defined over F_{q^m}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension e'-1. Since Y' has codimension one in the smooth variety X' and is itself smooth, it is an effective Cartier divisor: a closed immersion between smooth varieties over a field is regular, and a regular immersion of codimension one is locally defined by one non-zero-divisor. It is nonempty and a proper closed subset because its dimension is e'-1<e'. Apply lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement to X' over F_{q^m} (legitimate because q^m is a prime power) and to Y'. It gives H^j_et,c((X' minus Y')_k,Q_l)=0 for every integer j<e'. This is exactly (HC). We prove by strong induction on d>=0 the following statement P(d): for every t>=1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety W over F_{q^t} of pure dimension d, the operator F_t(W) is semisimple on H^n_et(W_k,Q_l) for every n>=0. Before the induction, record the degree-zero fact. If Z is a connected scheme over k and F:Z->Z is an automorphism, then F^* on H^0_et(Z,Q_l) is the identity. Indeed H^0_et(Z,Q_l) is the group of locally constant Q_l-valued functions on the underlying topological space of Z; because Z is connected these functions are exactly the constant functions, and pullback by any map leaves constant functions unchanged. For W smooth projective geometrically connected over F_{q^t}, W_k is connected, so F_t(W) acts as the identity on H^0_et(W_k,Q_l). The identity on Q_l is semisimple. Base case d=0. Let W be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension 0 over F_{q^t}. The preceding paragraph gives semisimplicity on H^0. For n>0, W_k is a projective scheme over k of pure dimension 0 (base change preserves projectivity and pure dimension), so lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing gives H^n_et(W_k,Q_l)=0. The unique operator on the zero vector space is semisimple. Thus P(0). Base case d=1. Let W be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^t}. H^0 is semisimple by the degree-zero fact. For H^1, apply the hypothesis of the lemma with e=1, t=t, and V=W. It says that F_t(W) is diagonalizable over Qbar_l on H^1_et(W_k,Q_l); by lemma_5 this is equivalent to semisimplicity over Q_l. For H^2, apply lemma_428 to X=W, m=t, and n=0. The lemma requires semisimplicity on H^0, which we have, and it concludes semisimplicity on H^{2*1-0}=H^2. For n>2, lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing gives H^n=0, hence semisimplicity is trivial. Thus P(1). Inductive step. Assume d>=2 and that P(r) holds for every r<d. Let W be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^t}. Lower degrees n<d. Apply lemma_below_middle_induction with s=t and e=d. Its compact-support vanishing hypothesis (HC) was verified above. Its lower-dimensional hypothesis is precisely P(d-1), because P(d-1) gives semisimplicity of F_{t'}(V) on H^n for every t', every smooth projective geometrically connected V of pure dimension d-1 over F_{q^{t'}}, and every n>=0, in particular for 0<=n<=d-1. The conclusion of lemma_below_middle_induction is that F_t(W) is semisimple on H^n_et(W_k,Q_l) for every integer n<d. Middle degree n=d. Apply the hypothesis of the lemma with e=d, t=t, and V=W. It gives diagonalizability over Qbar_l on H^d_et(W_k,Q_l), and lemma_5 converts this to semisimplicity over Q_l. Upper degrees d<n<=2d. Put r=2d-n. Since d<n<=2d, we have 0<=r<d. By the lower-degree case just proved, F_t(W) is semisimple on H^r_et(W_k,Q_l). Apply lemma_428 to X=W, m=t, and n=r. It yields semisimplicity on H^{2d-r}_et(W_k,Q_l)=H^n_et(W_k,Q_l). Degrees n>2d. By lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing applied to the projective scheme W_k over k of pure dimension d, H^n_et(W_k,Q_l)=0, so semisimplicity is trivial. The cases n<d, n=d, d<n<=2d, and n>2d partition all integers n>=0, so this completes the proof of P(d) and hence the induction. Finally, let W be any smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_{q^t} and let n>=0. By the pure-dimension observation, W has pure dimension d for some d>=0. P(d) gives that F_t(W) is semisimple on H^n_et(W_k,Q_l). Since this vector space is finite-dimensional over Q_l, lemma_5 implies that F_t(W) is diagonalizable over Qbar_l on H^n_et(W_k,Q_l) tensor_Q_l Qbar_l. This is exactly the desired conclusion. QED.

lemma_441.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), and let \(r\ge1\) be an integer. Then \(T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) if and only if \(T^r\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_441.proof:
We prove both implications after reducing to operators over the algebraically closed field K := \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.

**Step 0: Reduction to K = \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.** Put K := \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, W := V \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} K and \tilde T := T \otimes \mathrm{id}_K. Since K is flat over \mathbb Q_\ell, W is a K-vector space of dimension n := \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} V, and since T \in \mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V) with inverse T^{-1}, the map \tilde T lies in \mathrm{GL}_K(W) with inverse \widetilde{T^{-1}} (using (f\otimes 1)\circ(g\otimes 1)=(f\circ g)\otimes 1, which holds because both sides send v\otimes c to f(g(v))\otimes c). Iterating, \tilde T^{\,r}=(T\otimes 1)^{r}=T^{r}\otimes 1=\widetilde{T^{r}}. By definition, "T is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell" means exactly that \tilde T is diagonalizable as a K-linear automorphism of W; by lemma_5 (eoinm, lemma_5) this is the same as T being semisimple on V, so the two formulations in the conjectural dictionary agree. Hence the target statement for (V,T) is precisely the statement for (W,\tilde T): \tilde T diagonalizable over K \iff \tilde T^{\,r} diagonalizable over K. We prove this for an arbitrary finite-dimensional K-vector space, writing A for \tilde T and dropping the tilde. Note K is algebraically closed of characteristic 0. If n=0 the only operator is the identity on the zero space, which is diagonalizable, and both directions are vacuous; so assume n\ge 1. The case r=1 is trivial, so we may and do assume r\ge 1 generally (the argument below covers r=1 as well).

**Fact 1 (existence and minimality of the minimal polynomial).** Consider the \mathbb K[x]-module structure on W given by x\cdot w=A w. The \mathbb Q_\ell- (equivalently K-) vector space \operatorname{End}_K(W) has dimension n^2, so the n^2+1 operators \mathrm{id}_W, A, A^2,\dots,A^{n^2} are K-linearly dependent; hence some nonzero f\in K[x] satisfies f(A)=0. Among all such f choose \mu_A monic of minimal degree; call it the minimal polynomial of A. If g\in K[x] satisfies g(A)=0, write g=\mu_A q+\rho with q,\rho\in K[x] and \deg\rho<\deg\mu_A (Euclidean division in the PID K[x]). Then \rho(A)=g(A)-\mu_A(A)q(A)=0, and minimality of \deg\mu_A forces \rho=0. Thus \mu_A \mid g in K[x]; in particular \mu_A is unique.

**Fact 2 (diagonalizability criterion).** A is diagonalizable over K if and only if \mu_A splits in K[x] as a product of pairwise distinct linear factors.

*Proof of (\Rightarrow).* If A is diagonalizable, let \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s be its distinct eigenvalues and set q(x):=\prod_{i=1}^{s}(x-\lambda_i). For each i choose an eigenvector 0\ne v_i\in W with A v_i=\lambda_i v_i; the eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent (a standard Vandermonde argument: if \sum_{i\in I}c_i v_i=0 with I minimal, applying A-\lambda_j I for j\in I\setminus\{\min I\} and subtracting kills all but one term, forcing a coefficient to vanish). Diagonalizability says W is spanned by eigenvectors, so q(A) vanishes on a basis and hence q(A)=0. If g is any polynomial with g(A)=0 then 0=g(A)v_i=g(\lambda_i)v_i, so g(\lambda_i)=0 for every i, and since the \lambda_i are distinct and K[x] is a UFD, (x-\lambda_i)\mid g for each i, hence q\mid g. Thus q is the monic annihilating polynomial of least degree, i.e. \mu_A=q, a product of s distinct linear factors.

*Proof of (\Leftarrow).* Suppose \mu_A=\prod_{i=1}^{s}(x-\lambda_i) with the \lambda_i\in K pairwise distinct. For each i put f_i(x):=\prod_{j\ne i}(x-\lambda_j) and d_i:=f_i(\lambda_i)=\prod_{j\ne i}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)\in K^{\times} (nonzero because the \lambda_j are distinct), and set e_i(x):=d_i^{-1}f_i(x)\in K[x]; thus e_i(\lambda_j)=\delta_{ij}. Define E_i:=e_i(A)\in\operatorname{End}_K(W).
(a) \sum_i E_i=\mathrm{id}_W: the polynomial \sum_i e_i(x)-1 vanishes at each \lambda_j, hence (x-\lambda_j) divides it for every j; the (x-\lambda_j) are pairwise coprime, so \mu_A divides it, and evaluating at A gives \sum_i E_i-\mathrm{id}_W=0.
(b) \operatorname{im}E_i\subseteq\ker(A-\lambda_i): the polynomial (x-\lambda_i)e_i(x) vanishes at every \lambda_j (at j=i because of the factor x-\lambda_i, at j\ne i because f_i(\lambda_j)=0), so \mu_A\mid (x-\lambda_i)e_i(x), hence (A-\lambda_i)E_i=0.
(c) E_iE_j=0 for i\ne j: e_i e_j vanishes at every \lambda_k, so \mu_A\mid e_i e_j.
Now every w\in W equals \sum_i E_i w with E_i w\in\ker(A-\lambda_i) by (a),(b); so W=\sum_i\ker(A-\lambda_i). The sum is direct: if w_i\in\ker(A-\lambda_i) and \sum_i w_i=0, then applying E_j gives 0=E_j(\sum_i w_i)=\sum_i E_j w_i. For i\ne j, e_j(\lambda_i)=0 means (x-\lambda_i)\mid e_j, say e_j=(x-\lambda_i)h, whence E_j w_i=h(A)(A-\lambda_i)w_i=0; and E_j w_j=w_j because e_j(x)-1 vanishes at \lambda_j, so (x-\lambda_j)\mid(e_j-1) and (A-\lambda_j)w_j=0. Hence w_j=0 for all j. Taking a K-basis of each \ker(A-\lambda_i) and concatenating gives a basis of W consisting of eigenvectors of A, i.e. A is diagonalizable. This proves Fact 2.

**Step 1 (forward implication).** Assume A is diagonalizable, with a basis (w_1,\dots,w_n) of W and scalars \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\in K^{\times} (nonzero because A is invertible) such that A w_j=\alpha_j w_j. Then A^{r}w_j=\alpha_j^{r} w_j for every j, so the same basis diagonalises A^{r}. Hence A^{r} is diagonalizable over K.

**Step 2 (reverse implication).** Assume A^{r} is diagonalizable over K. By Fact 2 applied to A^{r},
\[\mu_{A^{r}}(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{s}(x-\mu_i)\]
with \mu_1,\dots,\mu_s\in K pairwise distinct.

*2a. Each \mu_i is nonzero.* Since A\in\mathrm{GL}_K(W), also A^{r}\in\mathrm{GL}_K(W). If some \mu_i were 0, then x would divide \mu_{A^{r}}, so \mu_{A^{r}}(x)=x\,g(x) with \deg g<\deg\mu_{A^{r}}. Evaluating at A^{r}: 0=\mu_{A^{r}}(A^{r})=A^{r}\circ g(A^{r}). As A^{r} is invertible, composing with its inverse gives g(A^{r})=0, contradicting the minimality of \mu_{A^{r}} (Fact 1). Hence \mu_i\in K^{\times} for all i.

*2b. A annihilates a squarefree split polynomial.* Define
\[p(x):=\prod_{i=1}^{s}\bigl(x^{r}-\mu_i\bigr)\in K[x].\]
Evaluation at A is a K-algebra homomorphism K[x]\to\operatorname{End}_K(W), so
\[p(A)=\prod_{i=1}^{s}\bigl(A^{r}-\mu_i\,\mathrm{id}_W\bigr)=\mu_{A^{r}}(A^{r})=0,\]
the last equality being \mu_{A^{r}}(A^{r})=0. By Fact 1, \mu_A\mid p in K[x].

*2c. p is a product of \deg p=s r pairwise distinct linear factors of K[x].* Fix i. Since K is algebraically closed and \mu_i\ne0, choose \beta\in K^{\times} with \beta^{r}=\mu_i. If \zeta\in K satisfies \zeta^{r}=1 then (\beta\zeta)^{r}=\mu_i, and conversely any root \gamma of x^{r}-\mu_i gives (\gamma\beta^{-1})^{r}=1, so the root set is \{\beta\zeta:\zeta^{r}=1\}. The polynomial x^{r}-1 has derivative r x^{r-1}; because \operatorname{char}K=0, r\ne0 in K, and 0 is not a root of x^{r}-1 (its value at 0 is -1), so \gcd(x^{r}-1,\,r x^{r-1})=1 in K[x]. Hence x^{r}-1 is squarefree; as it splits over K it has exactly r distinct roots, i.e. |\{\zeta\in K:\zeta^{r}=1\}|=r. Therefore x^{r}-\mu_i has exactly r distinct roots in K, and the r roots of the factor for i are \{\beta\zeta:\zeta^{r}=1\}\subset K^{\times}. If i\ne i', the root sets of x^{r}-\mu_i and x^{r}-\mu_{i'} are disjoint, for a common root \gamma would give \mu_i=\gamma^{r}=\mu_{i'}, contradicting 2a's distinctness of the \mu_i. Consequently p splits in K[x] as a product of sr distinct linear factors (x-\alpha), \alpha\in K^{\times}.

*2d. Conclusion.* Write p=\prod_{j=1}^{sr}(x-\alpha_j) with the \alpha_j\in K^{\times} pairwise distinct. Since \mu_A is monic and \mu_A\mid p, unique factorisation in K[x] gives \mu_A=\prod_{j\in J}(x-\alpha_j) for some subset J\subseteq\{1,\dots,sr\}: indeed p=\mu_A h with h monic, and each (x-\alpha_j) divides exactly one of \mu_A, h. Thus \mu_A is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors in K[x], and Fact 2 implies that A is diagonalizable over K.

**Step 3: Descent of notation.** We have shown for A=\tilde T=T\otimes\mathrm{id}_K that \tilde T is diagonalizable over K iff \tilde T^{\,r}=(T^{r})\otimes\mathrm{id}_K is diagonalizable over K. By the definition of "diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell" used in the statement (and lemma_5, which identifies this with semisimplicity on V), this is exactly the assertion that T is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell if and only if T^{r} is diagonalizable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. Note that the hypothesis T\in\mathrm{GL}(V) is essential and was used exactly in Step 2a: for a non-invertible operator the reverse implication fails (e.g. a nonzero nilpotent Jordan block T on \mathbb Q_\ell^{2} has T^{2}=0 diagonalizable while T is not).

This completes the proof of both implications in all cases (including n=0 and r=1), establishing the lemma. \hfill\blacksquare

lemma_444.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(f:Y\to X\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(N\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Then for every integer \(n\ge0\) there exists a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear homomorphism \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) such that \(f_*\) commutes with the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of source and target, and such that \(f_*\circ f^*=N\cdot\mathrm{id}\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), where \(f^*\) is pullback.
lemma_444.proof:
We keep the notation of the statement: $q=p^a$, $\ell\neq p$, $X$ and $Y$ smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge 1$ over $\mathbb F_q$, $f:Y\to X$ proper surjective generically finite of degree $N\ge1$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. For $Z\in\{X,Y\}$ write $H^j(Z):=H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and let $F_Z:H^j(Z)\to H^j(Z)$ denote the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^q$.

**Step 0 (Preliminaries: finite dimensionality and invertibility of $F_Z$).** Since $Z$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, applying eoinm/lemma_45_finite_frob to $K=\mathbb Q_{\ell,Z_k}$ (with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure) gives that $H^j(Z)$ is finite dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ for every $j$. eoinm/lemma_6a then says that $F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^j(Z)$ (with inverse the geometric Frobenius), so $F_Z^{-1}$ exists and may be used.

**Step 1 (Poincar\'e duality data).** eoinm/lemma_77 applies to $Z$ (with $m=1$, pure dimension $d$). Its part (a) provides the trace isomorphism
$$\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2d}(Z)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad \operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q],$$
which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ as multiplication by $q^{d}$. Its part (b) says that for every $0\le n\le 2d$ the pairing
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Z:H^n(Z)\times H^{2d-n}(Z)\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad \langle x,y\rangle_Z=\operatorname{tr}_Z(x\cup y),$$
is a **perfect** pairing of finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and that
$$\langle F_Zx,F_Zy\rangle_Z=q^{d}\langle x,y\rangle_Z\qquad\text{for all }x,y. \tag{1}$$
Since $F_Z$ is invertible (Step 0), substituting $y\mapsto F_Z^{-1}y$ in (1) yields the adjointness relation we shall use repeatedly:
$$\langle F_Zx,y\rangle_Z=q^{d}\langle x,F_Z^{-1}y\rangle_Z\qquad\text{for all }x,y. \tag{2}$$

**Step 2 (Naturality of Frobenius pullback).** Because $f$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$, the square
$$\begin{CD} Y_k @>{f_k}>> X_k \\ @V{F_Y}VV @VV{F_X}V \\ Y_k @>{f_k}>> X_k\end{CD}$$
commutes. Indeed, writing $Z_k=Y\times_{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,k$, both composites $Y_k\to X_k$ are the morphism over $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$ induced by the pair $(f,\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)$, i.e. on the level of the fibre product both are given by $f^\#\otimes\sigma$; uniqueness in the universal property of the fibre product gives equality. Applying the contravariant functor $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ gives, for every $n$,
$$f^*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f^*,\qquad\text{hence also}\qquad f^*\circ F_X^{-1}=F_Y^{-1}\circ f^*, \tag{3}$$
the second identity following from the invertibility of $F_X,F_Y$ (Step 0).

**Step 3 (Definition of $f_*$ for $0\le n\le 2d$).** Fix $n$ with $0\le n\le 2d$ and $u\in H^n(Y)$. Define $f_*(u)\in H^n(X)$ to be the unique element satisfying
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f_*(u)\cup x\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(u\cup f^*x\bigr)\quad\text{in }\mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad\text{for all }x\in H^{2d-n}(X). \tag{4}$$
*Existence and uniqueness.* By perfectness of $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_X$, the map $H^n(X)\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^{2d-n}(X),\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\bigr)$, $a\mapsto\bigl(x\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(a\cup x)\bigr)$, is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. The right-hand side of (4), as a function of $x$, is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear because $\cup$ is bilinear, $f^*$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear and $\operatorname{tr}_Y$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear. Hence there is a unique $f_*(u)$ satisfying (4). 
*Linearity.* For $u,v\in H^n(Y)$ and $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb Q_\ell$, the element $f_*(\lambda u+\mu v)$ is characterised by (4); by bilinearity of $\cup$ on $Y$ and linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_Y$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((\lambda u+\mu v)\cup f^*x\bigr)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}_Y(u\cup f^*x)+\mu\operatorname{tr}_Y(v\cup f^*x)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((\lambda f_*u+\mu f_*v)\cup x\bigr),$$
so uniqueness gives $f_*(\lambda u+\mu v)=\lambda f_*u+\mu f_*v$. Thus $f_*:H^n(Y)\to H^n(X)$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear.

**Step 4 (The case $n>2d$).** By Spark/lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing applied to the projective $k$-schemes $X_k$ and $Y_k$ of pure dimension $d$, $H^n(X)=H^n(Y)=0$ for $n>2d$. Taking $f_*=0$ (the only possible map) the required identities $f_*F_Y=F_Xf_*$ and $f_*f^*=N\cdot\mathrm{id}$ hold trivially on zero spaces. Henceforth assume $0\le n\le 2d$, so that $f_*$ is given by Step 3 (and note $2d-n\ge0$, so no negative-degree group occurs).

**Step 5 ($f_*$ commutes with Frobenius).** Let $u\in H^n(Y)$ and $x\in H^{2d-n}(X)$. Note $F_X^{\pm1}$ preserves $H^{2d-n}(X)$ and $F_Y^{\pm1}$ preserves $H^n(Y)$. Using (2) on $X$ with $a=f_*u$, $b=x$, then the defining property (4), then (3), then (2) on $Y$ with $a=u$, $b=f^*x$, we compute:
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((F_Xf_*u)\cup x\bigr)=q^{d}\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f_*u\cup F_X^{-1}x\bigr)=q^{d}\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(u\cup f^*F_X^{-1}x\bigr)=q^{d}\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(u\cup F_Y^{-1}f^*x\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((F_Yu)\cup f^*x\bigr).$$
The last expression is exactly the right-hand side of (4) with $u$ replaced by $F_Yu$, i.e.
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((f_*F_Yu)\cup x\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((F_Yu)\cup f^*x\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((F_Xf_*u)\cup x\bigr)\qquad\text{for all }x\in H^{2d-n}(X).$$
Perfectness of $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_X$ forces $f_*F_Yu=F_Xf_*u$. Since $u$ was arbitrary, $f_*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f_*$, which is the required commutation with the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of source and target.

**Step 6 (The identity $f_*\circ f^*=N\cdot\mathrm{id}$).** Let $\alpha\in H^n(X)$ and $x\in H^{2d-n}(X)$. By (4) applied to $u=f^*\alpha$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((f_*f^*\alpha)\cup x\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f^*\alpha\cup f^*x\bigr).$$
Pullback is a homomorphism of graded-commutative rings (functoriality of the cup product), so $f^*\alpha\cup f^*x=f^*(\alpha\cup x)$, where $\alpha\cup x\in H^{2d}(X)$. Thus
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((f_*f^*\alpha)\cup x\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f^*(\alpha\cup x)\bigr). \tag{5}$$
Now apply eoinm/lemma_top_trace_generically_finite. Its hypotheses are satisfied with the roles of its $(X,Y,D,d)$ equal to our $(Y,X,d,N)$: $f:Y\to X$ is proper, surjective and generically finite of degree $N\ge1$ between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$ (smooth and geometrically connected implies geometrically integral, so the degree is the function-field degree $[k(Y):k(X)]=N$, exactly the degree entering that lemma). Its trace isomorphisms are normalised on closed points by $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$, which is precisely the normalisation of the $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ of Step 1 (lemma_77(a), with $m=1$); hence the two lemmas use the same maps. The lemma then says that $\operatorname{tr}_Y\circ f^*\circ\operatorname{tr}_X^{-1}$ is multiplication by $N$ on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, i.e.
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f^*\omega\bigr)=N\,\operatorname{tr}_X(\omega)\qquad\text{for all }\omega\in H^{2d}(X). \tag{6}$$
Applying (6) to $\omega=\alpha\cup x$ in (5) and using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\cup$ and $\operatorname{tr}_X$ gives
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((f_*f^*\alpha)\cup x\bigr)=N\operatorname{tr}_X(\alpha\cup x)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((N\alpha)\cup x\bigr)\qquad\text{for all }x\in H^{2d-n}(X).$$
Perfectness of $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_X$ yields $f_*f^*\alpha=N\alpha$. As $\alpha$ was arbitrary, $f_*\circ f^*=N\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^n(X)$.

**Step 7 (Conclusion).** For each integer $n\ge0$ we have produced a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear homomorphism $f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ — namely the Poincar\'e-dual adjoint of $f^*$ defined by (4) when $n\le 2d$, and the zero map when $n>2d$ (where both groups vanish) — such that $f_*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f_*$ (Step 5, trivially true in the vanishing range) and $f_*\circ f^*=N\cdot\mathrm{id}$ (Step 6, likewise). This is exactly the required conclusion. $\blacksquare$

lemma_443.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Suppose that for every integer \(m\ge1\), every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(Y\) of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and every \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisor \(H\) with cycle class \(\xi\) and Lefschetz operator \(L\), hard Lefschetz holds for \(L\), and for every \(0\le r\le d\) and every embedding \(\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\), the primitive space \(P^r=\ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-r+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\) is stable under the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \(F\), and \(P^r\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C\) carries a positive definite Hermitian form \(h\) with \(h(F_\sigma x,F_\sigma y)=q^{mr}h(x,y)\), where \(F_\sigma=F\otimes\mathrm{id}\). Then for every integer \(m\ge1\), every smooth projective variety \(X\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and every integer \(n\ge0\), the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_443.proof:
We write k = \bar{\mathbb F}_q. Throughout, we fix once and for all a nonzero element \(u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\); this is the "trivialisation of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\)" with respect to which all \(\ell\)-adic cycle classes \(\operatorname{cl}(D)\in H^2_{\acute et}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) of divisors on all varieties below are taken. For a variety \(Z\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\) we denote by
\[
F_{Z,t}:=(\mathrm{id}_Z\times \operatorname{Spec}\sigma_t)^*,\qquad \sigma_t(c)=c^{q^t},
\]
the \(q^t\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^\bullet_{\acute et}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

By "semisimple on \(V\)" we mean semisimple as a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear operator; by lemma_5 (eoinm) this is equivalent to being diagonalizable on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), and we freely pass between the two formulations using lemma_5.

We shall prove the following statement, and then deduce the lemma from lemma_436 (Spark).

**Claim 1.** *Let \(t\ge 1\), \(e\ge 1\), and let \(V\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(e\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\). Then \(F_{V,t}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(0\le n\le e\) (in particular for \(n=e\)).*

*Proof of Claim 1.*

**(1) \(V\) is integral.** Being of finite type over a field, \(V\) is noetherian, and being smooth over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\) it is regular; regular local rings are domains, so every local ring of \(V\) is a domain. A noetherian scheme all of whose local rings are domains is reduced (its local rings are reduced). It is also irreducible: if \(V=Z_1\cup Z_2\) were a union of two distinct irreducible components, then \(Z_1\cap Z_2\neq\varnothing\) by connectedness of \(V\) (both are nonempty closed, and a connected noetherian space is not the disjoint union of two proper closed subsets); a point \(x\in Z_1\cap Z_2\) would have \(\mathcal O_{V,x}\) with at least two minimal primes, contradicting that \(\mathcal O_{V,x}\) is a domain. Hence \(V\) is irreducible and reduced, i.e. integral.

**(2) Existence of an \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\)-rational very ample divisor.** Since \(V\) is projective over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), there is a closed immersion \(V\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}\); put \(\mathcal L:=\mathcal O(1)|_V\), which is very ample, defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\). Very ampleness means the complete linear system \(|\mathcal L|=\mathbb P H^0(V,\mathcal L)\) defines the embedding, so \(H^0(V,\mathcal L)\neq 0\); choose \(0\neq s\in H^0(V,\mathcal L)\). Since \(V\) is integral, \(s\) is a non-zero-divisor on each \(\mathcal O_V(U)\), so its vanishing scheme \(H:=V(s)\), with the induced closed subscheme structure, is an effective Cartier divisor, defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), with conormal sheaf \(\mathcal I_H/\mathcal I_H^2\cong\mathcal L^{-1}|_H\), hence \(\mathcal O_V(H):=(\mathcal I_H)^{-1}\cong\mathcal L\) is very ample. Thus \(H\) is an \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\)-rational very ample divisor on \(V\). Also \(H\neq V\) since \(s\neq 0\) on the integral scheme \(V\).

**(3) Applying the standing hypothesis.** Apply the hypothesis of the lemma to \(Y=V\), \(m=t\), \(d=e\), and this \(H\). Writing \(\xi=\operatorname{cl}(H)\in H^2_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) (cycle class w.r.t. the fixed \(u\)) and \(L:=\xi\cup(-)\), we obtain:

 (a) *hard Lefschetz*: \(L^{e-n}:H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^{2e-n}_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le e\);

 (b) for every \(0\le j\le e\), the primitive space \(P^j:=\ker\bigl(L^{\,e-j+1}:H^j_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2e-j+2}_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\) is stable under \(F:=F_{V,t}\);

 (c) for every \(0\le j\le e\) and every embedding \(\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\), the \(\mathbb C\)-vector space \(P^j_\sigma:=P^j\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell,\sigma}\mathbb C\) carries a positive definite Hermitian form \(h_\sigma\) with \(h_\sigma(F_\sigma x,F_\sigma y)=q^{tj}\,h_\sigma(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\), where \(F_\sigma:=F\otimes\mathrm{id}\).

**(4) Finite dimensionality.** By lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) applied to \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\) (the constant sheaf, with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism) on the proper \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\)-scheme \(V\), each \(H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Hence so are all \(P^j\) and all \(L^r(P^{j})\).

**(5) The primitive pieces are diagonalizable.** Fix \(0\le j\le e\) and an embedding \(\sigma:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\). By (b), \(P^j\) is \(F\)-stable, and since \(F\) is an automorphism of the finite-dimensional space \(H^j\), the restriction \(T:=F|_{P^j}\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(P^j)\) is an automorphism. Its base change \(T_\sigma=F_\sigma\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb C}(P^j_\sigma)\) satisfies \(h_\sigma(T_\sigma x,T_\sigma y)=c\,h_\sigma(x,y)\) with \(c=q^{tj}\in\mathbb R_{>0}\subset\mathbb C^\times\). We first show \(T_\sigma\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb C\), by induction on \(\dim_{\mathbb C}P^j_\sigma\). The case \(0\) is trivial. Otherwise, since \(\mathbb C\) is algebraically closed the characteristic polynomial of \(T_\sigma\) has a root \(\lambda\), and \(\lambda\neq0\) since \(T_\sigma\) is invertible; choose an eigenvector \(v\ne0\). Put \(W_1:=\mathbb C v\); then \(T_\sigma(W_1)=W_1\). Positive definiteness gives \(h_\sigma(v,v)>0\), so \(W_1\cap W_1^{\perp}=0\) and \(P^j_\sigma=W_1\oplus W_1^{\perp}\). The orthogonal complement \(W_1^{\perp}\) is \(T_\sigma\)-stable: for \(x\in W_1\) and \(y\in W_1^{\perp}\), substituting \(u=T_\sigma^{-1}x,\ w=y\) into \(h_\sigma(T_\sigma u,T_\sigma w)=c\,h_\sigma(u,w)\) gives \(h_\sigma(x,T_\sigma y)=c\,h_\sigma(T_\sigma^{-1}x,y)=0\), because \(T_\sigma^{-1}x\in W_1\) and \(y\in W_1^{\perp}\). By induction \(T_\sigma|_{W_1^{\perp}}\) is diagonalizable, and \(T_\sigma|_{W_1}=\lambda\); hence \(T_\sigma\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb C\).

Now we descend this to \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\mu\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) be the minimal polynomial of \(T\). The minimal polynomial of \(T_\sigma\) over \(\mathbb C\) equals \(\sigma(\mu)\): indeed, by the structure theorem over the PID \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\), \(P^j\cong\bigoplus_i\mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(\mu_i)\) with \(\mu_1\mid\cdots\mid\mu_s=\mu\), and tensoring with \(\mathbb C\) (which is flat, indeed free, over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)) gives \(P^j_\sigma\cong\bigoplus_i\mathbb C[t]/(\sigma(\mu_i))\), whose annihilator is \((\sigma(\mu))\). Since \(T_\sigma\) is diagonalizable, \(\sigma(\mu)=\prod_{i=1}^{s'}(t-\lambda_i)\) with the \(\lambda_i\) pairwise distinct; hence \(\gcd(\sigma(\mu),(\sigma(\mu))')=1\) in \(\mathbb C[t]\). As \((\sigma(\mu))'=\sigma(\mu')\) and \(\sigma:\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\hookrightarrow\mathbb C[t]\) is injective and degree-preserving, \(\gcd(\mu,\mu')=1\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\), i.e. \(\mu\) is squarefree. Factor \(\mu=\prod_i p_i\) into distinct irreducibles in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\); since \(\operatorname{char}\mathbb Q_\ell=0\) each \(p_i\) is separable, so \(\mu\) splits over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) into pairwise distinct linear factors. Therefore \(T\otimes\mathrm{id}\) is diagonalizable on \(P^j\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), i.e. \(F|_{P^j}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) (equivalently semisimple, by lemma_5).

**(6) The Lefschetz decomposition.** Apply lemma_417 (Spark) with the prime power \(p^{at}\) in place of its \(q\), to \(X=V\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), the divisor \(H\), and the operator \(L\) (the same fixed trivialisation \(u\) is used in both places, so its \(L\) is our \(L\), and its \(P^m\) is our \(P^m\)); its hypothesis is exactly hard Lefschetz (3a). Its conclusion is that for every \(n\ge0\) the map
\[
\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,n-e)}P^{n-2r}\longrightarrow H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad (x_r)\longmapsto\sum_r L^r x_r,
\]
is an isomorphism (with \(P^m=0\) for \(m<0\)), and each subspace \(L^r(P^{n-2r})\subseteq H^n\) is stable under the \(q^t\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \(F\). For \(0\le n\le e\) this reads
\[
H^n_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\bigoplus_{0\le r\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor} L^r\bigl(P^{n-2r}\bigr)
\]
as an internal direct sum of \(F\)-stable \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspaces, and, because the displayed map is an isomorphism and the inclusion \(P^{n-2r}\hookrightarrow\bigoplus_r P^{n-2r}\) is injective, each
\[
L^r:\;P^{n-2r}\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ L^r(P^{n-2r})
\]
is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism.

**(7) Each summand is diagonalizable.** By lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable (eoinm) applied over the field \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\) (its \(q\) is our \(q^t\)), \(F\circ L=q^{t}\,L\circ F\) on every \(H^m\); iterating, \(F\circ L^{r}=q^{tr}\,L^{r}\circ F\). Fix \(r\) and set \(W_r:=L^r(P^{n-2r})\), \(\alpha:=L^r:P^{n-2r}\xrightarrow{\sim}W_r\), \(T_V:=F|_{P^{n-2r}}\), \(T_W:=q^{-tr}\,F|_{W_r}\). The relation above says precisely \(\alpha\circ T_V=T_W\circ\alpha\). By lemma_8 (eoinm), \(T_W\) is semisimple if and only if \(T_V\) is; by step (5) (with \(j=n-2r\), noting \(0\le n-2r\le n\le e\)) \(T_V\) is semisimple, so \(T_W\) is semisimple. Finally \(F|_{W_r}=q^{tr}T_W\) with \(q^{tr}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times\): multiplying by a nonzero scalar does not change the eigenspace decomposition after any field extension, so \(F|_{W_r}\) is again semisimple, hence diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) by lemma_5.

**(8) Conclusion of the claim.** The operator \(F|_{H^n}=\bigoplus_{0\le r\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor}F|_{W_r}\) is a finite direct sum of semisimple operators, hence semisimple by lemma_9 (eoinm), and diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) by lemma_5. Taking \(n=e\) gives the top-degree statement. \(\square\) (Claim 1)

**Part II: Conclusion of the lemma.** Claim 1 with \(n=e\) says precisely: for every \(e\ge1\), every \(t\ge1\), and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(V\) of pure dimension \(e\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), the \(q^t\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^t}\), is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^e_{\acute et}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). This is exactly the hypothesis of lemma_436 (Spark). Applying lemma_436 yields: for every \(t\ge1\), every smooth projective variety \(W\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), and every \(n\ge0\), the \(q^t\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Renaming \(t\) as \(m\) and \(W\) as \(X\), this is exactly the required conclusion. \( lacksquare\)

lemma_admissible_affine_poincare_duality.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field and let l be a prime different from char(k). Let X be a smooth projective connected variety of pure dimension d >= 1 over k, let Y \subsetneq X be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor that is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over k, and put U = X \ Y with its open subscheme structure. Then there exists a Q_l-linear isomorphism tr: H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_l) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_l(-d) such that for every integer j the pairing H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_l) \times H^{2d-j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_l) \to \mathbb Q_l(-d), (x,y) \mapsto tr(x \cup y), is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_l-vector spaces.
lemma_admissible_affine_poincare_duality.proof:
Proof. Let C = H_c^{2d}(U,Q_l). First we show that C is one-dimensional and that H^0_et(U,Q_l)=Q_l. Since X is smooth over k, it is regular. A connected Noetherian regular scheme is irreducible: each local ring is a domain, so each point lies on a unique irreducible component, hence irreducible components are open; connectedness leaves only one component. Thus X is irreducible. The divisor Y is a proper closed subset of X, so U = X \ Y is a nonempty open subset of an irreducible space; hence U is irreducible and connected. For a connected scheme, global sections of the constant sheaf Q_l on the etale site are Q_l (equivalently, a locally constant Q_l-valued function on a connected space is constant), so H^0_et(U,Q_l)=Q_l.

Because Y is an effective ample Cartier divisor, the line bundle L=O_X(Y) is ample and Y is the zero scheme of the canonical section s in H^0(X,L). Applying lemma_318 to (X,L,s) gives that U = X \ Y is affine. Also U is an open subscheme of the separated finite type k-scheme X, hence separated finite type, and it is pure of dimension d.

Now apply lemma_ample_complement_pairing with a=2d. It gives a perfect pairing C x H^0_et(U,Q_l) -> C, (x,lambda) |-> x cup lambda = lambda x. Since H^0_et(U,Q_l)=Q_l, perfectness says that the adjoint map Q_l -> End(C), lambda |-> (x |-> lambda x), is a Q_l-linear isomorphism. The same lemma says C is finite-dimensional. Therefore dim End(C)=1. If n=dim C, then dim End(C)=n^2, so n=1. Thus C is one-dimensional. Choose any Q_l-linear isomorphism tr:C -> Q_l(-d); this is possible because Q_l(-d) is also one-dimensional.

For each integer j with 0 <= j <= 2d, lemma_ample_complement_pairing gives a perfect pairing beta_j: H_c^j(U,Q_l) x H^{2d-j}_et(U,Q_l) -> C, (x,y) |-> x cup y. Define P_j(x,y)=tr(x cup y). If beta:A x B -> C is perfect and phi:C -> C' is a linear isomorphism, then phi o beta is perfect: the adjoint A -> Hom(B,C') is the composite of the adjoint A -> Hom(B,C) with postcomposition by phi, and postcomposition by phi is an isomorphism Hom(B,C) -> Hom(B,C'); the argument for B is analogous. Hence P_j is perfect. The lemma also gives finite-dimensionality of both factors.

It remains to handle j outside [0,2d]. Negative cohomology groups are zero by definition. For ordinary cohomology, U is affine of dimension d. Applying lemma_ordinary_vanishing_affine_cover to the one-element affine cover of U gives H^n_et(U,Q_l)=0 for every n>d; in particular for n>2d. For compact supports, let u:U -> X be the open immersion and i:Y -> X the closed immersion. The extension-by-zero sheaf gives a short exact sequence of etale sheaves of Q_l-vector spaces 0 -> u_!Q_l -> Q_l -> i_*Q_l -> 0. Exactness is checked on geometric stalks: over U the stalk of u_!Q_l is Q_l and the stalk of i_*Q_l is 0, while over Y the stalk of u_!Q_l is 0 and the stalk of i_*Q_l is Q_l. The associated long exact sequence identifies H_c^n(U,Q_l) with H^n(X,u_!Q_l). For n>2d, lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing gives H^n(X,Q_l)=0 and also H^{n-1}(Y,Q_l)=0, because Y is projective of pure dimension d-1 and n-1 > 2(d-1). The exact sequence segment H^{n-1}(Y,Q_l) -> H_c^n(U,Q_l) -> H^n(X,Q_l) therefore forces H_c^n(U,Q_l)=0.

If j<0, then H_c^j(U,Q_l)=0 by definition and H^{2d-j}_et(U,Q_l)=0 by the ordinary vanishing above, since 2d-j>2d. If j>2d, then H_c^j(U,Q_l)=0 by the compact-support vanishing above and H^{2d-j}_et(U,Q_l)=0 because its degree is negative. In both cases both factors are zero, and the zero pairing between zero vector spaces is perfect (both adjoint maps are 0 -> 0). It is finite-dimensional. Thus the pairing (x,y) |-> tr(x cup y) is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional Q_l-vector spaces for every integer j. This completes the proof.

lemma_442.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(H\) be an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisor on \(X\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be its cycle class via a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), and let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\). Let \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the Poincare duality trace and let \(\Lambda\) be the unique degree-\(2\) endomorphism of \(V=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{2d}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) such that \(\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y)\) for all homogeneous \(x,y\). Let \(F\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(V\), and let \(F_u\) be its unipotent part. Then \(F_u\) commutes with \(L\) and \(\Lambda\).
lemma_442.proof:
Write Q := q^m. Then Q is a prime power, \(\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_Q\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q\), and the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of the statement is the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Throughout we substitute the prime power \(Q\) for the parameter \(q\) in every cited lemma whose statement is phrased over \(\mathbb F_q\) (so that, e.g., the factor \(q^{md}\) of eoinm:lemma_77 becomes \(Q^{1\cdot d}=Q^d\)). Put \(V^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}V^n\); the operator \(L:V\to V\) is cup product with \(\xi\in V^2\), hence \(L(V^n)\subseteq V^{n+2}\).

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of \(F\)). Apply eoinm:lemma_45_finite_frob with \(\mathcal K=\mathbb Q_\ell\) the constant sheaf and \(\phi=\psi\) its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \(F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\): for every \(n\), \(H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V^n\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), and the canonical Frobenius automorphism it produces is exactly the arithmetic Frobenius. By eoinm:lemma_6a (with \(q\) replaced by \(Q\)), \(F:=F_{\mathrm{ar}}=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^Q\), is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of each \(V^n\) with inverse \(F_{\mathrm{geo}}=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*\). Hence \(F\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\); moreover \(V\) is finite-dimensional since it is a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional spaces, and \(F\) preserves each graded piece \(V^n\) because pullback preserves cohomological degree.

Step 2 (vanishing outside \([0,2d]\)). \(X_k\) is a projective scheme over \(k\) of pure dimension \(d\ge1\), so Spark:lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing gives \(V^n=0\) for all \(n>2d\); and \(V^n=0\) for \(n<0\) since étale cohomology of a sheaf vanishes in negative degrees. Thus \(V=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{2d}V^n\), and any degree lying outside \([0,2d]\) is handled by this vanishing.

Step 3 (the pairing, and existence/unipotence-free definition of \(\Lambda\)). Let \(f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q\) be the structure morphism. eoinm:lemma_77(a),(b), applied with \(q:=Q\) and \(m:=1\) to the smooth projective geometrically connected \(d\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F_Q\)-variety \(X\), supplies an isomorphism \(\operatorname{tr}_0:V^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) (the trace induced by the cycle-class/Gysin isomorphism \(\mathbb Q_\ell(d)[2d]\to Rf^!\mathbb Q_\ell\), normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_0(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_Q]\)) such that, writing \(\langle u,v\rangle_0:=\operatorname{tr}_0(u\cup v)\),
\[(\mathrm{P}1)\quad V^a\times V^{2a'}\ \text{with } a'=2d-a:\ V^a\times V^{2d-a}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\ \text{is a perfect pairing for every }0\le a\le 2d;\]
\[(\mathrm{P}2)\quad \langle Fu,Fv\rangle_0=Q^{d}\langle u,v\rangle_0\ \ \text{whenever }\deg u+\deg v=2d.\]
The \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) of the statement is the Poincaré duality trace; the Poincaré duality trace is determined up to a scalar of \(\mathbb Q_\ell^\times\) (the target \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) is one-dimensional and \(F\) acts on it as the scalar \(Q^d\), so every \(\mathbb Q_\ell^\times\)-multiple of \(\operatorname{tr}_0\) is again a Frobenius-equivariant Poincaré duality trace, and conversely). Both properties used below — perfectness, and the equivariance factor \(Q^d\) — are preserved under multiplying the trace by a scalar of \(\mathbb Q_\ell^\times\), and the defining identity of \(\Lambda\) has \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) on both sides, hence is also unaffected. We may therefore, and do, take \(\operatorname{tr}_X=\operatorname{tr}_0\); write \(\langle u,v\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}_X(u\cup v)\) for homogeneous \(u,v\) with \(\deg u+\deg v=2d\). Extend \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) to all of \(V\) by declaring it \(0\) on \(V^m\) for \(m\ne 2d\); with this convention \(\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup \Lambda y)\) holds for all homogeneous \(x,y\), since if \(\deg x+\deg y\ne 2d\) both sides are the trace of an element of some \(V^m\) with \(m\ne2d\), hence both are \(0\).

Existence. Fix \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2d-2\) and \(y\in V^n\). The map \(\varphi_y:V^{2d-n-2}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\), \(x\mapsto\langle Lx,y\rangle\), is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear (cup product is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear, \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear; it is defined because \(Lx\in V^{2d-n}\) and \((2d-n)+n=2d\)). By perfectness of \(V^{2d-n-2}\times V^{n+2}\) (an instance of (P1), legitimate since \(0\le 2d-n-2\le 2d\) and \(0\le n+2\le 2d\)), there is a unique element \(\Lambda_n y\in V^{n+2}\) with \(\langle x,\Lambda_n y\rangle=\varphi_y(x)\) for all \(x\in V^{2d-n-2}\). For \(n\ge 2d-1\) we have \(V^{n+2}=0\) by Step 2, so we set \(\Lambda_n:=0\); the defining identity then holds trivially: for \(n=2d-1\) the product \(Lx\cup y\) lies in \(V^{2d+2}=0\), and for \(n=2d\) there is no nonzero admissible \(x\) since \(V^{2d-n-2}=V^{-2}=0\). For \(n<0\) or \(n>2d\), \(V^n=0\). Define \(\Lambda:=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}\Lambda_n\); it is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear endomorphism of \(V\) with \(\Lambda(V^n)\subseteq V^{n+2}\) (degree \(2\)) satisfying \(\operatorname{tr}_X(Lx\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\Lambda y)\) for all homogeneous \(x,y\).

Uniqueness. If \(\Lambda'\) is another degree-\(2\) endomorphism with the property, then for homogeneous \(y\in V^n\) and every \(x\in V^{2d-n-2}\) one has \(\langle x,(\Lambda-\Lambda')y\rangle=0\) with \((\Lambda-\Lambda')y\in V^{n+2}\) and \((2d-n-2)+(n+2)=2d\); perfectness (P1) forces \((\Lambda-\Lambda')y=0\) (and for \(n\ge2d-1\) both vanish on \(V^n\) since \(V^{n+2}=0\)). Hence \(\Lambda'=\Lambda\).

Step 4 (\(F_u\) commutes with \(L\)). eoinm:lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable, applied with \(q:=Q\) to the smooth projective pure-\(d\) \(\mathbb F_Q\)-variety \(X\) and the \(\mathbb F_Q\)-rational very ample divisor \(H\), gives \(F\circ L=Q\,L\circ F\) on every \(V^m\); equivalently \(FLF^{-1}=Q\,L\). Since \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) has characteristic \(0\), \(F\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\) admits a unique multiplicative Jordan decomposition \(F=F_sF_u=F_uF_s\) with \(F_s\) semisimple and \(F_u\) unipotent. Applying Spark:lemma_418 with \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\), the finite-dimensional space \(V\), \(T=F\), \(c=Q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times\) (\(Q=p^{am}\ne0\)) and \(A=L\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\) — the hypothesis \(TAT^{-1}=cA\) being exactly \(FLF^{-1}=QL\) — yields
\[F_uL=LF_u.\tag{4.1}\]

Step 5 (the identity \(F\Lambda F^{-1}=Q\,\Lambda\)). First note \(F\Lambda F^{-1}\) has degree \(2\), because \(F^{\pm1}\) preserve each \(V^j\) (Step 1) and \(\Lambda\) raises degree by \(2\). We prove \(\Lambda=Q^{-1}F\Lambda F^{-1}\) on homogeneous elements; by additivity over the grading this gives \(F\Lambda F^{-1}=Q\Lambda\) on \(V\). Also record, from \(FL=Q\,LF\) by composing with \(F^{-1}\) on both sides, the relation
\[F^{-1}L=Q^{-1}LF^{-1}.\tag{5.0}\]

Case \(n\ge 2d-1\): for \(y\in V^n\), \(\Lambda y\in V^{n+2}\) with \(n+2\ge 2d+1>2d\), so \(\Lambda y=0\) by Step 2; and \(F^{-1}y\in V^n\), so \(\Lambda F^{-1}y=0\) and \(F\Lambda F^{-1}y=0\). The equality holds trivially.

Case \(0\le n\le 2d-2\): let \(y\in V^n\) and let \(x\in V^{2d-n-2}\) be arbitrary. The degrees are: \(\deg x=2d-n-2\), \(\deg Lx=2d-n\), \(\deg y=n\), \(\deg\Lambda y=n+2\), \(\deg F^{-1}x=2d-n-2\), \(\deg F^{-1}y=n\), \(\deg F^{-1}Lx=2d-n\), \(\deg LF^{-1}x=2d-n\), \(\deg\Lambda F^{-1}y=n+2\), \(\deg F\Lambda F^{-1}y=n+2\). In particular each pairing appearing below is between degrees summing to \(2d\), so each is defined.

First expression — the defining property of \(\Lambda\) applied to \(x\in V^{2d-n-2}\) and \(y\in V^n\) (valid since \(\deg x+\deg\Lambda y=(2d-n-2)+(n+2)=2d\) and \(\deg Lx+\deg y=(2d-n)+n=2d\)):
\[\langle Lx,y\rangle=\langle x,\Lambda y\rangle.\tag{5.1}\]

Second expression:
\[\langle Lx,y\rangle=Q^{d}\langle F^{-1}Lx,F^{-1}y\rangle=Q^{d-1}\langle LF^{-1}x,F^{-1}y\rangle=Q^{d-1}\langle F^{-1}x,\Lambda F^{-1}y\rangle=Q^{d-1}\cdot Q^{-d}\langle x,F\Lambda F^{-1}y\rangle=Q^{-1}\langle x,F\Lambda F^{-1}y\rangle.\tag{5.2}\]
Justification of each equality in (5.2), in order:
(i) (P2) applied to \(u=F^{-1}Lx\in V^{2d-n}\) and \(v=F^{-1}y\in V^{n}\), whose degrees sum to \(2d\): \(\langle Fu,Fv\rangle=Q^d\langle u,v\rangle\) reads \(\langle Lx,y\rangle=Q^d\langle F^{-1}Lx,F^{-1}y\rangle\).
(ii) \(F^{-1}Lx=Q^{-1}LF^{-1}x\) by (5.0), together with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linearity of the pairing in the first slot.
(iii) the defining property of \(\Lambda\) applied to \(F^{-1}x\in V^{2d-n-2}\) and \(F^{-1}y\in V^{n}\) (degrees \((2d-n-2)+(n+2)=2d\) after applying \(\Lambda\), and \((2d-n)+n=2d\) before).
(iv) the equivalent form of (P2), namely \(\langle F^{-1}u,F^{-1}v\rangle=Q^{-d}\langle u,v\rangle\) (obtained from (P2) by substituting \(F^{-1}u,F^{-1}v\) for \(u,v\); their degrees sum to \(2d\) exactly when those of \(u,v\) do), applied to \(u=x\in V^{2d-n-2}\) and \(v=\Lambda F^{-1}y\in V^{n+2}\), whose degrees sum to \((2d-n-2)+(n+2)=2d\).

Subtracting (5.2) from (5.1) gives \(\langle x,\ \Lambda y-Q^{-1}F\Lambda F^{-1}y\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in V^{2d-n-2}\). The element \(w:=\Lambda y-Q^{-1}F\Lambda F^{-1}y\) lies in \(V^{n+2}\), and \((2d-n-2)+(n+2)=2d\) with \(0\le 2d-n-2\le 2d\) and \(0\le n+2\le 2d\), so (P1) asserts that \(V^{2d-n-2}\times V^{n+2}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) is a perfect pairing; non-degeneracy on the right forces \(w=0\). Hence \(\Lambda y=Q^{-1}F\Lambda F^{-1}y\).

Case \(n<0\) or \(n>2d\): \(V^n=0\) by Step 2, nothing to prove.

Thus \(\Lambda y=Q^{-1}F\Lambda F^{-1}y\) for every homogeneous \(y\), hence for all \(y\in V\) by additivity over the grading, i.e.
\[F\Lambda F^{-1}=Q\,\Lambda.\tag{5.3}\]

Step 6 (\(F_u\) commutes with \(\Lambda\)). Apply Spark:lemma_418 with \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\), the finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-space \(V\), \(T=F\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\) with Jordan decomposition \(F=F_sF_u\) as in Step 4, \(c=Q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times\), and \(A=\Lambda\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\). Its hypothesis \(TAT^{-1}=cA\) is exactly (5.3), and its conclusion is
\[F_u\Lambda=\Lambda F_u.\tag{6.1}\]

Step 7 (conclusion). (4.1) and (6.1) together say precisely that the unipotent part \(F_u\) of the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \(F\) commutes with both \(L\) and \(\Lambda\). \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_448.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(m\ge1\), let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be its cycle class under a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and let \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace. For an integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d\), the map \(L^{\,d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective if and only if the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear form \((x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(L^{\,d-n}x\cup y)\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is perfect.
lemma_448.proof:
Write $\Q:=q^{m}=p^{am}$ (again a prime power), $k=\overline{\F}_q$, and abbreviate $H^{j}:=H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\Q_\ell)$. The class $\xi\in H^{2}$ is the cycle class of the very ample divisor $H$, and $L:H^{j}\to H^{j+2}$ denotes $\Q_\ell$-linear cup product with $\xi$; since $\xi$ has degree $2$, $L^{d-n}$ is $\Q_\ell$-linear of degree $2(d-n)$, hence indeed a map $L^{d-n}:H^{n}\to H^{2d-n}$ (note $0\le n\le d$ guarantees $d-n\ge0$). Set $T:=L^{\,d-n}$ and, for $a\in H^{2d-n}$, $b\in H^{n}$, put
\[
\langle a,b\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}_X(a\cup b)\in\Q_\ell,\qquad
B(x,y):=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(Tx\cup y\bigr)=\langle Tx,y\rangle\qquad(x,y\in H^{n}).
\]
We must prove: $T$ is injective $\Longleftrightarrow$ $B$ is a perfect pairing on $H^{n}$.

**Step 1 (finite-dimensionality).** $X$ is smooth projective over $\F_{\Q}$, hence proper; the constant sheaf $\Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ is an object of $D^b_c(X_k,\Q_\ell)$ (the stratification with the single stratum $X_k$ exhibits it as lisse of rank $1$) and carries its natural arithmetic-Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:\Frob_{\Q}^{*}\Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\Q_\ell$. Applying eoinm/lemma_45_finite_frob with $\Q$ in place of $q$ and $K=\Q_\ell$, $\phi=\psi$, we obtain that every $H^{j}=H^{j}(X_k,\Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\Q_\ell$.

**Step 2 (Poincar\'e duality pairing is perfect).** By eoinm/lemma_77(a), applied to $X$ over $\F_{\Q}=\F_{q^m}$, there is a canonical trace isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{can}}:H^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}\Q_\ell(-d)$; in particular $\dim_{\Q_\ell}H^{2d}=1$. The trace $\operatorname{tr}_X$ occurring in the statement is, by hypothesis, an isomorphism $H^{2d}\xrightarrow{\sim}\Q_\ell$. After the trivialisation $\Q_\ell(-d)\simeq\Q_\ell$ determined by the fixed nonzero element of $\Q_\ell(1)$, both $\operatorname{tr}_X$ and $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{can}}$ are isomorphisms from the $1$-dimensional space $H^{2d}$ to $\Q_\ell$, so they differ by a scalar: $\operatorname{tr}_X=c\cdot\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{can}}$ for some $c\in\Q_\ell^{\times}$. By eoinm/lemma_77(b), $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{can}}(u\cup v)$ is a perfect pairing $H^{n}\times H^{2d-n}\to\Q_\ell(-d)$; multiplying by the non-zero scalar $c$ and using the trivialisation, $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{can}}$-pairing composed with $c$ is again perfect. Hence
\[
\text{the pairings }H^{n}\times H^{2d-n}\to\Q_\ell,\ (u,v)\mapsto\langle u,v\rangle\text{ and }H^{2d-n}\times H^{n}\to\Q_\ell,\ (a,b)\mapsto\langle a,b\rangle\text{ are perfect.}\tag{1}
\]
(Perfectness in the two orders is equivalent because cup product is graded-commutative: for $a\in H^{2d-n}$, $b\in H^{n}$ one has $a\cup b=(-1)^{(2d-n)n}b\cup a$, so $\langle a,b\rangle=(-1)^{(2d-n)n}\langle b,a\rangle$ in the other order, and $(-1)^{(2d-n)n}\in\Q_\ell^{\times}$.)

From the second perfectness in (1), the map
\[
\Psi:H^{2d-n}\xrightarrow{\sim}(H^{n})^{\vee},\qquad \Psi(a)(b):=\langle a,b\rangle=\operatorname{tr}_X(a\cup b)
\]
is an isomorphism of $\Q_\ell$-vector spaces.

**Step 3 (the two left/right maps attached to $B$).** Define the two $\Q_\ell$-linear maps associated with $B$:
\[
\Phi:H^{n}\to(H^{n})^{\vee},\ \Phi(x)(y):=B(x,y);\qquad \Phi':H^{n}\to(H^{n})^{\vee},\ \Phi'(y)(x):=B(x,y).
\]
By definition of $B$ and of $\Psi$, for all $x,y\in H^{n}$,
\[
\Phi(x)(y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(Tx\cup y)=\Psi(Tx)(y),
\]
so $\Phi=\Psi\circ T$. Likewise, since $Ty\in H^{n+2(d-n)}=H^{2d-n}$,
\[
\Phi'(y)(x)=\operatorname{tr}_X(Tx\cup y)=(-1)^{(2d-n)n}\operatorname{tr}_X(y\cup Tx)=(-1)^{(2d-n)n}\Psi(Ty)(x),
\]
so $\Phi'=\varepsilon\,(\Psi\circ T)$ with $\varepsilon=(-1)^{(2d-n)n}\in\{\pm1\}$. As $\Psi$ is an isomorphism and $\varepsilon\neq0$,
\[
B\text{ is perfect }\Longleftrightarrow\ \Phi\text{ is an isomorphism }\Longleftrightarrow\ \Phi'\text{ is an isomorphism }\Longleftrightarrow\ T\text{ is an isomorphism.}\tag{2}
\]
(Here "perfect" means both $\Phi$ and $\Phi'$ are isomorphisms, i.e. trivial left and right radicals; by the displayed identities the two conditions coincide and are equivalent to $T$ being bijective. In particular, if $H^{n}=0$ then $\Phi,\Phi',T$ are all the zero map $0\to0$, hence isomorphisms, so the equivalence holds in this degenerate case as well.)

**Step 4 (injectivity $\Rightarrow$ bijectivity of $T$).** The first perfectness in (1) identifies $H^{n}\simeq(H^{2d-n})^{\vee}$; since both spaces are finite-dimensional (Step 1), $\dim_{\Q_\ell}H^{2d-n}=\dim_{\Q_\ell}(H^{2d-n})^{\vee}=\dim_{\Q_\ell}H^{n}$. Thus $T:H^{n}\to H^{2d-n}$ is a linear map between finite-dimensional spaces of the same dimension $r$. If $T$ is injective, rank--nullity gives $\dim_{\Q_\ell}\operatorname{im}T=\dim_{\Q_\ell}H^{n}-\dim_{\Q_\ell}\ker T=r-0=r=\dim_{\Q_\ell}H^{2d-n}$, so $\operatorname{im}T=H^{2d-n}$ and $T$ is an isomorphism. The converse (isomorphism $\Rightarrow$ injective) is immediate.

**Step 5 (conclusion).** Combining Step 4 with (2):
\[
T=L^{\,d-n}\text{ is injective}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ T\text{ is an isomorphism}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ B\text{ is perfect},
\]
which is exactly the required statement: $L^{\,d-n}:H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\Q_\ell)$ is injective if and only if $(x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(L^{\,d-n}x\cup y)$ is a perfect $\Q_\ell$-bilinear form on $H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\Q_\ell)$. All cases $0\le n\le d$ (including $n=0$, $n=d$, and $H^{n}=0$) are covered by the argument above. $\qquad\blacksquare$

lemma_450.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\). Then \(T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) if and only if \(T^{-1}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_450.proof:
Write K = \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) and \(\Omega=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). For a finite-dimensional K-vector space W and a K-linear endomorphism S of W, write \(W_\Omega := W\otimes_K\Omega\) and \(S_\Omega := S\otimes_K \mathrm{id}_\Omega\in \mathrm{End}_\Omega(W_\Omega)\). By definition, S is "diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)" means precisely that \(S_\Omega\) is a diagonalizable \(\Omega\)-linear operator, i.e. \(W_\Omega\) admits a basis consisting of eigenvectors of \(S_\Omega\). The assertion to prove is thus: \(T_\Omega\) is diagonalizable \(\Longleftrightarrow\) \((T^{-1})_\Omega\) is diagonalizable.

Step 1 (base change commutes with inversion). Since \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_K(V)\), we have \(T\circ T^{-1}=T^{-1}\circ T=\mathrm{id}_V\). Extension of scalars is a functor \(\mathrm{Mod}_K\to\mathrm{Mod}_\Omega\) and on morphisms \((S_1\circ S_2)_\Omega=(S_1)_\Omega\circ(S_2)_\Omega\); indeed both sides send a simple tensor \(v\otimes c\) to \(S_1(S_2(v))\otimes c\). Hence
\[ T_\Omega\circ (T^{-1})_\Omega=(T\circ T^{-1})_\Omega=\mathrm{id}_{V_\Omega},\qquad (T^{-1})_\Omega\circ T_\Omega=\mathrm{id}_{V_\Omega}. \]
Thus \(T_\Omega\in\mathrm{GL}_\Omega(V_\Omega)\) and
\[ (T_\Omega)^{-1}=(T^{-1})_\Omega. \tag{1}\]

Step 2 (eigenspace characterisation of diagonalizability). Let W be a finite-dimensional \(\Omega\)-vector space and \(U\in\mathrm{End}_\Omega(W)\). For \(\alpha\in\Omega\) put \(W_\alpha:=\ker(U-\alpha\,\mathrm{id})\). Then U is diagonalizable if and only if \(W=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Omega}W_\alpha\).
Proof. (\(\Leftarrow\)) Choosing a basis of each nonzero \(W_\alpha\) and taking their union gives, by the direct-sum decomposition, a basis of W consisting of eigenvectors of U. (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(\mathcal B\) is an eigenbasis, every \(w\in W\) is a finite K-linear combination of elements of \(\mathcal B\), each of which lies in some \(W_\alpha\); hence \(W=\sum_\alpha W_\alpha\). It remains to see the sum is direct: suppose \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\) are pairwise distinct and \(v_1+\cdots+v_r=0\) with \(v_j\in W_{\alpha_j}\). Applying \(U^k\) for \(k=0,1,\dots,r-1\) gives \(\sum_j\alpha_j^{k}v_j=0\) for all such k. The \(r\times r\) matrix \((\alpha_j^{k})_{0\le k\le r-1,\,1\le j\le r}\) is a Vandermonde matrix with determinant \(\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_j-\alpha_i)\neq0\) since \(\Omega\) is a field and the \(\alpha_j\) are distinct; multiplying the system by its inverse yields \(v_j=0\) for every j. So the sum is direct. This proves Step 2.

Step 3 (forward implication). Assume T is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), i.e. \(T_\Omega\) is diagonalizable. By Step 2,
\[ V_\Omega=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Omega}(V_\Omega)_\alpha,\qquad (V_\Omega)_\alpha=\ker(T_\Omega-\alpha\,\mathrm{id}). \]
Because \(T_\Omega\) is invertible (Step 1), \((V_\Omega)_0=\ker T_\Omega=0\); hence only indices \(\alpha\neq0\) occur. Let \(\alpha\neq0\) and \(v\in (V_\Omega)_\alpha\). Then \(T_\Omega v=\alpha v\). Applying \((T_\Omega)^{-1}\) to both sides gives \(v=\alpha\,(T_\Omega)^{-1}v\), and since \(\alpha\neq0\) in the field \(\Omega\),
\[ (T_\Omega)^{-1}v=\alpha^{-1}v. \]
Thus \((V_\Omega)_\alpha\subseteq \ker\big((T_\Omega)^{-1}-\alpha^{-1}\mathrm{id}\big)\). Writing \(\beta=\alpha^{-1}\) (so \(\beta\) ranges over \(\Omega^*\), and \(\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{-1}\) is a bijection of \(\Omega^*\) onto itself), we obtain
\[ V_\Omega=\sum_{\alpha}(V_\Omega)_\alpha\;\subseteq\;\sum_{\beta\in\Omega^*}\ker\big((T_\Omega)^{-1}-\beta\,\mathrm{id}\big)\;\subseteq\;V_\Omega, \]
so equality holds: \(V_\Omega\) is the sum of the eigenspaces of \((T_\Omega)^{-1}\). By the independence argument of Step 2 that sum is automatically direct (eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues are independent). Hence by Step 2, \((T_\Omega)^{-1}\) is diagonalizable. Using (1), \((T^{-1})_\Omega\) is diagonalizable, which is exactly the statement that \(T^{-1}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).

Step 4 (converse). Assume \(T^{-1}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). Since \(T\in\mathrm{GL}_K(V)\), also \(T^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}_K(V)\) and \((T^{-1})^{-1}=T\). Apply the already-proved forward implication (Step 3) to the invertible operator \(S:=T^{-1}\): S is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), hence so is \(S^{-1}=T\). This is the converse implication.

Edge cases. If \(V=0\) then \(V_\Omega=0\), the empty family is a basis, and both \(T_\Omega\) and \((T^{-1})_\Omega\) are diagonalizable, so the equivalence holds trivially; the argument above covers this case as well, since the direct sum over an empty index set is the zero space. If \(V\neq0\), every eigenvalue that occurs is nonzero because \(T_\Omega\) (resp. \((T_\Omega)^{-1}\)) is invertible, which is exactly the point used in Step 3.

Optional cross-check via minimal polynomials (not needed for the argument): if \(T_\Omega\) is diagonalizable with distinct eigenvalues \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\in\Omega^*\), its minimal polynomial is \(m(t)=\prod_i(t-\alpha_i)\), which is squarefree and has nonzero constant term \(a_0=(-1)^r\prod_i\alpha_i\neq0\). Then \(q(t):=a_0^{-1}t^{r}m(t^{-1})=a_0^{-1}\prod_i(1-\alpha_i t)\cdot(-1)^r\prod_i\alpha_i^{-1}\cdot\prod_i (t-\alpha_i^{-1})/\prod_i(t-\alpha_i^{-1})\), i.e. concretely \(q(t)=\prod_i (t-\alpha_i^{-1})\), is a squarefree polynomial over \(\Omega\) whose roots are the distinct \(\alpha_i^{-1}\); from \(m(T_\Omega)=0\) one checks \(q\big((T_\Omega)^{-1}\big)=0\) by multiplying the identity \(\sum_k c_k T_\Omega^{k}=0\) (with \(c_0\neq0\)) by \((T_\Omega)^{-r}\). Hence the minimal polynomial of \((T_\Omega)^{-1}\) divides the squarefree polynomial q and is itself squarefree with all roots in \(\Omega\), so \((T_\Omega)^{-1}\) is diagonalizable — consistent with Step 3.

Combining Steps 3 and 4, T is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) if and only if \(T^{-1}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_447.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(f:Y\to X\) be a finite locally free surjective morphism, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi_X\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(\xi_Y\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle classes of \(H\) and \(f^*H\) under a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), and let \(L_X\) (resp. \(L_Y\)) be cup product with \(\xi_X\) (resp. \(\xi_Y\)). If for some integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d\) the map \(L_Y^{\,d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective, then \(L_X^{\,d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism.
lemma_447.proof:
Write H^i(X) := H^i_et(X_k, Q_ell) and H^i(Y) := H^i_et(Y_k, Q_ell), and write L_X^{d-n}, L_Y^{d-n} for (d-n)-fold cup product with xi_X and xi_Y respectively.

Step 1 (the degree of f). Since f is finite locally free, f_* O_Y is a locally free O_X-module; its rank is a locally constant function on X, and X is connected (geometrically connected implies connected), so f_* O_Y has constant rank N. Since f is surjective and X is non-empty (X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d >= 1, hence non-empty), the generic fibre of f is non-empty, so N >= 1. Thus f is finite locally free surjective of degree N >= 1.

Step 2 (pullback on cohomology is a split monomorphism). By the proved lemma lemma_426 (Spark), applied to X, Y (both smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_q) and to f (finite locally free surjective of degree N >= 1), for every integer n >= 0 the pullback
   f^*: H^n(X) -> H^n(Y)
is a split monomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces. In particular f^* is injective in every degree. (The Frobenius-equivariance part of that lemma is not needed here.)

Step 3 (functoriality of the cycle classes: xi_Y = f^* xi_X). The divisor H is very ample, hence in particular an effective Cartier divisor on X, with associated invertible sheaf O_X(H), which is very ample. Since f is finite locally free it is flat, so the scheme-theoretic inverse image of H is again an effective Cartier divisor on Y, namely f^*H, and there is a canonical isomorphism O_Y(f^*H) ≅ f^* O_X(H) (pullback of Cartier divisors under a flat morphism commutes with the construction of the associated invertible sheaf).

For any scheme Z over k and any effective Cartier divisor D subset Z, the cycle class of D, expressed through the fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1), is the image of c_1(O_Z(D)) in H^2(Z, Q_ell). Indeed, the ell-adic first Chern class c_1: Pic(Z) -> H^2(Z, Z_ell(1)) is the connecting homomorphism
   delta: H^1(Z, G_m) -> H^2(Z, mu_{ell^r})
coming from the Kummer short exact sequence of etale sheaves 1 -> mu_{ell^r} -> G_m -> G_m -> 1 (last map g |-> g^{ell^r}), after the identification H^2(Z, mu_{ell^r}) ≅ H^2(Z, Z/ell^r(1)) and passage to the inverse limit and then to Q_ell; and for a line bundle L the class delta(L) is exactly c_1(L), while the class of an effective Cartier divisor D is c_1(O(D)).
