**Step 3: eigenvalues of \(T_\iota\).** Since \(T_\iota=\gamma U\), the operator \(T_\iota\) is diagonalisable over \(\mathbb C\) and its eigenvalues are \(\gamma\beta\) with \(|\beta|=1\); hence every eigenvalue \(\beta'\) of \(T_\iota\) satisfies \(|\beta'|^2=\gamma^2=c=\iota(c)\).

**Step 4: the minimal polynomial of \(T\) splits with distinct roots over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).** By Fact A applied to \(S=T_\iota\) over \(K=\mathbb C\), diagonalisability of \(T_\iota\) implies \(\mu_{T_\iota}\) is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors in \(\mathbb C[t]\). By Fact B, \(\mu_{T_\iota}=\iota(\mu_T)\). By Fact C, \(\mu_T\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) is then a product of pairwise distinct linear factors in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]\):
\[ \mu_T=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(t-\alpha_i),\qquad \alpha_i\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\ \text{pairwise distinct}. \]

**Step 5: \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\), hence diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).** Since \(\mu_T\) has no repeated root in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), \(\gcd(\mu_T,\mu_T')=1\) in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]\); the Euclidean algorithm computing this gcd takes place in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\), so \(\mu_T\) is squarefree in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\). Write \(\mu_T=\prod_{j=1}^{s}f_j\) with the \(f_j\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) distinct monic irreducibles. The Chinese remainder theorem gives an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-algebras
\[ \mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(\mu_T)\xrightarrow{\sim}\prod_{j=1}^{s}\mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(f_j)=\prod_{j=1}^{s}K_j, \]
with each \(K_j\) a field. Via \(t\mapsto T\), the space \(V\) is a module over \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) annihilated by \(\mu_T\), hence a \(\prod_jK_j\)-module; the idempotents of \(\prod_jK_j\) give \(V=\bigoplus_jV_j\) with \(V_j:=e_jV\), and each \(V_j\) is a \(K_j\)-vector space (the image of \(K_j\) in \(\mathrm{End}(V_j)\) is \(K_j\) itself, since \(e_j\mu_T/f_j\) acts as \(1\) on \(V_j\) and \(f_j\) acts as \(0\)). As a \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\)-module, \(V_j\) is therefore a direct sum of copies of the simple module \(K_j=\mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(f_j)\) (simplicity because \(f_j\) is irreducible), so \(V_j\) is semisimple, and so is \(V\). That is, \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\). By lemma_5 (eoinm), \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\) if and only if it is diagonalizable on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\); hence \(T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).

**Step 6: the eigenvalue modulus condition.** Let \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) be an eigenvalue of \(T\), i.e. an eigenvalue of \(T_W=T\otimes\mathrm{id}\) on \(W=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). By Step 5, \(T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), so the eigenspace decomposition \(W=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Sigma}E_\alpha\) of Part I holds, where \(\Sigma\) is the set of eigenvalues of \(T\) (the roots of \(\mu_T\), by Fact A). Repeating the base-change argument of Part I (which used no hypothesis beyond diagonalisability), \(\Phi\) identifies \(V_{\mathbb C}\) with \(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Sigma}E_\alpha\otimes_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell,\iota}\mathbb C\) and \(T_\iota\) with \(\iota(\alpha)\) on the \(\alpha\)-summand, each summand being non-zero. Hence \(\iota(\alpha)\) is an eigenvalue of \(T_\iota\), and by Step 3,
\[ |\iota(\alpha)|^2=\gamma^2=c=\iota(c)=\iota(c). \]
This is exactly the required condition \(|\iota(\alpha)|^2=\iota(c)\) for every eigenvalue \(\alpha\) of \(T\).

Combining Part I and Part II, the equivalence is established. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_467.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(d\ge1\), and let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\). Then there exist an integer \(m\ge1\) and a morphism \(f\colon X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\to \mathbb P^d_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) which is finite, locally free and surjective.
lemma_467.proof:
Proof. Let k be an algebraic closure of F_q. Since X is projective over F_q, choose a closed immersion i: X -> P^N_{F_q}. Let S = F_q[x_0,...,x_N]/I_X be the homogeneous coordinate ring, with standard grading S = direct sum_{n>=0} S_n, S_0=F_q, generated by S_1, and Proj S = X. Put S_k = S tensor_{F_q} k.

Dimension of S_k. The base change X_k is smooth over k, hence regular, and geometrically connected, hence connected. A noetherian regular connected scheme is irreducible: regular local rings are domains, so irreducible components of a regular noetherian scheme are open and closed. Thus X_k is integral. Therefore S_k is a standard graded k-domain with Proj S_k = X_k of dimension d. For a standard graded k-domain R with Proj R of dimension d, dim R = d+1; indeed homogeneous prime chains in Proj can be extended by the irrelevant maximal ideal, and dimension of a standard graded ring is computed using homogeneous primes. Hence dim S_k = d+1.

Linear Noether normalization. We use the following sublemma. Let R be a standard graded algebra over an infinite field K, generated by R_1 over K, with dim R = r+1. Then there exist y_0,...,y_r in R_1 such that R/(y_0,...,y_r) is Artinian. If R is a domain, the induced map K[T_0,...,T_r] -> R is injective.

Proof of sublemma. We construct y_i by induction. Suppose y_0,...,y_{n-1} have been chosen and put R_n = R/(y_0,...,y_{n-1}). Assume dim R_n = s+1. Let Min_s(R_n) be the finite set of minimal primes p of R_n with dim R_n/p = s+1. For each p in Min_s(R_n), p_1 is a proper K-subspace of R_{n,1}: if p_1=R_{n,1}, then p contains the irrelevant ideal R_{n,+}; since R_n is generated by R_{n,1}, R_n/p=K, contradicting s+1>0. Since K is infinite, a finite union of proper subspaces cannot cover R_{n,1}; choose y_n in R_{n,1} outside the union of these p_1. Then y_n lies in no maximal-dimensional minimal prime of R_n. By Krull's principal ideal theorem, every minimal prime of R_n/(y_n) has height at most one over a minimal prime of R_n contained in it; because y_n is not in a maximal-dimensional minimal prime, the relevant height is one. Since finitely generated algebras over a field are catenary, dim R_n/(y_n)=s. This completes the induction. When s=0 the quotient is noetherian of dimension zero, hence Artinian.

For injectivity in the domain case, let A=K[y_0,...,y_r] be the subalgebra generated by the chosen linear forms. The quotient R/(A_+R) is Artinian, hence finite-dimensional over K. Choose a finite-dimensional graded K-subspace V of R mapping onto R/(A_+R). Since R is generated over K by R_1, it is generated over A by V; more precisely R=AV+A_+R. Induction on degree gives R=AV, so R is finite as an A-module. Finite integral extensions preserve dimension, so dim A=dim R=r+1. But A is a quotient of K[T_0,...,T_r]. If the kernel were nonzero, its dimension would be at most r. Thus the kernel is zero.

Apply the sublemma to R=S_k and r=d. We obtain linear forms l_0,...,l_d in S_{k,1} such that S_k/(l_0,...,l_d) is Artinian and the map k[T_0,...,T_d] -> S_k is injective. Let A_k denote the image, a polynomial ring in d+1 variables, and note that S_k is finite over A_k.

Descent to a finite field. The finitely many l_i have coordinates in a finite extension K of F_q. Let S_K = S tensor_{F_q} K and let A_K = K[T_0,...,T_d] -> S_K be the map sending T_i to l_i. Base change from K to k is the injective map A_k -> S_k. Since k/F_q is faithfully flat, A_K -> S_K is injective. The quotient S_K/(l_0,...,l_d) becomes Artinian after base change to k; field extension preserves Krull dimension of finitely generated algebras, so S_K/(l_0,...,l_d) is Artinian. By the same graded Nakayama argument, S_K is finite over A_K.

Construction of f. Since A_K is polynomial in d+1 variables, Proj A_K = P^d_K. The graded inclusion A_K -> S_K induces a morphism f: Proj S_K -> Proj A_K. But Proj S_K = X_K. Because S_K is finite over A_K, f is finite: on each standard affine open D_+(T_i), the degree-zero part of (S_K)_{T_i} is finite over the degree-zero part of (A_K)_{T_i}.

Surjectivity. The scheme X_K is irreducible, smooth, and of pure dimension d. Finite morphisms are closed. Let Z be the reduced closed image of f in P^d_K. The induced map X_K -> Z is finite and surjective, hence dim Z = dim X_K = d. A closed subset of P^d_K of dimension d is all of P^d_K, because P^d_K is irreducible. Thus f is surjective.

Flatness. We check flatness on stalks. Let y be a point of P^d_K and let x be a point of X_K mapping to y. Put A=O_{P^d_K,y} and B=O_{X_K,x}. Since f is finite, B is a finite A-algebra. Smoothness of P^d_K and X_K implies that A and B are regular local rings. Because f is finite surjective and X_K and P^d_K are irreducible of dimension d, dim B=dim A. Indeed, if X_x and Y_y denote the closures of x and y, then f(X_x)=Y_y and finite surjective maps preserve dimension, so dim X_x=dim Y_y; for an irreducible catenary variety of dimension d, dim O_{Z,z}=d-dim closure{z}.

We now use miracle flatness. If A is a regular local ring, B is a Cohen-Macaulay local ring finite over A, and dim B=dim A, then B is flat over A. For completeness: A regular local ring has finite global dimension. The Auslander-Buchsbaum formula gives pd_A B + depth_A B = depth A = dim A. For a finite local A-algebra, depth_A B=depth_B B because the extension of the maximal ideal of A is primary to the maximal ideal of B. Since B is regular local, it is Cohen-Macaulay, so depth_B B=dim B=dim A. Hence pd_A B=0, so B is free, in particular flat, over A. Applying this to every stalk shows that f is flat.

Finally, a finite flat morphism is locally free: over an affine open Spec R of P^d_K, the corresponding module is finite and flat; over each local ring R_p it is free. Thus f is finite, locally free, and surjective. The field K is a finite extension of F_q, so K=F_{q^m} for some m>=1. This completes the proof.

lemma_472.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be prime, let m≥1, and let k=overline(F_q). Let X and Y be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension d≥2 over F_{q^m}, and let f:Y→X be proper surjective generically finite of degree N≥1. Let H_X be an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor on X, let ξ_X∈H^2_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) be its cycle class under a fixed nonzero element of Q_ℓ(1), and let L_X be cup product with ξ_X. Let H_Y=f^*H_X, let ξ_Y∈H^2_et(Y_k,Q_ℓ) be its cycle class, and let L_Y be cup product with ξ_Y. If L_Y:H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ℓ)→H^{d+1}_et(Y_k,Q_ℓ) is injective, then L_X:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)→H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) is injective.
lemma_472.proof:
Proof. Write H^i(Z) for H^i_et(Z_k,Q_l). Since k is also an algebraic closure of F_{q^m}, apply lemma_444 with the prime power q^m in place of q. The morphism f:Y -> X satisfies its hypotheses: X and Y are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=1 over F_{q^m}, and f is proper, surjective, generically finite of degree N>=1. Therefore, for n=d-1, lemma_444 gives a Q_l-linear map f_*:H^{d-1}(Y) -> H^{d-1}(X) such that f_* o f^* = N id on H^{d-1}(X). Since N is a positive integer, it is nonzero and invertible in Q_l. Hence f^* is injective: if f^*x=0, then x=(1/N)f_*(f^*x)=0.

Next record compatibility of pullback with the Lefschetz operators. The class xi_X is the cycle class of H_X, and xi_Y is the cycle class of f^*H_X. For a Cartier divisor D, its cycle class is the first Chern class of O(D); pullback of Cartier divisors corresponds to pullback of the associated line bundles, and first Chern classes are functorial. Since f is dominant and Y is smooth (hence regular integral), f^*H_X is a Cartier divisor, and under the fixed identification of Tate twists we have f^*xi_X=xi_Y. Pullback is also a ring homomorphism for the cup product. Hence for every x in H^{d-1}(X), f^*(L_X x)=f^*(xi_X cup x)=(f^*xi_X) cup f^*x=xi_Y cup f^*x=L_Y(f^*x). This is an equality in H^{d+1}(Y).

Now let x in H^{d-1}(X) satisfy L_X x=0. Then L_Y(f^*x)=f^*(L_X x)=0. By the hypothesis that L_Y:H^{d-1}(Y) -> H^{d+1}(Y) is injective, f^*x=0. By the injectivity of f^* proved above, x=0. Thus ker(L_X)=0, i.e. L_X:H^{d-1}(X) -> H^{d+1}(X) is injective.

lemma_471.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(m\ge1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and \(Y\subsetneq X\) a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), let \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) and \(\operatorname{tr}_Y\) be the Poincar\'e duality traces normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(Y\), let \(\xi_Y=i^*\xi\), and let \(L_X\) (resp. \(L_Y\)) be cup product with \(\xi\) (resp. \(\xi_Y\)). Then for every \(0\le n\le d-1\) and all \(x,y\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \[\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(L_Y^{\,d-1-n}(i^*x)\cup i^*y\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(L_X^{\,d-n}x\cup y\bigr).\]
lemma_471.proof:
Write H^n(Z) for H^n_et(Z_k, Q_l). All cup products are taken in the cohomology ring with Q_l coefficients, and all traces are the untwisted traces obtained from the fixed nonzero element of Q_l(1); these are exactly the normalised traces appearing in Spark lemma_gysin_projection_formula_all_degrees.

Since Y is a very ample Cartier divisor, it is ample. Hence Spark lemma_gysin_projection_formula_all_degrees applies. Let
  i_!: H^r(Y) -> H^{r+2}(X)
be the unique Q_l-linear map such that, for every a in H^r(Y) and every b in H^{2d-2-r}(X),
  tr_X(i_! a cup b) = tr_Y(a cup i^* b).
The same lemma also gives the projection formula
  i_!(i^* u) = u cup i_!1
for every u in H^r(X).

First we identify i_!1. For every b in H^{2d-2}(X), take a=1 in the defining identity for i_!. Since 1 is the unit of H^0(Y) and i^*1=1, we obtain
  tr_X(i_!1 cup b) = tr_Y(1 cup i^* b) = tr_Y(i^* b).
By the standard divisor-class characterisation of the cycle class of a smooth effective Cartier divisor, the class xi of Y satisfies the same identity:
  tr_X(xi cup b) = tr_Y(i^* b)
for every b in H^{2d-2}(X). This is the usual trace compatibility for the Gysin map of a divisor, written after the fixed Tate-twist identifications. Uniqueness of an element of H^2(X) with this property follows from perfectness of the Poincare duality pairing
  H^2(X) x H^{2d-2}(X) -> Q_l
(after the fixed Tate-twist identification), which is supplied by eoinm lemma_77. Therefore
  i_!1 = xi.

Now fix an integer n with 0 <= n <= d-1 and elements x,y in H^n(X). Put
  z = xi^{d-1-n} cup x cup y.
This is an element of H^{2d-2}(X), because deg(xi)=2 and deg(x)=deg(y)=n, so
  deg(z)=2(d-1-n)+n+n=2d-2.
Since i^* is a ring homomorphism and xi_Y=i^*xi, we have
  i^*z = (i^*xi)^{d-1-n} cup i^*x cup i^*y
       = xi_Y^{d-1-n} cup i^*x cup i^*y
       = L_Y^{d-1-n}(i^*x) cup i^*y.
Thus the left hand side of the desired identity is exactly tr_Y(i^*z).

Apply the defining identity for i_! with a=i^*z in H^{2d-2}(Y) and b=1 in H^0(X). It gives
  tr_X(i_!(i^*z) cup 1) = tr_Y(i^*z cup i^*1) = tr_Y(i^*z).
Hence
  tr_Y(i^*z) = tr_X(i_!(i^*z)).
By the projection formula from Spark lemma_gysin_projection_formula_all_degrees,
  i_!(i^*z) = z cup i_!1.
Using i_!1=xi, this becomes
  i_!(i^*z) = z cup xi.
Therefore
  tr_Y(i^*z) = tr_X(z cup xi)
             = tr_X(xi^{d-1-n} cup x cup y cup xi).
Since xi has degree 2, moving xi past x cup y, whose degree is 2n, introduces no Koszul sign. Hence
  xi^{d-1-n} cup x cup y cup xi = xi^{d-n} cup x cup y.
Consequently
  tr_Y(i^*z) = tr_X(xi^{d-n} cup x cup y)
             = tr_X(L_X^{d-n}x cup y).
Substituting the expression for i^*z above gives
  tr_Y(L_Y^{d-1-n}(i^*x) cup i^*y) = tr_X(L_X^{d-n}x cup y).
The exponent d-1-n is nonnegative because 0 <= n <= d-1, so all powers are defined. This proves the required identity for every allowed n,x,y.

lemma_weight_separated_crt_projector.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space with a decomposition \(V=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{N}V_j\) into \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspaces, let \(T\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\) preserve each \(V_j\), and let \(w_0,\dots,w_N\) be pairwise distinct non-negative real numbers such that for every \(j\), every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of \(T|_{V_j}\) and every field embedding \(\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) satisfy \(|\iota(\alpha)|=w_j\). Then for each \(0\le n\le N\) there exists \(P\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) such that \(P(T)|_{V_n}=\mathrm{id}_{V_n}\) and \(P(T)|_{V_m}=0\) for all \(m\ne n\).
lemma_weight_separated_crt_projector.proof:
We prove the statement by pure linear algebra over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); none of the geometric lemmas is needed, and no semisimplicity or diagonalisability of \(T\) is used.

NOTATION AND CONVENTIONS. Since each \(V_j\) is \(T\)-stable, \(T_j:=T|_{V_j}\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_j)\) is a well-defined operator. We use the standard definition of eigenvalue over a non-algebraically-closed base field: for a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-space \(W\) and \(S\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W)\), an element \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is an eigenvalue of \(S\) if there is \(0\neq w\in W\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) with \((S\otimes\mathrm{id})w=\alpha w\). Choosing a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-basis of \(W\) and letting \(A\) be the matrix of \(S\), the induced \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-basis of \(W\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) gives \(S\otimes\mathrm{id\) the same matrix \(A\); hence this definition is equivalent to \(\det(tI-A)(\alpha)=0\), i.e. to \(\chi_S(\alpha)=0\) where \(\chi_S(t):=\det(t\,\mathrm{id}_W-S)\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) is the characteristic polynomial. In particular an operator on the zero space has no eigenvalue.

STEP 1 (one fixed embedding suffices). We first record that the set of field embeddings \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) is non-empty. Indeed \(|\mathbb Q_\ell|=|\varprojlim_n\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z|=\aleph_0^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}\), and the algebraic closure of an infinite field has the same cardinality as the field, so \(|\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell|=2^{\aleph_0}\). For an algebraically closed field \(K\) of characteristic \(0\) with transcendence degree \(\kappa\) over \(\mathbb Q\), \(K\) is the algebraic closure of \(\mathbb Q(t_i\,:\,i\in I)\) with \(|I|=\kappa\), and \(|\mathbb Q(t_i:i\in I)|=\max(\kappa,\aleph_0)\); hence \(|K|=\max(\kappa,\aleph_0)\). Applying this to \(K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) and to \(K=\mathbb C\) (using \(|\mathbb C|=2^{\aleph_0}\)) gives \(\operatorname{trdeg}(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell/\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{trdeg}(\mathbb C/\mathbb Q)=2^{\aleph_0}\). By the Steinitz classification of algebraically closed fields (two algebraically closed fields are isomorphic over their prime field iff they have the same characteristic and the same transcendence degree over it), \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\cong\mathbb C\) over \(\mathbb Q\); restricting such an isomorphism to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) yields a field embedding \(\iota_0:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\).

The hypothesis quantifies over ALL embeddings; restricting it to the single embedding \(\iota_0\) we obtain
\[(*)\qquad\text{for every }j\text{ and every eigenvalue }\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\text{ of }T_j,\quad |\iota_0(\alpha)|=w_j.\]
Everything below uses only \((*)\).

STEP 2 (minimal polynomials and evaluation on the graded pieces). Fix \(j\).

If \(V_j=0\), set \(\mu_j:=1\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\).

If \(V_j\neq0\): consider the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-algebra homomorphism \(\mathrm{ev}_j:\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_j)\), \(f\mapsto f(T_j)\), and let \(I_j:=\ker\mathrm{ev}_j\). This ideal is non-zero: \(\chi_j(t):=\det(t\,\mathrm{id}_{V_j}-T_j)\) is monic of degree \(d_j:=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_j\ge1\), and by the Cayley--Hamilton theorem \(\chi_j(T_j)=0\), so \(\chi_j\in I_j\setminus\{0\}\). Since \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) is a Euclidean domain, hence a PID, \(I_j=(\mu_j)\) for a unique monic \(\mu_j\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\); this is the minimal polynomial of \(T_j\). Consequently, for every \(f\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\),
\[f(T_j)=0\iff f\in I_j\iff \mu_j\mid f\ \text{ in }\ \mathbb Q_\ell[t].\tag{2.1}\]
Moreover \(\mu_j\) is non-constant: if \(\mu_j=1\) then \(0=\mu_j(T_j)=\mathrm{id}_{V_j}\), forcing \(V_j=0\), a contradiction.

We also record that evaluating a polynomial with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients at \(T\) and then restricting to \(V_j\) is the same as evaluating at \(T_j\). Indeed, by induction on \(k\ge0\) one has \(T^k|_{V_j}=T_j^k\): for \(k=0\) this is \(\mathrm{id}_{V_j}\); and for \(v\in V_j\), using \(T^kv\in V_j\) (stability), \(T^{k+1}v=T(T^kv)=T_j(T_j^kv)=T_j^{k+1}v\). Hence for \(f=\sum_k a_kt^k\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\), \(f(T)|_{V_j}=\sum_ka_kT^k|_{V_j}=\sum_ka_kT_j^k=f(T_j)\). \tag{2.2}

STEP 3 (roots of \(\mu_j\) \emph{are exactly} the eigenvalues of \(T_j\)). We claim: for each \(j\),
\[\{\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell:\mu_j(\alpha)=0\}=\{\text{eigenvalues of }T_j\},\]
both sets being empty when \(V_j=0\).

(\(\supseteq\)) Let \(\alpha\) be an eigenvalue of \(T_j\), and choose \(0\neq w\in V_j\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) with \(S w=\alpha w\), where \(S:=T_j\otimes\mathrm{id}\). First, \(S^kw=\alpha^kw\) for all \(k\ge0\), by induction: \(k=0\) is clear, and \(S^{k+1}w=S(\alpha^kw)=\alpha^kSw=\alpha^{k+1}w\) by \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-linearity of \(S\). Hence for any \(f=\sum_{k=0}^rc_kt^k\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]\), \(f(S)w=\sum_kc_kS^kw=\big(\sum_kc_k\alpha^k\big)w=f(\alpha)w\). Now the map \(\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_j)\to\mathrm{End}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}(V_j\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\), \(U\mapsto U\otimes\mathrm{id}\), sends \(\mathrm{id}\) to \(\mathrm{id}\) and \(T_j\) to \(S\), and is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear, so it sends \(g(T_j)\) to \(g(S)\) for every \(g\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\). Applying this to \(g=\mu_j\) and using \(\mu_j(T_j)=0\) gives \(\mu_j(S)=0\). Therefore \(0=\mu_j(S)w=\mu_j(\alpha)w\), and since \(w\neq0\) we get \(\mu_j(\alpha)=0\).

(\(\subseteq\)) Let \(V_j\neq0\) and let \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) satisfy \(\mu_j(\alpha)=0\). We first show \(\mu_j\mid\chi_j\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) (all polynomials here have \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients, so the division algorithm takes place in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) and produces quotient and remainder in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\)). Divide: \(\chi_j=q\mu_j+r\) with \(q,r\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) and \(r=0\) or \(\deg r<\deg\mu_j\). Evaluating at \(T_j\) and using Cayley--Hamilton and \(\mu_j(T_j)=0\) gives \(r(T_j)=q(T_j)\mu_j(T_j)-\chi_j(T_j)=0\), so \(r\in I_j=(\mu_j)\). If \(r\neq0\) then \(\deg\mu_j\le\deg r<\deg\mu_j\), impossible; hence \(r=0\) and \(\mu_j\mid\chi_j\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\). Evaluating this identity at \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) gives \(\chi_j(\alpha)=0\). By the equivalent characterisation of eigenvalues recalled at the outset (\(\chi_j(\alpha)=0\iff\det(\alpha I-A)=0\iff\ker(S-\alpha)\neq0\)), there exists \(0\neq w\in V_j\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) with \(Sw=\alpha w\); that is, \(\alpha\) is an eigenvalue of \(T_j\).

If \(V_j=0\), then \(\mu_j=1\) has no root and \(T_j\) has no eigenvalue, so the claim holds trivially.

Combining the claim with \((*)\) we obtain the key fact
\[(\dagger)\qquad\text{every root }\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\text{ of }\mu_j\text{ satisfies }|\iota_0(\alpha)|=w_j.\]

STEP 4 (the \(\mu_j\) are pairwise coprime). Let \(j\neq m\). Suppose \(\delta\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) were a common divisor of \(\mu_j\) and \(\mu_m\) of positive degree; taking an irreducible factor of \(\delta\) we may assume \(\delta\) irreducible. Then \(\delta\) is a non-unit, so \(\deg\delta\ge1\), and since \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is algebraically closed \(\delta\) has a root \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). By Step 3, \(\alpha\) is simultaneously an eigenvalue of \(T_j\) and of \(T_m\); by \((\dagger)\), \(w_j=|\iota_0(\alpha)|=w_m\), contradicting the pairwise distinctness of \(w_0,\dots,w_N\) (as \(j\neq m\)). Hence \(\mu_j\) and \(\mu_m\) have no common irreducible divisor, i.e. \(\gcd(\mu_j,\mu_m)=1\) in the UFD \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\). (If \(V_j=0\) or \(V_m=0\) then one of the two polynomials equals \(1\) and the conclusion is immediate.)

STEP 5 (Chinese remainder / Bézout construction of \(P\)). Fix \(n\) with \(0\le n\le N\), and put
\[M_n:=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le N\\ k\neq n}}\mu_k\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\]
(the empty product, equal to \(1\), when \(N=0\)). We claim \(\gcd(\mu_n,M_n)=1\). Indeed, if an irreducible \(\delta\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) divided both \(\mu_n\) and \(M_n\), then, \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) being a PID and hence a UFD in which irreducibles are prime (Euclid's lemma), \(\delta\) would divide \(\mu_k\) for some \(k\neq n\); then \(\delta\) is a common irreducible divisor of \(\mu_n\) and \(\mu_k\) with \(n\neq k\), contradicting Step 4. Since \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) is a PID, the ideal \((\mu_n,M_n)\) is the whole ring, so there exist \(a,b\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) with
\[a\,\mu_n+b\,M_n=1.\tag{5.1}\]
Define
\[P:=b\,M_n\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t].\]
(When \(V_n=0\) we have \(\mu_n=1\) and may take \(a=1,\ b=0\), i.e. \(P=0\); when \(N=0\) we have \(M_0=1\) and may take \(a=0,\ b=1\), i.e. \(P=1\). Both are legitimate instances of (5.1).)

STEP 6 (verification). All evaluations below are of a polynomial \(P\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\), hence are \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear endomorphisms of the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-spaces \(V_j\), and (2.2) applies.

(a) Let \(m\neq n\). By construction \(\mu_m\mid M_n\mid P\), so \(P\in(\mu_m)=I_m\) and therefore \(P(T_m)=0\) by (2.1). Using (2.2), \(P(T)|_{V_m}=P(T_m)=0\).

(b) For \(j=n\): by (5.1), \(P-1=bM_n-1=-a\,\mu_n\), so \(\mu_n\mid(P-1)\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\). Hence \((P-1)(T_n)=0\) by (2.1), i.e. \(P(T_n)-\mathrm{id}_{V_n}=(P-1)(T_n)=0\), so \(P(T_n)=\mathrm{id}_{V_n}\). Using (2.2), \(P(T)|_{V_n}=\mathrm{id}_{V_n}\). (If \(V_n=0\) then \(\mu_n=1\), \(P=0\), and both \(P(T)|_{V_n}\) and \(\mathrm{id}_{V_n}\) are the zero map on the zero space, so the equality holds.)

Together (a) and (b) give exactly the required properties of \(P\).

STEP 7 (edge cases and what was NOT used). 
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Non-invertibility of \(T\).} Nowhere did we use that \(T\) (or any \(T_j\)) is invertible. If \(0\) is an eigenvalue of \(T_j\) then \(t\mid\mu_j\) and \((\dagger)\) forces \(w_j=|\iota_0(0)|=0\); this is consistent with the hypothesis (which allows \(w_j=0\)) and does not disturb any step.
\item \emph{Vanishing pieces.} \(V_j=0\) is handled by the convention \(\mu_j=1\): it has no root, so it never obstructs coprimality, and it divides every polynomial so that the corresponding \(P(T)|_{V_j}=0\) is automatic.
\item \emph{Degenerate cases.} If \(N=0\) the construction gives \(P=1\) and \(P(T)|_{V_0}=\mathrm{id}_{V_0}\) with no other pieces to kill. If all \(V_j=0\) then \(V=0\) and the assertions are vacuous (the constructed \(P=0\) works).
\item \emph{No semisimplicity.} At no point did we assume or use that any \(T_j\) is diagonalisable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), nor that the eigenvalues within a single piece are distinct, nor that the \(\mu_j\) are irreducible. The only property of the weights that is used is their pairwise distinctness, entered through \((\dagger)\) via the single embedding \(\iota_0\).
\end{itemize}

Thus for every \(0\le n\le N\) the polynomial \(P\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) constructed in Step 5 satisfies \(P(T)|_{V_n}=\mathrm{id}_{V_n}\) and \(P(T)|_{V_m}=0\) for all \(m\neq n\), which is the desired conclusion. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_473.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m >= 1, let d >= 2, let k be an algebraic closure of F_q, and fix a nonzero element of Q_l(1). Suppose that for every t >= 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected variety V of pure dimension d-1 over F_{q^t}, and every F_{q^t}-rational very ample divisor on V, with cycle class xi_V and L_V cup product by xi_V, the map L_V^{(d-1)-j}:H^j_et(V_k,Q_l)->H^{2d-2-j}_et(V_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism for every 0 <= j <= d-1. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor on X, and let L be cup product by xi. If L:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_l) is injective, then L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= d.
lemma_473.proof:
PROOF.

Setup and conventions. Put Q := q^m = p^{am}; this is again a prime power, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q = \overline{\mathbb F}_Q, and X is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_Q. Every auxiliary lemma quoted below is stated for an arbitrary prime power in the role of "q"; we therefore apply them with q replaced by Q (equivalently, we regard \mathbb F_{q^m} as the ground field). Note that the maps L^{d-n} whose bijectivity we must establish are purely \mathbb Q_\ell-linear cup-product maps and do not involve Frobenius, so this change of ground field affects nothing in the conclusions. Write H^n := H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for short, let H \subsetneq X be the given \mathbb F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let \xi = \mathrm{cl}(H) \in H^2 be its cycle class computed with the fixed nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell(1) (which we use, as in the quoted lemmas, to identify each \mathbb Q_\ell(r) with \mathbb Q_\ell), and let L: H^n \to H^{n+2}, x \mapsto \xi \cup x.

Step 0 (finite dimensionality, and "injective iff bijective" in the Lefschetz range).
(a) X is proper over \mathbb F_Q. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) to K = \mathbb Q_\ell on X_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \psi: F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell. It gives that H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = H^n is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell for every n \ge 0.
(b) Apply lemma_77 (eoinm), part (b), to X over \mathbb F_Q of pure dimension d: for every 0 \le n \le 2d the pairing H^n \times H^{2d-n} \to \mathbb Q_\ell(-d), (x,y) \mapsto \mathrm{tr}_X(x \cup y), is PERFECT. A perfect pairing between two finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces forces their dimensions to be equal; hence
  dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^n = dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^{2d-n}  for all 0 \le n \le 2d.   (*)
(c) Combining (a) and (*): for each integer n with 0 \le n \le d, the endomorphism-pair map L^{d-n}: H^n \to H^{2d-n} is injective if and only if it is an isomorphism. Indeed, "isomorphism \Rightarrow injective" is formal. Conversely, if L^{d-n} is injective then, since domain and codomain are finite-dimensional of the same dimension by (*), the image has dimension dim H^n = dim H^{2d-n}, so the map is also surjective, hence an isomorphism. (This equivalence is precisely the content of lemma_hard_lefschetz_reduces_to_injectivity (Spark), applied to X over \mathbb F_Q with the ample line bundle \mathcal O_X(H), which is very ample hence ample and defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}; we cite that lemma as the formal justification and record (a)-(b) as the verification of its mechanism.)

Step 1 (the range 0 \le n \le d-2).
The hypothesis of the present lemma is word-for-word the hypothesis of lemma_low_degree_lefschetz_isomorphisms (Spark): it asserts that for every t \ge 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected V of pure dimension d-1 over \mathbb F_{q^t}, and every \mathbb F_{q^t}-rational very ample divisor on V, with cycle class \xi_V taken via the same fixed nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell(1) and L_V = \xi_V \cup (-), the map L_V^{(d-1)-j}: H^j(V_k) \to H^{2(d-1)-j}(V_k) is an isomorphism for every 0 \le j \le d-1. Since d \ge 2, that lemma applies and yields: for every t \ge 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected W of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_{q^t}, and every \mathbb F_{q^t}-rational very ample divisor on W, cup product with the (d-n)-th power of its cycle class is an isomorphism H^n(W_k) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^{2d-n}(W_k) for every 0 \le n \le d-2. Specialising to W = X and t = m (permitted because our divisor H is \mathbb F_{q^m}-rational and its cycle class is exactly the \xi of the statement), we obtain
  L^{d-n}: H^n \xrightarrow{\sim} H^{2d-n}  is an isomorphism for every 0 \le n \le d-2.   (1)

Step 2 (the middle degree n = d-1).
By assumption the map L: H^{d-1} \to H^{d+1} is injective. Since d-(d-1) = 1 and 2d-(d-1) = d+1, this map is exactly L^{d-n} for n = d-1. By the equivalence of Step 0(c) (i.e. lemma_hard_lefschetz_reduces_to_injectivity over \mathbb F_{q^m}, with the very ample line bundle \mathcal O_X(H)), injectivity implies bijectivity, so
  L^{d-(d-1)} = L: H^{d-1} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^{d+1}   (2)
is an isomorphism.

Step 3 (the middle degree n = d).
For n = d we have d-n = 0 and 2d-n = d, so L^{d-n} = L^0 = id_{H^d}: H^d \to H^d, which is an isomorphism.
  L^{d-d} = \mathrm{id}_{H^d}: H^d \xrightarrow{\sim} H^d.   (3)

Conclusion. Because d \ge 2, the integers n with 0 \le n \le d split as the disjoint union {0,1,\dots,d-2} \sqcup \{d-1\} \sqcup \{d\} (and d-2 \ge 0, so the first set is nonempty and lies strictly below d-1). Equation (1) gives the required isomorphism for n in the first set, (2) for n = d-1, and (3) for n = d. Hence L^{d-n}: H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is an isomorphism for every 0 \le n \le d. \hfill $\blacksquare$

Remark on the role of the hypotheses. The inductive hypothesis on dimension d-1 is used only to feed lemma_low_degree_lefschetz_isomorphisms, which supplies every degree strictly below the middle; the single extra input "L is injective in the middle degree H^{d-1}" is then promoted to an isomorphism by Poincar\'e duality (equal Betti numbers in degrees n and 2d-n), and degree d is trivial because L^0 is the identity. No Frobenius semisimplicity is used anywhere, so there is no circularity.

lemma_474.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let g >= 1, let V be a K-vector space of dimension 2g, and let omega in wedge^2 V^* be a nondegenerate alternating form. For 0 <= n <= 2g let L:wedge^n V^* -> wedge^{n+2} V^* be wedge product by omega. Then L^{g-n}:wedge^n V^* -> wedge^{2g-n} V^* is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= g.
lemma_474.proof:
Let K be a field of characteristic 0, g >= 1, V a K-vector space with dim_K V = 2g, and omega in wedge^2_K V^* a nondegenerate alternating form. By definition, nondegeneracy means that the K-linear map

  phi: V -> V^*,   v |-> ( w |-> omega(v,w) )

is an isomorphism. (Since omega is alternating, phi(v) = 0 says exactly that v lies in the radical {v : omega(v,w) = 0 for all w}, so this is the usual notion.)

We prove that for every 0 <= n <= g the (g-n)-fold iterate of L, namely L^{g-n}: wedge^n V^* -> wedge^{2g-n} V^*, is an isomorphism.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 1. L^{g-n} is wedging by omega^{g-n}.

The wedge product on wedge^* V^* is associative, so for every k >= 0 and every alpha in wedge^n V^* one has, by induction on k,
  L^k(alpha) = omega wedge ( omega wedge ( ... (omega wedge alpha) ... )) = (omega^{wedge k}) wedge alpha =: omega^k wedge alpha,
where omega^k denotes the k-th power of omega in the graded algebra wedge^* V^*. (Base case k = 0: L^0 = id and omega^0 = 1 in K = wedge^0 V^*, and 1 wedge alpha = alpha. Inductive step: L^{k+1}(alpha) = omega wedge L^k(alpha) = omega wedge (omega^k wedge alpha) = (omega wedge omega^k) wedge alpha = omega^{k+1} wedge alpha.) Thus the map whose bijectivity we must prove is
  mu_{n}: wedge^n V^* -> wedge^{2g-n} V^*,   alpha |-> omega^{g-n} wedge alpha,   for 0 <= n <= g.
(No sign appears relative to the statement of the cited lemma, since deg(omega^{g-n}) = 2(g-n) is even, so omega^{g-n} wedge alpha = alpha wedge omega^{g-n} by graded-commutativity.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 2. Symplectic basis for (V, omega).

Claim. There exist e_1,...,e_g, f_1,...,f_g in V forming a K-basis with
  omega(e_i,e_j) = 0,  omega(f_i,f_j) = 0,  omega(e_i,f_j) = delta_{ij}  for all i,j.

Proof of the claim, by induction on g. For g = 1: pick 0 != e_1 in V. Since phi is an isomorphism, phi(e_1) != 0, so there is w in V with omega(e_1,w) != 0; put f_1 = omega(e_1,w)^{-1} w, so omega(e_1,f_1) = 1. Then e_1, f_1 are linearly independent (a relation a e_1 + b f_1 = 0 pair with e_1 and with f_1 gives b = a = 0 using alternation omega(e_1,e_1) = omega(f_1,f_1) = 0), hence a basis, and the required relations hold trivially.

Inductive step, g >= 2: choose e_1, f_1 as above with omega(e_1,f_1) = 1, and set U := K e_1 (+) K f_1. The restriction of omega to U has matrix ((0,1),(-1,0)) in the basis (e_1,f_1), so U cap U^perp = 0, where S^perp := { v in V : omega(v,s) = 0 for all s in S } for any subspace S. Since phi: V ->~ V^* is an isomorphism, for every subspace S the composite V ->~ V^* -> S^* (restriction of functionals; surjective because functionals on a subspace of a free module extend) is surjective with kernel S^perp, hence
  dim_K S^perp = dim_K V - dim_K S = 2g - dim_K S.      (*)
Applying (*) to S = U gives dim U^perp = 2g - 2, and V = U (+) U^perp.

We check that omega_1 := omega|_{U^perp wedge U^perp} is nondegenerate. Let v in U^perp with omega(v,u) = 0 for all u in U^perp; then v in (U^perp)^perp. Using U cap U^perp = 0 and (*) twice: dim (U^perp)^perp = 2g - dim U^perp = 2 = dim U, and U subset (U^perp)^perp (immediate from the definition), so (U^perp)^perp = U. Hence v in U cap U^perp = 0, proving omega_1 nondegenerate. By the induction hypothesis applied to the (2g-2)-dimensional space U^perp with the nondegenerate alternating form omega_1, there is a symplectic basis e_2,...,e_g, f_2,...,f_g of U^perp. Since U^perp pairs trivially (for omega) with U, the 2g vectors e_1,...,e_g, f_1,...,f_g form a symplectic basis of V; they form a basis because V = U (+) U^perp. This proves the claim. (Note also that this shows omega nondegenerate forces dim V even, consistent with 2g.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 3. Expansion of omega in the dual basis.

Let e^1,...,e^g, f^1,...,f^g in V^* be the dual basis of (e_1,...,e_g,f_1,...,f_g); it is a K-basis of V^*. We claim
  omega = sum_{i=1}^{g} e^i wedge f^i   in wedge^2 V^*.
Both sides are alternating bilinear forms on V, so it suffices to check equality on pairs of basis vectors of V. For the right-hand side R := sum_i e^i wedge f^i we have, for a,b in V,
  (e^i wedge f^i)(a,b) = e^i(a) f^i(b) - e^i(b) f^i(a),
hence R(e_i,e_j) = 0 - 0 = 0 = omega(e_i,e_j); R(f_i,f_j) = 0 - 0 = 0 = omega(f_i,f_j); and R(e_i,f_j) = delta_{ij} - 0 = delta_{ij} = omega(e_i,f_j). So omega = R.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 4. omega^g != 0 in wedge^{2g} V^*.

Put alpha_i := e^i wedge f^i in wedge^2 V^*. Since deg alpha_i = 2, graded-commutativity gives alpha_i wedge alpha_j = (-1)^{2*2} alpha_j wedge alpha_i = alpha_j wedge alpha_i, and
  alpha_i wedge alpha_i = e^i wedge f^i wedge e^i wedge f^i = - e^i wedge e^i wedge f^i wedge f^i = 0,
because e^i wedge e^i = 0 (again graded-commutativity with odd degree, or alternation).
Expanding by the multinomial theorem in the commutative (in even degrees) subalgebra generated by the alpha_i,
  omega^g = ( sum_{i=1}^{g} alpha_i )^g = sum_{(i_1,...,i_g) in {1,...,g}^g} alpha_{i_1} wedge ... wedge alpha_{i_g}.
Every tuple with a repeated index contributes 0, and the surviving tuples are exactly the permutations sigma in S_g, each contributing alpha_{sigma(1)} wedge ... wedge alpha_{sigma(g)} = alpha_1 wedge ... wedge alpha_g (the alpha_i commute). Therefore
  omega^g = (g!) alpha_1 wedge ... wedge alpha_g = (g!) e^1 wedge f^1 wedge ... wedge e^g wedge f^g.
Now e^1, f^1, ..., e^g, f^g is a K-basis of V^*, so their wedge is a basis element of the 1-dimensional K-vector space wedge^{2g} V^*, in particular nonzero. Since char K = 0, the integer g! is nonzero in K, hence a unit of the field K. Thus omega^g != 0.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 5. Apply the proved symplectic Lefschetz lemma.

Take W := V^* as the K-vector space in lemma_symplectic_exterior_lefschetz (user_id Spark). Then:
  - K has characteristic 0 and g >= 1 (hypotheses of that lemma);
  - dim_K W = dim_K V^* = dim_K V = 2g, since V is finite dimensional (a basis e_1,...,e_{2g} of V has a dual basis e^{*1},...,e^{*2g} of V^*, which spans: if lambda = sum c_i e^{*i} then c_i = lambda(e_i), and is linearly independent: sum c_i e^{*i} = 0 evaluated at e_j gives c_j = 0);
  - our omega lies in wedge^2_K V^* = wedge^2_K W;
  - omega^g != 0 in wedge^{2g}_K W = wedge^{2g}_K V^* by Step 4.
All hypotheses of lemma_symplectic_exterior_lefschetz are satisfied, so for every integer n with 0 <= n <= g the K-linear homomorphism
  wedge^n_K W -> wedge^{2g-n}_K W,   alpha |-> omega^{g-n} wedge alpha,
is an isomorphism.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 6. Conclusion.

Identifying W with V^*, the above map is exactly mu_n of Step 1, which by Step 1 equals L^{g-n}: wedge^n V^* -> wedge^{2g-n} V^*. Hence L^{g-n} is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= g, which is the desired statement. (The edge cases are included: for n = g the map is L^0 = id on wedge^g V^*, and for n = 0 the map K = wedge^0 V^* -> wedge^{2g} V^*, 1 |-> omega^g, is an isomorphism because omega^g != 0 and both spaces are 1-dimensional; both are covered by Step 5.) QED.

lemma_hypersurface_top_class_nonzero.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m >= 1, and put k = overline(F_q). Let X be the zero scheme in P^{d+1}_{F_{q^m}} of a homogeneous polynomial of positive degree, and suppose X is smooth, projective, geometrically connected, and of pure dimension d >= 1. Let xi in H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell) be the pullback of c_1(O_{P^{d+1}}(1)) under the closed immersion X -> P^{d+1}_{F_{q^m}}. Then xi^d is nonzero in H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ell).
lemma_hypersurface_top_class_nonzero.proof: Let F_0=F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_l(1), so that Chern classes and Tate-twisted trace targets are identified with Q_l as in the cited lemmas. Since ell != p and finite extensions of F_0 are p-powers, the hypotheses ell != p of the cited cohomological lemmas hold after any finite base change we make. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant sheaf on the proper varieties over F_Q considered below, all etale cohomology groups used are finite-dimensional Q_l-vector spaces. Let e be the positive degree of the given homogeneous polynomial. The closed subscheme X is proper and has pure dimension d, while P^{d+1}_{F_0} has dimension d+1, so X is not the whole projective space. Its complement U is a nonempty open subscheme of a finite type scheme over the finite field F_0; hence U has a closed point with finite residue field F_Q/F_0. This gives an F_Q-rational point P of P^{d+1} not lying on X_{F_Q}. Replacing F_0 by F_Q does not change k=overline F_q, because F_Q is finite over F_0. Smoothness, projectivity, pure dimension, and the hyperplane class are preserved by this base change; geometric connectedness is also preserved, since a disconnection of X_{F_Q} would become a disconnection after base change to k. If we prove nonvanishing for X_{F_Q}, it gives the original statement because (X_{F_Q})_k=X_k and the hyperplane class base changes. Choose an F_Q-linear projective automorphism g of P^{d+1}_{F_Q} sending P to P_infty=[0:...:0:1]. Let X'=g(X_{F_Q}) and let xi' be its hyperplane class. The automorphism g pulls O(1) to O(1), so g^*xi'=xi_Q, where xi_Q is the base-changed hyperplane class on X_{F_Q}. Pullback by g is a cup-product preserving Q_l-linear isomorphism on etale cohomology over k, so it suffices to prove (xi')^d !=0 for X'. The transformed defining polynomial F' is homogeneous of the same positive degree e, because an invertible linear change of homogeneous coordinates acts invertibly on the vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree e, and the automorphism pulls back the defining ideal sheaf, so X' is the zero scheme of F'. Since P_infty is not in X', F'(0,...,0,1) !=0; this number is the coefficient of T_{d+1}^e, so after scaling F' we may assume F' is monic in T_{d+1}. Define f: X' -> P^d_{F_Q} by [T_0:...:T_{d+1}] -> [T_0:...:T_d]. This is well-defined because P_infty is not in X'. We show f is finite locally free of rank e. Cover P^d by the standard affines U_i=D_+(T_i), i=0,...,d. On U_i put u_j=T_j/T_i for j != i,d+1 and s=T_{d+1}/T_i. Then f^{-1}(U_i)=Spec(A_i[s]/(f_i)), where A_i=F_Q[u_j] and f_i(u,s)=F'(u_0,...,1,...,s). Since F' is monic of degree e in T_{d+1}, f_i is monic of degree e in s. By the division algorithm for monic polynomials, A_i[s]/(f_i) is a free A_i-module with basis 1,s,...,s^{e-1}. Hence f is finite locally free of rank e. Finite morphisms are proper. A finite locally free morphism of positive rank is surjective: over any point y, the fiber coordinate ring is a free module of rank e over the residue field at y, hence nonzero. The target P^d_{F_Q} is integral. The source X' is integral: smoothness over a field gives regular local rings, regular local rings are domains, so X' is locally integral; if two irreducible components met, the local ring at a point of intersection would have at least two minimal primes and would not be a domain, while if they were disjoint the noetherian scheme would be disconnected, contradicting geometric connectedness. Thus X' is integral. Since f is finite and surjective, it is dominant. The generic fiber is obtained by localizing the coordinate ring of an integral affine open subset of X' at the nonzero elements of the function field K of P^d, so it is a domain; it is finite over K and has K-vector-space dimension e, so it is a finite field extension of K of degree e. Therefore f is a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree e between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension d over F_Q. Let h=c_1(O_{P^d}(1)). The sections T_0,...,T_d of O_{P^{d+1}}(1) restrict to sections of O_{X'}(1) with no common zero, because a common zero would be P_infty, which is not in X'. They generate O_{X'}(1), and f is the morphism given by this generating linear system. Hence f^*O_{P^d}(1) is isomorphic to O_{X'}(1). By functoriality of Chern classes, f^*h=xi', and therefore f^*(h^d)=xi'^d. Apply lemma_201 to P^d_{F_Q}, with q replaced by Q. It identifies the cohomology ring with Q_l[t]/(t^{d+1}) by t^i -> h^i. Since t^d is nonzero in this quotient, h^d !=0 in H^{2d}_{et}(P^d_k,Q_l). Apply lemma_77(a) to P^d_{F_Q}: the normalized trace tr_{P^d}: H^{2d}_{et}(P^d_k,Q_l) -> Q_l(-d) is a Q_l-linear isomorphism, so tr_{P^d}(h^d) !=0. Apply lemma_top_trace_generically_finite to f. It gives tr_{X'} o f^* o tr_{P^d}^{-1}=multiplication by e on Q_l(-d), hence tr_{X'}(xi'^d)=tr_{X'}(f^*(h^d))=e tr_{P^d}(h^d). The integer e is positive, hence nonzero in Q_l, and Q_l(-d) is a one-dimensional Q_l-vector space; therefore e times the nonzero vector tr_{P^d}(h^d) is nonzero. Thus tr_{X'}(xi'^d) !=0. Apply lemma_77(a) to X'_{F_Q}: tr_{X'} is a Q_l-linear isomorphism, in particular injective, so xi'^d !=0 in H^{2d}_{et}(X'_k,Q_l). Pulling back by the isomorphism g gives xi_Q^d !=0 in H^{2d}_{et}((X_{F_Q})_k,Q_l). Since (X_{F_Q})_k=X_k and xi_Q is the base change of xi, this is exactly xi^d !=0 in H^{2d}_{et}(X_k,Q_l). QED.

lemma_477.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(m\ge1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) and \(Y\subsetneq X\) a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(Y\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and for \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\). Let \(i_!:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map with \(\operatorname{tr}_X(i_!a\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b)\) for all \(a\in H^{d-1}(Y_k)\), \(b\in H^{d-1}(X_k)\). If \(i_!\) is injective and \(i_!(1)=\xi\), then \(\ker\bigl(L:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)=\ker\bigl(i^*:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\).
lemma_477.proof:
Write all étale cohomology groups with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients on the geometric fibre over \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and abbreviate
\[
V:=H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k),\qquad V':=H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k),\qquad W:=H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k).
\]
These are finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces (\(X\) and \(Y\) are proper over the algebraically closed field \(k\)). The maps under consideration are
\[
i^*:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad i_!:W\longrightarrow V',\qquad L:V\longrightarrow V',\ \ x\longmapsto x\cup\xi .
\]
(\(L\) is well defined by the stated convention that \(L\) is cup product with \(\xi\); since \(\deg\xi=2\) is even, graded commutativity of the cup product gives \(x\cup\xi=\xi\cup x\), so no sign ambiguity arises.)

**Step 1: The trace pairings are perfect, hence \(i_!\) is uniquely determined by its defining relation.**
Apply the Poincaré duality lemma (lemma_poincare_duality_smooth_projective_not_connected) to the smooth projective pure-dimensional \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-schemes \(X\) (dimension \(d\)) and \(Y\) (dimension \(d-1\)): after the identification of Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) coming from the chosen nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), the pairings
\[
H^n(X_k)\times H^{2d-n}(X_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell,\quad (u,v)\mapsto \operatorname{tr}_X(u\cup v),\qquad
H^m(Y_k)\times H^{2d-2-m}(Y_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell,\quad (a,b)\mapsto \operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup b)
\]
are perfect. In particular, for \(n=d+1\) the pairing \(V'\times V\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) is perfect. Consequently, two \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear maps \(\varphi,\psi:W\to V'\) satisfying
\(\operatorname{tr}_X(\varphi(a)\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_X(\psi(a)\cup b)\) for all \(a\in W,\ b\in V\) must coincide: \(\operatorname{tr}_X((\varphi(a)-\psi(a))\cup b)=0\) for every \(b\in V=H^{d-1}(X_k)\) forces \(\varphi(a)=\psi(a)\) by perfectness. Thus there is at most one map \(W\to V'\) with the defining property in the statement.

**Step 2: Identification of \(i_!\) with the Gysin pushforward of the projection-formula lemma.**
Consider the cited projection-formula lemma (lemma_gysin_projection_formula_all_degrees). Its hypotheses are exactly ours: \(q=p^a\) a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\), \(m\ge1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\); \(X\) a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\); \(Y\subsetneq X\) a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\); a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) used to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); and the traces \(\operatorname{tr}_X,\operatorname{tr}_Y\) normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\), exactly as in the present statement. That lemma provides, for each \(n\ge0\), the unique map
\[
i_!:H^n(Y_k)\longrightarrow H^{n+2}(X_k)\quad\text{with}\quad \operatorname{tr}_X(i_!a\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b)
\]
for all \(a\in H^n(Y_k)\) and \(b\in H^{2d-2-n}(X_k)\). Taking \(n=d-1\), we have \(2d-2-n=2d-2-(d-1)=d-1\), so the defining property reads: for all \(a\in H^{d-1}(Y_k)=W\) and \(b\in H^{d-1}(X_k)=V\),
\[
\operatorname{tr}_X(i_!a\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b),
\]
which is verbatim the defining property of the map \(i_!:W\to V'\) appearing in the present statement. By the uniqueness established in Step 1, the two maps coincide. Hence we may (and do) use the projection-formula identity of the cited lemma for our \(i_!\).

**Step 3: The key identity \(L=i_!\circ i^*\).**
The cited lemma asserts, for every \(n\ge0\) and every \(x\in H^n(X_k)\),
\[
i_!(i^*x)=x\cup i_!(1),
\]
where \(1\) denotes the unit of \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k)\). Specialising to \(n=d-1\) and \(x\in V\), and using the hypothesis \(i_!(1)=\xi\in H^2(X_k)\), we obtain
\[
i_!(i^*x)=x\cup i_!(1)=x\cup\xi=L(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in V .
\]
Thus \(L=i_!\circ i^*\) as maps \(V\to V'\).

**Step 4: Computation of the kernel.**
We prove the two inclusions.

(\(\supseteq\)) Let \(x\in V\) with \(i^*x=0\). Then, by Step 3 and \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linearity of \(i_!\),
\[
L(x)=i_!(i^*x)=i_!(0)=0,
\]
so \(x\in\ker L\).

(\(\subseteq\)) Let \(x\in V\) with \(L(x)=0\). By Step 3, \(i_!(i^*x)=0\). Now \(i^*x\in W=H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k)\), and by hypothesis the map \(i_!:W\to V'\) is injective; hence \(i^*x=0\), i.e. \(x\in\ker i^*\).

Both inclusions give
\[
\ker\bigl(L:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)
=\ker\bigl(i^*:H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr),
\]
as required. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_475.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let < , > be a perfect bilinear form on V, let T in GL(V), and let c in K^* satisfy <Tx,Ty>=c<x,y> for all x,y. Extend < , > and T to V tensor_K K_bar, where K_bar is an algebraic closure of K. For alpha,beta in K_bar^*, let V_alpha and V_beta be the generalized eigenspaces of T for alpha and beta. If alpha beta != c, then V_alpha and V_beta are orthogonal under the extended pairing.
lemma_475.proof:
We write $K$ for the ground field, $W:=V\otimes_K\overline K$ for the scalar extension, $\langle-,-\rangle_W$ (abbreviated $\langle-,-\rangle$ once no confusion is possible) for the extended pairing, and $S:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\overline K}\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ for the extension of $T$. For $\gamma\in\overline K$ the generalized eigenspace is $V_\gamma:=\bigcup_{M\ge1}\ker(S-\gamma\,\mathrm{id})^M=\ker(S-\gamma\,\mathrm{id})^{\dim W}\subseteq W$; it is an $S$-stable and $S^{-1}$-stable $\overline K$-subspace. The claim to prove is: for $\alpha,\beta\in\overline K^{*}$ with $\alpha\beta\ne c$, one has $\langle x,y\rangle=0$ for all $x\in V_\alpha$, $y\in V_\beta$.

Step 1 (the extended pairing is perfect). Choose a $K$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $V$ and let $G=(\langle e_i,e_j\rangle_V)\in M_n(K)$ be the Gram matrix. Since $\langle-,-\rangle_V$ is perfect, the map $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_V:V\to V^{\vee}$ is a $K$-linear isomorphism; in the basis $e_i$ and its dual this map is represented by $G$, so $\det G\ne0$. The family $f_i:=e_i\otimes1$ is a $\overline K$-basis of $W$, and by definition of the extended pairing $\langle f_i,f_j\rangle_W=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle_V$, so the Gram matrix of $\langle-,-\rangle_W$ in the basis $f_i$ is the image of $G$ in $M_n(\overline K)$, which is still invertible. Hence $\langle-,-\rangle_W$ is perfect: both $y\mapsto\langle-,y\rangle_W$ and $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_W$ are $\overline K$-linear isomorphisms $W\xrightarrow{\sim}W^{\vee}$, and in particular $\langle x,z\rangle_W=0$ for all $x$ implies $z=0$, and likewise on the other side.

Step 2 (the similitude identity extends). For pure tensors $a=v\otimes\lambda$, $b=w\otimes\mu$ one has, using $\overline K$-bilinearity of both sides,
$\langle Sa,Sb\rangle_W=\lambda\mu\,\langle Tv,Tw\rangle_V=\lambda\mu\,c\,\langle v,w\rangle_V=c\,\langle a,b\rangle_W,$
where the middle equality is the hypothesis on $T$ (and $c\in K^{*}\subset\overline K^{*}$). Both $ (a,b)\mapsto\langle Sa,Sb\rangle_W$ and $(a,b)\mapsto c\langle a,b\rangle_W$ are $\overline K$-bilinear maps $W\times W\to\overline K$ agreeing on pure tensors, hence
(2)  $\langle Sx,Sy\rangle_W=c\langle x,y\rangle_W\qquad$ for all $x,y\in W$.

Step 3 (the adjoint, and the two identities it satisfies). Let $\varphi:W\to W^{\vee}$, $\varphi(y)=\langle-,y\rangle_W$, which is an isomorphism by Step 1, and let $S^{t}:W^{\vee}\to W^{\vee}$, $S^{t}(\psi)=\psi\circ S$, be the transpose. Define
$S^{\dagger}:=\varphi^{-1}\circ S^{t}\circ\varphi\in\mathrm{End}_{\overline K}(W).$
Then for all $x,y\in W$,
$\langle x,S^{\dagger}y\rangle_W=\varphi(S^{\dagger}y)(x)=(S^{t}\varphi(y))(x)=\varphi(y)(Sx)=\langle Sx,y\rangle_W,$
so we have established explicitly the LEFT-slot identity
(a)  $\langle Sx,y\rangle_W=\langle x,S^{\dagger}y\rangle_W\qquad$ for all $x,y\in W.$
Moreover $S^{\dagger}$ is the UNIQUE endomorphism with property (a): if $A$ also satisfies (a) then $\langle x,(A-B)y\rangle_W=0$ for all $x$, so right nondegeneracy (Step 1) gives $(A-B)y=0$ for all $y$, i.e. $A=B$.

We now identify $S^{\dagger}$. Apply (2) with $(a,b)=(x,S^{-1}y)$ (legal since $S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$):
$\langle Sx,y\rangle_W=\langle Sx,S(S^{-1}y)\rangle_W=c\,\langle x,S^{-1}y\rangle_W=\langle x,\,cS^{-1}y\rangle_W,$
the last equality using $\overline K$-linearity of the pairing in the second slot. Thus the endomorphism $cS^{-1}$ satisfies property (a), and uniqueness forces
(3)  $S^{\dagger}=cS^{-1}.$
From (3) we now verify the RIGHT-slot identity as a separate displayed computation: for all $x,y\in W$,
$\langle S^{\dagger}x,y\rangle_W=\langle cS^{-1}x,y\rangle_W=c\,\langle S^{-1}x,y\rangle_W,$
while (2) applied with $(a,b)=(S^{-1}x,y)$ gives $\langle x,Sy\rangle_W=\langle S(S^{-1}x),Sy\rangle_W=c\,\langle S^{-1}x,y\rangle_W$. Hence
(b)  $\langle S^{\dagger}x,y\rangle_W=\langle x,Sy\rangle_W\qquad$ for all $x,y\in W.$
Identities (a) and (b) are both proved, and (3) replaces any one-sided-inverse argument.

Step 4 (adjointness for powers and polynomials). We prove by induction on $k\ge0$ that
(4)  $\langle S^{k}x,y\rangle_W=\langle x,(S^{\dagger})^{k}y\rangle_W\qquad$ for all $x,y\in W.$
For $k=0$ this is $\langle x,y\rangle_W=\langle x,y\rangle_W$. For $k=1$ it is exactly (a). For the induction step $k\to k+1$ (using (a) with the vector $S^{k}x$ in the first slot, and the induction hypothesis with the vector $S^{\dagger}y$, which is simply a vector of $W$, in the second slot):
$\langle S^{k+1}x,y\rangle_W=\langle S(S^{k}x),y\rangle_W\overset{(a)}{=}\langle S^{k}x,S^{\dagger}y\rangle_W\overset{\text{IH}}{=}\langle x,(S^{\dagger})^{k}(S^{\dagger}y)\rangle_W=\langle x,(S^{\dagger})^{k+1}y\rangle_W.$
Now let $P(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}a_kt^{k}\in\overline K[t]$. Since the pairing is $\overline K$-BILINEAR (not sesquilinear), scalars may be pulled out of either slot identically, so
$\langle P(S)x,y\rangle_W=\textstyle\sum_k a_k\langle S^{k}x,y\rangle_W=\sum_k a_k\langle x,(S^{\dagger})^{k}y\rangle_W=\langle x,P(S^{\dagger})y\rangle_W.$
Thus
(5)  $\langle P(S)x,y\rangle_W=\langle x,P(S^{\dagger})y\rangle_W\qquad$ for all $P\in\overline K[t]$ and all $x,y\in W$ (no conjugation of coefficients occurs).

Step 5 (a shift by a non-eigenvalue is an automorphism of a generalized eigenspace). Let $\lambda\in\overline K$ and let $N_\lambda:=(S-\lambda\,\mathrm{id})|_{V_\lambda}\in\mathrm{End}_{\overline K}(V_\lambda)$; by definition of $V_\lambda$ this is nilpotent, say $N_\lambda^{\,r+1}=0$ for some $r\ge0$. Let $\mu\in\overline K$ with $d:=\lambda-\mu\ne0$. Then on $V_\lambda$,
$(S-\mu\,\mathrm{id})|_{V_\lambda}=(S-\lambda\,\mathrm{id})|_{V_\lambda}+(\lambda-\mu)\,\mathrm{id}=N_\lambda+d\,\mathrm{id}=d(\mathrm{id}+U),\qquad U:=d^{-1}N_\lambda,$
with $U^{r+1}=0$. We check directly that $\mathrm{id}+U$ is invertible with inverse $\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^{k}U^{k}$:
$(\mathrm{id}+U)\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^{k}U^{k}=\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^{k}U^{k}+\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^{k}U^{k+1}=\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^{k}U^{k}+\sum_{k=1}^{r+1}(-1)^{k-1}U^{k}=\mathrm{id}+(-1)^{r}U^{r+1}=\mathrm{id},$
where in the last sum we reindexed with the sign $(-1)^{k-1}$, the intermediate terms cancelling pairwise, and the surviving term is $(-1)^{r}U^{r+1}=0$. Since both factors are polynomials in the single operator $U$ they commute, so this one-sided check gives a two-sided inverse. Hence $(S-\mu\,\mathrm{id})|_{V_\lambda}$ is invertible in $\mathrm{End}_{\overline K}(V_\lambda)$, with inverse $d^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^{k}U^{k}$; in particular it is a BIJECTION of $V_\lambda$ onto itself. Consequently every positive power $\big((S-\mu\,\mathrm{id})|_{V_\lambda}\big)^{M}$, $M\ge1$, is also an automorphism of $V_\lambda$.

Step 6 (generalized eigenspaces of $S$ and of $S^{\dagger}$). Let $\mu\in\overline K^{*}$. Using (3),
$S^{\dagger}-\mu\,\mathrm{id}=cS^{-1}-\mu\,\mathrm{id}=S^{-1}(c\,\mathrm{id}-\mu S),$
and the two factors commute because both are polynomials in $S$ and $S^{-1}$. Hence for every $M\ge1$,
$(S^{\dagger}-\mu\,\mathrm{id})^{M}=S^{-M}(c\,\mathrm{id}-\mu S)^{M}.$
Furthermore, since $\mu\ne0$,
$c\,\mathrm{id}-\mu S=(-\mu)\big(S-\tfrac{c}{\mu}\,\mathrm{id}\big)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (c\,\mathrm{id}-\mu S)^{M}=(-\mu)^{M}\big(S-\tfrac{c}{\mu}\,\mathrm{id}\big)^{M}\ \ \text{for each }M\ge1,$
so that
$(S^{\dagger}-\mu\,\mathrm{id})^{M}=(-\mu)^{M}S^{-M}\big(S-\tfrac{c}{\mu}\,\mathrm{id}\big)^{M}.$
Because $S^{-M}$ is an automorphism of $W$, $w\in\ker(S^{\dagger}-\mu\,\mathrm{id})^{M}$ if and only if $\big(S-\tfrac{c}{\mu}\,\mathrm{id}\big)^{M}w=0$. Taking the union over $M\ge1$ (both unions stabilise, e.g. at $M=\dim W$) gives, for every $\mu\in\overline K^{*}$,
(6)  $V_\mu(S^{\dagger})=V_{c/\mu}(S).$

Step 7 (orthogonality). Let $\alpha,\beta\in\overline K^{*}$ with $\alpha\beta\ne c$, and take $x\in V_\alpha$, $y\in V_\beta$. Both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are nonzero, which is used twice below: to form $c/\beta\in\overline K^{*}$ and to multiply the inequality $\alpha\beta\ne c$ by $\beta^{-1}$.

Set $\mu:=c/\beta\in\overline K^{*}$. Note $\alpha\ne\mu$, for $\alpha=\mu$ would give $\alpha\beta=\mu\beta=c$. By the definition of generalized eigenspaces choose $M_2\ge1$ with $(S-\alpha\,\mathrm{id})^{M_2}x=0$, and by (6) applied with this $\mu=c/\beta$ we have $y\in V_\beta(S)=V_{c/\beta}(S^{\dagger})$, so choose $M_1\ge1$ with $(S^{\dagger}-\tfrac{c}{\beta}\,\mathrm{id})^{M_1}y=0$. Put $M:=\max(M_1,M_2)\ge1$ and $P(t):=\big(t-\tfrac{c}{\beta}\big)^{M}\in\overline K[t]$.

Since $\alpha\ne c/\beta$, Step 5 applied with $\lambda=\alpha$ and $\mu=c/\beta$ shows that $(S-\tfrac{c}{\beta}\,\mathrm{id})|_{V_\alpha}$ is an automorphism of $V_\alpha$; hence $P(S)|_{V_\alpha}=\big((S-\tfrac{c}{\beta}\,\mathrm{id})|_{V_\alpha}\big)^{M}$ is also an automorphism of $V_\alpha$. As $x\in V_\alpha$, there exists $w\in V_\alpha$ with $P(S)w=x$. Therefore, using (5) for the polynomial $P$ and then the annihilation of $y$ by $P(S^{\dagger})$ (valid because $M\ge M_1$),
$\langle x,y\rangle_W=\langle P(S)w,y\rangle_W=\langle w,P(S^{\dagger})y\rangle_W=\Big\langle w,\Big(S^{\dagger}-\tfrac{c}{\beta}\,\mathrm{id}\Big)^{M}y\Big\rangle_W=\langle w,0\rangle_W=0.$

Since $x\in V_\alpha$ and $y\in V_\beta$ were arbitrary, $V_\alpha$ and $V_\beta$ are orthogonal for the extended pairing $\langle-,-\rangle_W$. This is exactly the required conclusion (the case $V_\alpha=0$ or $V_\beta=0$ is covered, as then there is nothing to check).

Remark on the hypotheses: only $c\in K^{*}$, $\alpha,\beta\in\overline K^{*}$ and $\alpha\beta\ne c$ were used, together with perfection of the form; the characteristic-$0$ assumption on $K$ is stronger than needed but is part of the statement and is harmless. No external lemma is invoked: the argument is elementary linear algebra (extension of scalars, the adjoint of a similitude, and the inverse of a nilpotent perturbation of a scalar operator).

lemma_476.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(m\ge1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(H\) be an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisor with cycle class \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) under a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), and let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\). Suppose \(L^{\,d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\), and put \(P^r=\ker\bigl(L^{\,d-r+1}:H^r\to H^{2d-r+2}\bigr)\) for \(0\le r\le d\). Let \(F\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(\bigoplus_n H^n\) and \(F_u\) its unipotent part. If \(F_u\) acts as the identity on \(P^r\) for every \(0\le r\le d\), then \(F\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_476.proof:
Let V^n = H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) and let V = direct sum_{n >= 0} V^n. By lemma_45_finite_frob, each V^n is finite-dimensional and carries the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism; by lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing, V^n = 0 for n > 2d, so V is finite-dimensional. Let F denote the direct-sum q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius operator on V.

1. Eigenvector property of xi. Let L_H = O_X(H). Since H is defined over F_{q^m}, L_H is pulled back from X_{F_{q^m}}. More explicitly, let p: X_k -> X_{F_{q^m}} be the base-change map. Then L_H = p^* M for some line bundle M on X_{F_{q^m}}. The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F_X satisfies p o F_X = p, hence there is a canonical isomorphism F_X^* L_H = F_X^* p^* M = p^* M = L_H. Let c_1(L_H) in H^2(X_k,Q_l(1)) be the first Chern class. Functoriality of Chern classes gives F_X^* c_1(L_H) = c_1(F_X^* L_H) = c_1(L_H) in H^2(X_k,Q_l(1)), where F_X^* denotes the twisted arithmetic Frobenius action on Q_l(1)-coefficients.

Choose the fixed nonzero element e in Q_l(1). The cycle class xi is the unique class in H^2(X_k,Q_l) such that xi tensor e = c_1(L_H). The arithmetic Frobenius acts on the coefficient module Q_l(1) by multiplication by some nonzero scalar mu in Q_l. Therefore
F(xi) tensor F(e) = F(xi tensor e) = F(c_1(L_H)) = c_1(L_H) = xi tensor e.
Since F(e) = mu e and tensoring with e identifies H^2(X_k,Q_l) with H^2(X_k,Q_l(1)), we obtain F(xi) = mu^{-1} xi. Thus there exists lambda in Q_l^* such that F(xi) = lambda xi.

2. Equivariance of the Lefschetz operator. For alpha in V^n, the pullback by Frobenius is a ring homomorphism on etale cohomology: cup product is induced by the diagonal morphism, and pullback commutes with pullback along the diagonal and with the coefficient action. Hence
F(L alpha) = F(alpha union xi) = F alpha union F xi = F alpha union lambda xi = lambda L(F alpha).
By induction on k >= 0, we therefore have
F L^k = lambda^k L^k F
as operators on the graded vector space V.

3. Stability of the primitive spaces. Fix r with 0 <= r <= d and let x in P^r. By definition, L^{d-r+1} x = 0. Applying F and using step 2 gives
0 = F(0) = F L^{d-r+1} x = lambda^{d-r+1} L^{d-r+1} F x.
Since lambda is nonzero, it follows that L^{d-r+1} F x = 0. Hence F x in P^r, so P^r is F-stable.

4. Diagonalizability on the primitive spaces. Take the Jordan decomposition
F = F_s F_u = F_u F_s
of the Q_l-linear operator F on the finite-dimensional vector space V. Over Qbar_l, F_s is diagonalizable and F_u is unipotent. The hypothesis says that F_u acts as the identity on every P^r; in particular, each P^r is F_u-stable. Since each P^r is also F-stable by step 3, the operator
F_s = F F_u^{-1}
preserves each P^r. Indeed, if x in P^r, then F_u^{-1} x = x and F x in P^r, so F_s x = F x in P^r.

On P^r, F_u is the identity, so
F|_{P^r} = F_s|_{P^r}.
After extending scalars to Qbar_l, the subspace P^r tensor Qbar_l is invariant under the diagonalizable operator F_s. The restriction of a diagonalizable operator to an invariant subspace is diagonalizable: the spectral projections of F_s are polynomials in F_s, hence preserve the invariant subspace, and the subspace decomposes as the direct sum of its intersections with the eigenspaces of F_s. Therefore F is diagonalizable over Qbar_l on P^r for every 0 <= r <= d.

5. Conclusion. The assumptions of lemma_466 are now satisfied: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, H is an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor with cycle class xi and Lefschetz operator L, the hard Lefschetz isomorphisms L^{d-n}: H^n -> H^{2d-n} are assumed for all 0 <= n <= d, the spaces P^r are defined exactly as in lemma_466, and step 4 proves that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F is diagonalizable over Qbar_l on each P^r. By lemma_466, F is diagonalizable over Qbar_l on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every n >= 0. This is exactly the desired conclusion.

lemma_463_n0.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(H\) be an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisor on \(X\) with cycle class \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) under a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), and let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\). Then \(L^{\,d}:H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism.
lemma_463_n0.proof: We prove a stronger induction statement P(d). Let K be any finite extension of F_q, write K=F_Q, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d>=1 over K. Let H be a K-rational very ample divisor on X, let A=O_X(H), let xi be the cycle class of H on X_k under the fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1), and let L be cup product with xi. We prove that L^d:H^0_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism. The desired lemma is the case K=F_{q^m}. Throughout k is the fixed algebraic closure of F_q, and all finite extensions are regarded as subfields of k. The fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1) is used to identify all Tate twists with Q_ell and to normalize all cycle classes and Poincare traces as in the cited lemmas. Base case d=1. Apply lemma_hard_lefschetz_curve with q=Q, C=X, and the very ample divisor H. Since K=F_Q and k=overline{F}_Q, it gives exactly that L:H^0_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^2_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism. Induction step. Assume P(d-1) for every finite extension of F_q, and let d>=2. Apply lemma_437 to X/K and the ample line bundle A, very ample implies ample, with q replaced by Q. It gives a finite extension K_1/K, an integer r>=1, and a section s of A_{K_1}^{r} whose zero scheme Y=V(s), with its induced closed subscheme structure, is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor on X_{K_1}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1 over K_1. Let i:Y->X_{K_1}. Since s is a regular section of the line bundle A_{K_1}^{r}, its ideal sheaf is (A_{K_1}^{r})^{-1}, hence O_{X_{K_1}}(Y) is isomorphic to A_{K_1}^{r}. Because A is very ample, A_{K_1}^{r} is very ample: if A=f^*O(1) for a closed immersion f, then A^r is the pullback of O(1) by the r-th Veronese embedding. Therefore Y is a very ample divisor on X_{K_1}. Let eta=cl_{X_{K_1}}(Y) under the fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1). The cycle class of an effective Cartier divisor is the first Chern class of its associated line bundle, and c_1 is additive under tensor product and compatible with pullback and base change. Hence eta=c_1(A_{K_1}^{r})=r c_1(A_{K_1})=r xi. Let B=O_Y(Y)=i^*O_{X_{K_1}}(Y). This is very ample because it is the restriction of the very ample line bundle O_{X_{K_1}}(Y) to the closed subscheme Y. Choose an embedding of Y into P^N_{K_1} defined by B. In the dual projective space parameterizing hyperplanes of P^N_{K_1}, the hyperplanes containing the embedded image form a proper closed subset: the condition is closed, and it is proper because the image is nonempty and is not contained in every hyperplane. Let U be the nonempty open complement. Since U is a nonempty scheme of finite type over the finite field K_1, it has a closed point z; its residue field K_2=Kappa(z) is a finite extension of K_1. The point z corresponds to a K_2-rational hyperplane h_z not containing Y_{K_2}. Let sigma_z be the corresponding section of B_{K_2}. Since h_z does not contain Y_{K_2}, sigma_z is not identically zero. The variety Y_{K_2} is smooth, projective, and geometrically connected over K_2; these properties are stable under finite field extension. Smoothness over a field gives regularity, and a connected regular noetherian scheme is integral, so Y_{K_2} is integral. A nonzero section of a line bundle on an integral scheme has an effective Cartier zero scheme; let D be the zero scheme of sigma_z. It is nonempty: if it were empty, sigma_z would be nowhere zero and would trivialize B_{K_2}, but a trivial line bundle on a positive-dimensional proper geometrically connected variety is not very ample, because its global sections are only the constants, so the associated morphism is constant and cannot be a closed immersion. Thus D is a nonempty K_2-rational effective Cartier divisor on Y_{K_2}. Its associated line bundle is O_{Y_{K_2}}(D)=B_{K_2}=i^*O_{X_{K_1}}(Y)_{K_2}, so D is very ample. Let delta=cl_{Y_{K_2}}(D). By the same cycle-class and Chern-class properties, delta=c_1(O_{Y_{K_2}}(D))=c_1(i^*O_{X_{K_1}}(Y)_{K_2})=i^*c_1(O_{X_{K_1}}(Y)_{K_2})=i^*eta. Apply P(d-1) to Y_{K_2}/K_2 and the very ample divisor D. Let L_D be cup product with delta. Then L_D^{d-1}:H^0_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism. By lemma_77(a) applied to Y_{K_2}, the trace tr_Y:H^{2d-2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell(-d+1), identified with Q_ell, is an isomorphism, so H^{2d-2} is nonzero. Hence H^0 is nonzero; the unit 1 is nonzero because a nonzero unital algebra cannot have zero unit. Therefore delta^{d-1}=L_D^{d-1}(1) is nonzero. Now apply lemma_471 to X_{K_2}/K_2, the divisor Y_{K_2}, the cycle class eta of Y_{K_2}, and xi_Y=i^*eta=delta. The traces tr_X and tr_Y are the normalized Poincare traces over the finite field K_2, using the same closed-point normalization and the same fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1). Take n=0, x=1, and y=1 in lemma_471. Since i^*1=1, L_Y^{d-1}(1)=delta^{d-1}, and L_X^{d}(1)=eta^{d}, lemma_471 gives tr_Y(delta^{d-1})=tr_X(eta^{d}). By lemma_77(a) for Y, tr_Y is injective, so the nonzero element delta^{d-1} has nonzero trace. Hence tr_X(eta^{d}) is nonzero. Since eta=r xi and r is a positive integer, hence nonzero in Q_ell because Q_ell has characteristic zero, tr_X(eta^{d})=r^{d}tr_X(xi^{d}); therefore tr_X(xi^{d}) is nonzero. Finally apply lemma_77(a) and lemma_77(b) to X_{K_2}. Lemma_77(a) says tr_X:H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell(-d), identified with Q_ell, is an isomorphism; hence H^{2d} is one-dimensional and tr_X is injective. The nonzero trace of xi^{d} implies xi^{d} is nonzero. Lemma_77(b) says the pairing H^0_et(X_k,Q_ell) x H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell(-d), identified with Q_ell, is perfect. Since H^{2d} is one-dimensional and nonzero, H^0 is one-dimensional. The unit 1 in H^0 is nonzero. The map L^d sends 1 to xi^{d}, a nonzero vector in a one-dimensional target, and its domain is one-dimensional. Therefore L^d is an isomorphism. It remains to note that proving P(d) over K_2 proves it over K. Indeed (X_{K_2})_k=X_k canonically, the cycle class of H_{K_2} is the pullback of xi and is identified with xi under this canonical isomorphism, and the operator L^d is unchanged. Thus P(d) holds for K. This completes the induction and proves the lemma.

lemma_481.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\) prime, \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and \(X\) a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\). Let \(Z\in\mathrm{CH}^d(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}X)_{\mathbb Q}\) be a correspondence such that \(\int_{X\times X}\mathrm{cl}(Z)\cup(\mathrm{cl}(A)\times \mathrm{cl}(B))=0\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) for every \(i\ge0\) and all \(A\in\mathrm{CH}^i(X)_{\mathbb Q}\), \(B\in\mathrm{CH}^{d-i}(X)_{\mathbb Q}\). Then the endomorphism \(Z_*:\alpha\mapsto \mathrm{pr}_{2*}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha\cup \mathrm{cl}(Z))\) of \(\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is nilpotent.
lemma_481.proof:
The statement as written is false, so no proof of it can be correct. We give an explicit counterexample (in fact for every prime power q).

Choose an elliptic curve E over F_q as follows. If p=2, take E to be the smooth projective curve given by y^2 + y = x^3 + x. If p is odd, take E to be the smooth projective curve given by y^2 = x^3 - x. In both cases E has the rational point O at infinity, is smooth, projective, geometrically connected, and has pure dimension d=1.

Let k=overline(F_q), let l != p be prime, and let f=[-1]_E be the inverse morphism for the elliptic curve group law. Explicitly, f(x,y)=(x,y+1) in characteristic 2 and f(x,y)=(x,-y) in odd characteristic. Define the correspondence
Z = [Gamma_f] - [Delta] in CH^1(E x E)_Q,
where Gamma_f is the graph of f and Delta is the diagonal.

We first verify the hypothesis of the lemma. For a smooth projective curve, CH^0(E)_Q = Q[E]. Also the cycle class map CH^1(E)_Q -> H^2_et(E_k,Q_l) factors through the degree map: if B is a 0-cycle of degree b, then cl(B)=b h, where h is the cohomology class of a point. Let A=a[E] with a in Q, and let B have degree b. For any automorphism g of E, the projection pr_2: Gamma_f -> E is an isomorphism, hence pr_{2*} cl(Gamma_g)=cl(E); similarly pr_{1*} cl(Gamma_g)=cl(E). By the projection formula,
int_{E x E} cl(Gamma_g) cup (1 cup cl(B)) = int_E cl(pr_{2*} cl(Gamma_g)) cup cl(B) = int_E cl(E) cup b h = b.
The same computation holds for the diagonal Delta. Therefore for Z=[Gamma_f]-[Delta],
int_{E x E} cl(Z) cup (cl(A) times cl(B)) = a b - a b = 0.
The case A in CH^1(E)_Q and B in CH^0(E)_Q is identical, using pr_1 instead of pr_2. Thus the required vanishing holds for all A,B.

Now compute the induced endomorphism Z_* on total cohomology. For alpha in H^1_et(E_k,Q_l),
Z_*(alpha) = f^*(alpha) - alpha.
We claim that f^* acts as multiplication by -1 on H^1_et(E_k,Q_l). By functorial Kummer theory (eoinm lemma_kummer_h1), H^1_et(E_k,Q_l(1)) is canonically the inverse limit of Pic(E_k)[l^n]. For an elliptic curve, Pic^0(E_k) is canonically isomorphic to E_k, so this inverse limit is the l-adic Tate module V_l(E). The morphism [-1]_E acts on E[l^n] by P -> -P, hence as multiplication by -1 on V_l(E). By eoinm lemma_tate_rank, V_l(E) is a finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space, and the Kummer identification is functorial for pullback. The Tate twist Q_l(1) is pulled back trivially by f. Hence f^*=-1 on H^1_et(E_k,Q_l).

Consequently Z_* = -2 id on H^1_et(E_k,Q_l). Since Q_l has characteristic 0, -2 is nonzero. Therefore (Z_*)^n = (-2)^n id on H^1_et(E_k,Q_l) for every n>=1, and no power of Z_* is zero on H^1_et(E_k,Q_l). Hence Z_* is not nilpotent on the total cohomology.

This Z satisfies all hypotheses stated in lemma_481, but its induced endomorphism is not nilpotent. Therefore lemma_481 is false as written.
